## EDITOR'S INTRODUCTION

<!-- p. 1 -->

IN the year 1738 Jonathan Edwards preached a series of sermons on 1 Corinthians 13. This sermon series is printed first in this volume of his ethical writings because it came first chronologically, but more because it is an extraordinary, systematic treatise on the Christian moral life. By contrast, the two philosophical-theological dissertations completing this volume are sustained essays on particular topics.[^003-note1] The series is printed here rather than among the volumes of sermons in the Yale edition because these sermons gained a historical identity of their own when, more than a hundred years after they were preached, Tryon Edwards published them as a series of "Lectures" under the title *Charity and Its Fruits*.[^003-note2] The text printed here is a nineteenth-century copy of Edwards' sermon notebooks (which Tryon probably discarded). The copy is in the Edwards collection at Andover-Newton Theological Seminary.

When Edwards preached his sermons in praise of charity, he was in his thirty-fifth year, about midway through his ministry at Northampton. The first revival (1734–36) was but a vivid memory, its fervor dampened. "Surprising works" of the Holy Spirit were again to descend in 1740–43 (this revival, known as the Great Awakening, encompassed the Middle and Southern colonies and the itinerancy of George Whitefield). Edwards was busy recording, explaining, analyzing, and defending the phenomena of the Northampton revival. *A Faithful Narrative of the Surprising Work of God* (begun as a letter to Benjamin Coleman in 1735) was first published in London in 1737, the year before the

<!-- p. 2 -->

charity sermons. Two years later, *The Distinguishing Marks of the Work of the Spirit of God* was delivered as a commencement address at Yale College on September 10, 1741. *Some Thoughts Concerning the Revival* was published in Boston in 1743. Throughout this period Edwards carried on a voluminous correspondence with both critics and supporters of the revivals.[^003-note3]

In the midst of these events and controversies, Edwards preached three remarkable series of sermons. The first of these was his hymn to charity in 1738, printed here. The following year he used thirty pulpit occasions to preach a lengthy sermon-discourse on Isaiah 51:8, which (at least after the fact) he planned to develop into a treatise on the work of redemption.[^003-note4] The third was a series on 1 Peter 1:8, preached probably in 1742 and 1743. Edwards rewrote and published this last in 1746 as *A Treatise Concerning Religious Affections*,[^003-note5] the finest fruit of the revival controversy, generally regarded as a major work in the psychology of religion. *Affections* can also be read as moral theology; and when so read, *Charity* is clearly superior to it.

Of these three important series of sermons, *Charity* came closest in time to the fervor and ferment of the first revival in Northampton under Edwards' preaching. Students of Edwards need to take into account these discourses to the glory of divine love— when, for example, interpreting *Distinguishing Marks* or *Some Thoughts* or the section on "Distinguishing Signs of Truly Gracious and Holy Affections," Pt. III of *Affections*. The seeds and more than the seeds of these attempts to sort out the "raised" affections are already in *Charity*.

Therefore, the sermons on 1 Corinthians 13 may be interpreted (a) as a finely woven systematic treatise on the Christian moral life, (b) as one that follows the story line of the work of redemption, and (c) as one of Edwards' major accounts, composed in the context of the revivals, of gracious affections (divine love) in heart and life. The first two of these three ways of reading the charity sermons— true virtue and its virtues— are summarily restated in Edwards' abbreviated account of a right holy life in *True Virtue*.[^003-note6] The third reading is amply indicated in my footnotes to

<!-- p. 3 -->

the sermons. In these notes I correlate "fruits" of charity with Edwards' account of one or another of the "marks" or "signs." The connection between the first "ethical writing" in this volume and Edwards' writings on the Great Awakening is often one of verbally identical expression, not merely similar meaning.

It is a major fault in any scholar to treat the charity sermons as a surd among Edwards' works. A student's first effort must be to understand Edwards *whole*, in the integrity of all parts of his writings on theological subjects. For some such reason, I believe, H. Richard Niebuhr chose the works to be included in the present volume (which he had intended to edit), despite the decades separating the 1738 sermons from the posthumously published works.

The title page of Tryon Edwards' nineteenth-century edition of the charity sermons states that he edited them from the original manuscripts. In addition, Tryon's Preface[^003-note7] claims that the 1738 sermons were "apparently designed by himself for publication." Mere association with Edwards' "discourses" the following year on the history of redemption— which it is known, he intended should be published— is not a very good reason for that supposition. Tryon gave as another reason the fact that the sermon booklets were "written out in full." If Tryon meant that the booklets he edited (and probably discarded from the collection) had Scripture verses fully written out, he had better reason for supposing that Jonathan Edwards planned to publish the series. In footnotes to the text[^003-note8] I draw attention to the skilled way in which it uses moral terms drawn from Scripture. It strains belief that a *copyist* located from scriptural verses and lists of spiritual gifts the exact precept or disposition of heart Edwards had in mind, and so unerringly filled in the blank lines that ordinarily follow Scripture citations in Edwards' sermon booklets. If writing out biblical verses indicates Edwards' design to publish, then we have the unanswerable question why he did not do so— since, as they stand, the series is already one connected discourse.

Tryon Edwards' Preface further states that after Jonathan Edwards' death the charity sermons were "selected for publication by Dr. Hopkins and Dr. Bellamy; and by the latter were in part copied out and prepared for the press, when for some reason he was interrupted in their publication." How could Tryon know this, so many decades after the event?

There is an indeterminate reference to sermons in a letter from Samuel Hopkins to Joseph Bellamy concerning their joint publishing project that by some stretch of the imagination *might* be a reference to the partial copy of the charity sermons by Bellamy, which later, in the nineteenth century, Tryon somehow knew about. From Great Barrington, Massachusetts, on January 4, 1764, Hopkins wrote Bellamy concerning the transcription of some sermons:

> I should be glad if you would transcribe some of the sermons you mention without any *ifs or ands*. I and my brother have transcribed 10 sermons which I hope to send to Boston soon, but these with the life and the 6 Mr. Searl has transcribed, will not be enough to make one Vol. 16 sermons will be about 200 pages... Most of the sermons have blanks. Where I think it not possible or proper to fill them up, I draw a ___, of which the reader must be notified in an advertisement.[^003-note9]

<!-- p. 4 -->

Hopkins' *Memoir* on Jonathan Edwards was first published in 1765 with eighteen "Sermons on Various Important Subjects."[^003-note10] His preface to the *Memoir* is dated August 20, 1764; his preface to the eighteen sermons printed with it, April 25, 1765. Likely, only two sermons had to be added to the sixteen Hopkins mentioned in the letter quoted above. Hopkins was not waiting to receive sermons transcribed by Bellamy to be added to his volume.[^003-note11] He was simply urging Bellamy to speed up his transcription of another set of sermons altogether, by pressing him to "transcribe some of the sermons you mention without any *ifs or ands*." These expressions are consistent with Hopkins' having knowledge of the special importance of the sermons Bellamy had begun to transcribe. Was Hopkins referring to the 1738 charity sermons, which (according to Tryon Edwards'

<!-- p. 5 -->

Preface) both men selected for publication and Bellamy began to copy? All one can say is that Hopkins' language is consistent with that supposition; perhaps for this reason, he pressed Bellamy to go forward without delay with his transcription. These conjectures led, in 1982, by remote and chance connections, to the discovery and correct identification of three four-page fragments of Joseph Bellamy's part-copy, classified as Bellamy sermons in the collection in the Hartford Seminary Library. The story continues, the three fragments are printed, and some passages from them are compared with Tryon's edition and with the text of the present edition, in Appendix I below.

The second and third of the three works comprising this volume are *Two Dissertations. I. Concerning the End for Which God Created the World. II. On the Nature of True Virtue*.[^003-note12] I ought rather to have said, the *second of two* works comprising this volume, for Edwards intended these dissertations to be published together. The one is the mirror image of the other; the "end" for which God created the world must be the "end" of a truly virtuous and holy life. The present volume reproduces the unity and the sequence of the component parts of the original edition of *Two Dissertations*. The use of that short title might help avoid some misinterpretations of Edwards' ethics.

In recent years the second of the two dissertations has frequently been printed and circulated alone under the title *The Nature of True Virtue*.[^003-note13] It

<!-- p. 6 -->

is one of the most widely known of Edwards' works, if not indeed the most well known. No admirer of the thought and writings of Edwards can regret the attention paid to any single one of his major works. Still, interpretations of *True Virtue* made without regard to its connection with *End of Creation* have fostered inadequate and even quite mistaken understandings of his ethical writings.[^003-note14]

<!-- p. 7 -->

Placing *Charity* first in this volume of Edwards' *Ethical Writings* is obviously justified, because the sermon series was the first of the three ethical writings the author produced. However, one might still question whether *End of Creation* should precede *True Virtue*, or the other way round. The fact that they were originally printed with *End of Creation* first does not quite settle the issue, since we do not know how Edwards left them tied together. In footnotes to the text below, I argue for the priority of *End of Creation* from the fact that (as Austin pointed out) in *True Virtue* there are two bracketed references (in subsequent editions turned into footnotes) to *End of Creation*, as if to a former companion treatise. These notes specifically say "former." Yet the question might continue to be debated on the basis of external evidence, for these references could have been inserted by the editor or the printer in 1765. One reference to *End of Creation* as the former treatise, however, seems to me to settle the matter. There, the reference is more than a mere citation or cross-reference that credibly might have been inserted by a later hand. Instead, Edwards' argument is greatly foreshortened at that point in the text of *True Virtue*, so much so that to comprehend it would require rereading the argument of *End of Creation*. Edwards expected his readers already to have gone through *End of Creation*; and, with both dissertations in hand, to be able to refer to it, and reread, when first reading *True Virtue*. This internal evidence seems to me compelling.[^003-note15] The reader now has the two dissertations before him in the sequence in which Edwards intended them to be understood— plus the prospect of beginning with Edwards' first and major account of a truly virtuous and holy life, for which objective moral end God created the world.

When I assumed responsibility for the volume of ethical writing in the Yale edition, Thomas A. Schafer transcribed for me "The Nature of True Virtue" from Edwards' massive unpublished "Book on Controversies."[^003-note16] This has been invaluable to me and, I believe, also for readers of the present volume and future interpreters of Edwards. There are three

<!-- p. 8 -->

brief notes to himself at the beginning of this section of the "Book on Controversies"; these are integral to the main body of it. One of these notes reads, "No true virtue without supreme love to god and making God our supreme end. See Miscell. 1208 B. 8." That reference is to Miscell. no. 1208. END OF CREATION. GLORY OF GOD. Nature of REDEMPTION. SATISFACTION OF CHRIST. Nature of TRUE VIRTUE AND RELIGION. Schafer dates this entry not later than mid— 1753, and he dates the "Controversies"— draft of *True Virtue* later that year or early 1754.[^003-note17] This means that by 1753–54 Edwards had written out the entirety of *Two Dissertations* in far more than outline form and frequently with verbally identical elaboration of arguments. These are actually penultimate drafts of *End of Creation* and of *True Virtue*, page after page marked, when later used, by lines along the left margin. Only the topic "satisfaction" was eliminated from Miscell. no. 1208.[^003-note18]

<!-- p. 9 -->

Since the entire argument of *Two Dissertations* is fully rendered in these earlier versions, footnotes are frequently required to identify the connections and to offer readers the opportunity to compare passages from Edwards' penultimate version with his final revision. This I also undertake to do at significant points in Edwards' lifelong wrestle with these themes in the "Miscellanies."[^003-note19] But there is little that needs to be said after the years 1753–54 as background for understanding *Two Dissertations*. Indeed, by then Edwards had all his great, late works firmly in mind, spelled out in notebooks, and woven together in an integrated system of thought.

His puzzlement was how he would allocate them to volumes and in what order. Another note at the beginning of the "Controversies"— draft, for example, reads: "Observe how whatever modern philosophers call natural moral taste is a different thing from virtue and the love of virtue. Treat of this either here or in the Discourse on Original Sin according as which is published first. See on Orig. Sin p. 97. a." That reference to a draft of *Original Sin* earlier in the "Controversies" notebook (where there is a cross-reference to the note just quoted) reads: "Perhaps under the head of original sin treat of MORAL TASTE."[^003-note20] (This note is cancelled by a vertical line about an inch from the left margin— a

<!-- p. 10 -->

line that may have been drawn when Edwards decided to ready *Original Sin* for publication.[^003-note21])

Indeed, Edwards' notes concerning method of publication indicate that he considered issuing the various treatises that neared completion together in the last several years of his life in a work that we might call "Three Dissertations," or "Four." In the middle of MS p. 102 of "Original Sin" in the "Book on Controversies" he wrote (this note is also cross-referenced and cancelled):

> METHOD. Perhaps in more volumes than one a treatise the first part concerning the nature of true virtue, and in this treat of God's end in creating the world, and in the next part concerning original sin an inquiry into the truth of the doctrine, both as to the corruption of nature and imputation [...] and its total corruption, and then concerning infused habits and concerning saving grace's differing from common grace in nature and kind, and concerning that natural taste that natural men [have] to show that there is nothing of true virtue in it.

In fact, all these works— together with Edwards' constant probing of these and other topics in the "Miscellanies"— were expected to be parts of his "Rational Account."

Does the foregoing passage contain reference to a treatise on grace, in addition to true virtue, God's end, and original sin? If so, was this the *Treatise on Grace* that Grosart published in the nineteenth century from among papers given him by Tryon Edwards?[^003-note22] These questions have no certain answers. But from several leaves found in the Andover collection,[^003-note23] Thomas A. Schafer estimates the original MS on grace to have been written earlier, between 1739 and 1743. This span of time was shortly after Edwards delivered the charity sermons. So the reader will want to pay attention to the structural similarity between Edwards on grace and Edwards on divine love in the heart.[^003-note24]

Edwards finished *Original Sin* and sent it off to the press. That left God's end and true virtue, of the topics mentioned as publishable together one way or another. In *Original Sin*, published shortly after his death, Edwards wrote:

<!-- p. 11 -->

As to the arguments made use of by many late writers, from the universal moral sense, and the reasons they offer from experience, and observation of the nature of mankind, to shew that we are born into the world with principles of virtue; with a natural prevailing relish, approbation, and love of righteousness, truth and goodness and whatever tends to the public welfare... a native bent in mankind to mutual benevolence, tender compassion, etc. those who have had such objections against the doctrine of original sin, thrown in their way, and desire to see them particularly considered, I ask leave to refer them to a *Treatise on the Nature of True Virtue*, lying prepared for the press, which may ere long be exhibited to view.[^003-note25]

Thus the decision was made *not* to include in *Original Sin* the reflections and argument on "moral taste" that Edwards had accumulated over a lifetime in his "Miscellanies." Nevertheless, the last work Edwards sent to press was itself directed against philosophers who affirmed man's natural worthiness to receive God's favor, or even that our natural goodness is in some way the measure of God's goodness or of his worthiness to be worshiped.

Throughout his entire life Edwards returned again and again to such topics as moral taste, God's end in creation, the history of redemption, original sin, the nature of true virtue and a right holy life, gracious affections, infused virtue, divine love, the Trinity; and these interrelated themes, as it were, crowded together into the treatises he wrote during his years at Stockbridge. *Any* decision Edwards might have made, or did make, concerning publication required tearing apart the integrated exposition and argument he had time and again set down in notebooks. The multiple titles he gave to numerous entries in the "Miscellanies" are sufficient alone to show that (in order to have a mind rightly prepared to read the present volume) it is a grave error, now or ever, to separate Edwards' philosophy from his theology, or his moral philosophy from his theological ethics.

One thing more needs to be noted from the "Controversies"— draft of *True Virtue*. Toward the end Edwards wrote another note to himself, which reads "METHOD. Show how all the virtues are derived from pure benevolence."[^003-note26] This one-line paragraph was cancelled when done. But the plan was executed in only one page of *True Virtue*, in Edwards' terse list of several virtues derived from pure benevolence alone: a virtuous

<!-- p. 12 -->

pity, virtuous gratitude, a virtuous love of justice, a virtuous sense of desert, a virtuous conscientiousness (sanctified conscience), a virtuous love of parents and children, "yea, and a virtuous love between the sexes."[^003-note27] Any promise Edwards might have made to elaborate fully upon how all the virtues derive from pure benevolence was adequately executed in the corpus of Edwards' writings only in the charity sermons preached nearly twenty years before he wrote that note.[^003-note28]

I have now discharged the main part of the first duty of an editor, namely, to tell the reader what he has in his hands.[^003-note29] Let this suffice also to explain why in the following sections of this introduction I undertake a *systematic* analysis of important themes in Edwards' ethical writings, with only light stress on the times and circumstance of their composition. One needs first of all to comprehend Edwards' ethics whole and entire and appreciate the integrity of internally related concepts which run through the three (or two) works printed here.[^003-note30]

I have chosen the alternative of systematic analysis of selected themes chiefly because the power and the coherence of Edwards' ethical writings demand such treatment. One studies the times and backgrounds of some men in order to understand them. Others have such rare greatness that one studies *them* in order to understand their times, or even to comprehend the deepest meaning of the intellectual and other influences that were effectual upon them. Jonathan Edwards was such an original.

*Self-Love, Love of Happiness, Love to God and to Neighbor*

In one of the "Miscellanies" Edwards asks the question whether each and every one of the desires of human hearts has become exorbitant as a

<!-- p. 13 -->

consequence of the Fall. He answers no— because love of happiness (which necessarily means love of one's own happiness) cannot be too much. A cynic always wins the debate over whether all people are selfish by failing to distinguish between a blameworthy selfishness and the general human endowment to love happiness. Yet a love of happiness is evidently different from always finding that happiness in a narrow, confined love of self as if the self were all— in Ibsen's apt description of Peer Gynt, living in "a cask of self, stopped with a bung of self."

Contemporary ethicists often break apart these two meanings of self-love by speaking of the grammatically "ambiguous genitive" case in present-day English language usage in such expressions as "the love of God" or "the love of self." The love of God can mean either God's love to us or our love to God. The love of self can mean the self's love to itself only (or to an extended social ego), or it may mean the self's love of whatever the self loves, whether that is its love to itself as object, or its love to God or to neighbor, or its love of learning, beauty, sensual pleasure, or anything else.

Edwards does not employ this distinction between the objective and subjective genitive. Instead, he plays out the same analysis in terms of what can only be called the "ambiguous pronoun." A man's love of his own happiness, he writes, is "ambiguous... as the pronoun ‘his own’ is equivocal" and can be taken in "two very different senses." A self's love of its own happiness limited to love to self is narrow, confined. But a self's love of its own happiness may simply mean the self's love of whatever is "grateful[^003-note31] and pleasing," more often than not found in other objects than the self *sole*.

Love of one's own happiness is "universal" in all, the same degree in all. To resolve the will and action of moral agents into nefarious self-love on the grounds that the propensity of will and action is our own happiness was for Edwards nonsense. That amounts to saying that there is something censurable in the fact that moral agents have wills, and differ from "stones and trees, which love nothing and hate nothing." Within the definition of self-love as love of one's own happiness, to put the

<!-- p. 14 -->

question "whether all our love... don't arise from self-love" is an "impropriety and absurdity." For this is only to say,

> self-love is a man's liking, and being suited and pleased in that which he likes, and which pleases him; or that 'tis a man's loving what he loves. For whatever a man loves, that thing is grateful and pleasing to him, whether that be his own peculiar happiness, or the happiness of others. And if this be all that they mean by self-love, no wonder they suppose that all love may be resolved into self-love. For it is undoubtedly true that whatever a man loves, his love may be resolved into his loving what he loves— if that be proper speaking. If by self-love is meant nothing else but a man's loving what is grateful or pleasing to him, and being averse to what is disagreeable, this is calling *that* "self-love" which is only a general capacity of loving, or hating; or a capacity of being either pleased or displeased: which is the same thing as a man's having a faculty of will.

The notion that men can fail to love their own happiness in whatever they find objectively "grateful" or pleasing amounts to the absurdity that they "incline to nothing and will nothing." This is one main theme running through Edwards' ethics: I have just been quoting from his treatment of it in *True Virtue*.[^003-note32]

Such "self-love taken in the most extensive sense" was already Edwards' analysis twenty-three years before *True Virtue* when he wrote Miscell. no. 530. LOVE TO GOD. SELF-LOVE (*c*. 1731–32), at twenty-nine years of age.[^003-note33] Again, some seventeen years before *True Virtue* was written,

<!-- p. 15 -->

Edwards made the same point preaching on a text that uses the ambiguous pronoun, charity "seeketh not her own" (one of his famous 1738 series on 1 Corinthians 13). That cannot possibly mean that a Christian spirit is contrary to all self-love, contrary to all love of one's own happiness. Love of one's own happiness is as necessary to man's nature "as a faculty of will is." To destroy that would be "to destroy the humanity." Thus in the seventh sermon of the charity series, Edwards signals the importance of this question by affirming that the point "needs to be well stated; for the resolution of many scruples and doubts, which persons have, depends upon it."[^003-note34] The first step is to fix firmly in mind that what is censurable in self-love does not consist in love of our own happiness "being absolutely considered in too high a degree." Man cannot love happiness too much, if such love is viewed *simpliciter*. Such love is not "a thing liable to diminution or increase." It is "alike in all" because it belongs to the "nature of all intelligent beings" as necessary to their nature "as a faculty of will is." Love of one's happiness is without degree.

Such self-love our first parents had before the Fall, in high degree, in no degree too great; or better to say, simply in no degree, since it was a thing not to be compared. "Saints and sinners" in this life "love happiness alike, and have the same unalterable propensity to seek and desire happiness." Finally, in the redemption of creatures on earth, it would be an absurdity to suppose that happiness increases as the love of it decreases upon the infusion of love to God; or that the holy saints above are happy, but their *love* of happiness diminished as their holiness increased. The saints and angels in heaven love their own happiness. If this were not so, heaven "would be no happiness to them; for that which anyone does not love, he can enjoy no happiness in."

Here we have a correlation of the nature of the will with love, and of love with happiness, that cannot be other than "one's own" while it is willed and loved and enjoyed— a correlation matched only by that in Augustine.[^003-note35] Since will and love are alike in all, the meaning of inordinate

<!-- p. 16 -->

self-love, to which a Christian spirit is contrary, cannot lie in too much love of one's happiness.

So far, we have one "principle" founded in human hearts. Edwards used the word "principle" in the sense of the Latin *principium* or the Greek *arché*. The word "principle" means a source or beginning or spring of disposition and action. But it also means the direction, shape, or contours of human hearts and lives, as in the root of our word "archetype," or the *arché* or formative power of Plato's ideas, such as justice or beauty, or triangularity. So when the first verse of St. John's Gospel reads "In the beginning was the Word," that in Greek is *en arché* and in Latin *inprincipio*. The verse not only points to the source and beginning of all things, without whom "was not anything made that was made." These verses also tell us something about the channel in which the whole creation runs, its shape, meaning, and direction.

A universal and ineradicable will and love of happiness, Edwards says in his sermon, makes the world go round. But that propensity of "intelligent willing perceiving" beings explains nothing specific. It does not explain why we find one particular object of love "grateful and pleasing" and not another. It does not explain the reason why such and such things become an agent's happiness, or why we *look on* others as ourselves, and so on their happiness as *our own*. Consider also Edwards' exclamation, "What can more properly be called love to any being, or any thing, than to place one's happiness in that thing?"[^003-note36] and his use of "placing" happiness to depict the goodness of Christ and of the saints in the charity sermons. An agent's general capacity to *place* his love of happiness anywhere or in any object, somewhere or in some object, and to *find bis*, own happiness therein, "can never be a reason why men's love is placed in such and such objects" and not in others. A "capacity of enjoying happiness, cannot be the reason why such and such things

<!-- p. 17 -->

become his happiness."[^003-note37] The difference between Hitler and you and me, and between Mother Teresa and you and me, lies not in our common love of happiness, but rather in what each of us looks on as that in which our own happiness consists. We need other principles to explain why we creatures move the world the way we do.

Two questions then: What accounts for the fact that love to God, and glorifying him and praising him forever, becomes a human heart's delight? What accounts for the fact that a moral agent lights upon the happiness of another human being as that in which love of his own happiness is gratified? Edwards' answer to this twofold question (which is the question asked of us by the twofold love commandment) is that only some "compounded self-love" can be any further explanatory— that is, love of happiness compounded with some other principle laid in human hearts and lives. This notion of principles conjunctively explanatory of *particular* loves and *particular* joys was best expressed in Miscell. no. 530. Compounded self-love, Edwards wrote,

> arises from the necessary nature of a perceiving and willing being, whereby he loves his own pleasure or delight; but not from this alone, but it supposes also another principle, that determines the exercise of this principle, and makes that to become its object which otherwise cannot: *a certain principle uniting this person with another*, that causes the good of another to be its good. The first arises simply from his own being whereby that which agrees immediately and directly with his own being, is his good; the second arises also from *a principle uniting him to another being*, whereby the good of that other being does in a sort become his own.[^003-note38]

Once more the mouth of the cynic must be stopped. The cynic is liable to say that love of our own happiness can be stretched to explain, by itself, every particular love. We secondarily and circuitously love another person because we first and primarily love our own specific happiness. All other-love is for our own sakes.[^003-note39]

<!-- p. 18 -->

This may be the case in the world as it is, because of a principle of sin acting conjunctively with willing beings' love of their own happiness. Indeed, love to self or to some extensive "private system" is the principle treated at length in *True Virtue*, Ch. IV, and in sermon seven. Still, another principle in the heart was, for Edwards, not a metaphysical impossibility: there is no contradiction in assuming that a human being *first* loves another and *then* finds or places his own happiness in the other's happiness, looks on that other's happiness as his own.[^003-note40]

Indeed, he argued in *True Virtue* that such a cynical location of a selfish system in the *nature* of the will (rather than in its corruption) is nonsense. That account makes the effect (our own happiness) "the cause of that of which it is the effect." It makes "our happiness, consisting in the happiness of the person beloved... the cause of our love to that person." Plainly the truth must be the other way round: "our love to the [other] person is the cause of our delighting, or [as an effect] being happy in his happiness. How comes our happiness to consist [particularly] in the happiness of such [persons] as we love, but our hearts being

<!-- p. 19 -->

*first united to them* in affection, so that as it were, *we look on them as ourselves*, and so on their happiness as our own?"[^003-note41]

So the question is, How comes the universal nature of a willing perceiving being, loving its own happiness, to be compounded with a principle of unitive love or truly virtuous benevolence and unalloyed goodwill toward another? In the familiar language of Scripture, How come love to God and love to neighbor to be what our happiness consists in? How can we creatures, who are on earth and not in heaven, place our happiness in God's glory and look on another person's happiness as our very own? Only if, in truth, we are first made one with them in "pure" or "absolute" benevolence, Edwards answers.

We are approaching, with increasing celerity, the very center of Christian theology. On the relation to God and his creatures, first let us ask Edwards, in the simplest terms, Whence come any knowledge of God and any love of God?

In the twentieth century Karl Barth answered, "Only God can reveal knowledge of God." That statement, on simple inspection, clearly must be true. No one would think of denying it but for the fact that man is (as Plato said) that most religious of animals and (as Calvin taught) the human mind a veritable factory of approximate ideas about the ultimate nature of things.

Jonathan Edwards in the eighteenth century said *why* only God can reveal knowledge of God: because God's knowledge of himself *is the only knowledge of God there is*. I cannot get to know you, i.e., I cannot get to know anything about you that is of any importance to you or to me, unless you communicate yourself to me in words without dissimulation or in actions that are authentically yours. These remain your words and actions, though they resonate in my heart and life. If the word from you that I hear is not and does not remain yours in reality, or if my hearing is only some echo of your word, I will never know more than something *between* us, nor know any more than something *about* you, but never *you*. In self-disclosure, the word sent forth and the hearing of it are one. In like manner, knowledge of God cannot be knowledge about God or knowledge of him from a distance.[^003-note42]

<!-- p. 20 -->

So if there is knowledge of God communicated to any human understanding, this is God's very own knowledge of himself, for that happens to be the only knowledge of God there is in heaven or on earth. If there is any love to God enkindled in any human will, this must be God's own love spread abroad in human hearts. If there is in human affections any happiness, joy, and delight in God, this must be God's own felicity communicated to us. These are the divine principles needed to "further inform" natural principles. When mingled and compounded with love of our own happiness, they direct and channel that love into love to God in particular, so that our greatest good and happiness consists in his glory.

We have now come upon expressions that look like "ambiguous genitives," but according to Edwards only seem so: the knowledge of God, the love of God. The two possible meanings of these expressions are not equivocal. Indeed, there are *not* two meanings. As a datum in our language, of course, "the knowledge of God" can mean either our knowledge of God or God's knowledge of himself; but according to Edwards these two are but one and the same thing. If there is any such thing as a creature's knowledge of God, this must be the creature's participation in God's knowledge of himself. "The love of God" grammatically can mean either our love of God or God's own love in himself; but according to Edwards, these are but one and the same thing. If there is any such thing as a creature's love to God, this must be an infusion of God's own love.

The simple fact that in past times English-speaking people used both *of* and *s* in genitives bears out the foregoing interpretation of Edwards. They wrote and said, "the house of my father's" for "my father's house." Similarly, in Miscell. no. 1084 Edwards wrote that John 17:26[^003-note43] expressed "two ways of God's flowing forth and being communicated... viz. manifesting God's name and communicating his love; or in other words Christ being in the creature in the name, idea or knowledge

<!-- p. 21 -->

of God being in them, and the Holy Spirit's being in them in the love of God's being in them." Edwards himself punctuated that last line. He awkwardly (it seems to us) wrote, "the love of God's being in them," where ordinarily he would write "love to God" or "divine love" dwelling in the heart. I suggest that his rare use here of the ambiguous genitive "the love of God," which is our usual practice today, followed by a possessive *s* ("the love of God's being in them") reinforces the conclusion that, for Edwards, if an intelligent, willing perceiving creature is disposed and determined to love to God, this must be from partaking of the divine love. Edwards might also have punctuated the preceding phrase to read "Christ being in the creature in the name, idea or knowledge of God'*s* being in them." No creature has a natural capacity to actualize in itself knowledge of or love to God; that is the common teaching of classical Christian theology. In evangelical Christianity in America this was, of course, and still should be, the meaning of being "born again."

Unique to Edwards is only the philosophical setting of this understanding of God and his creatures. Thus Edwards believed that "perceiving being only, is properly being"; minds, spirits only, are properly beings; to speak of material things as "beings" is to speak improperly. God "communicates himself properly only to spirits; and they only are capable of being proper images of his excellency, for they only are properly beings... Yet he communicates a sort of shadow or glimpse of his excellence to bodies which... are but the shadows of being, and *not real beings*."[^003-note44] In one of his notes on "The Mind," Edwards asks us to make the following supposition: "Suppose that we received none of the sensible qualities of light, colors, etc. from the resisting parts of space (we will suppose it possible for resistance to be without them), and they were to appearance clear and pure, and all that we could possibly observe was only and merely resistance." Suppose, in other words, that we are hummingbirds bumping into the clear glass of a window pane. Then all we would observe of "solidity" would be "that certain parts of space... resist anything coming within them." We would never bump into matter. All we would experience would be "impenetrability"; and all we need to suppose to account for the bump-up-againstness is some immediate *action* that prevents coming within various parts of space. We are stopped here and now, and not elsewhere or later. According to Edwards, God's immediate action accounts for the resistance bumped into whenever we encounter solid, impenetrable bodies. *No matter there*. Of course, it is

<!-- p. 22 -->

natural for men to suppose that there is "some latent substance, or something that is altogether hid," which upholds every moment the solidity of created bodies. "All therefore agree that there is *something* that is there, and upholds these properties; and it is most true, there undoubtedly is. But men are wont to content themselves in saying merely that it is something; but that ‘something’ is *he by whom all things consist*."[^003-note45]

This is the ontology into which Edwards set his understanding of God and his creatures. He is nothing if not ontological and theological or biblical at the same time. Here we have a sort of "scale of being." As surely as an archangel is further removed from nonentity than is a worm or a flea,[^003-note46] so spiritual beings— the only proper beings— are further removed from nonentity than bodies. To this we can now add that "*understanding* and *will* are *the highest kind of created existence*," higher than merely perceiving being. Then to that we can add: understanding and will in exercise are higher in actuality than those faculties dormant. Finally "and certainly the most excellent *actual knowledge and will* that can be in the creature is the knowledge and the love of God.[^003-note47]

A being to whom has been imparted knowledge of God and love to God is the being of a creature furthest removed from nonentity. This was Edwards' interpretation of St. Paul's "if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature" (2 Corinthians 5:17).

> The increasing knowledge of God in all elect creatures to all eternity is *an existence*, a *reality*, infinitely worthy to be in itself... *If existence is more worthy than defect and nonentity*, and if any created existence is in itself worthy to be, *then this knowledge of God and his glory is worthy to be*. The existence of the created universe consists as much in it as in anything, yea, *it is one of the highest, most real* and *substantial* parts of all created existence; *most remote from nonentity* and defect."[^003-note48]

Thus, the "new creation" is the name, idea or knowledge of God'*s*, being in human understanding; the love of God'*s*, being in human wills, and the joy of God'*s*, being in human affection. This was the original ultimate end God had in the creation of the world.

So Edwards in the eighteenth century joins Barth in the twentieth in

<!-- p. 23 -->

the belief that it is not God whose existence needs proof, but rather the existence of anything other than God, any world at all, that needs explaining. Edwards' cosmic teleology was ultimately Christological; the work of redemption accounted for the history of the universe at large. God's end in the natural world was the end of the moral world, the end of the moral order was the end of the good part of the moral world, the end of the good part of the moral world was the end of the saints at their best, venting their souls in praise of God, and the end of the best part of the moral world at their best was what Jesus Christ sought as his last or ultimate end, in his "great request" in what we call his High Priestly prayer: "that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves"; "that they all may be one; as thou Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they may be one in us... that they may be one, even as we are one" (John 17:13, John 17:21–22).[^003-note49] That was Edwards' ultimate answer to the question, Whence came knowledge of God to any human understanding, and whence any love to God? Since the being of that knowledge, love, and joy is existence most worthy of being, most remote from nonentity, the same was his answer to the perplexing question— if this be proper speaking— why on earth there is any being outside of God himself.

"Divine love" in the heart also goes out to our fellow creatures. Characteristically, Edwards always spells out "Do unto others as you would that others do to you" by adding "If you were in their circumstances and they in yours." That is, he spells out the golden rule to mean "swapping places" in order to tell what we should do. Moses' command, "Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself" also puts you in your neighbor's place, and he in yours.

Modern moral philosophy calls this the "reversibility" test, crucial in golden rule arguments generative of specific moral conclusions, or verdicts concerning right or wrong. Since philosophers talk that way, it looks as if there can be a truly virtuous love of neighbor *without* divine love in the heart. Before letting ourselves be culture-bound to that view, however, consider the extraordinary conclusions Edwards drew from "swapping places." In his sermon on "Charity suffereth long and is kind," Edwards commented as follows on Jesus' parable, Luke 10:25–37: "if the Samaritan was neighbor to the Jew, his enemy, so the Jew was neighbor to the Samaritan; because neighborhood is a mutual relation equally predicable of both those between whom there is such a

<!-- p. 24 -->

relation."[^003-note50] So Moses' "as thyself" entails love of alien or enemy neighbors no less than those who are friendly. In the application of this sermon, Edwards reformulates "neighborliness" (in terms of golden rule reversibility) in words that in their extremity must include freely doing good to enemies no less than to friends, strangers or the poor. "If others have a hearty good will to us," he wrote, "and there is a great deal of kindness, and they are ready to help us when we stand in need of help, and to that end are free to do for us, to labor for us, to give to us, to suffer for us, and help bear our burdens, and share with us in our calamities, are free and cheerful in it, and seem to be open-hearted and liberal in it, *this we approve of when we are the objects*; this we highly commend; *... we are not apt to think that they exceed their duty*."[^003-note51] While yet an enemy we would not think such beneficence exceeded the duties of neighborhood if we were the object helped. "Swapping places" requires that if *I* am hostile and an implacable enemy to someone, yet am in serious need of help, I ask myself whether I would approve or disapprove of aid kindly given me by my implacable enemy; and go now and do likewise to him.

Now that is truly extraordinary. Edwards assumes that people, whose only obvious "mutual relation equally predicable" is that of stranger, alien, venomous hostility, may also become sharers in an equally predicable mutual relation of neighborhood; and that then anyone can know quite well the right disposition and action due to a hateful enemy by imagining that we are in his place and he in ours when we see him suffering under great calamity. If we suffered similarly, we would not say *he* "exceeded his duty" by helping *us*. But the language of "duty" or obligation may be questioned here.

Not many of us are likely to believe that love of enemies (real enemies, not ideal or imaginary ones) is a duty. Indeed, it is reasonable to argue that the expression "the duties of charity" is a contradiction in terms. In the Roman Catholic tradition of ethics, "counsels of perfection" placed less strain on ordinary, reasonable people's conception of their bottom-line obligations. And in Lutheran and Reformed traditions, the first function of the example of Christ, the perfection of righteousness he taught, the "love one another as I have loved you" of John 13:34, was to cast people down in their own eyes so that they realize they have no health in them, and can do nothing but seek a Savior. Yet, as we have just seen, Edwards' shared neighborhood consists of moral roles, relations, and duties having extraordinarily elevated standards of bottomline

<!-- p. 25 -->

expectations, which he tries to show are entirely reasonable. His demonstration consists in a use of the reversibility test, which ordinarily aims at attaining an unbiased derivation to others of the self's natural inclinations and preferences. On its face that reasoning fails to reach the moral dispositions and actions Edwards commends. The reverse of love of self is not naturally love of enemies. How are we to explain the remarkable meaning Edwards finds in the "as thyself of the Mosaic law? Does what he says really follow from a rational use of reversibility or golden rule arguments?

In his sermon on "seeketh not her own," Edwards wrestles with why Christ called "love one another as I have loved you" a new commandment in "rule and motive." This was a problem since he believed the *love*, the matter of the command, is the same as the old "as thyself"; the "substance" is the same but with "a new enforcement and light annexed," a "new rule and motive." What he says under these heads is all very puzzling. It explains nothing. No answer can be given to those who demand a "rational" explanation of how the rule of loving others as Christ has loved us only "more clearly" shows our obligation in respect to our neighbor. "In a further degree" hardly describes the remarkable meanings Edwards draws from the "swapping places" that Moses and modern moral philosophy command.[^003-note52] Reason alone teaches no such thing to be the meaning of virtuous benevolence.

Typology is the key to understanding Edwards on the sum of the moral law, Old and New. Typology, or figural interpretation, was the way Puritan exegetes held on to the narrative unity and truth of the whole of Scripture, without either fundamentalist literalism or medieval allegorization. The story of Jonah, for example, was a marvelous type; its real but veiled meaning was unveiled and made manifest in the antitype, the entombment of Jesus Christ— who, risen from the dead, also reveals in the Great Commission (Mark 16:15) the true meaning and scope of preaching God's forgiveness to the Ninevites. The blessed land of Canaan, passing over Jordan into the promised land, Zion, Jerusalem were all remarkable types whose meaning will be fully manifest only in the future the New Testament promises God's people.

In like manner, the old commandment contains the new under a veil; the new is the old unveiled and made clear. Love of neighbor "as thyself" is a typical adumbration of the antitypical love to one another "as I have loved you." Therefore, I suggest, "swapping places" (with the remarkable meaning Edwards finds in that interchange) is a type

<!-- p. 26 -->

whereby we substitute ourselves in the stead of others as Jesus Christ stood in ours. Or rather, substituting Jesus Christ in the stead of others (when *he* was in prison, etc. [Matthew 25:35–40], when *he* went down from Jerusalem to Jericho or up to Golgotha) "derives to others" our own position when we were dead by the roadside and the Good Samaritan freely shared with us in our own calamities. We are not apt *then* to think excessive duty was done them. I can conceive of no other grounds than these for deriving *to* myself *from* my implacable enemy succor for me when he catches me in distress, as the standard for what *I* his implacable enemy should be and do towards him in disposition and in action in his calamities. Of course, there is the example of David who, after Saul became his "enemy continually," yet spared Saul's life when Saul was resting in a cave from pursuing him. But in this and other respects David was for Edwards a type of Christ.[^003-note53] Thus the gospel meaning of "pure benevolence" was contained in the old rule, "as thyself"; and thus only is it discoverable by reversibility or golden rule arguments.

Given Puritan typology, it should surprise no one that Christ substituting himself for us gives the meaning to golden rule arguments; that the doctrine that Christ looked on our happiness as his own, placed his happiness in ours, placed his glory in our glorification with him gives the meaning of pure benevolence to our neighbor; or that looking on others' happiness as our own, placing or finding our own happiness in theirs is the manifest meaning of the "as thyself." For the matter of the old law, the meaning of swapping places, types out Jesus' taking our place. Truly virtuous love to neighbor, if there is any such goodwill in human hearts, must be love "so great as to be justly looked upon as a thorough union with them"; so great as the friendship of Christ for his people, which was a love "justly looked upon as making himself *one with them*, as is thoroughly assuming them into *union with himself*."[^003-note54] John 17:21–22 is the manifest, fully unveiled meaning of goodwill among men.

By this measure, we who do not reveal ourselves to one another without dissimulation and are not united in affection can hardly have virtuous and holy goodwill among us. It begins to look as if no one in this life has a native capacity for the first act of truly virtuous benevolence to our neighbors— as was said of love to God. A perfect conjunction of love of our own happiness consisting in their happiness must be the effect (and

<!-- p. 27 -->

not the cause, nor we the cause) of our first being united with them.[^003-note55] There must be an assumption of their happiness into the will and love of our own happiness, as Christ assumed our own nature into his. Mostly, love of our happiness and of theirs runs on two tracks; or sometimes so, sometimes not; sometimes converging, sometimes diverging. Our wills and loves to happiness are compatibly similar— *homoiousios*, I am tempted to say. Still our own happiness does not consist in theirs. There remains an iota between us; my happiness is not *homoousios* with theirs, placed in theirs by our first being united in perfect affection.

In the Christian life, according to Edwards, the old creature has passed away, yet not perfectly; all things are made new, yet none perfectly.

*Consent to Being*

The second dissertation analyzes the topic announced by its title only in the first two chapters. The first of these uses the metaphysical language of "being"; the second translates that into theological language. Decisive for understanding Edwards' ethics is, first of all, the way in which one "unpacks" the extraordinarily compressed exposition of chapter one. Edwards begins with preliminary definitions and initial steps designed to bring his readers into agreement with him concerning the likely location of true virtue. These opening pages, written in nontechnical language, extend down to Edwards' introduction of his distinction between the primary (first) object and the secondary object of virtuous benevolence (propensity) of heart. At that point Edwards also introduces his contrived "term of art"— "‘absolute Benevolence’ (if I may so call it)"— and here rigorous analysis and argument begins.[^003-note56] The paragraphs immediately preceding this point serve only as a ground-clearing elimination of both love of complacence and love of benevolence, as ordinarily understood, from eligibility to be crowned true virtue.

These introductory pages also include the statement, "True virtue most essentially consists in benevolence to Being in general." But that is not Edwards' true starting point. For he immediately signals: "Or perhaps to speak more accurately, it is that *consent, propensity* and *union* of heart to Being in general, that is immediately *exercised in* a general good

<!-- p. 28 -->

will."[^003-note57] That "more accurate speaking" is put fully to work in his later exact definition of terms as he means them, and his later complex logical argument. This, I suggest, serves to qualify his use of the shorthand expression "general benevolence" throughout the dissertation (and his introductory distinction between general and particular beauty, which is preliminary in any case).

Edwards has signaled another thing in these earlier pages. He tightens the circle around the sort of beauty and excellency that everyone will agree true virtue consists in to include only the moral beauty of the "heart" (the disposition and will) of mankind. Having thus stipulated that only intelligent willing beings are "capable subjects" of true virtue, Edwards then announces that by "Being in general" he thereby means "*intelligent* Being in general."[^003-note58] The reader should note this description of the only capable *object* of true benevolence, for it prepares the ground for the second chapter's translation of the first into theological language. It also anticipates Edwards' logical argument in this first chapter, which begins, not with general benevolence, but with "consent, propensity and union" of the heart of a capable subject to the only capable object of true virtue.

Edwards' move is from the particular ("beings' *uniting* love to being") to the general, not the other way round. Consider the relationship between his "first" and "second" objects of virtuous benevolence. First, there is benevolence to Being. Second, benevolence to benevolent Being. In the course of explaining this, a certain priority, even a causal priority, is ascribed to Being— Being itself, Being simply considered, or Being itself, simply considered— over Being in general as the capable object of consent, propensity and union of heart. The difference between the first cluster of expressions and "Being in general" must have some significance. In asking what that significance may be, consider the sequence in the two following, crucial elaborations in Ch. I: (1) "propensity and union of heart to Being simply considered; *exciting* ‘absolute Benevolence’ (if I may so call it) to Being in general"; and (2) "pure benevolence

<!-- p. 29 -->

in its *first* exercise is nothing else but being's uniting,[^003-note59] consent, or propensity to Being; appearing true and pure *by its extending* to Being in general, and inclining to the general highest good, and to each being, whose welfare is consistent with the highest general good."[^003-note60] Edwards' basic premise is the definition he gives to a truly virtuous relation of being to Being. From that he moves to generality. Precisely the same sequence he expresses in terms of "implication" in Ch. VI, where he tests instinctual affections (and finds them wanting, whether exercised to

<!-- p. 30 -->

some only of our fellow creatures or "towards men in general") by "a principle of virtue" which has been "*proved* to be union of heart to Being simply considered; which *implies* a disposition to benevolence to Being in general."[^003-note61] This reading of Edwards is confirmed, it seems to me, by the interchangeability of "beings" and "persons" in his discussion in Ch. VII of the remarkable and misleading resemblance between a truly virtuous love and love that has nothing of "pure" benevolence in it.

The movement from the first to the second object of virtuous benevolence (and the logic of most of the numbered paragraphs in Ch. I) is at least closely coordinated with the movement from love to Being simply considered to love to Being in general. Edwards comes last to "general beauty" or what is "beautiful in a comprehensive view as it is in itself, and *as related to everything that it stands in connection with*,"[^003-note62] adumbrated but not proved in his introductory pages.

We may ask, How does one get to such general beauty or general excellency? The great stride toward extension or universalization is taken by moving to the second object of virtuous love, which is benevolence to *benevolent* being. In this secondary context, it is fitting to speak of "general benevolence." Such general benevolence is now fully demonstrated to mean the heart's relish and cordial union with the supremely benevolent supreme Being. In context with this second object, benevolent Being itself (Edwards' appropriate metaphysical referent to God) and "Being in general" are interchangeable. "Pure" or "absolute" benevolence to Being in general concisely encapsulates the complex "proportion *compounded* of the greatness of the benevolent being, or the degree of *being* and the degree of *benevolence*,"[^003-note63] which is Edwards' criterion or test for love's rectitude. In relation to the greatest Being's benevolence to all being, and only in propensity to union with him, is the soul "related to everything it stands connected with" or does it become the capable

<!-- p. 31 -->

subject of moral beauty in the most comprehensive view of it. Norman Fiering is exactly right when he says that "Edwards meant by ‘being in general’ the transcendent God *plus* His ordered creation."[^003-note64] But that was the conclusion of his argument in chapter one, not an axiom with which to begin. In the movement of his thought, Edwards comes last to "Being in general" and to full warrant for the use of "general benevolence" to abbreviate his more exact definition of terms.

Chapter II of *True Virtue* translates the foregoing metaphysical language into biblical theological language. The reference to "created beings" in its title, and the expression in its first sentence of love to "the Being of beings," make it clear that "Being in general" does not point simply to all-encompassing being, nor does virtuous love to God direct us to a Whole of parts that are lesser wholes, etc., down to particular loves. Readers who have followed my interpretation so far will not be surprised to find that Edwards anchors the evidentiality of substituting "love to God" for true, absolute, or general benevolence in both the "*first* objective ground" (benevolence to Being) and the "*secondary* objective ground" (benevolence to *benevolent* Being). I need only draw attention here to the biblical character of Edwards' love to God (his glory in human understanding, his fullness in our "esteem" and our joys) and of his "benevolence to created beings" (loving *for* them *with* them their knowledge of God, and their loving union and joy in him). The following is a typical paragraph:

> By these things it appears that a truly virtuous mind, being as it were under the sovereign dominion of *love to God*, does above all things seek the *glory of God*, and makes *this* his supreme, governing, and ultimate end: consisting in the expression of God's perfections in their proper effects, and in the manifestation of God's glory to created understandings, and the communications of the infinite fullness of God to the creature; in the creature's highest esteem of God, love to God, and joy in God, and in the proper exercises and expressions of these. And so far as a virtuous mind exercises true virtue in benevolence to created beings, it chiefly seeks the good of the creature, consisting in its knowledge or view of God's glory and beauty, its union with God, and conformity to him, love to him, and joy in him. And that temper or disposition of heart, that consent, union, or propensity of mind to Being in general, which appears chiefly in such exercises, is virtue, truly so called; or in other words, true grace and

<!-- p. 32 -->

 real holiness. And no other disposition or affection but this is of the nature of true virtue.[^003-note65]

That was Edwards' rendering of the two love commandments. At least, it will seem so to a reader not bemused by the metaphysical language of being, and not driven to try to prove that, shortly before his death, America's greatest theological mind loosened his bonds to biblical ethics when writing on true virtue. That is the grave mistake fostered by separating the second from the first dissertation, where are to be found Edwards' scriptural evidences and theological arguments. Still, an implied contrast between metaphysical and biblical theological language entails no necessary conflict for Edwards. Before the modern period, classical Christian theology did not play these options against one another. Theological language was not set over against metaphysical language, nor biblical against theological.

Some interesting similarities and differences may, in conclusion, be noted between Edwards and, for example, the theological language and analysis of Thomas Aquinas. In Aquinas *ipsum esse* functions as a reference or name for God, for all practical purposes. This is Edwards' "Being itself." Both theologians orient the human being upon the *summum ens* (supreme being) or *ens primum*, and not only upon a summum bonum (highest good). Interpreters of Edwards can hardly demonstrate that the "new sense of the heart"— his "voluntarism"— excluded conviction of the truth and reality of divine things; or even that the heart leads the head. Yet the traditional telos of the intellect to being and of the will to good is not exactly replicated. In his thought, greater being (an archangel in comparison with a flea) has greater worth, even before consulting the "secondary object," the consenting or the benevolence to being on the part of that greater or lesser being. This seems rather like saying that the *summum ens* is worthy to be, and to be loved, before consulting *bonum* as one of the "transcendental" attributes of *ipsum esse* (Being itself). Entity itself is worthy of being. In this, Edwards distinguishes more than Aquinas did between greatness and goodness, even in holding them together in God, and in depicting the restored image of God in the virtuous love of the saints. Therefore, in devising his philosophical equivalent of a principle of divine love in the heart going out towards God and towards neighbor,[^003-note66] Edwards found it necessary to define true virtue (or "primary" beauty) as consent, propensity, and

<!-- p. 33 -->

union of heart proportionate to the degree of greatness of the being loved in combination with the degree of benevolence or goodness of that being. Finally, "Being simply considered" may introduce a divergence: Aquinas' *ens simpliciter* (being wherever found) is always used in contrast to *secundum quid* (modality of being). However, the fact that Aquinas never uses *ens simpliciter* (Edwards' "Being simply considered"?) interchangeably with *summum ens* or *ipsum esse* should not detract too greatly from the degree of similarity between these philosophical theologies.

*The Splendor of Common Morality*

It is a mistake to treat Edwards' moral philosophy apart from his moral theology, his theological ethics. That would be to separate the merely distinguishable. It is a mistake also to separate the four principles that comprise his account of common or natural morality. These elements, sources, or *principia* are (1) our sense of the secondary beauty in moral dispositions and relations, (2) self-love extended by association of ideas, (3) natural conscience, and (4) instinctual kind affections: pity and familial affection. Yet another mistake would be to reduce these principles to one only, e.g., self-love understood to be utterly nefarious; and then to understand the other principles as simply and overwhelmingly subject to the inroads of nefarious self-love.

Edwards' well-known thesis, of course, is that there is nothing of the nature of true virtue in the morality arising from these four principles; such natural dispositions are "entirely diverse" from truly virtuous goodwill. Still he is equally concerned to show that, working together or separately, these four principles adequately account for a common morality which, both in its nature and its effects, greatly "resembles" and is "agreeable" to true virtue and readily mistaken for it.

So for Edwards ordinary morality was a rather splendid thing. Here we need not and should not appeal to the grace or the gifts of the Holy Spirit that are "common" to the godly and ungodly alike: common illuminations, common awakenings, common inspiration, common convictions, common religious experience, common humiliations, etc. These restraints or aids accompany the redemption God is working in every age from the Fall to the end of the world. Edwards was not one to use prevenient grace, restraining grace, or common grace to account for the *natural* moral competence of fallen humanity, and to avoid the belief that we good people are only "miserable sinners" and not totally deprived of true virtue.

<!-- p. 34 -->

*True Virtue* should first be read as Edwards' *ethics of creation*. Indeed, if anyone wants to know the meaning of the "natural image" of God in intelligent willing creatures, in distinction from the lost and to-be-restored "spiritual image" of God, I know no better place to send the questioner than to the second dissertation. While these are "entirely diverse" and there is nothing of the nature of the spiritual image in the natural, God has so made our "frames" that we instinctually, silently, insensibly are moved— our dispositions and actions are directed and shaped— by those four principles. Christianity is not built on the ruin of reason, nor on the ruin of morality within the competence of ungraced moral agents.

In addition to principles planted in our natures from creation, God's "laws of nature" or his "moral constitutions" complete Edwards' account of common morality. These also are components of an ethics of creation. A law of nature refers to God's governance of the creation, its moral part no less than what we today call "nature." Laws governing physical nature or intelligent moral beings are immediate arbitrary constitutions. "When I call this an arbitrary constitution," Edwards wrote, "I mean that it depends on nothing but the divine will; which *divine will* depends on nothing but the *divine wisdom*."[^003-note67] In the moral order or in the physical order, a "new effect is consequent on the former, only by the established laws, and settled course of nature: which is allowed to be nothing but the continued immediate efficiency of God, according to a constitution that he has been pleased to establish." So "God's *preserving* created things in being is perfectly equivalent to a *continued creation*, or to his creating those things out of nothing at each moment of their existence."[^003-note68] As the world is not a machine set going by a perfect watchmaker, neither is it a system of orbiting and moving creatures whose designed courses the Space Director must constantly correct, thus "preserving" planets in being, preventing collisions or cosmic grid-lock. "So that truly the giving the world a being at the first no more differs from preserving it through all successive moments, than the giving the last moment differs from the giving a supported being this moment."[^003-note69] We may also say that the giving the moral world a being this moment, lawfully and beautifully connected with a previous moment, differs in no significant respect from giving the moral world a being the first moment. The creation of an intelligent willing being the first moment was

<!-- p. 35 -->

not *without* the moral world that God, in his wisdom, was pleased to create and continues to constitute. So Edwards' natural laws and moral constitutions are ordinances of creation. No reference need yet be made to God's providential rule and overruling, since the immediate telos of general or special providence is the redemption, as is expressly the case with prevenient or restraining grace "common" to the godly and the ungodly alike.

Edwards' radical doctrine of creation-every-moment needs to be brought to mind whenever one is attempting to understand his view of principles and moral constitutions, whether "natural" or "divine." Thus, apart from God's laws of nature, the beautiful harmonies of sight and sound, the consent of minds, fitting moral relations of any sort, the virtues of the pagans or of the regenerate would have no continuity or duration or any being at all. With respect to the four principles of common morality, a moral order by God's immediate "arbitrary" constitution figures prominently in Edwards' account of secondary beauty in insuring that the effects of self-love are an extensive and rather admirable love for others and in instinctual kind affections (which serve not only to preserve the world but also to give us pleasure and comfort on the earth). Without God's laws of nature, there would be no common notions of *desert* or *justice* from our sense of the secondary beauty in fit or proportionate moral relations, or in conscience. Self-love would incurve on itself at once, with no propensity to include other-love, nor any sort of consent to another. Calamities would have destroyed all human creatures long since (without pity) and men and women, parents and children, would have no continuance at all of any affection or comfort on the earth.

SECONDARY BEAUTY. Edwards observed beauty in the symmetry of buildings, in melodies, in the infinite number of equalities in a rose, a countenance, or the solar system. But this inferior sort of beauty or excellency was also in immaterial things. An orderly working together in society is beautiful. So is wisdom "consisting in the united tendency of thoughts... to one general purpose." An adaptedness of things one to another— in, e.g., the proper returns of love— is the beauty of natural justice. There is also "a becoming *gratitude*."[^003-note70]

"The *cause* why secondary beauty is grateful to *men* is only a *law of nature*, which God has fixed, or an *instinct* he has given to mankind."[^003-note71] He

<!-- p. 36 -->

made the answerableness in the natural world and in our common moral world beautiful because therein is "*some image* of the true, spiritual original beauty," consisting in "the union of minds or spiritual beings in a mutual propensity and affection of heart... And it pleases God to observe analogy in his works... and especially to establish *inferior things in an analogy to superior*."[^003-note72] The whole creation (natural and moral), and this first element of ordinary morality, is an analogy of "cordial union" with God.

By using the term *analogy* Edwards does not suggest ascent from a taste for well-known inferior beauty to a taste for primary beauty or excellency. Comparison with Barth's analogy of faith or analogy of relationship may not be entirely apt, but certainly no comparison is to be made with the analogy of being. For when Edwards speculates why God was pleased to observe analogy in all his works, he thinks of no influence of secondary beauty toward bringing about true spiritual beauty in human hearts or moral relations. Nevertheless, the image— secondary beauty, whether material or immaterial— has "a tendency to *assist* those whose hearts are [already] under the influence of a truly virtuous temper, to *dispose them* to the exercises of divine love, and *enliven* in them a sense of spiritual beauty."[^003-note73] Cordial consent or pure love must first *be* in order to be enlivened by the beauties abroad in the natural and moral worlds. Very much this same relation of asymmetrical, dependent reciprocity is again expressed by Edwards when he briefly brings morality from divine principles and from natural principles together at the end of Ch. VII, in a sentence that calls to mind the "instinctual *kind* affections": "a principle of general benevolence softens and sweetens the mind, and makes it more susceptible of the proper influence and exercise of the *gentler* natural instincts."[^003-note74]

The extent and the kind of duties to which our sense of secondary beauty inclines are quite remarkable. This inferior sort of beauty is the ground of "most of the duties incumbent on us" in justice, the "duties of friendship and good neighborhood," and "all duties whatsoever, considered as required by God, and as branches of our duty to him." So "religion" was for Edwards, as for Aquinas and many others, a species of justice. And finally, since true religion has been made known, the answerableness of acts to their occasion, or rendering God his due, also encompasses all duties "considered as what are to be performed with

<!-- p. 37 -->

a regard to Christ, as acts of *obedience* to his precepts, and as *testimonies of respect* to him, and of *our regard to what he has done for us*, the virtues and temper of mind he has exercised towards us, and the benefits we have or hope for therefrom."[^003-note75]

But the goodness of these beauties, even the "becoming" beauty of gratitude, is entirely "diverse" from the beauty of holiness, and there is nothing of the nature of true virtue in them. Men may be disposed to and capable of "great performances" and "great sufferings"[^003-note76] in which there is an inherent moral beauty, but this is only secondary if these dispositions and performances are not from a propensity to unition of heart with God and relish for the primary beauty of holiness. A taste for love to God is as different from a taste for the beauty of justice to God as it is from a taste for harmony, honey, or the smell of a rose.

This brings us to the proof Edwards offers for this diversity— an argument used in the case of each of the four cooperating principles of common morality. If primary and secondary beauty were not diverse, "men's sense of secondary beauty would increase in proportion to their virtue," and truly virtuous love would increase in proportion to men's capacity for secondary beauty. But experience teaches that spiritual beauty and secondary beauty are independent variables. A good ear for music, a good eye for painting or for architecture, appreciation of beautiful systems in physics or philosophy, eligibility for the Metropolitan Opera Company, good citizenship, virtuosity in what *we* (not Edwards) call golden rule morality, the administration of justice or the harmonious arrangement of political society evidently do not vary directly with true virtue.

Edwards sometimes uses a stronger form of this argument, which gives instances of the entire separation of apparent from true virtue. Serpents can be charmed by the beauty of a tune! Whatever we may think of classing secondary beauty in moral matters with the beauty of melodies to serpents, I see no reason to deny that, for example, beneficence may be inherently a very beautiful thing, fitting real benefits to real occasions, even without true benevolence.

SELF-LOVE. By "association of ideas... vastly heightened by education,"[^003-note77] self-love is a principle or spring of disposition and action productive of an extensive love to others. A genuine "love to some others [and to many others] may truly be the effect of self-love." Self-love, of

<!-- p. 38 -->

course, has no power by itself to do this. Still, anyone experienced in loving himself well will have a sort of other-love. Such an association of the idea of others' good with our own is because of a law of nature God has fixed. There is no "metaphysical necessity" that from regard to our own interest we should love those that love us; the contrary would imply "no contradiction."[^003-note78] It could be that— however we exert ourselves to promote our own interest by promoting the interest of some others— we could never do so that way. It could be that self-love spins only on the spot, that each and every moral agent remains alone, with no mutual benefits flowing from other-love and no sense that this is so, that love to self and of private interest are of the self *sole*, that the self's loves are becalmed at sea, governed by no moral laws and therefore associated with no others, going out to none. Just so, the gravity that draws parts of our globe toward its center might be different from the gravity that draws our globe to other planets. In both instances, we have to look to see. And when we look to see, we see that self-love (even censurable selfishness) is very often commonly and best gratified by love to others. God's moral constitution sustains and bends purely private personal self-love to extension into larger communities of common interest.
