No one rightly reads Edwards if he does not understand that for this, too, the Creator is to be praised.

We not only learn to love other specific persons (and common causes) from love of their love to us, which is a love *derived to them* from an experienced love to self. In the course of individual moral development we also learn to love certain "qualities and characters" abstracted from the particular persons who originally taught our love to self to love those characteristics in others. It takes no "great degree of metaphysical refining" to see that this is the reason men approve of others they hear of at a distance, or read of in history, or in a romance, or see represented on the stage from whom they expect no profit or advantage; and why they

<!-- p. 39 -->

disapprove of other moral characters from which they expect no injury. Our initial approval of the "character" was because from experience "its nature and tendency falls in with the nature and tendency of self-love." So from association of ideas first imprinted and fixed in the mind by experienced deadly danger or experienced pleasure, a child learns to respond to the picture of a snake, painted fruit, or the figure of a bird, without any expectation of being bitten, or tasting or hearing these representations.[^003-note79]

This approval of "qualities and characters" extends to "meekness, peaceableness, benevolence, charity, generosity, justice, and the social virtues in general." Edwards goes so far as to say that from love to self can be derived by fixed association of ideas a sort of love of enemies, if in their "quality and character" we discern a *stoutness* or a high degree of strength to overcome obstacles which in our own moral development we learn to value in others who are friendly to us.[^003-note80]

*Justice*, or *desert*, are among those qualities. This virtue of persons and in moral relations, we saw, also springs from the secondary beauty of uniformity and proportion. Since one of these principles is never without the other, Edwards does not undertake to determine whether extended self-love or the secondary beauty of moral and social relations better accounts for justice in common morality. I judge that the excellency of symmetry in moral relations exerts the stronger influence. But Edwards does not decide this question. Instead, he compounds the effects of these two first principles in yet another "association of ideas." Our "approbation of justice and desert, arising from a sense of the beauty of natural agreement and proportion" strengthens by "a kind of reflex... influence" men's claims to justice and desert, and concordant exercises of their own agency, from self-love. Association of ideas brings the first two sources of common morality together. So "some vices may become in a degree odious by the influence of self-love, through an habitual connection of ideas of contempt with it; contempt being what self-love abhors." Concurrently, the same idea of odiousness attaches to qualities and characters because of their incongruity or natural ugliness or deformity— the abstracted contrary of secondary beauty in moral matters and relations of which we have a sense to disapprove.[^003-note81]

Thus anger and gratitude are justly deserved manifestations of self-love "when others' hearts oppose us, and they from their hearts do us

<!-- p. 40 -->

hurt" or "when they love us, and do us good." At the same time, gratitude flows from our "sense of a beauty in moral things," which Edwards calls "a kind of moral sense"[^003-note82] (reserving this designation, unqualified, for conscience); and resentment from our sense of incongruity in moral matters. There is a "natural agreement, proportion, and adjustment" between others' dispositions and actions and, respectively, their suffering "in like manner as we have suffered" or our gratefully loving them and doing them good. Two different pairs of things are here joined together in a morally experienced self-love: (1) self-love and fixed attitudes toward "qualities and characters" of persons, and (2) self-love and "a kind of reflex and indirect influence" of "a sense of the beauty of natural agreement and proportion." Either or both together cause men to approve justice or desert; and as well, to approve ordinary benevolence and disapprove malice.[^003-note83]

To this he adds a final explanation: the "almost irrefragable association, in innumerable instances, of ideas which have no connection any other way than by education... greatly strengthening that association, or connection, which persons are led into by other means."[^003-note84] That is, education *transmits* the moral notions men were led to, even after the strong, fixed connection that was experienced has been forgotten. Children are morally educated in the virtues in a tradition of ordinary morality, who no way have experienced their connection with self-love. A tradition commending virtues that originally arose from morally experienced self-love, with its esteem of qualities and characters from association, will continue in moral education long after memory of that connection is lost. This is precisely the "lapsed link" theory used by British utilitarians to explain why people persist in the belief that virtue and vice— and judgments about right and wrong actions— are not to be explained by their usefulness in obtaining beneficial and avoiding evil consequences.[^003-note85]

<!-- p. 41 -->

Finally, Edwards gives two examples to show that gratitude and anger arising from self-love do not vary directly with public benevolence. These are independent variables. The case of the conspiratorial crew and the gang of robbers provides evidence that there is no virtuous benevolence in the love to others, with its becoming gratitude and anger, that may be *derived to them* from self-love. Nevertheless, love to self as a source of moral disposition can account for gratitude and angers that are fitting and those that are not; and that is important, morally, without true virtue.[^003-note86]

CONSCIENCE. The element in Edwards' account of conscience that is original with *True Virtue* reaches back to pick up a theme in Edwards' first Miscellany on the Trinity. This entry argues that, since any idea "perfectly like a thing, *is* that thing" and "wants nothing that is in the thing, substance nor nothing else," the Son, who is the "express and

<!-- p. 42 -->

perfect image of God, is God's idea of his own essence." There is "some image" of this in human self-knowledge. Thus, Edwards continued:

> Man is as it were two, as some of the great wits of this age have observed: a sort of genius is with a man, that accompanies him and attends him wherever he goes; so that *a man has a conversation with himself*, that is, he has a conversation with his own idea. So that if his idea be excellent, he will take delight and happiness in conferring and communing with it; he takes complacency in himself, he applauds himself; and wicked men accuse themselves and fight with themselves as if they were two. And man is truly happy then, and only then, when these two agree, and they delight in themselves, and in their own idea and image, as God delights in his.[^003-note87]

In like manner, in *True Virtue* conscience consists in "a disposition in man to be uneasy in a consciousness of being inconsistent with himself and, as it were, against himself in his own actions." Ease of conscience is consistency with self: integrity. There is a sort of "self-love, or self-*union*"[^003-note88] that is with man, that accompanies him wherever he goes. The reflex action of conscience is at least one element in what Edwards means by intelligent willing creatures being in the "natural image" of God. In conscience there is some image of the primary beauty of both the paradigm union and consent between the Father and the Son, and of truly virtuous consent to "persons and beings."

Immediately after introducing the notion of self-union, Edwards writes that disturbance of conscience "appears particularly in the inclination of the mind to be uneasy in the conscience of doing to others what he should be angry with them for doing to him, if they were in his case, and he in theirs." Thus common morality so far as it arises from conscience encompasses what we today call golden rule arguments, or the reversibility or "swapping places" test for whether the action we are contemplating is moral or immoral. This is the constant element in Edwards' many notes on natural conscience written over a lifetime. The new stress in *True Virtue* is on the *contradiction* within the self, which disapproves when one is "conscious *to* oneself"[^003-note89] of having done as one would not be done by, and which arises spontaneously, insensibly, etc., in the mind. The spontaneous reflex of ease or dis-ease may be the reason Edwards is willing to have *his* understanding of conscience called the

<!-- p. 43 -->

"moral sense." The reader should recall, however, that a sense of secondary beauty also spontaneously registers the harmony or proportion of answerable actions and moral relations, without our having any knowledge of nature's laws. In any case, conscience is not an intuition. It is not Francis Hutcheson's "moral sense" that registers approbation upon an apprehension of benevolence wherever it may be found, in oneself or in others, similar in manner of operation to the other senses we have of the world. For Edwards, conscience is, itself, a relation. It is golden rule morality writ small in the self's consciousness *to* self.

> To do that to another which we should be angry with him for doing to us... if we were exactly in the same case, is to disagree with ourselves, and contradict ourselves. It would be for ourselves both to choose and adhere to, and yet to refuse and utterly reject, as it were, the very same thing. No wonder this is contrary to nature... and inward war with a man's self.[^003-note90]

So in some sense conscience prescribes reversibility (not, in the first place, to make universal). If an agent does not abide by this, if his disposition and action go against natural integrity, an uneasiness of conscience warns him that wrong has been done, in that he *claims* such and such disposition or action to be moral and yet would not prescribe that it be directed by others toward himself in similar circumstances. This is a practical contradiction— disunion with self— in a moral agent since he is by nature "conscious *to*" his own will and action. Edwards believed that "unless men's consciences are greatly stupefied" such golden rule approvals and disapprovals are "naturally and necessarily suggested" and "habitually, spontaneously, instantaneously, and as it were insensibly arise in the mind"— no need to read contemporary moral philosophy. Any person "easily and quietly sees" whether he, being in another's place, should "approve or condemn, be angry or pleased as he is."

So far we have ascribed to conscience only the *formal* capacity for swapping places to distinguish right from wrong. This formal test of self-consistency, by itself, would be empty. Indeed, it could mandate evil-doing, if natural conscience has no other foundation of its rectitude. We still need to ask, therefore, concerning the material content an agent should prescribe when he puts himself in the place of another. Our sense of secondary beauty informs conscience concerning the excellency of justice or desert; these material judgments, indeed, "must precede" formal self-consistency. "There is another thing that must precede," Edwards

<!-- p. 44 -->

writes, "and be the foundation" of the "uneasiness" of conscience which he explored."[^003-note91]

If my reading is correct, Edwards held that natural morality was a rather splendid thing— though there is no true virtue in it. He ascribed to natural conscience the capacity to "swap places" even with God and to determine what is justly *his* due. If persons have any idea of divine things, they have a conscience which will excite within them "resentments which would be occasioned in themselves by an injurious treatment in any wise parallel" to their own failure to give God his due.[^003-note92]

Because of the concurrence of "self-union" (and all that means) with a taste for secondary beauty and excellence in moral matters (and all that means in material moral judgments that are fit, amiable and worthy) the power of conscience seems unlimited. So Edwards affirms:

> Approbation and disapprobation of conscience, in the sense now explained, will extend to all virtue and vice; to everything whatsoever that is morally good or evil, in a mind which does not confine its view to a private sphere, but will take things in general into its consideration, and is free from speculative error... Thus natural conscience, if the understanding be properly enlightened, and errors and blinding stupefying prejudices are removed, concurs with the law of God, and is of equal extent with it, and joins its voice with it in every article. And thus, in particular, we may see in what respect this natural conscience that has been described, extends to true virtue, consisting in union of heart to Being in general, and supreme love to God. For,

<!-- p. 45 -->

 although it sees not, or rather does not taste its primary and essential beauty, i.e. it tastes no sweetness in benevolence to Being in general, simply considered, or loves it not for Being in general's sake (for nothing but general benevolence itself can do that), yet this natural conscience, common to mankind, may approve of it from that uniformity, equality and justice which there is in it... Men by natural conscience may see the justice (or natural agreement) there is in yielding all to God, as we receive all from God; and the justice there is in being his that has made us, and being willingly so... and also the justice there is in our supreme love to God, from his goodness— the natural agreement there is between our having supreme respect to him who exercises infinite goodness to us, and from whom we receive all well-being.[^003-note93]

Nevertheless, to know the justice of duties to God and Christ, and to perform some or any of them for conscience's sake, is evidently not the same thing as to know and do his will from love and propensity of heart to union with him.

The foregoing passages carry the mind back to *End of Creation*, the "former treatise," where the same moral reasoning was used. To show that "reason teaches," no less than Scripture, that the end God had in creating any world at all was for his glory, praise, and name's sake, Edwards wrote:

> When we are considering with ourselves, what would be most fit and proper for God to have a chief respect to, in his proceedings in general, with regard to the universality of things, it may help us to judge of the matter with the greater ease and satisfaction to consider what we can suppose would be judged and determined by some third being of perfect wisdom and rectitude, neither the Creator nor one of the creatures, that should be perfectly indifferent and disinterested. Or if we make the supposition that wisdom itself, or infinitely wise justice and rectitude were a distinct disinterested person... now such a judge... would weigh things in an even balance; taking care that greater, or more existence should have a greater share than less, that a greater part of the whole should be more looked at and respected than the lesser in proportion (other things being equal) to the measure of existence, that the more excellent should be more regarded than the less excellent: so that the *degree of regard* should always be in a proportion *compounded* of the proportion of existence

<!-- p. 46 -->

 and proportion of excellence, or according to the degree of *greatness* and *goodness* considered *conjunctly*... To determine, then, what proportion of regard is to be allotted to the Creator, and all his creatures taken together, both must be as it were put in the balance; the Supreme Being, with all in him that is great, considerable, and excellent, is to be estimated and compared with all that is to be found in the whole creation: and according as the former is found to outweigh, in such proportion is he to have a greater share of regard. And in this case, as the whole system of created beings in comparison of the Creator would be found as the light dust of the balance (which is taken no notice of by him that weighs) and as nothing and vanity; so the arbiter must determine accordingly with respect to the degree in which God should be regarded by all intelligent existence, and the degree in which he should be regarded in all that is done through the whole universal system... And as the Creator is infinite, and has all possible existence, perfection and excellence, so he must have all possible regard. As he is every way the first and supreme, and as his excellency is in all respects the supreme beauty and glory, the original good, and fountain of all good; so he must have in all respects the supreme regard... Thus we must conclude such an arbiter as I have supposed would determine in this business, being about to decide how matters should proceed most fitly, properly, and according to the nature of things. He would therefore determine that the whole universe, including all creatures animate and inanimate, in all its actings, proceedings, revolutions, and entire series of events, should proceed from a regard and with a view to *God*, as the supreme and last end of all...[^003-note94] Thus I have gone upon the supposition of a third person, neither Creator nor creature, but a disinterested person stepping in to judge of the concerns of both, and state what is most fit and proper between them. The thing supposed is impossible; but the case is nevertheless just the same as to what is most fit and suitable in itself. For it is most certainly proper for God to act according to the greatest *fitness*, in his proceedings; and he knows what the greatest *fitness* is, as much as if perfect rectitude were a distinct person to direct him. As therefore there is no third being beside God and the created system, nor can be, so there is no need of any, seeing God himself is possessed of that

<!-- p. 47 -->

 perfect discernment and rectitude which have been supposed. It belongs to him as supreme arbiter, and to his infinite wisdom and rectitude, to state all rules and measures of proceedings... For being interested unfits a person to be an arbiter or judge, no otherwise than as interest tends to blind and mislead his judgment, or incline him to act contrary to it. But that God should be in danger of either is contrary to the supposition of his being possessed of discerning [discernment] and justice absolutely perfect... [I]t therefore belongs to God whose are all things, who is perfectly fit for this office, and who alone is so, to state all things according to the most perfect fitness and rectitude, as much as if perfect rectitude were a distinct person. We may therefore be sure it is and will be done. I should think that these things might incline us to suppose that God has not forgot himself, in the ends which he proposed in the creation of the world; but that he has so stated these ends (however he is self-sufficient, immutable and independent) as therein plainly to show a supreme regard to himself. Whether this can be, or whether God has done thus, must be considered afterwards, as also what may be objected against this view of things.[^003-note95]

Edwards' stunning use of an independent arbiter to show God himself to be the supremely worthy and fit end in creation may be compared with the "ideal observer" theory of ethics proposed in the twentieth century.[^003-note96]

<!-- p. 48 -->

This brings us to Edwards' standard argument: that there is no true virtue in conscientious morality. The weaker form of this argument is that these two moralities are distinct; even when together, they are independent variables. Not all approbations and condemnations of conscience, experience teaches, are in proportion to virtuous temper of mind.[^003-note97]

However, the stronger form of the argument is the more striking. The "greatest reason" Christians have for believing that true virtue is not the same as that which conscience dictates is that they believe there will be a day and a state of affairs in which the two are entirely separate. Then and there, no "thought experiment" or search for supposable examples of robber bands will be required to tell the difference.

> Christians have the greatest reason to believe from the Scriptures that in the future day of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, when sinners shall be called to answer before their Judge, and all their wickedness, in all its aggravations, brought forth, and clearly manifested in the perfect light of that day; and God will reprove them, and set their sins in order before them; their consciences will be greatly awakened and convinced, their mouths will be stopped, all stupidity of conscience will be at an end, and conscience will have its full exercise... And this, according to the notion I am opposing, would be the same thing as then being brought to the fullest repentance; their hearts being perfectly changed to hate sin and love holiness; and virtue or holiness of heart in them will be brought to the most full and perfect exercise. But how much otherwise have we reason to suppose it will then be?... 'Tis proper for a judge when he condemns a criminal to endeavor so to set his guilt before him as to convince his conscience of the justice of the sentence. This the Almighty will do effectually, and do to perfection, so as most thoroughly to awaken and convince the conscience... But supposing natural conscience to be what has been described, all these difficulties and absurdities are wholly avoided. Sinners, when they see the greatness of the Being, whom they have lived in

<!-- p. 49 -->

 contempt of, and in rebellion and opposition to; and have clearly set before them their obligations to him as their Creator, Preserver, Benefactor, etc. together with the degree in which they have acted as enemies to him, may have a clear sense of the *desert* of their sin, consisting in the natural agreement there is between such contempt and opposition of such a Being, and his despising and opposing them; between their being and acting as so great enemies to such a God, and their suffering the dreadful consequences of his being and acting as their great enemy: and their being conscious within themselves of the degree of anger which would naturally arise in their own hearts in such a case, if they were in the place and state of their Judge. In order to these things there is no need of a virtuous benevolent temper, relishing and delighting in benevolence, and loathing the contrary. The conscience may see the natural agreement between opposing and being opposed, between hating and being hated, without abhorring malevolence from a benevolent temper of mind, or without loving God from a view of the beauty of his holiness. These things have no necessary dependence one on the other.[^003-note98]

There's nothing like the Day of Judgment for concentrating the mind!

Edwards' appeal to those to be condemned on the Day of Judgment was, for him, an appeal to real states and intelligences *to clarify the nature of natural conscience* in any intelligent willing creature when conscience alone is perfectly in exercise. In this world of trial, the conscience of saints is often dim. God's common grace often assists conscience to do its office more fully in the unregenerate. In this world of trial, saints and sinners alike may ask, Who? Me? Why me? (Matthew 25:31–46). But when perfect judgment is come, their deeds will be set in order before them (Psalms 50:21). The perfection of judgment requires both that all mankind be judged together and that the occasion be public for justice to be fully manifest. And finally, those sentenced must have no doubt about the justice of the sentence. If they still ask, Who? Me? Why me? the Judge has not *perfectly* judged them.[^003-note99]

<!-- p. 50 -->

It is a serious error to read the case of the Judgment Day as denying the worth of conscientious morality; or to say that in this time of trial conscience produces no fruits in justice done, only approbations; or to say that grace alone enables men to do what justice requires, i.e., conscience itself has no motivational power. We need to remember that in Edwards' example from Christian belief the present moral world has come to an end. God's moral constitution of it has come to an end. Presumably there is no more secondary beauty imaging the divine beauty, no more God's laws of nature sustaining the derivation of love to some and many others from love to self, no pity or familial kind affections (to which we next turn), and, I judge, no more of the fruits of conscience's golden rule morality in actual justice done and to be done, nor need for that. The point was simply to show decisively that in this life— as on that Day when men will have (in words from Miscell. no. 623)[^003-note100] "an illumination of conscience far beyond any have in this world"— our conscience (which is "nothing else but a sense of the equality and answerableness" of God's judgment upon our sins) never disposes us to see "the hatefulness or deformity," the true ugliness from a sense of the heart, of sin in general, or of our sins in particular so as to dispose human hearts to do justice— or anything else— from pure benevolence to God.[^003-note101] If this were so, the Day of Judgment would be a day of universal conversion to love to God!

INSTINCTUAL KIND AFFECTIONS. Since Edwards called our sense of secondary beauty in moral matters an "instinct" of nature, we need to pay careful attention to his definition of this fourth and final element in his account of common morality. "Instincts" are "inclinations natural to men... determining their minds to certain affections and actions *towards particular objects*." These instincts differ from our "instinctual" sense of beauty in their degree of specificity. But although instinctual kind affections are oriented toward particular persons or particular occasions, they (like the other principles) lead to admiration for or aversion to general qualities and characters. The last terse paragraph of this chapter states that "natural instinct, disposing men to pity others in misery," is also "a source of a kind of abhorrence in men of some vices, as cruelty and oppression; and so, of a sort of approbation of the contrary virtues, humanity, mercy, etc." Edwards' criticism of the virtues enkindled

<!-- p. 51 -->

by natural pity is limited to "so far as they arise from this cause *only*."[^003-note102] And the same word "kind" in this chapter and in 1 Corinthians 13:4 adumbrates a convergence of some sort between virtues infused with or by charity and virtues based on natural principles— to be discussed later. Edwards chooses to discuss two sorts of instinctual kind affections that move us to particular others, or to others under specific circumstances.

(1) Familial "kind affections" join together husband and wife, parents and children. Edwards expressly refuses to dispute with anyone who refers what we today call "special moral relations" (and he called "relative duties") to extended self-love. "In my opinion both [these accounts] are true," he writes, "viz. that natural affection is owing to natural instinct, and also that it arises from self-love." Again we see that Edwards' account of common morality is multifactoral. Between husband and wife "there is doubtless a disposition both to mutual benevolence and mutual complacence [esteem] that are not naturally or necessarily connected with any sensitive desires."[^003-note103] Sexual attraction serves the preservation of mankind; so it seemed obvious to Edwards that in addition kind affections provide us comfort on earth in congenial community. My guess is that, of the familial loves mentioned, there is between husband and wife more complacence (pleased by the good) than benevolence; between parents and children, more benevolence (good-giving) than complacence; between children and parents, more complacence (or esteem) than benevolence. These are the loves familiar in moral discourse; and, again, the same-named loves (we shall see) also arise from absolute or pure benevolence to God. Relative duties and dispositions are also specifications of charity.

(2) There is a natural inclination to pity that is universally excited in all men on occasions proper to it. Pity is "uneasiness on the sight of others' extreme distress." When Edwards asks why the Creator implanted in us the kindly affection of pity, the reply is: "for the same purposes as most other instincts, viz. chiefly for the preservation of mankind, though not exclusive of their well-being."[^003-note104] My guess is that he would have said that familial kind affections are implanted chiefly for well-being and comfort.

Edwards believed that experience shows a correlation of pity with the purpose he ascribes to it in the designs of a wise and merciful God. He has

<!-- p. 52 -->

so made men that in cases of great calamity they rush to the aid of strangers, for it is then that men stand most in need of the help of others besides their near friends with whom they have closer ties of kind affection. Otherwise calamities would tend to men's destruction from the earth. From this we may see something of the reason God has so strangely endowed men with a natural sense of pity in the face of extreme calamity to persons indifferent, but not with an equal sense of rejoicing at the sight of others' great prosperity. This is "agreeable to the state that God designed mankind for here, where he intends their preservation, and comfortable subsistence."[^003-note105]

For preservation, pity and sexual instinct seem sufficient; for comfortable subsistence, familial kind affections. When we add to these final elements of God's moral constitution the sum of men's instinct for the secondary beauty of answerable moral relations in family, neighborhood, and civic friendship, the immediate and instantaneous operation of ease or dis-ease of conscience, and the fact that self-love is never exercised without God's ordering of it, there is no reason to ascribe to Edwards a bleak view of the life or the morality of mankind during this time of trial.

Nevertheless, his negative thesis still stands. There is nothing of true virtue in instinctual kind affections. The two are utterly diverse. In particular, familial affections arise from a quite different source and have no tendency to produce general benevolence. Affections and benevolence do not vary directly with each other.

With regard to pity Edwards uses the stronger form of his standard argument. Pity is shown to be entirely separable from true virtue, not merely distinguishable from it. Pity not only does not vary directly with goodwill; it can even consist with illwill. Therefore true benevolence must be a distinct thing, essentially different from pity— though Edwards has shown that pity produces approvals of "humanity, mercy, etc." and disapprovals of cruelty and oppression in general. For we feel pity toward persons in extreme anguish even though notice of their deaths would cause no great uneasiness. We are moved to pity brute creatures under extreme and long torments, but not— at least not to the same degree— by seeing them put out of all sensible pain or pleasure "at butchers' shambles in great cities."[^003-note106] We pity persons in great pain whose positive pleasure we may be very indifferent to. We pity others under

<!-- p. 53 -->

exquisite torment whose prosperity excites in us the "comparative spirit" of envy.[^003-note107]

*The Two Sources of Morality*

So there are two moralities: first, common morality from natural principles, and second, true virtue, pure holy goodwill, absolute benevolence to God. In the next section we shall see what this means in terms of various virtues in Christian moral life from the indwelling Spirit's infusing divine love in hearts and lives. Before concluding on the second dissertation, however, Edwards in Ch. VII offers four reasons why common morality, wholly diverse from true virtue, has "yet by many been mistaken for true virtue."

(1) The two resemble one another in nature. Ordinary morality has "something that *belongs to the general nature* of [true] virtue."[^003-note108] There is "a sort of love" from natural principles, both benevolence to "persons and beings" and complacence in anything in them resembling virtuous benevolence to being or beings. There are also fruits of these principles in qualities and characters, i.e., in natural virtues.

(2) The two resemble one another in tendency and effects. Both tend to the common good. There may be beneficent effects without pure benevolence. As Edwards wrote concerning judgments of desert and justice from secondary beauty or fitness in moral relations: "So that the tendency of general benevolence to produce justice, also the tendency of justice to produce *effects* agreeable to general benevolence, both render justice pleasing to a virtuous mind."[^003-note109]

(3) "There is indeed a true *negative* moral goodness" from natural principles. An intelligent willing being "framed" without them or created by God with no moral constitution, would manifest much greater evil. Men would be more vicious, would characteristically resemble true virtue less; and they would "in innumerable respects" be less restrained "from *acts* of true wickedness" than they actually are.[^003-note110]

This language calls for a reminder that Edwards is not here speaking of restraining grace, but of a negative moral goodness belonging to his

<!-- p. 54 -->

ethics of creation, his account of how God continually creates, rules, and preserves the moral world. There is no reference to either restraining or assisting "graces before grace" in Edwards' analysis of natural morality. (4) The last reason why those things that have not the essence of virtue are very often commonly mistaken for true virtue is most important for our present purposes. *Virtues are properly called by the same names whether they spring from natural principles or from benevolence*. "Another reason why these inferior affections, especially some of them, are accounted virtuous is that there are affections of the *same denomination* which are truly virtuous."[^003-note111] Here, I judge, we must cease to speak of two moralities— natural and inspirited— and must address ourselves directly to two sources of morality that are, in important respects, one and the same morality. Immediately following the sentence above, Edwards gives, as one example, a fruit of charity properly called by the same virtue term that he used to designate one of the two instinctual kind affections.

> Thus, for instance, there is a truly virtuous *pity*, or a compassion to others under affliction or misery from general benevolence. Pure benevolence would be sufficient to excite pity to another in calamity, if there were no particular instinct, or any other principle determining the mind thereto. It is easy to see how benevolence which seeks another's good should cause us to desire his deliverance from evil. And this is a source of pity far more extensive than the other. It excites compassion in cases that are overlooked by natural instinct.

"Virtuous *pity*" and the various virtuous dispositions in heart and life set forth in the sermons on 1 Corinthians 13 are *specifications* of charity alone. Overall, therefore, Edwards gives an account of virtues that are both theological and moral, and which are actualized on the same level as the natural virtues. Of these "theological moral" virtues he here says only that many Christian virtue terms are also fittingly used in common moral discourse to designate the fruits of natural principles.

All along in his several accounts of common morality, Edwards prepared for this by qualifying interjections ("Not but there can be..."), suggesting, for example, that there is gratitude from principles other than secondary beauty or extended self-love. In the technical language of *True Virtue*: "Respect to Being, in this proportion [compounded of respect to degree of greatness of being and respect to degree of its benevolence to being], is *the first and most general kind of justice; which will produce*

<!-- p. 55 -->

all the subordinate kinds

."[^003-note112] I take that sentence to mean the same as the one-line note to himself in the "Controversies"— draft, "The Nature of True Virtue" (MS p. 188), which reads: "METHOD. Show how all virtues are derived from pure benevolence."[^003-note113] Only the final brief paragraphs of Ch. VII of True Virtue cash in that promissory note. But surely the 1738 sermon series, which Tryon Edwards appropriately titled Charity and Its Fruits; Or Christian Love as Manifested in Heart and Life, dealt with that extensively. So there is a certain logic in the arrangement by which we come to the articulation of the virtues of true virtue last in this introduction.Before, however, enlarging upon the positive nature of true virtue (as Edwards did in *Charity* and in the twelve positive signs in *Affections*), I suggest an abbreviated comparison between the analysis of morality compressed into the last three paragraphs of Ch. VII of *True Virtue* and that to which Thomas Aquinas devoted many pages.

"Virtuous *pity*" and the other fruits of charity in the sermons on 1 Corinthians 13 call to mind Aquinas on the infused moral virtues. These were moral virtues infused with the theological virtues (faith, hope, and charity), parallel with his natural moral virtues, and to which he also gives the "same denomination," e.g., justice, courage, etc.[^003-note114] Edwards would agree with Aquinas that "charity is the mother and root of all the virtues."[^003-note115] If it is objected that, unlike Aquinas, he would not have continued that sentence with the words, "inasmuch as it is the form of them all," that depends on the meaning of *form*. First cause and the end or final cause (Alpha and Omega) were the important ones for Edwards; *formal cause* was swallowed up in the laws of nature and moral constitutions. Still, he used Augustinian analysis and the language of virtues "arising from" and as "forms of" love.[^003-note116] Aquinas' explanation of *form* in this context is the same: form is plastic to the surpassing *end* of charity. Charity is the mother of the other virtues, since she conceives within herself "the acts of the other virtues, by the desire of the last end." It is in this sense that "charity is said to be the end of other virtues, because it directs all other virtues to its own end." Thus "it is charity which directs the acts of all other virtues to the last end, and which consequently, also *gives the form* to

<!-- p. 56 -->

all other acts of virtue.[^003-note117] I know that elsewhere the philosophy of formmatter, and of virtues as excellences of divers faculties or appetites, remains intact. But in the contexts I have cited, the moral virtues seem to be specifications of charity alone. In these contexts Aquinas used Augustine to baptize Aristotle.

In addition, both Aquinas and Edwards teach that divine love in the heart penetrates and elevates natural morality. Charity perfecting the natural virtues in Aquinas (after infused moral virtues come the gifts and fruits of the Spirit, and the beatitudes) can be compared with Edwards' true virtue mixing its influence with natural principles, guiding and regulating their operation, which he treats in the final two pithy paragraphs summarily ending the seventh chapter. The more sweeping expression of Edwards' basic claim is that all virtues are specifications of charity, that for example, a virtuous pity or compassion would be a quality of Christian character even if men were without the same-named instinctual kind affection. His final, somewhat more limited assertion of that claim is that charity "excites compassion in cases that are *overlooked* by natural instinct." Having thus shown the preponderance of true virtue as a source of "theological moral" virtues when alongside homonymous natural moral virtues, he then proceeds to list "mixed fruits" of charity and natural principles. This should be read as yet another claim, corresponding to Aquinas' "grace perfecting nature":

> And even in those cases to which instinct extends, it mixes its influence with the natural principle, and guides and regulates its operations. And when this is the case, the pity which is exercised may be called a virtuous compassion. So [i.e., in like manner] there is a virtuous *gratitude*, or a gratitude that arises not only from self-love, but from a superior principle of disinterested general benevolence. As 'tis manifest that when we receive kindness from such as we love already, we are more disposed to gratitude, and disposed to greater degrees of it, than when the mind is destitute of any such friendly prepossession— therefore, when the superior principle of virtuous love has a governing hand, and regulates the affair, it may be called a virtuous gratitude. So [in like manner] there is a virtuous love of *justice*, arising from pure benevolence to Being in general, as that naturally and necessarily inclines the heart, that every particular being should have a share of benevolence as is proportioned to its dignity, consisting in the degree of its being and the degree of its

<!-- p. 57 -->

 virtue... And so [in like manner] it is easy to see how there may be a virtuous sense of *desert* different from what is natural and common. And so [in like manner] a virtuous *conscientiousness*, or a sanctified conscience. And as when *natural affections* have their operations mixed with the influence of virtuous benevolence, and are directed and determined hereby, they may be called virtuous, so there may be a virtuous love of parents to children, and between other near relatives, a virtuous love of our town, or country, or nation. Yea, and a virtuous love between the sexes, as there may be the influence of virtue mingled with instinct, and virtue may govern with regard to the particular manner of its operation, and may guide it to such ends as are agreeable to the great ends and purposes of true virtue. Genuine virtue prevents that increase of the habits of pride and sensuality, which tend to overbear and greatly diminish the exercises of the forementioned useful and necessary principles of nature. And a principle of general benevolence softens and sweetens the mind, and makes it more susceptible of the proper influence and exercise of the gentler natural instincts, and directs every one into its proper channel, and determines the exercise to the proper manner and measure, and guides all to the best purposes.[^003-note118]

The language of the final paragraph suggests the mingling of "Charity is... *kind*" (1 Corinthians 13:4) with "instinctual *kind* affections" in general, of which Edwards names and discusses only two.

What is this if not an account of the perfection of natural morality? *To perfect* means to bring to complete actualization; and by this Aquinas does not mean simply the complete actualization of virtues that are only specified by faculties of the soul. Instead, moral virtue in its perfect state "makes its possessor good."[^003-note119] Radically to be turned to the supreme end of charity makes *the man*, the moral agent, *good*, which seems more than simply to bring the virtues or excellence of his faculties to actuality. Because of the central role conscience plays in *True Virtue*, one might conjecture a parallel with prudence in Aquinas, in this respect only: that through conscience or through prudence charity perfects every virtue, and perfects the possessor of them. If by a "sanctified conscience" Edwards does not mean charity perfecting prudence by conceiving within herself its acts by desire of the last end, and so conceiving the acts of other virtues as well, thus making their possessor good, I suggest that significant difference may be located in their concepts of conscience or

<!-- p. 58 -->

prudence. The difference is in the moral philosophies of these two men, and not in their theologies of grace or divine love.

Finally, Aquinas' answer to the question "Whether a Man can Will or Do Good without Grace" does not support the notion that the natural or acquired virtues alone have an integrity that enables men to achieve their natural good, while grace only steps in to enable them to reach their supernatural end (the theological virtues, distinct from the natural). Aquinas believed that was true of human nature only in its prelapsarian state: "In regard to the sufficiency of his operative power, man in the state of pure nature could will and do, by his own natural power, the good proportionate to his nature, such as the good of acquired virtue, though not surpassing good such as the good of infused virtue." So even before the Fall, "he cannot by his own power fulfill the whole good that pertains to his nature," i.e., his eternal good. After the Fall, the natural power to will and to do the good proportionate to his nature was also lost. Explaining that "human nature is not so entirely corrupted by sin... as to be deprived of natural good altogether," Aquinas gives a rather astonishing rejection of any "hierarchical synthesis" of natural morality and grace. His explanation is that "even in a state of corrupt nature a man can do some particular good by the power of his own nature, such as build houses, plant vineyards, and things of this kind"![^003-note120] The good pertaining to man's nature which he can still will and do is practical reason in its exercise of making, not in its exercise of doing (ethics or politics). The "healing" fallen humanity needs lies in the very desire for the good, and in this man needs divine help, by which he is first moved to act well. Should we conclude that for Aquinas the grace of charity is needed to direct the acts of every natural, acquired virtue in fallen man to its own end? That after the Fall, all the virtues must be specifications of charity, conceiving in herself the acts of every virtue that can be in fallen creatures?

We seem to have arrived at the conclusion that Edwards' account of common morality is at least as favorable to the moral competence of the unregenerate, perhaps even more favorable, than that of Thomas Aquinas— if anyone supposes that praising fallen humankind is a test of the truth of Christian teaching, or even of what that teaching in fact is. It does seem that on the infused moral virtues, the gifts and fruits of the Spirit, and the beatitudes, Aquinas used Augustine to baptize Aristotle by total immersion three times (in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit). Concerning the grace of charity perfecting

<!-- p. 59 -->

rational, common, or natural morality, the two thinkers are most in agreement; most in disagreement on the need for charity to presuppose common morality (supposing that question asked of Edwards). At the same time, by Edwards' account, virtues from natural principles were never merely splendid vices (supposing Augustine to have thought so). Common morality has integrity without charity. There is a wholeness to moral life without charity, and a wholeness to moral life from charity. The former does not point to the latter, nor does the latter presuppose the former.

Other contexts may not support the interpretation and parallels I have suggested, and I do not know whether or when the Saint nodded. I am content with a weaker claim: from these comparisons it is reasonable to claim that these thinkers' music is the same, although the lyrics may have changed. This is to say, the main features— the general picture— of the Christian moral life is the same. It is the philosophy or metaphysics— and the science— of each that makes for any notable differences. The same can be said of any of the great doctors of grace in Christian history and tradition.

*Charity and Its Virtues*

These fifteen sermons unfold the meaning and movement of St. Paul's Hymn to Love, 1 Corinthians 13. Introductory to the whole are the first three sermons, whose Doctrines[^003-note121] are: (1) "All that virtue which is saving, and distinguishing true Christians from others, is summed up in Christian or divine love." (2) "The ordinary influence of God's Spirit, working saving grace... is a more excellent blessing than any of the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit," and (3) "All which men can do, and all which they can suffer, will not make up for the want of sincerity in the heart."

The love of which Edwards speaks is *one* in principle [*principium*, spring or source) flowing out toward diverse objects. One and the same Spirit infuses love, influences the heart to love God and fellow man. Moreover, these "are not two works of the Spirit of God, one to infuse a spirit of love to God, and another a spirit of love to men. But in doing one he doth the other."[^003-note122]

<!-- p. 60 -->

Nevertheless, the accent can fall on one or the other, love toward men or love to God. So following the three introductory sermons, Edwards' next seven sermons primarily concern the fruits of charity in disposition and action toward men. I call this division the "first table of love," reversing the order of the "tables" in the Decalogue. Here the Doctrines are: (4) "A Christian spirit disposes persons meekly to bear ill that is received from others, and cheerfully and freely to do good to others," (5) "A truly Christian spirit is opposite to an envious spirit," (6) "A Christian spirit is a humble spirit," (7) "A Christian spirit is opposite to a selfish spirit,"[^003-note123] (8) "Charity contrary to an angry spirit," and (9) "That a Christian spirit is contrary to a censorious spirit; or in other words, it is contrary to a disposition uncharitably to judge others." These are Christian virtues particularly related to our neighbors. The final sermon in this section— on ver. 1 Corinthians 13:6— is one in which Edwards reads the Apostle as cutting short his specifications and summarizing all that he has said, or that can ever be said about these first fruits of charity in the words "Rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth." From these words, Edwards derives the Doctrine (10) "All true Christian grace tends to holy practice."

In the second division or table of love, Edwards stresses love to God. Sermons eleven through fourteen, on ver. 1 Corinthians 13:7 and 1 Corinthians 13:8, expound the Doctrines: (11) "They who are truly gracious have a spirit for Christ's sake to undergo all sufferings to which they may be exposed in the way of their duty," (12) "There is a concatenation of the graces of Christianity," (13) "True Christian grace is that which nothing that opposes it can ever overthrow," and (14) "That great fruit of the Spirit in which the Holy Ghost shall not only for a season but everlastingly be communicated to the church of Christ is divine love." Readers will note more frequent use of "grace" and "graces" in this division of the sermons, as they will have noted that love to God is often given as a reason for the disposition that is a fruit of divine love going out primarily toward men.

The fifteenth and final sermon— ver. 1 Corinthians 13:8–10, on the theme (15) "Heaven Is a World of Love"— is Edwards' remarkable glorification of

<!-- p. 61 -->

divine love in every respect: perfect love for one another in indefectible love to God. This is Edwards' triumphant conclusion and eschatological verification of the wealth of particulars he found in the chapter as a whole. The rhetorical power of this last sermon is rivaled only by his other "virtuoso performance,"[^003-note124] "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God."

It is impossible, and would be a travesty for me to attempt, to summarize the rich texture of Edwards' phenomenology of the Christian moral life in the sermon series as a whole. Nevertheless, a sketch can be given of the more important interconnections in Edwards' reading of St. Paul's chapter as an account of the Christian moral life.

The third sermon, to which I give the short title[^003-note125] "Nothing Can Make

<!-- p. 62 -->

Up for Want of Sincerity in the Heart," both concludes the general introductory section and is transitional to the particular virtuous dispositions and actions that are the fruit of love to men, which Edwards depicts in analytical detail in the first table of love (sermons four through ten). Edwards' use of the plurals "performances" and "sufferings" indicates that he is still speaking in somewhat general terms of moral matters. By its extremity, giving all one's goods to feed the poor encompasses all performances. And giving one's body to be burned, by its extremity, encompasses all sufferings. If these extremes profit nothing and have no ultimate significance without sincerity in the heart, then nothing else of a "moral nature" can. So Edwards goes on to analyze in the following sermons particular moral qualities— seemingly less extreme— that are fruits of charity toward men.

To give all one's goods to feed the poor seems to be an action, and martyrdom looks like suffering an action by others. But both are a sort of *doing*, on Edwards' reading. Both are acts of giving. "When a man has given away all his goods," Edwards writes, "he has nothing remaining which he can give but himself." Yet giving himself, his own body, avails nothing "if the heart is withheld."[^003-note126] So "sincerity" in the heart means to be a self-giver.

We should take Edwards at his word when he says "great" performances and sufferings, for he uses it as a term of approval. These things are admirable *simpliciter*. "Many of the heathen... have been eminent for justice, and others for their great deeds which they have done for the public good"[^003-note127] So also of "great sufferings": "history gives an account of some who have yielded themselves to voluntary death out of mere stoutness and sturdiness of spirit, who have braved it out and died rather than yield to the demands of others when they might have saved their lives."[^003-note128] These words do not express a grudging admiration. True, Edwards speaks in this context of great performances or great sufferings done from mixed or false motives. But he deems these things "great" *simpliciter*. Moreover, he believes them often done from "natural principles" or motives that as such are admirable. Indeed, "it is hard to say how far natural principles may carry men in particular duties and performances."[^003-note129]

<!-- p. 63 -->

Edwards draws no hard-and-fast line between the fruits of natural principles and the fruits of divine love in the heart. Nor is there any reason to believe that he changed his mind about this subject between the sermon series and *True Virtue*, which analyzes, as we have seen, four sources of a common morality that Edwards knew to admire.

Edwards' standard of excellence, however, was different from the praiseworthiness of natural virtue or common morality. He assessed moral matters by their "worth in the sight of God." Recall that "Christian love is one and the same in principle" whether exercised toward God or toward fellow creatures. The test, then, is not the sincerity of love of neighbor in separation from love to God. There is no such love. Nor is it a heteronomous or pious standard of love to God in separation from love to fellow human beings. There is no such love. To ask whether there is any sincere regard to God in the matter is identical with asking whether there is any sincere love to fellow men in the hearts of those who do great deeds or suffer bravely in some cause. Charity alone in the hearts of moral agents is "amiable" to God. "Whatever is done or suffered, yet if the heart is withheld there is nothing really given to God."[^003-note130]

God delights in the giving heart, not in the gift he does not need. He delights in the cymbalist praising him, not in tinkling cymbals used in his praise. This, I suggest, is a definition of gift-giving to God; a gift is no gift without a willing giver, a *self-giver*. It is also a definition of gift-giving to neighbor. Without sincerity in the heart the essential gift is withheld. Charity, then, is Edwards' basic moral notion in terms of which every disposition or action is assessed, whatever be their greatness or goodness *simpliciter*, whatever principle is their source or spring, and whatever benefits result.

It may be helpful to interrupt my exposition of Edwards' series at this point in order to take up two different groupings of sermons, considering together certain related sermons out of the order of the verses in 1 Corinthians 13. First, I shall lift up to view the "progression" in Edwards' exposition of qualities of Christian life in sermons four, eleven, thirteen, and fourteen, whose texts are deceptively similar statements in ver. 1 Corinthians 13:4, 1 Corinthians 13:7, and 1 Corinthians 13:8. These qualities, fruits, or graces, I suggest, viewed in their significant sequence, manifest an increasing strength and an increasing unity of the whole company of virtues, which reflects the story of redemption. Then, second, we will view together sermons two and (again) fourteen, whose short titles are "Love More Excellent Than Extraordinary Gifts of the

<!-- p. 64 -->

Spirit" and "Divine Love Alone Lasts Eternally." In these two sets of sermons, I suggest, we more than glimpse the objective story line of the work of redemption that frames a "moral progression" of the church— individually or collectively, as Edwards puts it. After exhibiting this theological-moral story line throughout Edwards' exposition of the chapter as a whole, we return to his account of the remainder of the specific fruits of charity in the first and second tables of love, which in their variety are the sum of divine love in the heart and the sum of this, Edwards' most important treatise on Christian ethics.

A progression in moral matters running through the sermon series is the ingenious interpretation Edwards gives of four phrases in 1 Corinthians 13:4, 1 Corinthians 13:7, 1 Corinthians 13:8— "Charity suffereth long," "Beareth all things," "Endureth all things," and "Charity never faileth." These texts seem to say much the same thing, or at least to have largely overlapping meanings. Edwards devoted a sermon to each: "Long-suffering and Kindness" (sermon four), "Undergoing Sufferings a Duty to Christ" (sermon eleven), "Grace Never Overthrown" (sermon thirteen), and "Divine Love Alone Lasts Eternally" (sermon fourteen).

The first of these sermons, based on the text "Charity suffereth long and is kind," begins what I have called the first table— love to neighbor. The next two fall within my second table— love to God in this life. The fourth sermon, on "charity never faileth," is on the theme— if I may so phrase it— charity and its fruits gone to heaven. To follow this thread through the series enables us to grasp the movement Edwards saw in the chapter as a whole, from accent on love to men to accent on love to God, from grace to glory, from the indwelling Spirit's implanting divine love in the heart back to God as the heart's supreme object and enduring delight.

Suffering long in the face of ill received from others and being kind in doing good to others are the first pair of particular fruits of charity directed toward our fellowmen. Indeed, these two qualities or dispositions of moral agents interpenetrate each other. Edwards holds the two virtues— long-suffering and kindness— together in a single duplex sermon. The disposition "meekly to bear ill, what is received from others" and the disposition "cheerfully and freely to do good to others" are not properly understood as separate qualities. There is kindness to others already in meekly suffering ills done by them, and kindness in doing good to others must encompass long-suffering in this life, and is already freely and cheerfully willing to do so. The force and meaning of this extraordinary sermon was seriously impaired when Tryon Edwards divided

<!-- p. 65 -->

it into two "Lectures"— a fault repeated in all heretofore available editions which are only reprints of Tryon's publication.

But does not "Beareth all things" say the same thing as "Charity suffereth long"? Edwards thinks not. Just as the sermon on the twin themes of long-suffering and kindness is the first in the table of fruits of love to others, so the sermon on "Beareth all things" is the first in the table of fruits of love to God. In this phrase the Apostle proclaims the tendency of charity to dispose men and make them ready to undergo sufferings for Christ's sake; and so the short title given this sermon is "Undergoing Sufferings a Duty to Christ." Many have supposed the words "Beareth all things" to refer to suffering injuries from men. Edwards' interpretation is that they mean bearing all things "for the cause of Christ and religion."

He offers four reasons for rejecting the ordinary reading.[^003-note131] (1) We ought not to suppose that the Apostle "in reckoning up the various fruits of charity, would use a tautology, and now mention the same thing in this verse." (2) The Apostle "seems evidently to have done with fruits of charity of that nature," since he summed them all up in the previous, transitional verse on which Edwards preached his tenth sermon, "Grace Tends to Holy Practice." (3) Many times elsewhere the Apostle speaks of the great fruit of charity in suffering for the cause of Christ. And finally, (4) the words that follow in ver. 1 Corinthians 13:7— "believeth all things," "hopeth all things"— "all show that the Apostle has done with those fruits of charity, which immediately respect our neighbor."

Again, does not "Endureth all things" say the same thing as "Beareth all things"? Edwards thinks not. All these "synonymous expressions" are "vulgarly understood... as though the Apostle in all of them only said the same thing over and over in different words."[^003-note132] We can see upon close consideration that each "signifies a distinct fruit of charity." Meekly suffering injuries from men is one fruit. Bearing all things for the sake of Christ that are in the way of duty is another fruit. "Endureth all things" signifies something different still.

Edwards bases his reading of "Endureth all things" on the original Greek *panta hypomenei*, which he says means "remains under all things," i.e., endures under all opposition that can ever be brought against it. To get this reading out of the Greek πάντα ὑπομένει Edwards separates out the prefix ὑπο from μένει. Long before the New Testament was written, the prefix had merged with the substantive, as in our word "withstand."

<!-- p. 66 -->

To "endure under" is the meaning, just as we today might make a point by saying that to "withstand" has great strength because it means to "stand with." Edwards seems to be quite aware of what he is doing, since he does not claim his to be a literal reading. Instead, he says that a more "liberal" translation could be "remains under all things."[^003-note133]

More important to note is the fact that the movement of thought through these verses and sermons parallels Edwards' view of the history of the work of redemption. Concerning the first three texts, Edwards makes the same argument. These synonymous expressions are "vulgarly understood... as though the Apostle in all of them only said the same thing... in different words." But we ought not suppose the Apostle was a tautologist. On the story line of redemption, to endure or remain under all possible opposition is the final fruit of charity that Christians need in this life. This virtue strengthens the church for the final tribulation before the reign of Christ on earth.

The text of the final sermon in this group of four is "Charity never faileth." "Charity never faileth" seemed so obviously different from "Charity endureth all things" that Edwards did not trouble to defend the Apostle against uttering a tautology in this instance. Bearing up under all possible opposition is no longer needed as a fruit of charity. Neither is undergoing suffering for the sake of Christ in the way of duty, nor is kindly long-suffering in the face of ill done to us by others. "That great fruit of the Spirit in which the Holy Ghost shall not only for a season but everlastingly be communicated to the church of Christ is divine love" is Edwards' Doctrine, penultimate only to his great peroration, "Heaven Is a World of Love." Thus the saving gifts and graces move through these four sermons toward God's end in redemption, which is his end in creation. This progression is sufficient to show that the story line of the history of redemption governs Edwards' account of the Christian moral life. As Edwards reads the chapter, Christ is building up his kingdom in the soul, and among men.

Is there a progression in moral matters corresponding to this Christological-eschatological progression? Of course there is. But we need first to consider additional details concerning that objective story line by taking note of some significant differences between the second and fourteenth sermons in exposition of the passing away of the spiritual gifts.

Edwards' stress in the second sermon is indicated by its Doctrine: "The ordinary influence of God's Spirit, working saving grace in the

<!-- p. 67 -->

heart, is a more excellent blessing than any of the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit." To magnify the far-surpassing blessing of divine love in the heart, Edwards heaps praise on the excellency of those "wonderful" endowments given in times past.[^003-note134] These were the gifts spoken of in chapter twelve: the gift of tongues ("languages which they had never before learned"), the gift of prophecy, the gift of knowledge ("immediate revelation or inspiration," but including also "speculative knowledge"), and the faith of miracles.[^003-note135] This sermon introduces Edwards' distinction between "common" and "uncommon," or saving, gifts, crisscrossing the distinction in Scripture between ordinary and extraordinary gifts. Common to the godly and ungodly alike are some ordinary gifts as well as the extraordinary gifts just named. But there is one ordinary, uncommon gift, working grace and infusing divine love in the heart.

This saving gift of the Spirit— and what makes it uncommon— blesses men with "a quality inherent in the nature of him who is the subject of it," "makes a man's heart and nature excellent."[^003-note136] In this the Spirit— who is the Love of the Father and the Son— does "communicate himself in his own *proper* nature to the man," "impart itself in its holy nature."[^003-note137] The Spirit becomes "an indwelling vital principle in the soul." "[T]he subject becomes *a spiritual being*, denominated so from the Spirit of God which dwells in him and of whose nature he is *partaker*," "a partaker of the Spirit so as to become spiritual in himself and in his own nature." Indeed, this "more excellent blessing" is what Edwards means by "the *spiritual image* of God," the "amiable image and likeness of Christ."[^003-note138] Here is the first reference to the notion of "participation" in the "divine nature" (2 Peter 1:4) that became crucial for Edwards' demonstration that God's end in creation was "but one."

By contrast, the common influences of the Spirit are "adventitious"; they "produce effects in the man," or by him. They are like "garments" or— since Edwards speaks here only of the "common *extraordinary*" gifts, reserving the "common ordinary" ones for his later sermon— like "precious jewels, which a man carries about him." Miraculous gifts do not make "the very soul itself... a precious jewel."[^003-note139]

<!-- p. 68 -->

*Comparison of privileges* is the main point of the second sermon. Subordinate to this, Edwards discusses at some length— in language that anticipates *Distinguishing Marks* and *Affections*— what are "no certain sign of grace, nor anything saving,"[^003-note140] and from this he concludes: "All the fruit of the Spirit, upon which we are to lay weight as evidential of grace, is summed up in charity or Christian love, because this is the sum of all grace"; or is "comprehended in that charity which is the fruit of the ordinary influences of the Spirit."[^003-note141] Edwards' theme is *discerning* the Spirit.

One reason saving grace in the heart is more excellent is that divine love (summed up or comprehended in grace) was "*the end* of all extraordinary gifts," their end in the history of redemption.[^003-note142] In Edwards' rendering of the movement of the chapter, it is notable that the *purpose* of every common gift (ordinary and extraordinary alike) is fully developed only in sermon fourteen when the end of them all— indefectible perfection— comes more fully into view. Moreover, the class of "common ordinary" gifts is specified and given meaning only in the later sermon, when they, too, are then and then only viewed as having passed away from the church, collectively and individually.

The theme of sermon fourteen is divine love everlastingly communicated to the church of Christ; "that great fruit of the Spirit" gone to heaven and there "confirmed" forever. Several things are a consequence of this, looking back upon the movement of redemption on earth. For one thing, the division of the chapter at the sixth verse between charity going out primarily to our neighbors and charity going out primarily to

<!-- p. 69 -->

God and Christ is ignored, or rather becomes an indifferent distinction.[^003-note143] Another small but perhaps significant feature of sermon fourteen is the fact that there is a brief sketch of "certain seasons" in the work of redemption when extraordinary gifts were granted *before* the period from the coming of Christ to the closing of the canon. Without elaborating further on the redemption God has been working in every age since the Fall of man, this recital of past temporary displays of miraculous gifts starts with "the church before the beginning of the canon of Scripture; that is, before the writing of the book of Job[^003-note144] and the five books of Moses."[^003-note145]

Far more important to notice is that the perimeters of the time in which the church now lives are more sharply marked in sermon fourteen— with the near approach of the end time within which Christ will reign on earth, and the end of that end time. In the second sermon, which was mainly a comparative evaluation of excellences, Edwards had simply insisted that the extraordinary gifts have ceased since the closing of the canon of Scripture and are not to be expected in "the glorious future times of the church." The "calling of the Jews[^003-note146] and

<!-- p. 70 -->

the destruction of Antichrist"[^003-note147] are the only lines drawn on those approaching glorious times. For characterization of those coming times we have to turn to the later sermon. The moral features of life within those times or eons are worth noting.

Of course, Edwards continues to preach that gifts of miraculous inspiration ceased long ago and are no more to be expected. But now, following the movement of the chapter further along the story line of redemption into the end (he believed) of creation and providence as well, far more is said about that end, telos, or purpose. Edwards used means-end language to group extraordinary means with some external ordinary means granted the church on earth. "When those saints who once had the enjoyment and use of those means of grace came to heaven, the miraculous gifts as well as other means ceased. There is no occasion for any means of grace in heaven; either ordinary, such as stated ordinances of God's house, [as] sacraments and prayer, or extraordinary, as prophecy, and gifts of tongues, and gift of knowledge." The end toward which the whole creation moves with the story of redemption is "a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of *the fullness* of Christ."[^003-note148] As in the second sermon we located an early use by Edwards of the notion of "participation," so here we have *pleroma*, the fullness, which together with partaking of the divine nature clinch the argument of *End of Creation*.

Edwards deploys the full force of a means-end argument: this is the "one reason" he gives for the doctrine of this sermon. "Miraculous gifts being means to a further end are good no further than as they tend to that end, and so cease when that end is obtained. But divine love is that great good which is the end itself, and therefore remains when the means cease." Immediate revelations "were never given for any other end but only to promote the setting up and building up of Christ's kingdom in men's hearts."[^003-note149] Edwards' language here is almost exactly that of the sermon series he preached the following year on the story of the work of

<!-- p. 71 -->

redemption.[^003-note150] Clearly, also, the kingdom of Christ building up in the souls of men should never be separated from the kingdom of Christ building up in the world among men— certainly not in a sermon next to one in which heaven is a *world*, essentially not a gathering place for individuals.

Most important for comprehending every facet of Edwards' understanding of the Christian moral life is the class of "common ordinary" gifts, not developed at all in the second sermon. These are "common convictions of sin, common illuminations, common religious affections."[^003-note151] (He does not say "common *gracious* affections.") These gifts are common to the good and the bad, the godly and the ungodly alike; they are experienced by the Spirit's "adventitious" influence upon both those who are truly virtuous and those who are truly without virtue. Those, too, are means, and they have the same destination as wonder-working did. "They have no goodness in themselves, and are no further good than as they tend to promote grace and holiness radically and summarily consisting in divine love."[^003-note152] But these common ordinary gifts have not yet passed away; they still promote Christ's kingdom in converted or unconverted human hearts, and will do so in the world and in the church to the end of time. In the church this means until the deaths of "particular members" but "collectively as a body" until the Day of Judgment.

A final point might easily be missed by the reader. In the tenth sermon Edwards distinguished "that faith which is saving from that which is only *common*." There are then a sort of "faith" and also a sort of "hope" that are as common as religious experience generally. In the present sermon, he lists as fruits of the Spirit "that conviction, *that faith*, and illumination... common both to godly and ungodly." He speaks of "common *temporary* faith"; of when "tongues and *faith fail*." When wicked men die, "their common temporary faith which they have had, which has had no divine love as an ingredient in it and to be the soul of it

<!-- p. 72 -->

shall cease"; but when saints "come to die," they "shall leave all that was common in their *faith* and in their *hope* and all that did not appertain to divine charity."[^003-note153] When that which is perfect is come, that which is in part faith and in part hope will pass away, and only that in every virtue which appertains to divine charity, as an essential ingredient in it and the soul of it, shall last eternally.[^003-note154]

This completes the two groups of sermons I have chosen to lift out of sequence. First, the increasing perdurance or strength of the saints, individually and collectively, shown by Edwards' interpretation of the four synonymous expressions in ver. 1 Corinthians 13:4, 1 Corinthians 13:7, and 1 Corinthians 13:8. Second, the additional Christological-eschatological enforcement of our understanding of the story line of redemption by his two sermons on the extraordinary gifts, i.e., the theological-moral movement between sermon two and sermon fourteen. If such is the frame story of the charity sermons, then we would expect something of the same movement to be evident in Edwards' consideration of particular virtues, which I now resume. It is not too farfetched to surmise that Edwards assumed a movement in the Old Testament of the Decalogue downward, with a first table of commands primarily indicating duties to God, and a second, primarily duties to our fellow creatures— as he read St. Paul's chapter to be a continuation of that movement of a people, individually and collectively, back to God. This is his root metaphor, Alpha and Omega, expressed in a famous passage in *End of Creation* as God's fullness received and returned, both "emanation" and "remanation."[^003-note155] Turning now to Edwards' account of the virtues as specifications of charity or divine love in heart and life, we shall look at two things simultaneously: (1) the remarkable tapestry of virtues Edwards weaves and (2) some important moral progressions corresponding to the Christological-eschatological movement in the chapter.

One identifiable moral progression began with long-suffering and kindness— the first fruits of charity that have our fellow creatures as object directly and immediately. There is progression in perdurance, beginning with long-suffering and continuing in the sequence to "Charity never faileth." This is moral, not ontological only. "Greatness of soul" and Stoic *virtus* (which Christian long-suffering resembles) accent strength, not only a moral quality like sincerity or gentleness or kindness

<!-- p. 73 -->

that, standing alone, could be fragile. Christian *virtus* also goes on from strength to strength, from its beginning in divine love implanted in us and among us (the kingdom Christ is building up). That strength ultimately empowers the whole array of virtues.

Meekness was joined with long-suffering in the Doctrine of the fourth sermon. Edwards quickly wove into his tapestry the qualities of peaceableness, calmness, quietness and repose of mind, self-possession, and "smooth outward behavior." Long-suffering with these qualifiers means essentially "always continuing" to bear injuries, just as for Kierkegaard "charity hopeth all things" means essentially a love that is "always hopeful."[^003-note156] Edwards' characterization of this virtue often sounds positively Stoic in its imperturbability. Indeed, he calls this virtue "a godlike greatness of soul"; "a more noble and excellent valor and greatness of mind than great conquerors who subdued walled cities, [possessed]." By this virtue we are fitted "to live in such a world as this." The wise Christian is "like the moon walking in her brightness, while the dogs are barking at her she is not moved, but goes on in her own course placidly shining through the heavens still." But Christian long-suffering, unlike Stoic imperturbability, is not grounded in curbing the passions but in love to God, in gratitude, and imitation of Christ. This is what "sets persons very much above the injuries of men."[^003-note157] Therefore, suffering ill from others is already interpenetrated and suffused with kindness, a spirit of being willing freely and cheerfully to do good to them.
