Contrariwise, to be kind, to be free and cheerful in willingness to continue doing good to others, to the good and the bad, "both to friends and enemies," "to the thankful and the unthankful,"[^003-note158] in short, to all creatures who are in the natural image of God, has of necessity an ingredient of long-suffering in it.

Under "kindness" Edwards introduces the familiar loves of benevolence and complacence. These are but "various denominations" of Christian love. As charity goes out to others, he wrote, "as it respects the good enjoyed or to be enjoyed *by* the beloved, it is called *love of benevolence*; and as it respects good to be enjoyed *in* the beloved, it is called *love of complacence*." Of the two familiar loves, Edwards takes the love of benevolence to be the more fundamental, "most of an imitation of the eternal love and grace of God, and the dying love of Christ."[^003-note159] Evidently, however,

<!-- p. 74 -->

benevolence as ordinarily understood is only one "denomination," one of several "exercises" of charity. Here we have the seed of Edwards' devised term, "pure" or "absolute" benevolence, meaning love to God (and all that implies), which he uses in the first chapter of *True Virtue*.

Even ordinary love of benevolence is more than a "wishing good," for it disposes its subject to do something effectual. Thus Edwards' agent-morality holds together benevolence and beneficence, heart and life, an ethics of virtue and an ethics of action, which are often rendered too distinct today. Yet this beneficence evidently has charity in it, of which it is an exercise. For Edwards has been speaking of the cheerful giver of the first sermon, one who does not withhold the heart from benefits given away.

A second pair of distinguishing Christian virtues is drawn from "Charity envieth not" and "Charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up. Doth not behave itself unseemly." We should begin now to pay attention to the tapestry, or the architecture, of Edwards' systematic discussion of these virtues. "Suffering long" had respect to the ill received from others, and "kindness" treated good to be done to others. In the next pair, "envying not" has to do with the good or prosperity others possess, while "vaunting not" involves the good or prosperity we ourselves possess. These two virtues deal with good possessed, and are not as closely or as internally related virtues as the first pair; therefore Edwards devotes two different sermons to the opposite of envy and to humility.

The notion of comparison, we shall see, is used by Edwards in different ways to analyze each of these fruits. Envy is defined as "a spirit of opposition to others' comparative happiness."[^003-note160] This is evident when others' prosperity is *above* ours. But we may be envious of those equal or near us, lest they outdistance us in good or goods possessed; and of those below us who (a comparative spirit is quick to suspect) may be fast catching up. Thus an envious spirit seeks to be "singular." It finds occasion for bitterness by comparing one's own allotment with that of *anyone* else.

Edwards then promptly reserves the word "envy" for those equal or above us, and suggests that envy of those near or below us in good or goods is better called "grudging." In its extremity, envy or grudging shifts from others' prosperity to dislike and even to a settled hatred of their persons. Hatred of person is another sort of vice altogether. It (not selfishness) is the very opposite of charity itself. Having introduced grudging as a refinement of terms in moral discourse about envy, Edwards

<!-- p. 75 -->

invokes with mounting rhetorical power the fact that God in Christ did not grudge us anything there was in his possession or power, including bringing lowly sinners to glory with him.[^003-note161] This is important to note here because Edwards is going to deny that Christ in the divine nature had "humility"; his rather was the excellence of "grudging not." So also the superior saints in heaven begrudge not the lower, whose perfect solidarity with those above them is "envying not."[^003-note162] An ungrudging

<!-- p. 76 -->

spirit— introduced here in the sermon on envy— gains increasing sway, in sermons that follow, over the moral life that Christ is building up in and among his creatures.

A Christian spirit sees envy to be odious; it "*mortifies* such a principle or disposition in the heart"; it brings contentment and quietness of mind in relation to others' prosperity; it teaches us rather to rejoice therein.[^003-note163] Here the structure of Edwards' treatise on the Christian moral life again becomes visible. We are disposed to this virtue and to mortify the vice in two ways.[^003-note164] We are disposed to the virtue "envying not" first by charity immediately and "directly of its own tendency." We are disposed to it second by charity working indirectly and "mediately, as it works humility." Thus humility— which, we shall see, is a hinge or cardinal virtue in Edwards' system— is a mediating fruit of charity that promotes the virtue "envying not," even as also charity directly engenders that virtue. Put the other way round: Charity directly mortifies the vice of envy. This it does also "more mediately" by mortifying pride in the good or goods we possess.

Moreover, these pairs— pride/humility and envy/envying not— are mutually fructifying vices/virtues. As Edwards says in the next sermon, being puffed up with pride most provokes one to envy and is used to excuse envy. Conversely, an envious spirit fuels pride and provides an excuse for it. Rejoicing in the good others possess (contra envy) and humility in regard to the good we possess (contra pride) are evidently complementary and mutually supportive Christian dispositions.

For the text of his sixth sermon on humility, Edwards joins together the final words of ver. 1 Corinthians 13:4, "vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up," with the first phrase of ver. 1 Corinthians 13:5, "Doth not behave itself unseemly." These statements refer to a greater or lesser degree of pride, especially as being puffed up manifests itself in "vaunting" and other behaviors. My comment will stress humility as the struggle of a Christian spirit against pride, understanding these cardinal opposites to be Godward in orientation. Only a reading of the sermon itself will show how Edwards locates

<!-- p. 77 -->

humility among the dispositions of love primarily going out to our neighbors.

Just as the focus of "envying not" was upon the comparative good possessed by others, so humility is a "sense of our own comparative meanness" focused upon the good *we* possess. "Meanness" is not a demeaning term— except to moral agents who aspire to be "all" or "singular" in their autonomy. Edwards expressly excludes men's "low opinion of themselves as compared with other men from melancholy, or from the meanness of their circumstances, or from their natural constitution." Theirs is not true humility; indeed, one can ascribe to Edwards the belief that such men should think of themselves— in the natural image of God, or the spiritual— more highly than they do. Notice also that, in relation to our fellow creatures, Edwards' meaning is that "he who has a right sense of himself with respect to God will open his eyes to see himself *aright* in all respects." If a person sees how he stands with "respect to the first Being... it will tend greatly to help him to a *just* apprehension of the place in which he stands among his creatures."[^003-note165] It is fair to call this rectitude in self-esteem.

A contemporary reader is apt to be misled early in this sermon. Edwards first speaks of humility as "an excellency proper to all created intelligent beings," men or angels. It "primarily" consists of our sense of "meanness as compared with God or a sense of the infinite distance between God and us,"[^003-note166] entailing rectitude of self-esteem among men. This we may call "creature feeling," and "fellow-creature feeling." This sense of humility is proper to all creatures, great and small, to excellent and glorious beings. The saints and angels in heaven excel in it; and this same sense of proper "comparative littleness" was before the Fall.

But Edwards' next point is: "Humility in fallen man implies a sense of a twofold meanness before God, natural and moral."[^003-note167] In this world a humble person has not only a sense of his distance from God's greatness but also a sense of sin, filthiness, and pollution before God's infinite holiness. Here Edwards cites, among other scriptures, the passages from Isaiah and Job that Rudolf Otto later used as examples of creature feeling suffused with a sense of self-abhorrence, of uncleanness and

<!-- p. 78 -->

repentance in dust and ashes.[^003-note168] Both littleness and unworthiness are constitutive of humility as a Christian virtue in this life.

Still, a sense of both natural and moral meanness is a *Christian* virtue. The ungodly have no such sense. When Edwards says that man's "natural meanness is become much greater since the Fall," since the "moral ruin" that "greatly impaired his natural faculties, though it has not extinguished them,"[^003-note169] he does not mean that the ungodly need to acknowledge a greater natural meanness. Nor does he mean that only the ungodly— the fallen— are subjects of the second element in humility, a sense of their unworthiness. The contrary is the case. He means rather that insofar as a person is come to a knowledge of the first Being, only "so far is he let into the knowledge of other things." These words immediately precede the introduction of moral meanness as an ingredient of humility in fallen man.[^003-note170] Humility is a sense of our "natural meanness" before God's greatness along with a sense of our "moral meanness" before God's excellency and the beauty of holiness. The saints in heaven have both components. Indeed, the sense of moral meanness increases among the inhabitants of heaven as their sense of God's excellency increases. It is a mistake to suppose that moral meanness primarily respects the inherent vileness in only some or many men. It is also important for Edwards that our sense of moral unworthiness has respect first to God's excellency. "It is necessary that we should not only see," he wrote, "God's greatness, but also his excellence and holiness."[^003-note171] So in the end Edwards teaches that there can be no true humility— no true self-understanding— without a creature's taking his true measure by God's loveliness, excellency, and holiness. The beauty (*pulchrum*) of God's goodness (*bonum*) is the transcendental measure, not any trivial distinctions among fellow worms of the dust. Moreover, a sense of the divine loveliness works humility; a sense of vileness, never. This sequence, or at least the logical priority, is important for Edwards. From love to God

<!-- p. 79 -->

in the heart comes humility, and among men every "answerable" behavior.

Concerning other virtues so far considered, the claim was that they are fruits of charity, or are its "tendency" or "effects." Concerning humility, Edwards makes another and quite different claim, namely, that charity and the exercises of love drawn forth by the gospel imply humility. He does not mean, of course, logical implication. It is of the utmost importance for us to ponder this word's meaning, even if it cannot be made sun-clear. For here it is that Edwards gives the reason for his astonishing assertion that if everything could be stated about the many works or fruits of humility, that statement "would in some way or other include the whole of our duty, both towards God and towards men."[^003-note172] Christian humility seems, therefore, to be that in which the Christian life summarily consists, as was said of charity in sermon one. What then, we must ask, is the relation of charity and humility? Can we say more than that humility is in some way or other more than a tendency or an effect of charity? The notion "implication" is Edwards' word at this point for the difference between humility and the other virtues.

Edwards explains his strong claim that charity and gospel works "imply" humility simply by saying that charity "implies it as an *essential qualification*"; not only is it among love's effects. "True divine love is an humble love," he writes, it is "not true divine love" if it is "not an humble love."[^003-note173] He writes humility into the "essential" meaning of divine love. Charity enfolds humility in a way that goes to the essence of each, even more than the interpenetration of long-suffering and kindness. One has not said all that needs to be said about the nature and meaning of Christian love until one has brought humility as a component into the heart of the matter. Humility as an essential qualification of charity is one and the same work of the Spirit, just as love to God and to men are not two gifts of the Spirit but one. In this sense, a humble love is the sum of all virtues. The reason humility lies deep in the heart of charity is that both are immediate responses to the loveliness of God, to his moral excellency.

Of course, charity still tends to produce humility. In the case of humility, however, *implies* and *tends* or *causes* are not clearly distinguished in Edwards' exposition. "If the knowledge of God as lovely causes humility," he writes, "then a respect to God as lovely implies humility." Seeing therefore that "a sense of God's loveliness... works humility, hence

<!-- p. 80 -->

we may learn that divine love implies humility."[^003-note174] Thus Edwards seems to infer from the tendency of God's loveliness to cause humility that it can be said of the *nature* of the virtue that it is implied by divine love. We could go so far as to say that divine love and humility co-imply each other in that the same Spirit works both in the heart, and one cannot be what it is without the other. A love that is not humble is, by that negation, no true love, not essentially a virtuous love.

The drift of Edwards' subsequent interpretation of 1 Corinthians 13 will be to enlarge upon this notion of "implication" and to amplify its role, both in sermon twelve on the "concatenation" of all Christian graces, and in the sermon on heaven. "Implication" also proved crucial, along with "fullness" and "participation," in the argument that God's end in creation was "but one."[^003-note175] Here then— in a virtue's "essential qualification" of another virtue— is another moral progression corresponding to the story line of redemption.

Sermons on the next three texts— "Seeketh not her own," "Is not easily provoked," and "Thinketh no evil"— have in common a special concern with moral relations among persons. Left behind are the virtues of moral agents undergoing injuries or doing good and virtues respecting the goods or happiness possessed by ourselves or by others. Left behind are the more personal virtues. The focus of attention is now upon fruits of charity that are qualities inhering in men's attitudes toward one another. Edwards moves now to social virtues, to virtues of interpersonal relations. The move may be slight, but it is significant. While envy, for example, could wax so strong as to take the form of bitterness and hatred toward the *person* whose good or prosperity one envied, the vices brought

<!-- p. 81 -->

now into consideration begin with the person, or with the agent's relation to persons. Before, even in pride and humility, the comparison focused on good *belonging* to oneself or another. Now, the vices of selfishness, anger, and censoriousness are directed upon persons themselves.

We can pass by the seventh sermon (on selfishness) since love of one's own happiness and other-love has already been considered as a theme running through all three ethical writings. We come then to the eighth and ninth sermons on an angry spirit and on a censorious spirit. It is, of course, a fruit of charity to mortify each of this pair of vices directly and immediately. But there is more to be said about the fabric of the virtues of love Edwards is weaving. At the beginning of the sermon on an angry spirit Edwards groups this with censoriousness and looks upon the pair from the viewpoint of his two previous sermons. These vices of anger and censoriousness, he says, are "commonly the fruit of pride and covetousness." "Covetousness" is now his word for a selfish spirit that blocks out all virtuous other-love. The word is appropriate, for Edwards means that a principle of sin in the heart disposes us to covetousness seeking our happiness in only our own. Selfishness (covetousness) joins pride as "fountains" of an angry spirit and a censorious spirit. Indeed, "those two lusts of pride and covetousness... are, as it were, two *cardinal vices* or fountains of sin and wickedness in the heart."[^003-note176] As vices they have further fruits. So humility and uncovetous other-love are cardinal virtues that mediate charity's effects throughout the moral life by mortifying anger and censoriousness, which charity also works to mortify directly and immediately.

Edwards' sermon series is extraordinary as a phenomenological account of moral matters. The sermon on anger, in addition, indicates its remarkable moral psychology. I pick out only one point from among the many ways in which Edwards sorts out suitable anger from unsuitable anger. The anger that is contrary to a Christian spirit is anger without any end in view. Men who permit such anger to arise continue in it "without any consideration. Reason has no hand in the business. Their passions go before their reason." Such anger is "not the anger of men but of beasts. It is a kind of beastly fury, rather than any affection of a rational creature."[^003-note177] This sort of anger can be compared to *ire*, the name passion of the group Aquinas called *irascible*. *Ire* alone among them is

<!-- p. 82 -->

paired with no opposite passion toward good; even in respect to evil it spins on the spot and has no outcome.[^003-note178]

Here it is plain that Edwards means to say that the distinguishing fruits of love mix with natural morality— at least negatively. "If love be in exercise," he writes, "it will tend to keep men's irascible passions down in subjection, so that reason and love may have the regulation of them, and will prevent their being in inordinate degree, or of long continuance."[^003-note179] Evidently Edwards believed that charity infused in the heart reaches and influences the passions in such fashion that men can attain the ends reason proposes.

Take *ire*, or continuing in anger to no end, and join it with envy, which is a comparative spirit directed not only to those who are superior to us in good or possessions but also to those near us or below us who may yet be our rivals— envy leading even to bitter hatred toward their persons. Or join irrational anger with censoriousness in the next sermon. This was a hellish way to live, according to Edwards. My words are carefully chosen in saying this. For there is a coda in Edwards' peroration on "Heaven Is a World of Love," in which Edwards depicts hell as no "world"— no society— at all.[^003-note180] As heaven is a world in which creatures are united in love to one another in their love to God, so hell is a place where men are given up to their hatred of themselves and of one another in common but entirely divisive hatred of God. There is no uniting love there. They hate themselves and they hate one another. They torment themselves and they torment one another. Envy raised to the height of bitterness toward every other soul, censoriousness of everyone else and anger so undue as to have no telos in view, and so no finis, is their permanent plight.

The Doctrine of the ninth sermon defines a censorious spirit as "a disposition uncharitably to judge others." It consists in a disposition to think and judge evil of others with respect to three things: their state (saved or unsaved), their qualities, and their actions. My comment on this slender sermon can be brief, beginning with a summary of the tapestry of virtues Edwards has been weaving. Pride tends to selfishness; pride and selfishness (or lack of other-love) together tend to an angry spirit. So with judging uncharitably: "forwardness to judge and censure others shows a proud disposition"; pride tends to ill will to persons; "where hatred and ill spirit against others most prevail, there a censorious spirit

<!-- p. 83 -->

does most prevail."[^003-note181] Divine love in the heart mortifies censoriousness through this chain, and also directly. Thus, charity mortifies a censorious spirit mediately and immediately. Humility— the opposite of pride— does so also.

The position taken concerning judging others' "states" is a moderate one. "All positiveness in an affair of this nature seems to be without warrant from the Word of God. God seems to have reserved the positive determination of men's state in his own mind, as the only searcher of the heart, and trier of the reins of the children of men."[^003-note182] The same is not true of actions: "Some men's actions give such clear evidence of the badness of their intentions that it is no judging the *secrets* of the heart to judge that their designs and ends are naught. Therefore all judging ill," Edwards concludes, "of others' state, or qualities, or actions, is not an uncharitable censoriousness."[^003-note183] These statements show in the case of notably wicked actions a willingness to move from condemnation to action to censoring dispositions— and states (?). Issues such as these were to be involved in the church-covenant controversy that occasioned Edwards' dismissal from the church in Northampton.

Students of Edwards will want to note the tension in this sermon between knowing persons' qualities and states by their fruits and reserving to God the judgment infallibly concerning those states of soul. There is the same tension between this sermon and the next on holy practices, and by way of emphasis throughout Edwards' writings. Among the marks or signs of gracious affections, in general, the "certainter" the sign the less public it is. Nevertheless, greatest stress on openness to human judgment is to be found in the Twelfth Sign. Having shown that Christian practice is "a great and distinguishing sign," Edwards writes, "I may go further, and assert, that it is the *chief of all* the signs of grace, both as evidence of the sincerity of professors *unto others*, and also *to their own consciences*."[^003-note184] Edwards returned to this worrisome problem ten years later than the present sermon, preaching in 1748 again on 1 Corinthians 13:8–13.[^003-note185]

<!-- p. 84 -->

By the text of the tenth sermon, "Rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth," Edwards understands the Apostle to say in effect, "I have mentioned many excellent things to which charity has a tendency, and shown how it is contrary to many ill things; but I need not go on to multiply particulars, for in short charity is contrary to everything in life and practice which is bad, and tends to everything which is good."[^003-note186] Edwards defends his interpretation by citing the expression in 3 John 3: "thou walkest in the truth." Later on he reinforces this understanding by citation of other scriptures, including several from St. Paul. One example is the reference in Romans 2:8 to those who "do not obey the truth but obey unrighteousness." Later, he also supports his interpretation of this text by drawing attention to the word "know" in the Bible as meaning practical as opposed to speculative knowledge. "He who knows God sees him to be worthy to be obeyed."[^003-note187] So rejoicing in the truth and knowing God are not dormant but vital principles in the heart tending to every excellent behavior.

Edwards' proofs in this sermon are from the active nature of grace and of "particular graces." While the immediate "foundation" of grace is in the understanding, its immediate "seat" is in the will; and "all the executive powers of... man, whether of body or mind, are subject to the faculty of the will."[^003-note188] Later Edwards explains that, by locating the immediate "foundation" of grace in the understanding, he means in a conviction of the understanding; and conviction tends to practice. By conviction

<!-- p. 85 -->

he means the understanding's judgment that some "great things" are real and true. Conviction, then, cannot fail to move men and much alter their behavior.[^003-note189] So men's movement to love and to holy practices by the "seat" of grace in the will is, as it were, already under way in the certain conviction of the truth of the gospel in men's understanding of it, i.e., their "knowledge" of it.

The same conclusion follows from a correct understanding of "principle." "If grace be a principle," Edwards asks, "of what is it a principle but of action? Principles and acts are correlates... Thus the meaning of a principle of life is a principle of life which acts... So by a principle of sin is meant a principle whence flow acts of sin... And a principle of love is a principle whence flow acts of love. So when we say a principle of grace we mean a principle whence flow gracious actions... So it is absurd to talk of a principle that it does not tend to practice."[^003-note190]

Edwards' stress on practice is not surprising. More notable is the fact that he unhesitatingly spoke of "infused grace";[^003-note191] and throughout the charity sermons, and elsewhere in his writings, exhibited his belief that infused grace and love become qualities of the soul issuing in other moral qualities or dispositions and in holy practices. He speaks of infused love

<!-- p. 86 -->

and infused grace and infused virtues actually altering the quality of human hearts and life.[^003-note192]

This tenth sermon is transitional to the work of the Spirit imparting love that goes out primarily to God. So it seems appropriate that Edwards again discusses humility as a Christian virtue. While humility is only one of twelve particular graces that Edwards invokes to show that grace leads to holy practices, he again accords it a special place, as he did when this disposition was first viewed primarily as a source of virtuous behavior among men. He notes that the particular grace of humility is "abundantly recommended and insisted on in Scripture, and seems often to be spoken of as most distinguishing of true Christian virtue from that which is counterfeit."[^003-note193] Here— and in what was said about humble love in sermon six— humility rivals charity in the heart as that which disposes to every virtue and right action. Humility is an "essential qualification" of charity, even as pride is an essential quality of the heart that lacks love. But pride is not love's opposite; that title is reserved for hatred alone. In both contexts, Edwards' thought can also be rendered by saying that humility is a fruit or effect of love that begets or causes other fruits or virtues, even as pride is a vice that begets or causes other vices as well.

Holy practice, however, is his present theme. If a proud and scornful spirit has been mortified, and "humility implanted in his heart in the room of it, surely there will be an alteration in the carriage and practice; for humility of heart is a principle which has as much tendency to practice as pride of heart has."[^003-note194] Notice that in these words Edwards calls pride and humility principles of action. The same was said of divine love in the heart and, from this sermon on, will be said of grace in the heart. The same is not said so plainly of other particular graces.

Not too much should be made of the fact that of the twelve particular graces the word *principle* is used only of humility. For all are principles that must be principles of action. Edwards calls his discussion of these graces "an induction of practice." These graces are: a true and saving faith in Jesus Christ, the conviction of the understanding and judgment that is in saving faith, the act of will that is within justifying faith, true trust in God, true love to God, true and saving repentance, true humility, true fear of God, a spirit of thankfulness and praise of God, heavenly-mindedness, a spirit of Christian love to men, and a true and gracious

<!-- p. 87 -->

hope. Notice that love to God and love to men are particular graces; the first sermon's "goings out" of divine love in the heart toward God and toward men are here listed as different loves. Also, the wording of this list entails— and Edwards says as much— that there are "false faith," "false trust," "false hope." That faith which is saving is to be distinguished from faith that is "common,"[^003-note195] a true and gracious hope from its counterfeit. And— not mentioned in this sermon— legal humiliation is not the same as saving humility; there are a false fear of God, a sorrow for sin that is not saving repentance, a drivenness from the world that is not heavenly-mindedness.

More important to note is that we are moving along the story line of redemption toward the sermon on the concatenation of all Christian graces. Here holy practices are the tendency and effect of these graces or virtuous dispositions, as these presumably are the effects of the Spirit's working divine love in the heart. In addition to that, in the later, twelfth sermon the particular graces imply and are essential qualifications of one another. This has been said so far of only humility and charity. Simply reading Edwards' induction of practice, however, is enough to convey that these graces are qualities of heart that qualify one another; and that he has all but stated the concatenation or unity of the virtues as the possessor of them becomes "a perfect man" (Ephesians 4:13). And notice this is in a sermon that mainly summarizes— instead of continuing to itemize— virtues primarily directed to neighbors, and no more than points to greater absorption of moral life into love to God.

In proving that the particular grace of true love to God leads to practice, Edwards also appeals to natural loves as principles of action. "Love to creature objects, we see, does powerfully influence men in their actions and practice. Yea, what is it, which chiefly keeps the world of mankind in action from day to day, and from year to year, but love of some kind or other." Among the loves that make the world go round (love of money, honor), Edwards cites the love of friendship to show that "reason teaches that a man's actions are the most proper trial and evidence of his love." Thus, "reason... teaches all mankind that the most proper evidence of his being a real and hearty friend, as he professes, is his appearing a friend in his deeds." Edwards goes on to say— and this is worth more than a moment's thought— that a person's natural love of friendship will go so far as "to *suffer* in his private interest to do him a *kindness*."[^003-note196] With the introduction of these latter words, the reader should

<!-- p. 88 -->

be reminded of the sermon on "Long-Suffering and Kindness" and of the chapter in *True Virtue* on the instinctual kind affections. The convergence of divine love and the natural affection of friendship in long-suffering and kindness must mean that the same virtues may arise from either source or from both mixed together. This is the analysis of Christian moral life in the posthumously published dissertation, but generally not of *Charity*, where Edwards concentrated on showing the virtues to be specifications of charity. But here we have both kindness and long-suffering as natural and as infused virtues; and of the two, kindness surely lasts longer than this life of trial and tribulation. What else could be Edwards' name for the "answerable behavior" of the saints in heaven? So the love of friendship among "natural" persons is to be perfected and assumed into truly virtuous love.

Edwards' use of examples from ordinary morality in the charity sermons serves mainly to prove some point to be reasonable to believe, or for argument in the form of how much more so Christians ought to be or do. He uses natural loves as examples of the reasonableness of Christian practice from true love, sometimes as a positive measure of the sacrificial devotion to which neighbor-love leads. An exception to this is a final point worth noting in sermon ten, which now concerns a cluster of graces that surely are qualities of humility set over against natural or "pagan" morality. This may not be enough to show that Edwards' two treatments (so far) of humility replicates something of the larger movement through the chapter of moral progress in the history of the kingdom of Christ building up in the soul; but that, too, is worth pondering.

A possible movement in the nature of humility from the first table of love in transition to the second table— from humility among men to humility primarily before God— can be glimpsed by recalling Edwards' earlier praise of pagans who were eminent in virtue. No sharp contrast was drawn between their virtuous love of earthly causes and Christian virtues. Now, however, in the transitional tenth sermon, the eminence of pagan nobility is seen in a different light. We now see Christian humility stressed as a virtue in contrast to eminent natural virtues. Thus humility is elevated above the context in which Edwards formerly appealed to admirable natural virtue as an analogue to true love's fruits. Christian practices now are sharply distinguished from heathen, i.e., natural, morality. A chief component of this contrast is a "humble, meek, and self-denying, self-renouncing, and even heavenly walk and behavior." Measured by this, natural virtues come under a different assessment.

<!-- p. 89 -->

Many heathens were very eminent for many moral virtues, and wrote excellently of them; as of justice, and of generosity, and of fortitude and others. But they were far from a Christian poverty of spirit, and lowliness of mind; they sought their own glory, and gloried exceedingly in their virtue, and said nothing about such a walk as the gospel commands, a walking in self-emptiness, poverty of spirit, self-diffidence, self-renunciation. And they said little of meekness, and did not own love of enemies, and forgiveness to be any virtue. Therefore, these peculiarly Christian virtues are called Christian virtues by way of eminence.

Ask yourselves, Edwards exhorted his congregation, "if you are essentially distinguished and different in your spirit from the *mere moralist*, or the heathen sage or philosopher," whether you have "a spirit of special esteem for and delight in these virtues that do especially belong to the gospel."[^003-note197] There is a distinctive Christian morality, and there is a natural morality that Edwards did not despise by calling it heathen. So while grace in the heart disposes to every virtue and holy practice, there is a distinction in eminence to be drawn, for example, between justice, and humility or forgiveness. Some thinkers have developed and extended this distinction under the names of the theological and the natural virtues. By such a classification, humility was for Edwards a theological virtue, along with faith, hope, and charity. He was prevented from this hierarchical and more static view of the elevation and perfection of moral life by his view of moral progress within the narrative of the kingdom building up in the soul and among men.

Two triumphal sermons remain to be considered. "Believeth all things, hopeth all things" is the text of Edwards' twelfth sermon. A frequent misunderstanding (according to Edwards) is that by these words the Apostle meant that "charity disposes men to believe the best and hope the best of our neighbors in all cases." But he had done with that in the words "Thinketh no evil" (sermon nine). Just as the preceding words in the present verse, "Beareth all things," mean the grace to suffer all things in the way of duty to Christ (and not suffering long the ills done to us by our neighbors), so believing and hoping all things are fruits of charity "quite of another kind." And afterward the Apostle begins to speak of faith, hope, and charity— those "three great and principal graces of the gospel, which have God and Christ as their main and immediate object"— not our neighbors.[^003-note198]

<!-- p. 90 -->

This introduction hardly prepares the reader for Edwards' stunning development of the Doctrine, "There is a concatenation of the graces of Christianity." He means more than that the Christian virtues hang one from another as links in a chain, or that they are interlinked in some other fashion. The reader should let Edwards' forceful rhetorical reiteration of the expression "concatenated together"[^003-note199] make room for whatever meaning he puts into it. For no image of merely extrinsic connections can begin to convey the unity in plurality that this sermon teaches is the destiny of Christian moral life. And we need also to remember that in this sermon Edwards is still exhibiting Christian moral life actualized at a point in time within the story of redemption when, in his view, the church is still under tribulation. The next sermon has yet to treat of charity enduring under all things, all opposition that may be brought against it in this life; after that comes his sermon on "Charity never faileth" in heaven when all opposition has ceased. Still, in this sermon on "Christian Graces Concatenated Together," Edwards presents an extraordinary account of the concentration of the virtues, even during the church's militancy against opposition, in a life being made *wholly new*, and made *unifiedly* wholly new.[^003-note200]

The six "reasons"[^003-note201] for the doctrine are noteworthy in that as a group they exhibit Edwards' master image of "from Alpha to Omega." This metaphor for cause/end is also reproduced in one or more of them. But we are further along the story line of the work of redemption. The graces are more closely woven than when we began with the first fruits of charity flowing out directly and immediately to our neighbors. From the beginning there was a certain unity among various virtues because they were not distinguished as excellencies of various faculties of the soul, but rather as specifications of charity and of the answerable will and loves of unitary moral agents. This ground of unity of the virtues Edwards now expresses to the highest degree in terms of redemptive grace that concatenates them all together— both the Christian virtues that parallel natural virtues and those that do not. Divine love believing and hoping all things of God and Christ reaches back and concatenates together all the fruits of charity in a moral life made unifiedly wholly new. The unity of Christian life also refers to far more than the three theological virtues— faith, hope, and charity— to which the Apostle turns next.

<!-- p. 91 -->

By "concatenated together" Edwards means three things. All graces and virtuous dispositions (1) "go together, so that where there is one, there are all; and when one is wanting, all are wanting." But there is "not only a conjunction" among them. In addition (2) there is a "mutual dependence," a causal relation among them; one "promotes" the other. (3) "One is, in some respects, *implied* in the very nature of the other." One is "*essential to another, and belongs to the essence of it*."[^003-note202]

Essential implication is the interior meaning of concatenated together. This was said before of charity and humility. A sort of implication was also suggested in the transitional sermon by naming a number of graces or dispositions that are associated with or aspects of humility, and by listing that cardinal virtue alongside eleven other, lively particular graces that issue in practice. Edwards now states clearly and systematically that all the different graces of Christianity are *essential* to one another as qualities. This is true not only of faith, hope, love, and humility in the various combinations Edwards celebrates. Repentance and conversion, thankfulness and reverence, Christian patience and thankfulness are brought into the interchanges of divine love. They all are motions of faith, hope, and love, since each has God and Christ directly and immediately as object. So also is heavenly-mindedness moved by God's loveliness and excellency, as distinct from a weanedness from the world born of life's miseries. And each of the usually named theological virtues has these other essential ingredients in it (e.g., thankfulness), even as all mutually promote one another.

Not only so. The same is true of the virtues that have our neighbors directly and immediately in view (which latter certainly overlap with virtues in common or natural morality). Thus "a true love to God tends to love to men, who have the image of God," and the reverse: "love to the image cherishes love to the original."[^003-note203] Christian love to men is "a kind of mediate exercise of love to Christ." And "*that justice* and *truth* towards men which are truly Christian graces *have love in them*, and it is *essential* to them."[^003-note204] Natural virtues are also subsumed here. Edwards' fullest systematic account of principles of common or natural morality, and their fruits, that are admirable is in *True Virtue*. But in the sermon series and here in his twelfth sermon we have the fullest account of the abbreviated suggestion in *True Virtue*, that graces mix with those natural principles[^003-note205] to direct, elevate, and perfect them in a moral life made new

<!-- p. 92 -->

unifiedly. Edwards sums this up in his use of self-examination, which is one long exhortation to his congregation that they prepare their hearts for the unity in the manifoldness of Christian virtues. Try one by the other quality or character, is his repeated plea, for if one grace is wanting, nothing has begun to be made new. Remember that all vices are mortified together, or none are. As with the first birth, if any part is missing, there is a monster of a man.[^003-note206] In conclusion: be not "like a cake [not turned], which is half baked, half raw."[^003-note207]

Before coming to Edwards' final exultation concerning God and the saints glorified together in heaven, there are two additional matters from sermon fourteen that need noting here, and which manifest the dramatic logic in his placing intervening sermons (two steps, as it were, in progress in the durability of divine love to its perfection in indefectibility) between "concatenated together" and "glorified together."

The first could pass entirely unnoticed, yet is not without some significance. In the text explication of the preceding sermon, Edwards had just repeated once again the line of demarcation drawn across the series at the tenth sermon on holy practice, as the Apostle's ceasing abruptly from itemizing fruits of charity primarily respecting our neighbors. Then, preaching his penultimate sermon— on things that shall have passed away when love alone lasts eternally in the redeemed community— he reached back to make connection with ver. 1 Corinthians 13:1–3 and with his second sermon on the extraordinary gifts that have long since passed away.[^003-note208] This move traverses ver. 1 Corinthians 13:4–7 and, subordinately, has the effect of

<!-- p. 93 -->

grouping these verses (formerly split apart at ver. 1 Corinthians 13:6) together into one unitary account of Christian morality in this life. Looking back on the church's pilgrimage, individually and collectively, every virtuous disposition is looked on as belonging to one continuous movement toward the ultimate end for which God created the world, without division into primarily this or primarily that respect.[^003-note209] So, I suggest, holy practice respects not only our fellow creatures in this life. The saints above (being Puritans) are engaged in all manner of behaviors answerable one to another; they are not engaged simply in common contemplation and vision of God. There is then no great inconsistency in the shift of holy practice from the midpoint of the sermon series to its location as the final Twelfth Sign in *Affections*.

The second matter is more substantive for Edwards' theological ethics. From the beginning of the sermon series, the movement has been from God manward and returning to him. This is Edwards' master image or root metaphor. Divine love is a supernatural principle implanted in the heart. The ordinary saving gifts of the Spirit are qualities "inherent in the subject, making men's hearts and natures excellent." The Spirit "imparts himself to the soul in his own holy nature," "an indwelling vital principle in the soul."[^003-note210] So Edwards used the term *infused* of divine love and all other graces. Thus the movement manward goes to the bottom of our being, there to effect a "turning." And in the movement through the sermons of return to God, who graces broken and fragmented men and their communities, we have traced the increasing durability (the *virtus*) of the virtuous against all opposition.

What now happens when we come to love's everlastingness in heaven? It seems to me that now Edwards' language is that of atonement accomplished in finality, the covenant of redemption once enacted now complete for all eternity. The "purchase" has been paid. The great promise the Father made to the Son to make him Head of a redeemed people is not now looked on as future in any of its effects. So the great fruit of the Spirit is now looked on as everlastingly "communicated" to the church.

<!-- p. 94 -->

The Spirit indwelling in men becomes a "proper right." To divine love in the heart the saints have "sure title." Theirs is a "sure covenant" by which the Spirit is "made over" to believers, not only communicated in his own proper nature to them. Concerning saving grace, this implies "the continuance of it forever." A most telling expression of the indefectibility of that great gift in Edwards' penultimate sermon is: "Christ is become *theirs*, and therefore his fullness is *theirs*, his Spirit is *theirs*, the Spirit of Christ is their purchased and promised *possession*."[^003-note211]

Throughout the series, among people not yet made wholly new, the conflict has been between "other-love derived to them" from the self's love to self and "other-love derived to us" from our first being united with them in true affection as a specifying principle (working conjunctively with persons' general love of their own happiness). Now that struggle is over. In the description of the society of heaven in Edwards' final sermon, there are echoes of finding or placing our happiness in others, as Christ placed his glory in ours. But a most telling expression of the everlastingness of the end to which uniting love has come is Edwards' ringing rhetorical changes on "theirs." The language of the final sermon is that we have *propriety* in one another, belong to each other, are each other's *own*. All the saints are our possession, their happiness is ours, ours is theirs, even as Christ is become ours and theirs forever.

The fourteenth sermon's argument, then, is this: If there is in this life any quality inhering in the souls of men that endures under all opposition (sermon thirteen), that surely would be a senseless quality if it had exercise only against this— worldly opposition. Edwards' co-inhering argument for the perseverance of the saints in this life (their preservation) need only read the proposition just stated in the reverse direction: If it is true that "charity never faileth," as the Apostle testifies, then surely (looking back on earth) that same charity must endure against all opposition that can be brought against it in this life no less than it has strength to meet the demands of Christ in the way of duty and to suffer long and with kindness the ills that other persons do to us.

Suppose the saints might not persevere. Suppose grace in the heart could be overthrown. Then God might still be imagined to be engaged in some other sort of redemption. Generation after generation of men might be born to be reborn. As the Spirit works divine love in the hearts of some persons in every generation, others fall away. For we are supposing that there is only a fragile grace and love in their hearts. God could still be imagined to bring a people of his to the end of time. This could be

<!-- p. 95 -->

so if God is imagined to be constantly mending the "broken links as well as he can, and be rectifying his disjointed frame and [the] disordered movements"[^003-note212] of this church in every generation. As some fall out, others are graced and brought into some sort of continuing story of redemption. But then there would be nothing indefectible indwelling among men. There would be no surety that divine love lasts eternally. God's end in creation, providence, and redemption would not be inherently sure, but only contingently so (because he is powerfully good at mending fences). "[I]t must be so that there must be some way of influence, and some kind of fruit of the Spirit, which is unfailing and everlasting."[^003-note213] Why must this be so? Because otherwise, creation would be end-less, or without end, redemption would be without *its* end, without an end in character with the story of it, without any end that God has, in the course of it, disclosed to the minds of men to be his purpose. Such suppositions were for Edwards suppositions contrary to reality. He never supposed that *nothing* of what men now have indwelling in their hearts has a durability that participates in God's own eternal purpose.

Not only is the preservation of the saints assured, as Adam's righteousness was not. Also their "holiness or spiritual image of God" may be vastly more perfect, by virtue of God's further manifestations of his loveliness and benefits, than was Adam's in innocency.

> Adam's perfection in holiness did not render utterly impossible that he should love God more, let God make further manifestations of himself [whenever] he would, or whatever further obligations he might receive from God. 'Tis probable that some Christians have had higher exercises of love to God than ever our first parents had, and yet were exceeding far from sinless perfection which they had. The occasion we have to love God is now infinitely greater than that which they had. 'Tis probable that some Christians have had higher spiritual joys than ever Adam had.[^003-note214]

"Heaven Is a World of Love" must be read aloud to be appreciated. The reader may wish to do just that at this point. If commentary must intervene, the following may be of some help.

I begin with several questions, all arising from the problem of how to understand Edwards' striking statement that the communication of divine

<!-- p. 96 -->

love "shall be, as it were, the *only* gift or fruit of the Spirit, as being the most perfect and glorious, and which being brought to perfection *renders others*, which God was wont to communicate to his church on earth, *needless*."[^003-note215] That suggest, that the perfection of the righteous is a monadic unity, love alone remaining in glory. The question this raises is how to conceive the unity of the virtues in perfection. Moreover, on its face, the statement sharply divides this world from the next, rendering needless many fruits of charity so far considered. Finally, what of faith and hope if only charity lasts eternally?

Monadic unity cannot be Edwards' meaning, for "one alone cannot be beautiful,"[^003-note216] in God, in heaven, or on earth. "One alone, without any reference to any more, cannot be excellent; for in such a case there can be no manner of relation no way, and therefore, no such thing as consent."[^003-note217] This suggests— and the final sermon in its entirety confirms— that love is the only gift or fruit of the Spirit in heaven in the sense that all fruits, leaving aside those needed under trial and opposition, are gathered up perfectly concatenated together. The unity of the virtues in the church brought to "mature manhood" individually and collectively at which we have now arrived ought, perhaps, to be spoken of as their perfect "harmony." The singing of God's praise is heaven's delight; and unless the hearts of all heaven's hosts are to be open to one another's direct view, how they were to hear one another over such great distances, through what "medium," and by what faculties, so as to join chorus together, was a problem Edwards more than once addressed in his notebooks.[^003-note218] The secondary beauty of music was "some image" of the excellency

<!-- p. 97 -->

of heavenly society. Best of all, we need to keep in mind that the divine trinity was Edwards' paradigm.

Heaven does not consist in undifferentiated divine love that has left behind the virtues conceptually depicted throughout Edwards' exegesis of 1 Corinthians 13. Nor is heaven only the abiding place of "faith, hope and charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity." All virtuous dispositions are subsumed in charity, elevated and perfected with it as graces that participate *essentially* together. Not only humility (from the first table of love) but also justice and truth (i.e., all holy practices) are assumed into Edwards' final paradigm of the perfection of creatures. In the society of heaven, all fruits of charity in heart and life— one work of one and the same Spirit— never fail. What fails is only the respect in which Christian dispositions and behaviors were determined by the church's state of militancy against opposition and when Christians were beset by temptation.

Some virtues are patently earthbound. These are left behind with earth's trials and tribulations, for example, long-suffering. But not its kindred virtue, cheerfulness and kindness to others. Bearing all things in the way of duty to Christ, rejoicing not in iniquity, and enduring under all opposition are also virtuous dispositions that have no business in heaven, because the occasion for them has ceased. But only the occasions are removed; human moral agents in heaven have in perfection still the dispositions tested in this life. So cheerfully doing good to others (which was the kindred spirit of long-suffering in face of injuries done to us), envying not, grudging not, vaunting not oneself, not behaving oneself unseemly, thinking no evil, rejoicing in the truth (all holy practices), believing all things, hoping all things are surely virtuous dispositions that are subsumed and perfected (actualized) in the divine love that alone lasts eternally. The sermon series exhibits all these as graces concatenated together even in this life.

The crux of the matter is that for Edwards heaven will be a world in which there remain comparisons that shall last eternally, but there will

<!-- p. 98 -->

be no comparative spirit in that perfect society. Doubtless John, the beloved disciple, and the apostle Paul shall have precedence over all other saints in their discernment of the inexhaustible riches of God and in the perfection of their love of God and Christ. But everyone's love shall be "perfect in its kind," with a "perfection... proper to their nature," "commensurate with the capacities of their natures."[^003-note219] Heaven is a world of love that does not require egalitarianism as the precondition of its peace.[^003-note220]

"All that whole society rejoice in each other's happiness." Where love is perfect, "the greater the prosperity of the beloved is, the more is the lover pleased and delighted. For the prosperity of the beloved is, as it were, the food of love; and therefore the greater that prosperity is [in those above us], the more richly is love feasted" with delight and complacence in the moral beauty of another. Love is "in proportion to the perfection and amiableness of the objects beloved." So those who are "highest in glory," "highest in holiness," shall be most beloved by all the saints. The saints of whatever rank shall "love those most who are most holy, and so they will all rejoice in it that they are most happy. And it will be a damp to none of the saints to see them who have higher degrees of holiness and likeness to God to be more loved than themselves; for all shall have as much love as they desire, and as great manifestations of love

<!-- p. 99 -->

as they can bear."[^003-note221] So heaven will be a world of love in which envy of those above or near to us or those below us who may yet threaten us will have no place. But charity's contrariety to an envious spirit (a fruit in this life) will be fulfilled.

Likewise there will be no pride there. For those angels, apostles, or saints above us in holiness will also be superior in humility; "for their superior humility is part of their superior holiness." "As some will have greater degrees of divine knowledge than others, will have larger capacities to see more of the divine perfections, so they will see more of their own comparative littleness and nothingness, and therefore will be lowest abased in humility."[^003-note222] This final sermon is replete with vigorous terms and imagery stripping heaven of any blemishes people had in this life. Like all other objects in heaven, the saints are "all over lovely"; nothing vile or deformed infests heaven. Consistent with sermon six, however, the humility of even the superior saints must consist in both natural meanness before God's greatness and their comparative moral meanness before God's goodness and excellency fully revealed to them. The more sight and sense of God's glory, the more humble shall the most holy be.

As in this life, the more holy the superior saints are in humble love to God, the more they will be humble among their fellow creatures. So charity still promotes love to others directly, and mediately through humility. Edwards at once states this further point. Those who are highest will have more of a spirit of love to others. These superior saints "will love those who are below them more than other saints of less capacity" may be able to love others. Persons lower in discernment and love of God's inexhaustible excellency, Edwards says, "will be most beloved of those who are highest in glory, and the superior in glory will be so far from slighting those who are inferior, that they will have more abundant love to them, greater degrees of love in proportion to their superior knowledge and happiness; the higher in glory, the more like Christ in this respect. So that they will love them more than those who are their equals."[^003-note223]

Why *more* than their equals? Because more like Christ. Here surely Edwards moves from humility (which as comparative meanness should not be ascribed to God or Christ) to condescension, his not grudging us: these were his more exact and appropriate terms. The superior saints will be "the more like Christ in this respect. So that they will love them

<!-- p. 100 -->

[the lowest of the inhabitants of heaven] more than those who are their equals."[^003-note224] The superior saints will share more of Christ's condescension and will therefore ungrudgingly love those of lesser capacity— those with lesser degrees of charity— more than their own equals, more than themselves. When Edwards expresses his point here about humility/ condescension/grudging not by saying that the superior saints will look upon the lesser "as themselves," the reader should recall the explanation of "Love one another as I have loved you" as the "unveiled" meaning of the "as thyself."[^003-note225] That earlier depiction in sermon seven of the Christian moral life *in via* is now fulfilled: the greater holiness of some saints in heaven is perfectly formed and directed by God's condescension and his love for the lowest. Therefore no one in heaven has reason for either envy or pride. Everyone there has all the love and happiness they can bear.

Earth's greatest need is satisfied. Here is Edwards on nature perfected: "Love there always meets with answerable returns of love. Love is always mutual, and the returns are always in due proportion. *Love always seeks this*. In proportion as any person is beloved, in that proportion his love is desired and prized."[^003-note226] His proof of this point for all saints who in their degree love Christ with inconceivable ardor of heart is that he will "open to their view the great fountain of love in his heart far beyond what they ever before saw." This undoubtedly means that the ardor of human hearts shall be fully satisfied by the love of God and Christ now poured forth to them. But then, not surprisingly, Edwards says that this "love of God to the saints *cannot properly be called returns of love*, because he loved *them first*."[^003-note227] It would, therefore, be impertinent for even St. John or St. Paul to claim that they receive from Christ love answerable or proportionate to their love to him, although they are fully satisfied and shall forever receive all the love they have capacity to receive.

Between them and other near saints there may be love answerable to love. Moreover it might be an answerable or proportionate love by which they are more beloved by saints of lesser degree. But we cannot understand the superior saints' fullness of love to everyone who is lesser in heaven without positing a transformation, perfection, and redirection of what Edwards means by the "answerable returns" of love. He says as much. "The nearer any saint is to him [Christ], the more he is like him in

<!-- p. 101 -->

this respect, the fuller his heart is of love"[^003-note228]— with "first love," with condescending love, with love that seeks but does not depend upon the answering love it elicits. If the love of God to the saints cannot properly be called the returns of love, then the more the love of superior saints is like that of Christ, the more their love for the lesser cannot properly be called the returns of love. Yet in heaven divine love has become mutual. The higher saints' answer is to the outpouring of the love of God to them, and this suffuses the storied mansions of heaven. The returns of love, familial and other natural loves, golden rule interchanges, and the "as thyself" have been transformed, redirected, and perfected to accord with "love one another as I have loved you." Thus divine love is the mother of all virtues in that she conceives within herself the acts of them all, as Aquinas said.

"Uniting consent" of being to being has attained its goal. "And so the saints shall be Christ's, for he has bought them with a price, and he shall be *theirs*; for he who gave himself *for* them, will have given himself *to* them."[^003-note229] To be related to one another is not enough; fiduciary loyalty is not enough. We might say, the returns of love perceived on earth to be wanted are not enough. To have "*propriety* one in another" is heaven's perfection.[^003-note230] Placing one's happiness in that of others is no longer a needed intention. Finding one's own happiness in others' happiness is in no way contingent. "Other-love derived to self" from first being joined in affection with them is now effortless. The self's love of its own happiness has come to its own when, in heaven, we shall be each others' *own*.

<!-- p. 102 -->

The established order of things is that the joy and happiness of all others *belong* to each and every sainted intelligent moral agent in perfect society.

Next Edwards introduces an essentially Augustinian point. The inhabitants of heaven "shall forever be continued in the perfect enjoyment of each other's love." They "shall be in no fear of any end of this happiness, nor shall they be in any fear or danger of any abatement of it." This "blessed circumstance"[^003-note231] of the enjoyment of happiness is Edwards' equivalent of Augustine's argument that the summum bonum must also be *immutabile*. The good that entirely satisfies the human heart must not merely be the highest of all goods in rank of perfection. It must also, Augustine believed, be "something which cannot be lost against the will. For no one," he reasoned, "can feel confident regarding a good which he knows can be taken from him, although he wishes to keep and cherish it. But if a man feels no confidence regarding the good which he enjoys, how can he be happy while in fear of losing it?"[^003-note232] Indeed, the higher the good the more sorrow, if it were a good that passes away, or a good we fear may pass away despite our heart's will and love of it. In heaven that sorrow is no more. Not only is the good itself eternal. There also shall be no abatement— Edwards adds— through weariness of will or cloyed enjoying faculties. Augustine's surety was in the immutable unchanging goodness of God. Edwards' surety was in the end of the work of redemption: Christ's enthronement as Head of his people made one and the marriage of the Lamb to his promised bride, the church. It is divine love that is the *summum bonum et immutabile— et commune*. In philosophical language, divine love is the *ens realissimum et bonum— et perfectum*. Both theologians agree: the most perfect would still be lacking unless it is also most real.

Last, we come to the question raised about the other "abiding" virtues, faith and hope. Are these among the gifts of the Spirit "God was wont to communicate to his church on earth," rendered "needless when love shall be, as it were, the only gift or fruit of the Spirit as being the most perfect"? Speaking of "the way to heaven" as "the way of love," Edwards' final sentence is: "And if ever you arrive at heaven, faith and love must be the wings which must carry you there."[^003-note233] An alert reader is likely to raise the question whether faith and *hope* are not the wings. Did the Andover copyist err when he wrote "love"? I think not. The word

<!-- p. 103 -->

"love" is entirely consistent with the thrust of this brief concluding paragraph on the way to heaven.[^003-note234] Moreover, there is no intimation of an abiding hope in this sermon.[^003-note235] To find a place for a hope that abides with love one has to turn to the perorations on progress in heaven in *End of Creation*.[^003-note236]

But what of an abiding faith? Apparently Edwards does not join those who hold that faith disappears in sight and hope in realization, while only charity lasts eternally. He does not use Dante's vision of faith and hope as two angels leading the soul— first one and then the other— into love's final union with God.[^003-note237] Edwards surely believed that faith as conviction of the reality of divine things shall be in perfect exercise in heaven. He also believed— though the sermon does not tell us this— in an assured hope of the soul's eternal progress. There may be, of course, a deceptive faith and hope and love that the saints leave behind with their

<!-- p. 104 -->

common ordinary gifts when they come to die, else Edwards could not have spoken of a false faith that fails, etc.[^003-note238]

These three theological virtues are subsumed in the same sort of concentrated unity in plurality as we have observed of every other Christian virtue. Commenting on 1 Corinthians 13 in his "Notes on the Bible," Edwards wrote that the three "cannot be properly three *distributively* distinct graces, or saving virtues, because charity or love is the sum of all saving virtue... Love is an ingredient in saving faith, and is the most essential thing in it, is its life and soul, and so it is in hope."[^003-note239]

*Note on the Texts*

CHARITY. The copy-text for this edition of the charity sermons is an early nineteenth-century copy of Edwards' sermon booklets, in the Andover collection.[^003-note240] This copy of Edwards' original sermons, which are now lost, consists of fifteen booklets, corresponding to the fifteen booklets in the series, numbered consecutively in the upper left-hand corner of the first page of each booklet. Only booklets three, five, and six do not have, written in the upper right-hand corner, the month and year in which, between April and October, 1738, Edwards preached the series. The booklets are composed of quarto size pages and have no covers. They are made of heavy paper with rough uncut edges, hand stitched with a coarse thread. Each booklet is paginated consecutively to the end of the sermon, whether one or more than one preaching occasion was needed to complete delivery of the sermon as a literary form. Thus the fifteen booklets correspond to the fifteen sermons, even though sermons

<!-- p. 105 -->

four, six, seven, ten, and fifteen required more than one preaching occasion to complete. The consecutive pagination of the fourth booklet confirms that Tryon erred in dividing the fourth sermon into two, thus producing sixteen "Lectures."

All this can be seen from the five columns below. These columns indicate respectively (1) the booklet/sermon, by Roman numerals; (2) the total number of pages filled by the scribe, in arabic numerals; (3) next, also in arabic numbers, the number of pages remaining blank in the booklet (I count as unused a page on which only one or a very few words are written, e.g., booklets/sermons seven and eleven); (4) the number of preaching occasions, if more than one, i.e., "two" or "three"; and (5) the month in which the sermon was preached.

Specific details concerning the Andover copy are provided in my notes to the charity sermons. These footnotes, needed to inform the reader concerning my reconstruction of the text, are cumulatively overwhelming evidence in support of the choice of the Andover copy over Tryon Edwards' edition as the copy-text for the present volume. Any passage of only a few lines length is sufficient to show that the copy is obviously Edwardsean, in contrast to the "improvements" Tryon Edwards freely introduced. Consider two brief passages in parallel:

<!-- p. 106 -->

| *Edited text of Andover copy* | *Tryon Edwards' edition* |
| (6) Humility will tend to prevent a leveling behavior. They who are | Humility will further tend *to prevent a leveling behavior*. Some persons |
| under the influence of a humble spirit will not be opposite to giving to others the honor which is due them. They will be willing that their superiors should be known and acknowledged in their place, and it will not seem hard to them. [*Charity*, p. 242.] | are always ready to level those above them down to themselves, while they are never willing to level those below them up to their own position. But he that is under the influence of humility will avoid both extremes. On the one hand... and on the other hand, he will be willing that his superiors should be known and acknowledged in their place, and have rendered to them all the honors that are their due. [p. 206] |
| He [the Apostle] had been reckoning over various carriages towards our neighbor to which charity tended; but not to proceed to multiply any more instances, the Apostle sums up all in the last verse in words importing that charity rejoices in no bad carriage or behavior, but in all | He [the Apostle] had been rehearsing over the various points of good conduct toward our neighbor which charity tends to, |
| good ones. And having thus summed up things of that nature, he seems now to proceed to something else of another nature, and not to mention the same things over again in other words. [*Charity*, pp. 313–14] | and having summed up these in the above expression, he now seems to proceed to traits of another nature, and not to be repeating the same things over in other words, [p. 362] |

One example of a longer passage will suffice, in this instance showing Tryon Edwards' extreme compression of the exposition that, it seems clear, was behind the copy. The example is from the second "use" in the Application of sermon two on "Love More Excellent Than Extraordinary Gifts of the Spirit," pp. 168–70. Obviously, Tryon in the nineteenth century had less interest in Edwards' long analysis of the extraordinary manifestations that are "no certain sign of grace, nor anything saving, though it were real."
