<!-- p. 110 -->

Another instance of Tryon's abbreviation of Andover (or rather of the sermon booklet he edited) was his entire deletion of Edwards' use of Joseph as one of the "saints" of old who was "long-suffering" on account of the condition of Mary, his betrothed.[^003-note245] Tryon in the nineteenth century felt that illustration to be in bad taste, as Edwards did not in the eighteenth. This somewhat humorous instance is enough to show Andover's faithfulness to the text of the booklets. Only once does Tryon let Edwards say "concatenation" or "concatenated together" in sermon twelve. Instead, he used what he believed was simpler language. And throughout the charity sermons, Tryon goes out of his way fourteen times to avoid using "infused" or "infusion."[^003-note246]

In other instances, however, we must rely on Tryon to fill out Andover. His text is needed, for example, to complete sermon three. Another example is Tryon's seventh use of instruction and his third use of improvement in the Application of sermon one. In this case we have definitive proof, from the recently identified copy of the charity sermons begun by Joseph Bellamy and found among his papers, that we need not suppose that Tryon strayed unrecognizably far from the text, or put his own words extensively into Edwards' mouth without respect for the originals. Tryon did not do this for his ending of sermon one,[^003-note247] and so probably not for the ending of sermon three, or elsewhere. In sum, then, given the choice of Andover as the copy-text to be edited, Tryon is sometimes a necessary source, and a not entirely unreliable one. Construing the present text called for difficult editorial judgments at a number of points; such decisions are opened to the reader in footnotes and in App. I below.

The manuscript copy is written in a distinct and readable hand. The style itself is obviously closer to that of Edwards than Tryon Edwards' edition. The copyist did his work well— instructed as no doubt he was by his editor to lengthen Edwards' contractions ('em, 'tis, can't), to spell out Edwards' "chap." to "chapter" and his "ver." to "verse," to leave space where he could not read Edwards' writing or where the booklet was defective, etc. The copyist left spaces with some frequency. Most notably, Tryon's edition is needed to complete the third, fifth, sixth, and eighth sermons; and to fill in numerous gaps— sometimes running to several lines— in Andover. Where I use Tryon's words in reconstructing the text, these are enclosed within double brackets. My own insertions

<!-- p. 111 -->

are placed in single brackets; these indicate disagreement with Tryon or that he is no help, or that I have to rewrite his words to elide with the Andover text. Where the blank space in the copy allows for only one or two short missing words, I assume no further explanation is needed than placing these insertions in single or double brackets. There remain numerous longer insertions, where a larger number of words, sentences, lines, paragraphs, or entire sermon endings are missing. Tryon is our only source for these endings or omissions and, often, his text is needed to make sense of the Andover text. In every one of these instances I append a footnote at the omission (or bracketed passage), describe the copy— text at this point and, where needed, give the reasons for my editorial judgment.

The three principal parts of the Puritan sermon form are (1) Text, and explication; (2) Doctrine, with reasons or motives; (3) Application or Improvement, in "uses" of instruction, of self-examination, of exhortation, of comfort, etc. From text through doctrine the sermon moved to practical application. Tryon subordinates these divisions, which the Andover copy correctly makes prominent by using all capital letters for Doctrine and Application, as was Edwards' practice.

Studies in seventeenth— and eighteenth-century English and American preaching have long since demonstrated that sermon form and style were more than literary conventions: they identified theological positions and often also ecclesiastical parties. Within a particular congregation the preacher's prescribed sermon form, and his marginal numbers, facilitated instruction and notetaking. The reader may need to visualize the following numerical and subnumerical designations:

| under Explication of the text | I. |  |  |  |  |
|  |  | (I) |  |  |  |
|  |  |  | *I*. |  |  |
|  |  |  |  | a. |  |
|  |  |  |  |  | (a.) |
| under Doctrine and Application: | I. |  |  |  |  |  |
|  |  | *First*. |  |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  | I. |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  |  | (I) |  |  |  |
|  |  |  |  |  | *I*. |  |  |
|  |  |  |  |  |  | a. |  |
|  |  |  |  |  |  |  | (a.) |

This standard, adopted for the Yale edition, simply regularizes Edwards'

<!-- p. 112 -->

own layout and his way of bringing out the bone structure of sermons he himself published.

In the rank of descending numbered heads and subheads indicated above, sometimes there may be a first or superior head clearly implied, but to which *there is no corresponding text* or number. In such an instance, we assume the superior head, and proceed to use the next lower ones. Illustrations of this— the only examples in the case of the charity sermons— fall under the heads of Application. Sometimes Edwards, or rather the extant copy, expressly states a use of examination or a use of exhortation. Edwards' practice was to number these uses I and II; and, of course, this is also our notation under Application. Sometimes, however, the entire application is clearly one unannounced use of examination, for example, or a use of instruction, in several points. In such instances, we assume that the Roman numeral "I" has been implied, and so the several points of the application are designated by the next lower numbers, i.e., *First., Second*., etc. Use of exhortation is clearly implied, for example, in the seventh sermon. If there is a number in the manuscript having no parallel, it is deleted. Major corrections of Andover's numeration will be noted, e.g., in the list of particular Christian graces concatenated together in sermon twelve. Formal marginal titles for certain other numbered heads— "Proposition," "Question," "Objection," "Answer," "Observation"— are abbreviated (Edwards' usual practice) and italicized: "*Prop*.," "Ques.," "*Obj*.," "*Ans*.," "*Obs*."

Each sermon is given a brief title which can be used as a running head. Sermon titles reflect the Doctrine. Generally, I use the titles Tryon Edwards gave to his "Lectures," somewhat altered or shortened. One exception to this should be noted. The title of sermon three is Joseph Bellamy's, "Nothing Can Make Up for Want of Sincerity"— to which I add "in the Heart."[^003-note248]

In editing the Andover copy I have made a few corrections silently. For example, adding an *s* to make a plural, changing "that" to "than," "here" to "have," "Romans 8:12" to "Romans 12:8, " "whethersoever" to "whithersoever," striking out a duplicate article, as in "the the," and inserting a period or question mark.

The rule governing the editing of previously published works is: Do not change "can't," "ben't," "independent on," or "'em" or other spellings or usages that affect pronunciation. Those eighteenth-century usages appear in this volume only in *Two Dissertations*. The Andover copyist has written out all those contractions, as well as spelling

<!-- p. 113 -->

"chapter" and "verse" for "chap." and "ver.," which likely were in Edwards' sermon booklets.

This should suffice for the general reader and advanced scholars. For other editors and scholars doing very specialized studies of Edwards, it is the expectation of the Yale edition that the copy-texts used may be available in microfiche editions, with target cards— so that these may be compared in detail with the letterpress editions. The excellent manuscript copy of the charity sermons is in the collection at Andover-Newton Theological Seminary and may be studied there. As for *Two Dissertations*, the first edition (1765) is already available in the Evans microtext editions of works published in America before 1800, #9962. To this text I now turn.

TWO DISSERTATIONS. The letter of Hopkins to Bellamy on January 4, 1764, quoted above,[^003-note249] throws light also on the collaboration of the two men in the transcription and posthumous publication of Edwards' papers. Having estimated that sixteen sermons combined with his *Memoir* would be enough to make two hundred pages, Hopkins continued, "I design to proceed in transcribing," i.e., additional unpublished works. Concerning this,

> I hear nothing from Boston, which to me is unexpected but perhaps Kneeland and Searl can account for it. Is it not best for me to go down to Boston in February [i.e., next month!], if I hear nothing, or if from what I hear, it appears necessary that I should be there in order to forward the matter. As I may possibly prosecute this proposal, it will be needful that you send me that on Virtue the first safe opportunity, and the sermons you shall transcribe. Mr. Collins, I fear, will not return soon enough for this... I have just received a friendly letter from Mr. Finley in which he expresses his zeal and good wishes, with respect to the proposed publication of Edwards' works, etc. I have finished that on *the last End*; should be glad to come down to get your assistance in reviewing and comparing it with the original, but if I go to Boston at the time proposed, it seems impracticable.

These passages indicate a division of labor in preparing *Two Dissertations* for publication, Hopkins assuming responsibility for *End of Creation* and Bellamy for *True Virtue*. We may surmise that Hopkins made the trip to Boston to "be there in order to forward the matter." To consult in person with Bellamy would require Hopkins to go a long journey, down from

<!-- p. 114 -->

Great Barrington, Massachusetts, south to Bethlehem, Connecticut, where Bellamy lived, and then turn back northeast in order to go (as New Englanders say) "down" to Boston. It seems likely that Bellamy sent Hopkins "that on Virtue" by messenger, and that Hopkins went directly to Boston. If so, there was no time for the two to review together and compare their copies with the original dissertations.

Hopkins was clearly the leader in his and Bellamy's collaborative editorship.[^003-note250] The preface to *Two Dissertations* (dated July 12, 1765) is signed simply "The Editor." I can observe no marked discrepancy in

<!-- p. 115 -->

style, spelling, etc., that might be attributed to the fact that the dissertations were prepared for the printer by different copyists.

Most remarkable, and inexplicable, are the many differences between the original editions of Edwards' works printed in his lifetime by Kneeland in Boston and the text of this work published posthumously by the same house in 1765, only a few years later. It is not too harsh a judgment to say that a contemporary copyeditor or author would reject or radically correct the printer's proofs of *Two Dissertations*.

There is, it is true, regularity in the use of contractions: thro’, tho’, altho’, possess'd, consider'd, determin'd, design'd, obtain'd, it's. These contractions, which uniformly appear also in works printed in Edwards' lifetime, are replaced by modern spelling or punctuation in the present edition, since the pronunciation is the same. But words ordinarily capitalized, then and now, are lowercased in the first edition of *Two Dissertations*: holy scriptures, scriptures, christian divines, deists, jews, redeemer, creator, the father and the son, the apostle, judas, moses, and in at least one place, "jesus christ." There are signal discrepancies in spelling: virtue/vertue; inquire/enquire; meerly/merely; favor/favour; honour/honor; supreme/supream; publick/public. Once in a single sentence we read, "His rejoycing therein, is rather a rejoicing in his own acts...," while "rejoicing" is the spelling everywhere else the word occurs. There may, of course, be difference in stress where the original edition reads "independent on"; sometimes "not dependent upon"; and sometimes "independent of."

Some of these characteristics of Hopkins' (and Bellamy's) edition no doubt reflect Edwards' writing habits. After all, he reverently wrote the word "god" in lowercase. And we know that he changed his spelling to "rejoice." So the text may in some respects be a too faithful reproduction of Edwards' manuscript, without enough editing of the copies Bellamy and Hopkins made.

My sense is that there is less repetitious use of italics for the purpose of stressing again and again a concept once it was introduced in italics, than there is in, for example, the first edition of *Freedom of the Will*. But while this is the case for a considerable number of pages, the reader then comes to page after page sprinkled all over with italics. I do not know how to account for this. It is a fact, however, that in those days printers, who kept letters in italics in one box, Roman in another, would begin to use more italics or more Roman depending on which they saw running short. While I have reduced the use of italics in the present edition, I

<!-- p. 116 -->

have not done so to the extent this was required in my editing of *Freedom of the Will* in the 1950s.

Indeed, I have introduced italics of my own to deal with a special problem. In Ch. II of *End of Creation*, on what is to be learned from Holy Scripture, Sec. III (on places in Scripture which show God's glory was his ultimate end) and Sec. IV (on places in Scripture which show it was for his name's sake and for his praise), the text waxes eloquent by the use of all capital letters for emphasis within Scripture verses quoted. Thus Philippians 2:11: "and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, TO THE GLORY OF GOD THE FATHER"; and Ephesians 1:5–6: "Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children— TO THE PRAISE OF THE GLORY OF HIS GRACE." In no case have I cluttered the page by retaining this excessive use of capitals. I have, however, often reduced one or more of the words the copy-text stresses in this fashion to italics within the Scripture verses, and in Edwards' text as well.

The excessive use of dashes is eliminated. There is one instance, however, of which I am fond, where the repetition of dashes is essential to the cadence and movement of thought. This is where, to show the meaning of subordinate and ultimate ends, Edwards wrote, "As when a man sells a garment to get money— to buy tools— to till his land— to obtain a crop— to supply him with food— to gratify his appetite."[^003-note251]

I come, finally, to the single most important difference between texts published in Edwards' lifetime (or between *Original Sin*, sent to the press by him) and this 1765 posthumous publication. This difference decisively supports an editorial decision toward which I was impelled, anyway, by the content and argument of *True Virtue*. In earlier works common nouns were all capitalized.[^003-note252] Our editorial practice was to eliminate all such capitalization of common nouns.

In *Two Dissertations*, by contrast, common nouns are not capitalized. Among common nouns, only the word *being* is capitalized, and words following colons.[^003-note253] (These practices have erratic exceptions, like the spellings above.) This means that the word *being* is not a common noun

<!-- p. 117 -->

as it is used in *Two Dissertations*. In this instance, routinely to adhere to an editorial directive to eliminate excessive capitalization, which was devised for printed texts that capitalized *all* common nouns, would be a mistake. So in editing the text I retain "Being in general" and "Being, simply considered" in all instances; and also the capitalization of "Being" alone where it is obviously a reference to God.

Of course, I sometimes judge that lowercase should be used where the original edition uses a capital. This I do when *being* plainly refers to finite beings, and where the word is plainly used more as a metaphysical concept than as a reference to God. An example of the first is "the Being of beings" (not "the Being of Beings") in "For they must see that consent to Being in general, and supreme respect to the Being of beings, is most just."[^003-note254] (That sentence is about the Day of Judgment! Before whom do men stand consenting or not consenting from their hearts to Being in general if not God?) An example of the second sort of use of lowercase *being* in my edited text is: "So that if all virtue primarily consists in that affection of heart to being, which is exercised in benevolence, or an inclination to its good, then God's virtue is so extended as to include a propensity not only to being actually existing, and actually beautiful, but to possible being, so as to incline him to give being, beauty and happiness."[^003-note255] The first edition capitalizes "being" throughout that sentence; I do not.

Nevertheless, the word *being* (rarely a metaphysical concept only) most often serves as a reference to God in *Two Dissertations*, as surely as do Judge and Ruler (which are functional concepts, not names for God). It is true, Edwards never says outright, "Being in general (or Being, simply considered) is God." But Edwards *does* say that consent to Being *is* love to God. The whole point of the second chapter of *True Virtue* is to change the abstract language of the first chapter into biblical or theological language. The first sentence of the second chapter states its thesis: "From what has been said, 'tis evident that true virtue must chiefly consist in love to God; the Being of beings, infinitely the greatest and best of beings." If that is "evident," surely it is equally evident that Being, as Edwards very often uses the term, is God. The force is the same when Edwards says the same thing in reverse: "God himself is in effect Being in general."[^003-note256] Even in the abstract language of the first chapter Edwards "gives notice" that when speaking of "an *intelligent* being's having a

<!-- p. 118 -->

heart united and benevolently disposed to Being in general," he means by the object of such cordial unity no mere metaphysical entity or concept but "*intelligent* Being in general." Indeed, this must necessarily be the meaning of "being," capitalized or lowercased, since Edwards believed there was no substance, no beings, properly so called, except intelligent or mental beings. Immediately following the characterization of the *object* of virtuous consent as "intelligent Being in general," Edwards begins a discussion of the loves of benevolence and complacence; and, in this context, invokes the innertrinitarian love of Father and Son!

It is a sufficient defense of my retention of the capitals to argue simply that, where I do so, the word is used in the context as a reference to God, not as a name for God. But also Edwards believed on scriptural ground that "Being," or its equivalent in Scripture, was the *name* God gave himself and himself revealed to his people in the famous "I am that I am" passage. This was Edwards' interpretation of Exodus 3:14 when he was only nineteen years of age.[^003-note257] That was still his view thirty years later when he wrote the "Controversies"— draft of *True Virtue*. In a paragraph[^003-note258] not marked for use and not in the version left by Edwards for publication, Edwards wrote concerning God that "he possesses being in general, he is an all-comprehending being, his name is *Jehovah I am* or existence itself, absolute, universal, infinite existence, and all other existence is but a communication from him." When Edwards decided to limit his discussion to *the creature's* true virtue, to creatures' absolute or pure benevolence to Being (or supreme love to God), the paragraph containing the foregoing sentence was omitted from his final version, since it undertook to prove *God's* moral perfection and infinite virtue. The sentence containing the words "Jehovah I am" is preceded by "How evident it is that God must have such benevolence." And the immediately following sentence is: "Therefore, as he has benevolence to himself he has benevolence to being in general, and as the creatures are rays of existence from the infinite fountain of light they must partake of his benevolence." Given

<!-- p. 119 -->

contemporary practice, Edwards himself would have capitalized both God and Being. More often than not, his usage was lowercase in both instances, with no less than supreme respect to "god" or to "being" (in very many or most of its occurrences in *Two Dissertations*), i.e., to intelligent willing Being itself, the only "capable object" of cordial consent.[^003-note259]

The Andover copy never places parentheses around Scripture citations at the end of the verse quoted. Instead, the copyist (faithful to Edwards' practice) reads: "I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne... and his train filled the temple, Isaiah 6:1." Omission of parentheses can, in addition, suggest to the contemporary reader that Scripture citations were probably voiced by Edwards for the instruction and notetaking of his congregation. The same is the style of the first edition of the posthumously published *Two Dissertations*. I adopt this common practice, only standardizing the punctuation and abbreviations. In addition, I ordinarily do not use final parentheses when myself citing scriptures in footnotes, for agreement's sake and also in order not to burden many a page with both parentheses and bracketed inserts. Of course, there was never any reason to use parentheses around Scripture citations *introducing* quotations; nor in the many instances where the citation is simply the middle part of Edwards' sentence, set off by commas.

Another decision favoring uniformity throughout the volume was not to spell out "chapter" and "verse" as did the Andover copyist. I use instead "ch." and "ver." The copy-text of *Two Dissertations* uses "ver."; its "chap." I shorten. Thus "ch." and "ver." are used throughout this volume for consistency's sake. Whether the reference is to one or to more than one chapter or verse needs no other indication than the one or more following numbers. I also use "par." for one or more paragraphs. The reader should note that the sections of *End of Creation* are main units corresponding to the chapters of *True Virtue*.

My copy-texts (and Edwards himself) use "Gen.," for example, as a class name for a sequence of chapters in Genesis connected by "and" until one comes to a period. Then another book may begin to be cited in its order in the Bible. Using "Gen." as a class name, "Genesis 3" could then become a subclass name for verses following in sequence, requiring an "and" before going on to, say, chapter Genesis 24. Thus, "Genesis 3:5–7, Genesis 3:9, Genesis 3:12 and Genesis 24:13." I am persuaded that Edwards (and readers also) *thought* "Genesis 3" at each enumeration when he set down Genesis 3:1–7, Genesis 3:19–20 following that citation. This was not a nervous habit. (The latter excess I shorten to Genesis 3:1–7, Genesis 3:19–20.) These features of the texts, no less than

<!-- p. 120 -->

Edwards' listing of biblical citations in the order in which the books appear in the Bible, I called the "concordance" character of his writing. I retain as much of this feature as seems feasible. However, I use semicolons instead of the periods in references such as "Isaiah 42:12 and Isaiah 64:1–5. Jeremiah 31:10. John 12:17, John 12:19 and John 15:1, " in order to avoid an entirely novel style of punctuation.

Perhaps I should say, finally, that in fidelity to our literary heritage and to the integrity of the English language, for accuracy and for fluency in reading Edwards, I use "men" interchangeably with "creatures," as he consistently did.

A Fellowship from the Guggenheim Foundation and a Senior Fellowship from the National Endowment for the Humanities enabled me to begin and make substantial progress in editing the *Ethical Writings*. My colleague John Wilson and I were jointly the recipients of a grant from the editing division of the National Endowment for the Humanities. Major contributors to the matching funds required in this case were Marjorie Buchanan Kiewit and a former undergraduate student, the Hon. John C. Danforth, United States Senator from the State of Missouri. Subsidy to cover the cost of publication of this volume, and in support of graduate assistants, were provided by a similar joint grant from Laurance Rockefeller. Since my retirement in June 1982 from the Department of Religion, Princeton University, I have received annual appointments as a member of the Center of Theological Inquiry. It is fitting that my final debt of gratitude upon the completion of this work is owed to Dr. James I. McCord, the founder and director of this institution for advanced theological scholarship, whose dream was shared with him years ago by H. Richard Niebuhr and, in lesser ways, by me. May providence continue to look with favor, through such benefactors, upon the twentieth-century revival of interest in Jonathan Edwards, the founding father of philosophy and theology in America.

Over the years since not the least of my inheritance from H. Richard Niebuhr was the debt of filial piety to him and the opportunity to enter more fully into the world rendered by Jonathan Edwards, I have been assisted by far too many persons than can ever be named here. Among graduate student assistants whom I am happy to count as colleagues in this enterprise are Stephen Crocco, John Merrill, Leigh Schmidt, James Beumler, John R. Fitzmier, Alan Young, and, one summer, Cathleen Kaveny, the last of my many undergraduate advisees. Among senior scholars who have written on Edwards' ethics, Norman Fiering read my

introduction and Roland A. Delattre read the entire manuscript, and gave me the benefit of their opinions.

Gentle but firm supervision, as well as constant support, was provided by my intrepid editor at the Yale University Press, Mary Alice Galligan. Copyeditors usually assist their authors from behind a veil of anonymity. Nancy R. Woodington came to understand and greatly improved my text. Gratitude requires that she be named among my contributors. Gloria Kramer was my final, most expert typist. Her idea of perfection troubled her but profited me. The original typescript of the copy-texts was produced, years ago, by Doris (Mrs. Joel) Nystrom, long-time secretary of Princeton's Department of Religion, whose invaluable and generous assistance is acknowledged in a number of my other writings. Upon finishing the typing of the charity sermons, Doris wrote an anthem. That's one advantage in knowing what you're doing (as a word processor cannot). May the reader be similarly blessed in mind and heart and life.

Paul Ramsey

*Feast of St. Luke the Physician*

*September* 3, 1987

[^003-note1]: Four of the seven chapters of *True Virtue* (my short title referring to JE's second dissertation *On the Nature of True Virtue*) are devoted to secondary beauty, self-love, conscience, and instinctual kind affections as "principles" that together give rise to natural morality (five, if one adds Ch. VI, which undertakes to show why the foregoing, separately or together, are often *mistaken* for true virtue). By contrast, the charity sermons address at length the meaning of true virtue, and articulate various truly virtuous dispositions and actions.

An entirely different collection was published under the same title— "Sermons on Various Important Subjects"— in Boston, 1738 (and again in Edinburgh [1785]). The Boston edition— printed in the year the charity sermons were preached— is commonly referred to as *Five Discourses*.

[^003-note11]: Indeed, in the account Hopkins wrote of his own life, he claims that he transcribed "the most" of the sermons published with his *Memoir*. "And Mrs. Edwards solicited me to write the life of Mr. Edwards, to be published, with a number of his manuscripts. I considered myself very unequal to writing his life; but as by having possession of his manuscripts, I was under a better advantage to do it, than others, I engaged to do the best I could; and if it should be approved of by a number of friendly, judicious ministers, I would consent to have it published, on condition that my name should not be put on it. Accordingly it was published with a number of posthumous sermons, the most of which I transcribed myself from his manuscripts." *Sketches of the Life of the Late, Rev. Samuel Hopkins, D. D., Pastor of the First Congregational Church in Newport*, Written by Himself... Published by Stephen West, D. D., Pastor of the Church in Stockbridge (Hartford, 1805), pp. 57–58.

[^003-note12]: These treatises are edited from the first edition, published seven years after JE's death by Samuel Hopkins (Boston, S. Kneeland, 1765). Short titles: *End of Creation* and *True Virtue*.

[^003-note13]: For example, the Ann Arbor paperback ed., with introduction by William K. Frankena (Univ. of Michigan Press, 1960; reprint ed., 1969). The first edition of True *Virtue* to be published by itself was in 1778; of *End of Creation*, in 1788, both in England. See Thomas H. Johnson, *The Printed Writings of Jonathan Edwards* (Princeton, Princeton Univ. Press, 1940), pp. 81–82. Editions of collected works continued this practice. The Leeds edition (1806–11) and the first Worcester edition (1808–09) entirely separated the two dissertations; in Worcester, *True Virtue* was printed in Vol. 2; *End of Creation*, in Vol. 6. That reversed the order in which *Two Dissertations* was originally printed. *True Virtue* was actually made available before *End of Creation* as the volumes of these collections issued from the press. The editor of the first American collection (the eight-volume Worcester edition), Samuel Austin, explained how this separation came about by adding to his preface, dated November 1, 1808, the following note (1, viii):N. B. The reader will observe in the Treatise on the "Nature of Virtue," several references to that on "The End of God in creating the World," as a foregoing Treatise. These have heretofore been served together, so as to agree with the references. And it was our intention to have placed the latter Treatise at the end of the first volume, which was printed after the second. [That is, in the numerical order of the volumes, with *End of Creation* in vol. I and *True Virtue* in vol. II, the sequence of the two dissertations would have been retained.] But the other pieces swelled the volume, so that we had no room for it. The reader must of course look forward to the sixth volume for this Treatise. With the Dwight edition (1829–30) and the four-volume Worcester edition (1843), the two dissertations were brought together again, and in their original sequence; and, fortunately, the latter has been the most widely reprinted and available collected edition of the works of Jonathan Edwards. Incidentally, Sereno E. Dwight errs in saying in *The Life of President Edwards* (*The Works of President Edwards: With a Memoir of His Life* [10 vols., New York, 1829–30], 1, 544) that the two dissertations were first published in a "pamphlet" in Boston in 1788. The now widely circulated Banner of Truth edition prints the two dissertations in their proper sequence. The "Preface by the First Editor" (Hopkins' preface to both dissertations), however, appears as preface to *End of Creation* alone, whose title is placed before it. A note is then attached to Hopkins' first line, which reads: "This preface was originally prefixed to the two following Dissertations, ‘concerning the End for which God created the World, and the Nature of True Virtue,’ in one volume." See *The Works of Jonathan Edwards*, 2 vols. (Edinburgh, Scotland, and Carlisle, Pennsylvania, Banner of Truth Trust, 1974, 1976), 1, 95. In all these publications the references in *True Virtue* to the "preceding discourse" are footnotes, not bracketed parts of the text, as in the first edition.

[^003-note14]: One example is William A. Clebsch, *American Religious Thought: A History* (Chicago, Univ. of Chicago Press, 1973). Clebsch writes that by the time JE wrote *True Virtue* "he could restate the essence of his thought nontheologically"; and for proof, "The treatise contains only one quite incidental appeal to Scripture, and only three casual references to Christianity. God became ‘being in general, simply considered.’ Sainthood became true virtue. The leading category of religious experience became not salvation but beauty" (pp. 49–50). Clebsch mentions *End of Creation* only once, in a listing of the topics to which JE turned his attention in Stockbridge. Even Perry Miller fails to acknowledge that the treatises were complementary elements of a larger, unified theological-ethical reflection. Although Miller adopts the language of the first edition in his introductory remarks by calling them *Two Dissertations*, he treats them as independent. His remarks on *End of Creation* are shorter, and subordinate to his discussion of *True Virtue*, which he treats first. The two function together only in the respect that they were "intended to be digested into the ‘Rational Account’" (Perry Miller, *Jonathan Edwards* [New York, William Sloane Assoc, 1949], pp. 285–305). More recently, Norman Fiering has written that "Edwards's dissertation on *The Nature of True Virtue* is about God, to be sure, but it is an extraordinary fact that *Scripture is never cited in the work*, nor does Edwards draw on the theological tradition for support" (Norman Fiering, *Jonathan Edwards's Moral Thought and Its British Context* [Chapel Hill, The Univ. of North Carolina Press, 1981], p. 9. Ed. italics). The Scripture citations, exegetical study, and additional theological backing are, of course, in the first dissertation! Fiering's failure to read *True Virtue* in the light of *End of Creation* may account for his statement that "*Charity and Its Fruits* has peculiarities that are inconsistent with nearly all the rest of Edwards's extant writings. It may be that Edwards chose not to publish these sermons because of some doubts he had about them, or even that the text prepared by Tryon Edwards in the nineteenth century is corrupt" (ibid., p. 173). Fiering's book concentrates on Edwards' moral philosophy, but in his introduction and again in his final chapter, he refers to Edwards' moral theology as "synthetic ethics" and to his moral philosophy as "critical ethics." However, to abstract moral philosophy from its theological context tends to obscure JE's extraordinary confidence that the truths of faith and of reason are *one*. "Critical" is a good description of chapters three through six or seven of *True Virtue*, but that term does not fit the positive analysis and argument of the first two chapters. "God"— talk or "Being"— talk does not signal whether a particular work or chapter is theological or philosophical. Fiering's belief is correct that JE wrote for different audiences, provided one understands that *Two Dissertations* was addressed to both no less than was *Freedom of the Will*, which contains both proof from Scripture and proof from reason. On the central, organizing principle of Edwards' ethics, Fiering is exactly right in his identification: "true virtue (or holy love, or Christian charity— the terms all have the same meaning)" (ibid., p. 172). An entire separation of theology and philosophy, between the "younger" Edwards and the "older" Edwards, was reasserted by Stephen E. Berk, *Calvinism versus Democracy: Timothy Dwight and the Origins of American Evangelical Orthodoxy* (Hamden, Conn., Archon, 1974).

[^003-note16]: Sec. 4, MS pp. 180–89, Yale coll., folder 28. I shall refer to this as the "Controversies"— draft. My numerous quotations from this penultimate draft are from Schafer's transcription, only slightly edited.

[^003-note17]: Schafer's reasons for this dating are too numerous and complicated to be stated fully here. In sum, his estimate is based on comparison of the light gray ink of Miscell no. 1208 and the "Controversies"— draft with that of JE's "Catalogue of Books," which begins using that same ink (and hand) at p. 29. Items on that and following pages of the "Catalogue" cite issues of the *Monthly Review* of 1752–53. There, too, JE begins to cite George Turnbull's *Moral Philosophy* and his *Christian Philosophy*. Add to this the fact that JE's references to Turnbull near the beginning of the "Controversies"— draft are as integral to it as his notes on method and the reference to Miscell. no. 1208; and that JE copied passages from Turnbull in Miscell. nos. 1209–11. Schafer suggests that reading Turnbull may have "triggered" (i.e., occasioned) the writing of *The Nature of True Virtue* section. Wallace E. Anderson extends this mutually supportive cross-dating to include nos. 199–206 "Images or Shadows of Divine Things," forthcoming in the typology volume of the Yale ed. An ink that is darker, or alternatingly gray-brown, begins with the 1250s or 1260s of the "Miscellanies" and continues through no. 1346 (the last entry JE numbered). It may be that this brown ink was JE's last Stockbridge ink (it is the last in the "Catalogue" and "Images"). I mention the brown that succeeded the gray ink of no. 1208 and the ink of almost the entirety of the "Controversies"— draft because the last four paragraphs of the latter, on MS p. 189, are in the darker ink. These were probably added later than 1753–54, how much later we do not know. One of these paragraphs defines what JE will call "absolute" or "pure" benevolence in *True Virtue*: "'Tis a being's being dear to us, which includes a desire of *union* with the object as well [as] a desire of the welfare of the object. Or rather, it is *an union with the object*; it is in the creature a kind of enlargement of the heart whereby self takes in existence in general. And these desires of sensible union and intercourse with the object, and desires of its good (the ordinary meaning of "benevolence"], may be considered as consequences and fruits of it" (Ed. italics). Here we see JE formulating benevolence as his term of art. In the final of these paragraphs JE uses the expression "moral sense" for the first time— for what *he* meant by it, namely, "sense of justice," "conscience." Thus in the "Controversies"— draft, conscience is still a sense of being in another's place— not yet the uneasiness and self-contradiction in conscience prominent in the final version of *True Virtue*. See App. II.

[^003-note18]: There is a single paragraph entitled "SATISFACTION FOR SIN" (words in center of MS p. 55). This begins a consideration of "how a perfectly wise, holy disinterested arbiter whose office it should be to regulate all things within the whole compass of existence according to the most perfect propriety, would determine in case the creature should injure the most high, should cast contempt on the majesty & trample the authority of the infinite Lord of the universe... And that it was very requisite in order to things being regulated & disposed most fitly & beautifully, that such injuries should not be forgiven in the neglect of this or without due care taken of this matter." No more is said corresponding to "SATISFACTION OF X" announced among the titles of the entry. This par. interrupts the parallel to the "supreme arbiter" argument in *End of Creation*, at the point noted below (Intro., p. 46, n. 4; and *End of Creation*, p. 425, at n. 2). Immediately before that point JE inserted these words: "See papers on the End of Creation p. 22, 23, 24." This reference was written later than the entry itself, and must refer to the final draft in process, which Hopkins copied for publication, or to some intervening pages. See further "Note on the Texts" and *End of Creation*, p. 426, n. 4.

[^003-note20]: Later, on MS p. 180b, Edwards copied quotations from George Turnbull (who is given prominent consideration in *Original Sin*), beginning: "WHO IS A GOOD MAN and VIRTUOUS MAN according to Turnbull." Since, according to JE, Turnbull believed a good and virtuous man is one whose "chief delight" is in "rational exercises," the question can here be raised whether JE would have drawn a sharp distinction between rationalists and sentimentalists and (and how he would have distinguished between these different sorts of believers that true moral goodness springs from natural goodness) if true virtue and original sin had been themes woven together for publication. See Intro., text at n. 7 below, for the notice to readers inserted near the end of *Original Sin*; and JE on Matthew Tindal on "moral sense," App. II.

[^003-note30]: An editor might, by contrast, use an introduction to set Edwards' thought in its historical context, tracing the antecedents of particular ideas and expressions. That task is an important one, never fully completed. So long as the majority of Edwards' papers remains unpublished, the time is not yet ripe for that, and whoever ventures it has not a sufficient community of scholars to check his learned proposals. Readers who are already into debates over the lineage of *True Virtue* may, at this point, wish to read App. IV below.

[^003-note31]: JE uses "grateful" to qualify some object, relation, or event that is "pleasing to the mind or the senses; agreeable; acceptable; welcomed." Gratitude in the heart is directed to that which is objectively "grateful." The Oxford English Dictionary gives the following illustrations of this usage: "his coming was very grateful unto the king," 1656; "He is so far from being hateful, he is exceedingly grateful to the people of Rome," 1690; "In grateful sleep," 1725; "This is a doctrine grateful to scientific men who are afraid of being thought hostile to religion," 1867. JE's "grateful" finds in things or situations a pleasing quality; "gratitude" is in the heart's answerableness to the grateful. The word in this sense is suited to and frequently used in JE's proof that moral terms are founded "in the reason and nature of things," not in sentiment (*True Virtue*, Ch. VIII).

[^003-note32]: *True Virtue*, pp. 575–76. What makes an act to be "one's own" was the point of Edwards' *Freedom of the Will*; and the upshot for ethics and moral psychology was the same: "that act which is performed without inclination, without motive, without end, must be performed without any concern of the will... If the soul in its act has no motive or end; then in that act... it seeks nothing, goes after nothing, exerts no inclination to anything; and this implies that in that act it desires nothing, and chooses nothing; so there is no act of choice in the case: and that is as much as to say, there is no act of will in the case." Jonathan Edwards, *Freedom of the Will*, ed. Paul Ramsey, in *The Works of Jonathan Edwards* (New Haven, Yale Univ. Press, 1957), 1, 333.

[^003-note33]: JE's language then was not as carefully honed as in his later works and his thought perhaps not so clear. Still, he wrote of "self-love taken in the most extensive sense" as "a man's love of his own pleasure and happiness... or rather, 'tis only a capacity of enjoyment or suffering. For to say a man loves his own happiness and pleasure, is only to say that he delights in what he delights [in]... So that self-love is only a capacity of enjoying or taking delight in anything." Thus the young JE answered the question of this entry, "whether or no a man ought to love God more than himself." Self-love in "the most extensive sense" (i.e., a capacity of enjoying) and "love to God are not things properly to be compared one with another." "Proportionable to our love to God, is our disposition to delight in his good. Now our delight in God's good, can't be superior to our general capacity of delighting in anything; or which is the same thing, our delight in God's good can't be superior to our love to delight in general: for proportionably as we delight in God's good, so shall we love that delight." JE's generalization is that "the degree of delight in a particular thing, and the degree of love to pleasure or delight in general, ben't properly comparable one with another." But one reason given for this may be obscure: for the two "are not entirely distinct, but one enters into the nature of the other."

[^003-note34]: *Charity*, p. 255.

[^003-note35]: In the same breath, a radical difference between JE and the Augustinian tradition must be pointed out. In that tradition, a telling response to the account of the Augustinian "synthesis" in Anders Nygren's *Agape and Eros* (London, S. P. C. K., 1953) would be to carve out a legitimate place for *creatures'* "need-love" to God— as did C. S. Lewis in *The Four Loves* (New York, Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1960). JE would not have limited himself to that rejoinder. His point was not the nature of *creatures*' wills and loves, but that of *any* intelligent willing perceiving being. That includes *God's* self-sufficient acts of will. He, too, must love his own happiness if he is different from sticks and stones, which will nothing. This is the problem of the first dissertation, why God willed to create any world at all.

[^003-note36]: *Charity*, p. 258. A principle *uniting* one person to another was JE's formulation of the meaning of "pure" or "absolute" benevolence. See Miscell. no. 530 and App. III. The older Edwards said essentially the same thing as the young Edwards when he wrote in the second dissertation, "to speak more accurately, it [true virtue] is that consent, propensity and union of heart to Being in general, that is immediately exercised in a general good will"; or, still more precisely, true virtue "primarily consists... simply considered; exciting ‘absolute benevolence’ (if I may so call it) to Being in general"; and "pure benevolence in its *first* exercise is nothing else but being's uniting, consent, or propensity to Being." (see *True Virtue*, pp. 540, 544, 546). In some respects, JE's earlier "*uniting* principle" was a better expression of his meaning than the word "union" in *True Virtue*, which is less connotative of continuous action.

[^003-note37]: *True Virtue*, p. 576.

[^003-note38]: Cf. n. 6 above.

[^003-note39]: This notion derives other-love from "a love to love our own [specific] happiness," i.e., from the self's love of self. In Miscell. no. 530 JE contrasted "compounded self-love" with what he called "simple mere self-love." He gave a somewhat confused account of the latter. On the one hand, "simple self-love" was so called "because it arises simply from... the nature of a perceiving willing being." With no more said, such simple self-love would be equivalent to that general capacity or universal meaning of self-love amply endorsed in this entry. On the other hand, "simple mere self-love" is "a man's own proper, single and separate good," and *this* selfishness is said always to be "what arises simply and necessarily from the nature of a perceiving willing being." Love to God can't be superior to the former, while superior to the latter, "love to God can and ought to be." "Simple self-love" is, to say the least, ambiguous. Norman Fiering understands "simple self-love" to mean our love to "single and separate good" (*Jonathan Edwards's Moral Thought*, p. 157), "in common language, selfishness" (p. 159). He is mistaken, however, in taking "compounded self-love" to be "in an intermediary position in Edwards's theory" (p. 157), a "necessary *balance* between self-love and social love" (p. 158; cf. p. 167), only "an enlarged sense of one's own good, which may include others to greater or less degree" (p. 159), consequent upon a line of reasoning later called "enlightened self-interest" (p. 160). All this is laid upon or arises from a hedonic/eudaemonic law (pp. 153, 157), which seems too pejorative a reference to self-love taken in JE's most extensive sense, or to the nature of any perceiving willing being's love of its own happiness. Fiering then must deem the charity sermons to be idiosyncratic among JE's works, forgetful of his "earlier differentiation [in Miscell. no. 530] of three types of love: simple, compounded and holy" (p. 172). Instances of Fiering's natural, compounded self-love or natural affection (pp. 158–59) allow inroads of "social love," which is love to others from an extended egotism. So he reads the several principles explanatory of the ordinary morality of perceiving willing creatures in *True Virtue* as, to say the least, too readily overwhelmed by the inroads of nefarious self-love. The other principles of natural morality are stripped of their variety, richness, and mutual support, if not altogether reduced to a single foundation in selfishness. The alternative is that, when writing Miscell. no. 530 in his nineteenth year, JE already had in place his understanding of universal self-love as a general capacity of willing or delighting in anything, and that this is the meaning to be ascribed to "simple mere self-love." Without this reading, it is difficult to understand the corollary of this entry, that it is "impossible for any person to be willing to be perfectly and finally miserable for God's sake," or for him to love God supremely and have that be "further informative" of his own particular happiness. My reading of Miscell. no. 530 is consistent with JE's argument in *True Virtue*, that our hearts must first be united to others in affection; then their happiness becomes ours. See *True Virtue*, p. 577.

[^003-note40]: Such statements are true of regenerate creatures; there is no contradiction in saying so. On this meaning of metaphysical "necessity" and "possibility," see *True Virtue*, p. 579 and n. 4.

[^003-note41]: *True Virtue*, p. 577. Ed. italics.

[^003-note42]: I use an analogy to end the use of versions of *analogia entis* in interpreting JE. See the merely negative theology afforded by proceeding from man's natural knowing (*True Virtue*, pp. 591–92). My analogy itself— to interpersonal self-disclosure and communication— is appropriate if there is no reality more "other" to us than another person. So far, anthropomorphic language is not only proper in address to God but in any talk about God as well. Our way of knowing the core of Christian truth is not by analogy, or by metaphors drawn from common experience. JE's types are not veils of heavenly archetypes; his natural types are types of Christ; his notion of participation is grounded in the communication of divine and human qualities in the person of Christ (*communicatio ideomatum*). Thus, JE wrote in his early twenties: "love of god, as it is in the divine nature, is not a passion, is not such a love as we feel; but by the incarnation [it] is really become passionate to his own, so that he loves them with such a sort of love as we have to him or to those we most dearly love. This was one great end of his incarnation, a merciful High Priest. So that now, when we delight ourselves at the thought of God's loving us, we need not have that alloy of our pleasure which our infirmity would otherwise cause, that though he loved us, yet we could not conceive of that love. Now this passionate love of Christ, by virtue of the union with the divine nature, is in a sort infinite" (Miscell. no. z). See App. III, pp. 706–38 below.

(See *Jonathan Edwards's Moral Thought*, p. 324.) Ed. italics. This editor's view is that in the search for an adequate understanding of JE's meaning the reader should allow JE's three words to interpret each other. If, however, a choice must finally be made, and if virtuous love is the mirror image of John 17:21 at the center of *End of Creation*, then some variant of "union" must be accorded pride of place in the second dissertation.

[^003-note59]: This is the punctuation of the first ed. My conjecture is that JE used "uniting" as a gerund. Of course, he probably wrote the words "uniting consent or propensity" consecutively without commas, just as he wrote "intelligent willing perceiving being." William K. Frankena's Ann Arbor edition of *True Virtue* (p. 9) and many earlier editions omit the comma. This may have influenced Fiering's preference for the term *consent* (*Jonathan Edwards's Moral Thought*, p. 325, with n. 10; cf. p. 339). In any case, "uniting consent" is a fortunate flaw. As modifier or as gerund, "uniting" indicates continuous action; so "uniting consent" is a good rendering of JE's notion (leaving aside the issue of whether the expression was his or not). So also we might profitably ponder "uniting propensity," or "propensity to union," or "consenting union" when reflecting on JE's meaning. See n. 2 above, and the "uniting principle" of Miscell. no. 530. One or the other of these variants seems needed to capture something of JE's "further informative" principle, joined with love of one's own happiness, to account for *specific* loves. See Intro., p. 16 above, n. 9. Because "uniting" suggests energy and action, it may be needed— instead of "union"— if we are ever to understand the peroration on the soul's progressive, unending approach to God with which *End of Creation* ends. See pp. 443–44, 534–36 below and App. III.

[^003-note60]: *True Virtue*, pp. 544–46. Ed. italics. On any interpretation of this dense chapter, the distinction between the "primary" and "secondary" objects of virtuous benevolence is structurally the centerpiece. Fiering's *Jonathan Edwards's Moral Thought* suppresses or fragments this distinction in his arrangement of eleven "Corollaries of True Virtue" (pp. 328–40). His first three corollaries (three *consecutive* sentences) avoid mentioning this distinction by omitting the first and topic sentence of the paragraph. The sentence that heads these three corollaries introduced the distinction and the logical *sequence* I have stressed: "The *first* object of a virtuous benevolence is Being, simply considered: and if Being, simply considered, be its object, then Being *in general* is its object" (*True Virtue*, p. 545). Omitting that enforces the view that particular loves emanate from general love. Fiering's corol. 4 concerning "that object who has the most of being" truncates the sentence from which it was taken, which *begins*: "And further, if Being, simply considered, be the first object of a truly virtuous benevolence, then that Being who has *most* of being..." (ibid., p. 545). By that omission a reader's attention is again not directed to the "first object of virtuous benevolence— nor does it anticipate the second, to come in JE's next paragraph. Then corol. 5 skips over to the fifth in JE's list of six things to be "more particularly noted" concerning that "secondary ground," which Fiering does not introduce until corol. 6. Two effects of this rearrangement are significant here. (1) Being "in general" is used without articulation for the primary object (Being itself) and for the secondary (*benevolent* Being in general). And (2) Edwards' points 1–4 and 6 in further explication of the "secondary ground" (now attached to nothing) must then be elevated in status to corol. 7–11 in Fiering's "geometrical method" (p. 323). In my view, Edwards' first chapter is more of an *argument* than is suggested by Fiering's use of "deductive reasoning," his "apodictically," or by his "logical extension," drawing out "the elements in the basic definition or axiom" (pp. 322–24). But he cuts the ground from under his interpretation by this footnote: "The division of the corollaries into 11 is entirely my doing. I have ignored Edwards's numbering, which is erratic, and imposed my own, and changed the order of Edwards's propositions as I found necessary and convenient for clear presentation" (p. 324, n. 6).

[T]he certainty that is in things themselves, which is the foundation of the certainty of the knowledge of them; or that wherein lies the ground of the infallibility of the proposition which affirms them... The subject and predicate of a proposition, which affirms the existence of something, may have a full, fixed, and certain connection several ways. (1) They may have a full and perfect connection *in and of themselves*; because it may imply a contradiction or gross absurdity, to suppose them not connected." To suppose a world with a different law of gravity or without secondary beauty, or a world in which self-love spins on its own spot and can produce love to no others, implies no contradiction. There is no inconsistency in supposing a world in which Peer Gynt could live as an isolate, in "a cask of self, stopped with a bung of self." But that is not God's world, in which love to self is "naturally" inclined to love to some others, many others.

[^003-note85]: It was John Gay's essay *Dissertation Concerning the Fundamental Principle and Immediate Criterion of Virtue or Morality* (London, 1731) that freed utilitarianism to emerge from the "moral sense" school in the tradition of John Locke, by thus explaining in terms of utility the counterevidence of our terminal approvals of certain virtues and disapprovals of certain vices. In the brief final paragraph of Ch. IV of *True Virtue* JE presses the same account of moral education to discover again the connection, by lapsed association of ideas, of our approvals and disapprovals with self-love. Fiering, *Jonathan Edwards's Moral Thought*, pp. 180–81, also notes a remarkable similarity of JE's analysis to that of Gay. Fiering's stress is on approbation and disapprobation from *habitual* association, not on a *lapsing* of the liveliness of the connection of, e.g., gratitude, approval of certain virtues, and disapproval of certain vices, with self-love. But such a lapsing must be the point if what JE says about moral education is true. This is the place to note that John Locke was interested most of all in the compositive powers of the mind, e.g., in "mixed modes" [*Essay Concerning Human Understanding* [1690], Bk. II, ch. 22) by which the mind puts together simple ideas impressed on us through one sense (redness) with ideas from *other* senses (roundness, smoothness) to form the idea of an apple. In comparison, habits from association of ideas were rather random and accidental, and mainly a bad influence on human judgment and conduct (ibid., ch. 33). Such was also the view of Francis Hutcheson. According to Hutcheson, admiration of distant historical characters arises directly and mysteriously from moral sense; and swine, serpents, and some insects, which are "really beautiful enough," are beheld by many people with aversion because they "have got some *accidental Ideas associated* with them. And for Distastes of this Kind, no other Account can be given" than accidentally associated ideas of disgust [*An Inquiry into the Original of our Ideas of Beauty and Virtue* [London, 1725], sec. VI, art. iii). Edwards (and Gay) systematically pressed the association of ideas for all the explanatory power it was worth.

[^003-note86]: The stronger form of this argument— i.e., examples to show that elements of ordinary morality from self-love occur in *entire separation* from true virtue, and are not simply distinguishable from it— was sketched in JE's "Controversies"— draft. Under the head, "That MORAL TASTE that is naturally in men is not of the nature of true virtue and essentially differs from [it]," he argued that the passions of gratitude and anger do not arise from true virtue, since they are shared by the brutes, whose passions tell the difference between *their kind* and inanimate objects! Notice again his qualified use of the expression "moral sense": "But allowing that such a moral sense if it be proper to call it by that name is in some degree in many of the beasts, as they have such a thing as anger. *They are much otherwise moved when they suffer from an agent that has will than when they suffer by the wind or water or hail*. And nothing appears but that the same instinct joined with that reason and that vastly more extensive knowledge that is in men may cause all the anger that appears in natural man, and without anything more akin to virtue. So [also] there are appearances of gratitude in some of the brute creatures" (MS p. 181, par. 4. Ed. italics). JE dropped any reference to the beasts in the revision readied for publication. Why should he cite serpents charmed by melodies for their sense of secondary beauty but not the beasts' passions at this point in his final text? Possibly because his full-scale discussion of gratitude and anger is under his second principle of common morality— the derivation of other-love from love to self— and love requires "intelligent willing" subjects, not alone sensible ones.

[^003-note91]: Ibid. p. 593. A brief detour into contemporary moral philosophy may help us to understand the importance of JE's second element in conscience. R. M. Hare's universal prescriptivism invoked natural human inclinations and disinclinations (this is his "naturalism") to supply the material content of rationally consistent moral judgments of reversibility and universalization. He then proceeds to speculate whether, within the constraints of reversibility, it could ever be the case that a moral agent might say that his neighbor should be incinerated if he is a Jew— provided only that he himself would be willing in the Jew's place to be incinerated for the same reason. JE would have thought this an outrageously inadequate view of the competence of conscience. The self-consistency principle has its *prius* in what the consistency of golden rule interchange is all about. In place of Hare's human inclination or disinclination, JE says that self-union or consistency with self has desert and justice as its material content, deriving that content of conscience from the secondary beauty of symmetry and proportion in moral relations. Thus the material content of conscience should teach us that neither you nor your neighbor deserves to be incinerated because of Jewishness, even if a fanatic who believes so (who, Hare might say, has his natural inclinations stupefied) might well comply with the formal requirements of self-consistency or reversibility in this case. For Hare on the problem of the fanatic, see "Toleration and Fanaticism" in *Freedom and Reason* (New York, Oxford Univ. Press, 1963; reprint ed., 1964).

[^003-note96]: The leading proponent of the ideal observer theory is Roderick Firth of Harvard University. This school's understanding of the meaning of "X is right" is summarized by Firth: "If there were an ideal observer (i.e. a person who is omniscient, omnipercipient, disinterested, and dispassionate, but in other respects ‘normal’), this person would have a certain experience (e.g. a feeling of approval, an experience of apparent requiredness) with respect to X." Roderick Firth and R. B. Brandt, "Discussion: The Definition of an ‘Ideal Observer’ Theory in Ethics," *Philosophy and Phenomenological Research*, 75 (1955), 407–23. The ideal observer theory does not locate impartial wisdom in God. In the contemporary logic of ethics it ought not to do so, since ethical statements would then seem to be false if God does not exist, and this is not "what we intend when we use ethical terms." Roderick Firth, "Ethical Absolutism and the Ideal Observer," *Philosophy and Phenomenological Research*, 12 (1952). Reprinted in *Readings in Ethical Theory*, ed. W. Sellars and J. Hospers, 2d ed. (Englewood Cliffs, N. J., Prentice-Hall, 1970), p. 203. JE supposed what he believed to be impossible, namely, "some third being of perfect wisdom and rectitude... perfectly indifferent and disinterested." His God was not characterless; he was in fact that supposed being of perfect wisdom and rectitude. Present-day ideal observer theory depersonalizes (into a model for decision-making) the impartial judge who was for JE personal and most real. But the sense of the nature of moral judgments seems to me to be identical in most important respects. And finally it should be noted that while perfect wisdom and rectitude is ascribed to God alone— he alone is free from all "stupefying prejudices"— the same sort of competence is inherently ascribed to every rational moral agent, men and angels, saints and sinners— and to the condemned on the Day of Judgment. Stephen D. Crocco drew my attention, and that of Professor Firth, to the importance of the impartial-arbiter argument in JE.

Here, indeed, he repeats the word "infuse" where Andover does not, in "and another *to infuse* a spirit of love to men" (Ed. italics). And just above this sentence TE agrees with the Andover copy's "It is the Spirit which infuses love to God," citing Romans 5:5. In a total of fourteen instances, however, where Andover uses the language of infusion, TE avoids any such term. His circumlocutions are indicated in footnotes to the text of the sermons. Clearly the copyist had no reason to introduce such language, while in the nineteenth century TE had reason to eliminate it because of the growing Protestant aversion to what came to be deemed a Roman Catholic error entailing merit threatening, if not fatal, to the sovereignty of God's grace. There is independent evidence as well in numerous entries in the "Miscellanies" that support the accuracy of Andover. See App. IV.

[^003-note124]: Wilson H. Kimnach's characterization of both sermons; certainly, the final sermon in this series was among JE's masterworks. "Though the much-discussed *Sinners* remains Edwards' virtuoso piece," Kimnach writes, "there are a few other sermons in which the handling of imagery is comparably inspired. One sermon worthy of comparison with *Sinners*, and complementary to it in theme, is the concluding sermon of [the charity] series... a sermon of Dantean simplicity, scope, and grandeur... Perhaps for the same reasons that many who have read Dante's ‘Inferno’ have not read his ‘Paradiso,’ this sermon has not received the attention given *Sinners*, and yet I feel that its vision of heaven is perhaps the supreme example of Edwards' systematic massing of images about a theme." ("The Literary Techniques of Jonathan Edwards," Ph. D. diss., University of Pennsylvania, 1971 [University Microfilms 71–26, 039], pp. 320–21.) The sermon uses the entire repertoire of JE's essential divine images: sun, light, rays, flame, fountain, sky, garden (plants, vine, trees), river (stream, ocean), family, the body, musical sounds. Kimnach's summary estimation of JE's handling of imagery in "Heaven Is a World of Love" is: "At his best, Edwards has the truly integrative imagination of the finest metaphysical poets" (ibid., p. 327).

[^003-note125]: Taken in part from Joseph Bellamy's part-copy. See App. I below, pp. 663–64. JE uses the word *sincerity* with the second of the two meanings set forth in *Freedom of the Will*, pp. 316–18. The expression "sincere endeavors" is ambiguous. On the one hand it simply means that a person does will and endeavor something; he has the "woulding"; he is not pretending. The other meaning is full integrity and wholeness of will, which for JE was true or "virtuous sincerity." See also the section on sincerity in Miscell. no. 1153. MORAL INABILITY. FREE WILL. SELF-DETERMINING POWER (a lengthy entry composed not long after dismissal from the church in Northampton, and marked for use or when used at that place in *Freedom of the Will*). Norman Fiering, *Moral Philosophy at Seventeenth Century Harvard* (Chapel Hill, Univ. of North Carolina Press, 1981), p. 172, affirms that *hypocrisy* did not have our meaning of the deliberate deception of others; a hypocrite was rather someone self-deceived as to his own true motives; he lacked "sincerity." If this seems strange, illustrations from the Oxford English Dictionary may help. *Sincere* means (1) not falsified or perverted in any way; genuine and pure in the case of doctrine; uncorrupted and uncontaminated in the case of motive ("Keeping them pure and sincere against temptations," 1649); of material things, colors, or substances; pure, unmixed, free from any foreign element; unadulterated, genuine. The "sincere fat" in a bloated body, "sincere gall" issuing from an incision, and "wood is cheap and *wine sincere* outside the city gates" illustrate these meanings. Or *sincere* means (2) containing no element of deception; not feigned or pretended; real, true, i.e., "real" and "true" in a sense different from what those words mean under the first definition. Likewise, *sincerity* means (1) freedom from falsification in the sense of adulteration or alloy; purity, correctness ("the sincerity of the Hebrew text"; "profess the sincerity of the Gospel") or (2) freedom from dissimulation or duplicity; honesty, straightforwardness. While the second of these meanings is more common today, the two seem to run along together through most of the history of the English language. JE's meaning is the first of these alternatives, as norm for judging the second. There is in truth and reality but one way human hearts can be sincere.

[^003-note144]: The running title of Miscell. no. 810 (*c*. Great Awakening) raised this question about the book of Job: "SCRIPTURES of the Old Testament, why constituted of such parts, and particularly why such a book of job is inserted?" JE's answer was that, seeing that the church is in her militant state and must pass through great tribulation, "'tis therefore a great instance of the fatherly mercy and tenderness of God towards his church that he has given one book of divine revelation on purpose to instruct them and direct them, strengthen and comfort them under such circumstances. This book is exceedingly fitted for these ends," JE explained at length and in detail. This led to the following speculation concerning the origin and writing of the book of Job: "'Tis probable the time that this book was first given to the church of Israel was either the time of their affliction in Egypt, which was a type of the suffering state of the Christian [church] under Rome, or the time of their travail in the wilderness, a type of the same afflicted state of the church wherein she is represented as the woman in the wilderness; and that Moses either wrote the book in Midian or brought it thence with him written by another to his own people in Egypt, or else it was brought to him in the wilderness by Jethro or written by Moses there. And so the time of its being first given to the church of Israel agrees with that which I have supposed to be the special design of the book." In his general introduction to the book of Job ("Notes on the Bible," Dwight, *Works*, p, 333–34) JE favored the speculation that Elihu is not named among Job's friends who came to lament with him when they are first mentioned because he himself was the "historian and penman" of the book; that Jethro the priest of Midian had Elihu's book, which Moses translated into Hebrew to teach the children of Israel patience under affliction.

The world affords nothing else like it— a remarkable hand of providence. When they shall be called then shall that ancient people that were alone God's people for so long a time [come] to be God's people again, never to be rejected more." *Work of Redemption*, Sermon Twenty-Six, MS Bk. 11, leaf 13 verso.

[^003-note162]: These moral notions are extensively deployed in the next sermon on humility and in Sermon Fifteen. In face of Philippians 2:8, JE denied that humility was a virtue of the divine nature of Christ: "grudging not" is the proper notion. The devil envied or begrudged man's happy state in Eden. JE also believed that those angels who fell did so not so much from towering pride as from that vice in their hearts in the form of envy or grudging, when they learned that God had determined to raise human creatures below them in creation to a higher destiny than theirs in glory, i.e., to the highest honor and blessedness, in *union* with himself. The fallen angels begrudged the hypostatic union when they saw that the created nature to be united with uncreated nature was that of a man, not one of the angels; human, not angelic. Miscell. no. 833. OCCASION OF THE FALL OF THE ANGELS: "As the creation of the visible world was in sight of the angels, for them the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy, so this solemn investing Christ with dominion over the world on the finishing of the creation was doubtless visible to them." That investiture was of the Son, i.e., of Jesus Christ in the divine nature. Moreover, JE continues, "God on this occasion made known to the angels something of his design and end in this dispensation. And 'tis very probable that, as this was done immediately after the creation of man, the principal work of that part of the creation which the angels saw and which they most admired, that now was something revealed of that peculiar love to that race of beings that he had... [T]hat God intended to make them, though created after the angels and of a much inferior nature to them, the principal end of the creation... [T]hat the Son of God that was now invested with the dominion over the world should have dominion in that [human] nature as the Head of that race, and as such they were to be his subjects and servants and ministring spirits, *and that this was the occasion of the fall* [of the angels]. They thought they were unequally dealt with and hence pride arose and they could not deign for such purposes to be subject to the Son of God and to have this inferior nature so exalted above them" (Ed. italics). Such an account of the angelic sin is a rarity in theological tradition. Suarez, for example, held that the highest among the fallen angels desired the hypostatic union for his own person, while the lesser angels desired it for angelic nature as such. Lucifer desired his very person to be united with the divine; his hosts desired that an angel instead of a man be assumed into the divine nature. See Fr. Edward J. Montano, *The Sin of the Angels* (Washington, Catholic Univ. Press, 1955), p. 117. Was the fall of the angels from pride or from envy? In fact, JE's notion of pride was not the simple one of storming heaven's battlements to usurp God's throne. His was a more nuanced concept, essentially that of a "comparative spirit," that is, pride born of creatures' vulnerability to perceived threats to their dignity, not of inordinate strength or uncomplicated assurance. "Pride don't consist most essentially in a too high conceit of oneself, but in a disposition inordinately to affect our own *comparative dignity*" (Miscell. no. 747. SELF-RIGHTEOUSNESS. PRIDE [roughly contemporary with the charity sermons], Ed. italics). "Pride may be thus defined. It is that habit or state of a person's heart whereby he is inordinately disposed to exaltation amongst other beings as to his comparative dignity or worthiness of esteem and value... The immediate object of pride is not... a man's own excellency considered absolutely. 'Tis not a disposition in a person to seek his own excellency absolutely, or a disposition to be excellent. A man can't excessively affect his own excellency... he can't excessively desire to be excellent, to have those qualifications that will render him a just object of esteem... 'Tis only a comparative dignity that pride affects, or the height that one is in or may be conceived to be amongst other beings. Nor is it the love and esteem of others absolutely considered... It don't content pride to be esteemed and loved by others, and to be so much valued by them, but to be highly valued and esteemed comparatively. 'Tis a person's comparative exaltation [among superiors, equals, or inferiors]... whether those other beings with whom we compare our exaltation or dignity be God or creatures" (Miscell. no. 950. PRIDE. HUMILIATION [*c*. 1744]).

[^003-note175]: In the 1738 series, "partaking of the divine nature," 2 Peter 1:4, was introduced early in Sermon One; this, p. 132 below, distinguishes the spiritual from the natural image of God. In *End of Creation*, pp. 441–44, this notion of "participation" comes together with "fullness" and "implication" to clinch JE's argument that in purposing creatures' good God manifests a supreme and ultimate regard to himself in all his works. In the first dissertation, God's "fullness" had been introduced (at p. 433 below), "partly because I know no better phrase to be used... and partly because I am led hereto by some of the inspired writers, particularly the apostle Paul" (n. 7). And "implied in" is first found on pp. 436, 438. The same concentrated interplay of "fullness," "participation," and "implication" is in JE's ans. to obj. 4, pp. 458–60. All this is under the head of "what reason teaches"! In *End of Creation*, however, the closest one comes to a definition of *implied in* is JE's assertion that the various names Scripture uses to designate God's end are but different denominations "involving each other in their meaning," p. 526; so there is "but one" end. See Intro., pp. 34–35 above. An example of JE's extended use of this notion of implication is his view that accepting Christ in his kingly office and accepting him as priest "not only can't be separated, or be asunder, in their [human] subject; but they can't be considered as separate things in their nature, for they are implied one in another." Miscell. no. 855. JUSTIFICATION. FAITH CONDITION OF SALVATION (*c*. 1740–42, Great Awakening).
