*Second*. Another distinction which divines make of the gifts of the Spirit are of extraordinary and ordinary. The extraordinary gifts of the Spirit are the same with miraculous gifts; such as gifts of prophecy and working miracles, and others mentioned by the Apostle in the text and other parts of the epistle. These are called extraordinary gifts of the Spirit, because they are such as are not given in the ordinary course of God's providence. They are not bestowed in a way of God's ordinary providential dealings with his children; but only on extraordinary occasions, as they were bestowed on the prophets and apostles to enable them to reveal the mind and will of God before the canon of the Scripture was complete. And so they were bestowed on the primitive church in order to the founding and establishing the Christian church in the world. But since the canon of the Scripture has been completed, and the Christian church fully founded and established, those extraordinary gifts have ceased. The ordinary gifts of the Spirit are such as are continued to the church of God throughout all ages; such gifts as are granted in conviction and conversion, and such as appertain to the building up of saints in holiness and comfort.

So that you may observe, that the distinction of the gifts of the Spirit into ordinary and extraordinary is very different from the other distinction of his gifts into common and special. There is a difference between the ordinary and common gifts of the Spirit. For some of the ordinary gifts of the Spirit are not common gifts of the Spirit. Saving faith and saving love and hope are ordinary gifts of the Spirit, but they are not common gifts of the Spirit. They are such gifts as God ordinarily bestows on his church in all ages; but they are not common to godly and ungodly, for they are peculiar to the godly. And the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit are common gifts, such as the gift of prophecy, the gift of tongues. Though they are extraordinary gifts of the Spirit, yet they are common

<!-- p. 154 -->

gifts of the Spirit; for they are not ordinarily bestowed on the Christian church but only on extraordinary occasions, yet they are common to good and bad. Many bad men have had these gifts. Many will say at the last day, "Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?" [Matthew 7:22]. Such as these, who will plead that they have had extraordinary gifts of the Spirit, but no special and saving gifts of the Spirit.[^004-note41] By this you may better understand the meaning of the doctrine. I proceed now

II. To observe that the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit of God are indeed great privileges. When God endows anyone with a spirit of prophecy and favors him with immediate inspiration, or when he gives any a power of working miracles, healing the sick, casting out devils, and the like, these are great privileges which God bestows on men; they are the highest kind of privileges which he bestows on men next to saving grace. It is a great privilege to live in the enjoyment of the outward means of grace, and to be one who belongs to the visible church; but to be a prophet, or worker of miracles in the church, is yet a much greater privilege. It is a great privilege to hear the word which he has spoken by prophets and inspired persons; but a much greater for persons themselves to be the prophets who shall speak the word, and those who are inspired by God to make known his mind and will to others. It was a great privilege which God bestowed on Moses when he called him to be a prophet, and made him the instrument to reveal the Law to the children of Israel, and of delivering to the church so great a part of the written Word of God, and the first standing written revelation which was ever delivered to it, and in making him the instrument of working so many wonders in Egypt, and at the Red Sea, and in the wilderness. Great was the privilege which God bestowed on David in inspiring him, and making him the penman of so great and excellent a part of his Word for the use of the church in all ages, as he was of a great part of the book of Psalms. Great were the privileges which God bestowed on those great prophets Elijah and Elisha in enduing them with so much of his Spirit in the extraordinary gifts of it, and working so many miracles by them. The privilege was very great which God bestowed on Daniel, in giving so much of the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit, and giving him such understanding in the visions of God. This procured him great honor among

<!-- p. 155 -->

the heathen, and in the court of the King of Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar, that great, and mighty, and haughty monarch, so admired Daniel for it that he was about to worship him as a God. Daniel 2:46, "Then the king Nebuchadnezzar fell upon his face, and worshipped Daniel, and commanded that they should offer an oblation and sweet odors unto him." God honored Daniel herein above all the wise men, the magicians, astrologers, and soothsayers of Babylon, and caused the king and others to honor him above them. And now honorably does the queen speak of Daniel to Belshazzar on this account. Daniel 5:11–12, "There is a man in thy kingdom, in whom is the spirit of the holy gods; and in the days of thy father light and understanding, and wisdom, like the wisdom of the gods, was found in him; whom the king Nebuchadnezzar, thy father, the king, I say, thy father, made master of the magicians, astrologers, Chaldeans, and soothsayers. Forasmuch as an excellent spirit, and knowledge, and understanding, interpreting of dreams, and showing of hard sentences, and dissolving of doubts were found in the same Daniel, whom the king named Belteshazzar; now let Daniel be called, and he will show the interpretation." This privilege was very much the thing which gave Daniel also honor in the Persian court. It is said in the beginning of the sixth chapter [Daniel 6:1–3], that "it pleased Darius to set over the kingdom an hundred and twenty princes, which should be over the whole kingdom; and over these three presidents, of whom Daniel was first: that the princes might give accounts unto them, and the king should have no damage. Then this Daniel was preferred above the presidents and princes, because an excellent spirit was in him; and the king thought to set him over the whole realm." By that excellent spirit seems to be meant chiefly that spirit of prophecy and divine revelation, which he had; the same for which he had been so honored by the princes of Babylon.

It was a great privilege which Christ bestowed on the apostles in so filling them with extraordinary gifts of the Holy Ghost, inspiring them to teach all nations, and to be, as it were, next to Christ, the twelve precious stones which are called the twelve foundations of the church. Revelation 21:14, "And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and in them the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb." Ephesians 2:20, "Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone." And how highly was the apostle John favored when he was in the Spirit on the Lord's day, and had such extraordinary visions representing the great events of God's providence towards the church in all ages of it to the end of the world.

<!-- p. 156 -->

Such extraordinary gifts of the Spirit are spoken of in Scripture as extraordinary privileges. So was the privilege which God bestowed on Moses in speaking to him by way of extraordinary, miraculous revelation, as it were face to face. It was foretold as a great privilege which God would bestow on the Christian church in the early times of the gospel, that the spirit of prophecy should be poured out upon them in the before mentioned place in Joel. Christ spake of the gift of working miracles, and the gift of tongues, as great privileges which he would bestow upon them who should believe on him. Mark 16:17–18, "And these signs shall follow them that believe; in my name shall they cast out devils; they shall speak with new tongues. They shall take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not hurt them; they shall lay hands on the sick, and they shall recover." When God endues any persons with such gifts he puts great honor upon them. He makes them the instruments by which he speaks or works. Moses and Aaron were envied in the camp, because of the peculiar honor which God put upon them. Psalms 106:16, "They envied Moses also in the camp, and Aaron, the saint of the Lord." And so Joshua was ready to envy Eldad and Medad because they prophesied in the camp, Numbers 11:27. And when the angels themselves have been sent to do the work of prophets, to reveal things to come, it has been spoken of as a great privilege bestowed on them. The apostle John himself, in his great surprise, was once and again ready to fall down and worship the angel who was sent by Christ to reveal to him the future events of the church. The angel forbids him, acknowledging that the privilege which he had of the spirit of prophecy was not of himself, but that he had received it of Jesus Christ. Revelation 19:10, "And I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said unto me, See thou do it not. I am thy fellow servant and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus; worship God; for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy." And ch. Revelation 22:8–9, "And I John saw these things, and heard them. And when I had heard and seen, I fell down to worship before the feet of the angel which showed me these things. Then saith he unto me, See thou do it not; for I am thy fellow servant, and of thy brethren the prophets, and of them which keep the sayings of this book; worship God." The heathen of Lystra were so astonished at the power which Barnabas and Paul had to work miracles that they were about to offer sacrifice to them as Gods, Acts 14:11–13. Simon the sorcerer had a great desire for that gift which the apostles had of conferring the Holy Ghost by laying on their hands, and offered them money for it.

These extraordinary gifts are great privileges, as there is in them a

<!-- p. 157 -->

conformity to Christ in his prophetical office. And the greatness of the privilege appears in this, that, though they were sometimes bestowed on natural men, yet far more rarely. And commonly such as have had them bestowed have been only saints; yea, and the most eminent saints, except at that extraordinary time of the pouring out of the Spirit after Christ's ascension. 2 Peter 1:21, "Holy men of old spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost." These gifts have commonly been bestowed as tokens of God's extraordinary favor and love, as it was with Daniel. He was a man greatly beloved, and therefore was admitted to such a great privilege of having these revelations made to him, Daniel 9:23 and Daniel 10:11, Daniel 10:19. And the apostle John was the disciple whom Jesus loved, and therefore he was chosen from among all the apostles to be the man to whom those great revelations were made, of which we have an account in the book of Revelation.[^004-note42] I come now in the third place[^004-note43]

III. To show that though these are great privileges, yet that the ordinary influences of the Spirit of God working grace in the heart is a far greater privilege than any of them; a greater privilege than the spirit of prophecy, or the gift of tongues, or working miracles even to the moving of mountains; a greater blessing than all those miraculous gifts which Moses, and Elijah, and Daniel, and the twelve apostles were endued with. This will appear if we consider

*First*. This blessing of the saving grace of God is a quality inherent in the nature of him who is the subject of it. This gift of the Spirit of God, working a saving Christian temper and exciting gracious exercises, confers a blessing which has its seat in the heart; a blessing which makes a man's heart and nature excellent. Yea, the very excellency of the nature consists in it. Now it is not so with respect to those extraordinary gifts of the Spirit. They are excellent things, but not properly the excellency of a man's nature; for they are not things which are inherent in the nature. For instance, if a man is endued with a gift of working miracles, that

<!-- p. 158 -->

power is not anything inherent in his nature. It is not properly any quality of the heart and nature of the man, as true grace and holiness are. And though most commonly those who have these extraordinary gifts of prophecy, speaking with tongues, and working miracles have been holy persons, yet their holiness did not consist in their having these gifts; but holiness consists in having grace in the heart: grace and holiness are the same thing. Extraordinary gifts are nothing properly inherent in the man. They are something adventitious. They are excellent things; but they are not properly excellencies in the nature of the subject, any more than the garments are which he wears. Extraordinary gifts of the Spirit are, as it were, precious jewels, which a man carries about him. But true grace in the heart is, as it were, the preciousness of the heart, by which it becomes precious or excellent; by which the very soul itself becomes a precious jewel.

*Second*. The Spirit of God communicates itself much more in bestowing saving grace than in bestowing those extraordinary gifts. In those extraordinary gifts of the Spirit the Holy Ghost does indeed produce effects in the man, or by the man; but not so as properly to communicate himself in his own proper nature to the man. A man may have an extraordinary influence on his mind by the Spirit of God, whereby some future thing may be revealed to him; or he may have an extraordinary vision given him, representing some future event; and yet the Spirit not in the least impart itself in its holy nature by that. The Spirit of God may produce effects on many things to which it does not communicate itself. So the Spirit of God moved on the face of the waters, but not so as to impart himself[^004-note44] to the waters. But when the Spirit by his ordinary influences bestows saving grace, he therein imparts himself to the soul in his own holy nature; that nature on account of which he is so often called in Scripture the Holy Ghost, or the Holy Spirit. By his producing this effect the Spirit becomes an indwelling vital principle in the soul, and the subject becomes a spiritual being, denominated so from the Spirit of God which dwells in him and of whose nature he is a partaker [2 Peter 1:4]. Yea, grace is as it were the holy nature of the Spirit of God imparted to the soul. But the extraordinary gift of the Spirit, such as showing things to come, or having a power to work miracles, does not imply this holy nature; not but that when God gives the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit, he is commonly wont to give the [[ordinary]] influences of the Spirit

<!-- p. 159 -->

with it; but one does not imply the other. And if God gives only extraordinary gifts of prophecy and of working miracles, these alone will never make him a partaker of the Spirit so as to become spiritual in himself and in his own nature.[^004-note45]

*Third*. That grace and holiness, which is the effect of the ordinary influence of the Spirit of God on the hearts of the saints, is that in which the spiritual image of God[^004-note46] consists, and not in those extraordinary gifts of the Spirit. The spiritual image of God does not consist in having a power to work miracles, and foretell future events; but it consists in our being holy, as God is holy; in having a holy and divine principle in the heart, and[^004-note47] gracious and heavenly [[lives]]. Indeed there is a kind of assimilation to Christ in having a power of working miracles; for Christ had such a power, and wrought multitudes of miracles. John 14:12, "The works that I do he shall do also." But the amiable image and likeness of Christ does much more consist in our having the same mind in us which was in Christ, in having the same spirit which he was of, in being meek and lowly of heart, of a spirit of Christian love, and walking as Christ walked. This makes a man more like Christ than if he could work ever so many miracles.

*Fourth*. That grace which is the effect of the ordinary influence of the Spirit of God is a privilege which God bestows only on his own favorites and children. But the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit are not so. It has been before observed that God most commonly has chosen [saints], and eminent saints, upon whom he bestows extraordinary gifts of the Spirit, yet not always. But these gifts are some of the common gifts of the Spirit. They have been common to both godly and ungodly. Balaam is stigmatized in Scripture as a wicked man (see 2 Peter 2:15, Jude 11, Revelation 2:14). And yet he had extraordinary gifts of the Spirit of God for a time. He

<!-- p. 160 -->

foretold many things.[^004-note48] Saul was a wicked man; but we read once and again of his being among the prophets [1 Samuel 10:11; 1 Samuel 19:24]. Judas was one of those whom Christ sent forth to preach and work miracles. He was one of those twelve disciples of whom it is said as in Matthew 10:1, "And when he had called unto him his twelve disciples, he gave them power against unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal all manner of sickness and all manner of disease." And in the next verse we are told who they were, and the names of all are rehearsed, and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him, is mentioned with them. And in the eighth verse Christ says to them, "Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, raise the dead, cast out devils." The grace of God in the heart is a gift of the Holy Ghost peculiar to the saints. It is a blessing which God reserves only for those who are the objects of his special and peculiar love. But the extraordinary gifts are what God sometimes bestows on those for whom he has no love, but whom he hates; which is a sure sign that the other is an infinitely more precious and excellent gift than these. That is the most precious gift which is most of an evidence of God's love. But the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit were no sure sign of it. The prophets were not wont to build their hope of the favor and love of God on their being prophets, and having revelations; but on their being sincere saints. Thus David in the Psalms built his hopes of God's favor from his sincerity in grace, and not his privilege as being a prophet. See Psalms 17 at the beginning; and many places in the hundred-nineteenth Psalm and throughout the book of Psalms. So though the apostle Paul was so extraordinarily privileged with the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit, yet we do not find him comforting himself in these as signs of God's love,[^004-note49] so much as his being a sincere Christian, his having [faith] in him, and his having committed himself to him who was able to keep that which he had committed to him against that day, 2 Timothy 1:12; in his having fought a good fight [2 Timothy 4:7], his having sold all for Christ, and suffering the loss of all things if by any means he might attain unto the resurrection of the dead [Philippians 3:8, Philippians 3:11], and in his so running, not as uncertainly [1 Corinthians 9:26]. Hence we may argue

*Fifth*. From the infinitely more excellent fruit of that grace, which is

<!-- p. 161 -->

the effect of the ordinary gifts of the Spirit, than of the extraordinary gifts, since grace is saving but those extraordinary gifts are not.[^004-note50] The Apostle tells us in the text that those extraordinary gifts of the Spirit profit nothing without charity. A man may have them and go to hell. Judas Iscariot had them, and is gone to hell. And Christ tells us of many, who have had these extraordinary gifts, whom he will bid in that day to depart from him as workers of iniquity. Matthew 7:22–23, "Many will say unto me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works? And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you; depart from me, ye that work iniquity." And therefore when Christ promised the disciples the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit, such as casting out devils, and other extraordinary gifts, he bids them not to rejoice that the devils were subject to them; but rather that they should rejoice because their names were written in heaven; intimating that men may have this power of casting out devils, and their names not be written in heaven, Luke 10:20. This shows that grace which is the effect of the ordinary gift of the Spirit is infinitely a greater blessing than the extraordinary, since it carries eternal life in it. Eternal life is a thing of infinite worth and value. And that must be an excellent blessing indeed which has this as the fruit of it. The value of any possession is known by the fruit or profit which is obtained by it. Ecclesiastes 7:8, "Better is the end of a thing, than the beginning thereof." By this therefore, that blessing of the grace of God which is the fruit of the ordinary gifts of the Spirit is infinitely more precious than that of the extraordinary gifts.

*Sixth*. Happiness itself does more immediately and essentially consist in Christian grace wrought by the ordinary influences of the Spirit in the saints than in those extraordinary influences. Man's highest happiness consists in holiness. It is by this the reasonable creature is united to God, the fountain of all good. Happiness does so essentially consist in knowing and loving and serving God, and having a holy and divine temper of soul, and the lively exercises of it, that those things will make a man happy without anything else. But no other enjoyments or privileges whatever will make a man happy without this.

*Seventh*. This gift of the Spirit, which is the fruit of the ordinary influence of the Spirit in the saints, is the end of all extraordinary gifts of the Holy Ghost. God gave such gifts as prophecy, and the working of miracles, and speaking with tongues to the end to promote and establish true

<!-- p. 162 -->

religion, and propagate the gospel. And the end of promulgating the gospel is that men might be turned from sin to God, that they might be brought to be partakers of the grace of God, and that true holiness might be promoted. The end of all extraordinary gifts of the Spirit is the conversion of sinners, and the building up of saints in that holiness, which is the fruit of the ordinary influences of the Spirit. For this the Apostle had suffered the loss of all things; and for this were so many endued with the gifts of prophecy, the working of miracles, and speaking with tongues. This we are taught in Ephesians 4:11–12, "And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ." Here the extraordinary gifts are mentioned, and then we are told what the end is why they are given.[^004-note51] What kind of edifying of the body of Christ this is, we learn in ver. Ephesians 4:16, "From whom the whole body fitly joined together, and compacted by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part, maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love"; in love, which is the same thing with that charity mentioned in the text, and also in ch. 1 Corinthians 8:1, "Charity edifieth." But the end is more excellent than the means, by an universally allowed maxim. For the means has no goodness in it otherwise than as subservient to the end. The end, therefore, must be considered as superior in excellency.[^004-note52]

*Eighth*. The extraordinary gifts of the Spirit will be so far from profiting without that grace, which is the effect of the ordinary gifts of the Spirit, that it will but aggravate the condemnation of those who have them. Doubtless Judas' condemnation was exceedingly aggravated by his having been one who had had such privileges. And some who have had such extraordinary gifts have committed the sin against the Holy Ghost; and their having such privileges has been a principal thing which has rendered their sin the unpardonable sin, as appears from what the Apostle says, Hebrews 6:4–6, "For it is impossible for those, who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers

<!-- p. 163 -->

of the Holy Ghost, and have tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come, if they shall fall away, to renew them again unto repentance; seeing they crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh, and put him to an open shame." Those who fell away, of whom the Apostle here speaks, were those who apostatized from Christianity, who had formerly been professing Christians, and had the extraordinary gifts of the Holy Ghost, as most Christians in that day had. And[^004-note53] most of those things here mentioned, as their tasting of the heavenly gift and the like, mean the extraordinary gifts of the Holy Ghost, and not any saving influences of the Spirit.

And because this place of Scripture is an occasion of much stumbling and difficulty to many, I would here be a little particular in explaining it. And if we observe the foregoing verses, the meaning of the words will appear plain to us. In the three foregoing verses the Apostle exhorts those who have begun in Christianity to go on and make progress in it to higher attainments; that when we have once laid the foundation, we should go on and build the superstructure, and not lay the foundation again, not be always only beginning and laying the first foundation of Christianity, and so have occasion to lay it a second time. Hebrews 6:1, "Therefore leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection; not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith towards God." The foundation or beginning and first setting out in Christianity consists in these things: in repentance from dead works, and faith towards God, which foundation was laid when they first turned from their wicked ways and embraced Christianity. And next, here is mentioned the doctrine of baptism and of laying on of hands; that is, those doctrines or first principles which they were taught when they were baptized, and the apostles laid on their hands, that they might receive the Holy Ghost. We learn by the history of the New Testament that that was the manner when any were converted to Christianity for them first to be baptized, and then some of the apostles came and laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Ghost; that is, they received the Holy Ghost in extraordinary gifts, such as prophecy, the gift of tongues, and working of miracles. So it was given, you know, in Samaria [Acts 8:11–24].

<!-- p. 164 -->

And therefore when the Apostle speaks of the doctrine of baptisms and of laying on of hands, he means those first principles which they were taught when they were baptized, and had hands laid on them to receive the Holy Ghost at their first beginning, or laying the foundation of Christianity. And then the Apostle mentions several of those doctrines, viz. the resurrection of the dead, and the eternal judgment. What the apostles used chiefly to insist on in their preaching to Jews and heathens was the resurrection of the dead; that is, that Christ was risen from the dead, and would raise all mankind, and would come to judge the quick and dead, as you may see in Acts. And then when they were indoctrinated in those things, then they were baptized, and the apostles laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Ghost in his miraculous influences.

Now the Apostle would not have them after they had thus laid the foundation fall away, and so have the foundation to lay again. And he makes use of this as an argument to warn them, viz. that if they fell away after this, after they had been so indoctrinated in Christianity, and baptized, and had hands laid on them, and had received the Holy Ghost in his extraordinary gifts, that they would commit the sin against the Holy Ghost, as many had done. For, says the Apostle, it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, that is, indoctrinated in Christianity, taught the principles of the oracles of God, and brought out of heathenish or Jewish darkness, so as to understand and embrace Christianity. This is evidently what the Apostle in this epistle means by being enlightened or illuminated, as appears by ch. Hebrews 10:32, "But call to remembrance the former days, in which, after ye were illuminated, ye endured a great fight of afflictions." "Tasted of the heavenly gift"; that is, had received those extraordinary gifts of the Holy Ghost in the apostles' laying their hands on them, as was before said.[^004-note54] [To prepare them for

<!-- p. 165 -->

baptism, plain instructions were given them in the first principles of religion that they first began with. 'Tis probable that most of those who tasted the heavenly gifts and were everywhere made partakers of the Holy Ghost, in the laying on of hands and baptism, were true saints. Yet when this was not accompanied by gracious affections it was always accompanied with great common illuminations and common religious affections. 'Tis not probable that they should have the Holy Ghost with respect to his miraculous influences, and not feel anything of the power of it in their souls.] So Acts 19:2, "Have ye received the Holy Ghost since ye believed?"[^004-note55] And so "being made partakers of the powers of the world to come";[^004-note56] [meaning they felt the power of the invisible agent of that world upon their minds]." Tasted the good word of God"; meaning those common illuminations which were wont to accompany[^004-note57] [extraordinary gifts]. For though some who had those extraordinary[^004-note58] [gifts] had not saving illuminations, yet probably they had always great common[^004-note59] [convictions, illuminations, and affections]. They had tasted the good word of God in that sense that those in Matthew 13:20 hear the word of God, and anon with joy receive it.[^004-note60] Balaam,

<!-- p. 166 -->

when he had[^004-note61] [beaten his ass to get by the Lord's forbidding, came nevertheless to say, "Let me die the death of the righteous," Numbers 23:10, and to praise the tents, tabernacles, valleys and gardens of the Lord, Numbers 24:5–6. Yet he was a stonyhearted hearer. So also was Saul, of whom it is said, "And the Spirit of the Lord shall come upon thee and thou shalt prophesy with them and shall be turned into another man," 1 Samuel 10:6. Balaam and Saul had extraordinary gifts and probably also great common illuminations. Yet neither had "root in himself, but dureth for a while" and by and by was offended, and willfully sinned against the Holy Ghost.][^004-note62]

*Ninth*. And lastly. Another thing which shows the preferableness of the ordinary gifts of the Spirit to the extraordinary gifts of it is that the one will last, the other will not. This argument the Apostle uses in the context to show that divine love is preferable to those extraordinary gifts. Ver. 1 Corinthians 13:8, ["Charity never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away"]. Divine love will remain throughout all eternity. But these extraordinary gifts are only certain means of grace for the converting of sinners and fitting saints for glory. But when that end is obtained, they shall cease; but divine love shall still remain. But possibly more of this at another opportunity.[^004-note63] I now hasten to the

*Improvement*

Use may be of instruction.

*First*. If it be so as we have heard, that[^004-note64] [[saving grace is a greater blessing than the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit,]] we may doubtless hence argue that saving grace in the heart is the greatest privilege and blessing which God ever bestows on any persons in this world. For those

<!-- p. 167 -->

extraordinary gifts of the Holy Ghost such as the gift of prophecy, of tongues, and the working of miracles, are the highest kind of privileges which God ever bestows on natural men, and privileges which have been very rarely bestowed on such, unless [in the apostolic age].[^004-note65]

What greater privileges does God ever bestow on natural men than the gifts of inspiration, prophecy, and working of miracles? The saving grace of God in the heart, working a holy and divine temper of soul in the [[gift]] of faith and love must doubtless be the greatest blessing that ever men receive in this world; greater than any of the gifts of natural men, greater than the greatest natural abilities, greater than any acquired endowments of mind, greater than any attainments in learning, greater than any outward worth or honor, and a greater privilege than to be kings and emperors. Great was the privilege which God bestowed on David in taking him from the sheepcote, from following the sheep, and making him ruler over Israel. Great was the privilege which God bestowed on Solomon [in choosing him to build an house for the name of the Lord, 1 Chronicles 28:10; 2 Chronicles 2:1].[^004-note66]

<!-- p. 168 -->

"Then one said unto him, Behold, thy mother and thy brethren stand without desiring to speak with thee. But he answered and said unto him that told him, Who is my mother? and Who are my brethren? And he stretched forth his hand toward his disciples and said, Behold my mother, and my brethren. For whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother."

 Great was the privilege which God bestowed on the blessed virgin Mary, in granting that of her should be born the Son of God; that a person who was infinitely more honorable than the angels, who was the Creator and King of heaven and earth and the great Savior of the world, should be conceived in her womb, born of her, and nursed at her breast, was a far greater privilege than to be the mother of the child of the greatest earthly prince that ever existed. But yet, surely that was not so great a privilege as it was to have the grace of God in the heart, to have Christ, as it were, born in the soul, as Christ himself does expressly teach us. Luke 11:27–28, "And it came to pass as he spake these things, a certain woman of the company lifted up her voice, and said unto him, Blessed is the womb that bare thee, and the paps which thou has sucked. But he said, Yea, rather blessed are they that hear the word of God, and keep it." And once when some told him that his mother and brethren stood without desiring to speak with him, he thence took occasion to let them know that there was a more blessed way of being related to him than that which consisted in being his mother and brethren according to the flesh, viz. in having grace in the heart, and bringing forth the fruits of it in the life. Matthew 12:47–50, *Second*. Hence these two kinds of privileges are not to be considered by taking things which have some appearance of an extraordinary miraculous gift of the Spirit for sure signs of saving grace. As if persons at any time have some extraordinary impressions made upon their minds, which, they think, are from God, and are to reveal something to them which shall come to pass hereafter. This, if it were real, would argue an extraordinary gift of the Holy Ghost, viz. the gift of prophecy; and the doctrine shows that it would be no certain sign[^004-note67] of grace, nor anything saving, though it were real; though indeed we have no reason to look on such things, when pretended to in these days, as any other than delusions. So if at any time persons think they have an impression made on their minds, revealing something to them which is not revealed in the Bible, nor can be found out by reason only, but only they have an impression that such or such a thing is, that they are converted, or that another is converted, or that such an one is gone to heaven, or to hell, or that there is about to be a pouring out of the Spirit of God; if there be such impressions that are real, they are of the nature of an extraordinary gift of the Spirit. They are such inspiration as the prophets had, and therefore weight is not to be laid to them as anything saving. And it is the same thing, if persons think they have a spiritual communication to their minds, to reveal some particular event to come to pass hereafter, or something that is otherwise secret, weight is not to be laid to it.

Scriptures, when they come to the mind, let them come ever so suddenly, and with ever so great impression, are not to be taken as revealing any more to us than is contained in them as they lie in the Bible; that is, a scripture coming to the mind proves no more to be true than reading it proves. If reading any text of Scripture at any time, and at all times, as it lies in the Bible does not prove such a thing, then its coming suddenly into the mind does not prove it. For the scripture speaks just the same thing at one time that it does at another. The words have the same meaning when they are read in course as they have when they are suddenly

<!-- p. 169 -->

brought to the mind; and if any man therefore argues anything further from them, he proceeds without warrant. If any man thinks that such and such a thing will come to pass, because such a scripture came to his mind on such an occasion, if the scripture as it is to be read in the Bible does not prove it, he argues too much from it. So, if anyone thinks that he is in a good estate, because such a text of Scripture came suddenly to his mind, if the text does not prove it as it lies in the Bible, and if it would not have proved it if he had only read it in course, then he cannot know by that scripture coming to his mind that he is in a good estate, unless it be by way of immediate extraordinary revelation, in the way of an extraordinary gift of the Holy Ghost, which is not now to be expected.[^004-note68]

So, if anything appears to persons as though they had a vision of some visible appearance, and heard some voice, such things are not to be taken as signs of grace; for if they are real, and from God, they are not grace but extraordinary gifts of the Spirit, which we have shown are not saving. All the fruit of the Spirit, upon which we are to lay weight as evidential of grace, is summed up in charity or Christian love, because this is the sum of all grace. And the way, therefore, that we and all others are to argue is by discerning[^004-note69] the exercises of grace in our hearts, some exercise of this divine charity, and comparing this with the rule of God's Word, and so to conclude our good estate. The prophets and apostles themselves, who so abounded in extraordinary gifts of the Spirit, took this way to satisfy themselves of their good estate, and did argue[^004-note70] [[by discerning the exercises of this divine charity in their hearts]]. Not but

<!-- p. 170 -->

that God may and doubtless often does direct persons' thoughts to such and such scripture, to that end, to stir up the exercises of grace, to give some spiritual discovery of God and Christ, and excite the exercises of faith and love, and Christian submission and thankfulness. And when he does so, then that exercise of grace which is excited by Scripture is a sign of saving grace; because this is comprehended in that charity which is the fruit of the ordinary influences of the Spirit.[^004-note71]

*Third*. If it be as we have heard, then we cannot conclude from what the Scripture says of the gloriousness of the future times of the church that in those times there will be any extraordinary gifts of the Spirit of God. Many have been ready to think that in those glorious times of the church, which shall be after the calling of the Jews[^004-note72] and the destruction of Antichrist,[^004-note73] there will be many persons who will be inspired, and will be endued with a power of working miracles. But what the Scripture says of the gloriousness of those times does not prove any such thing, or make it probable. For by the doctrine we learn that the pouring out of

<!-- p. 171 -->

the Spirit of God in his ordinary saving operations to fill men's hearts with a Christian and holy temper, and leading them to the exercises of a divine life, is the most glorious way of pouring out the Spirit, more glorious than a pouring out of the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit. And therefore the glory of those times of the church does not require any such thing as the pouring out of the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit. Those times may be far the most glorious times of the church, that ever have been, without them. Their not having the gifts of tongues and of working miracles as they had in the apostles' times will not hinder their being far more glorious times than the apostles' times were, if the Spirit be poured out in greater measures in his sanctifying influences; for this, the Apostle expressly says in the last words before the text, is a more excellent way. This glory is the greatest glory of the church of Christ, and of any times of that church. This glory is what will make the church more like the church in heaven, where charity or love has a perfect reign, than any measure or degree of the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit could do. So that we have no reason upon this account, and perhaps not on any other, to expect that there will [be][^004-note74] any pouring out of the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit; for there will be no new dispensation to be made.[^004-note75] We have no reason to expect any new communication of Scripture to be made or

<!-- p. 172 -->

the Scripture to be added to and enlarged. In the end of this canon it seems to be intimated it will not be added to. Revelation, last verses: "For I testify unto every man that heareth the words of the prophecy of this book, If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues, that are written in this book. And if any man shall take away from the words of this prophecy, God shall take away his part out of the book of life, and out of the holy city, and from the things which are written in this book" [Revelation 22:18–19].

*Fourth*.[^004-note76] What cause have they to bless God and live to his glory who have received such a privilege, if we do but seriously consider of it? The godly, those who have that inestimable blessing, have cause to bless God which cannot be expressed. The[^004-note77] more we consider it, the more wonderful and inexpressible will it appear. When we read over the history of Moses, and how God appeared to him, and what wonderful works were wrought by his hands, and how he went up into the holy Mount, etc., etc. And when we read the history of Elijah, Elisha, Daniel, the Virgin Mary, the apostle Paul who was caught up to the third heaven, and consider what privileges these had and what high honors were done them, we are ready to admire at the greatness of those privileges by which they were distinguished from the others. But all those extraordinary privileges, considered in themselves, separately from the saving grace of God, are nothing compared to this.

Let those, therefore, who are thus highly favored, consider more than ever yet they have done, how great that blessing is which God has bestowed upon them of his mere free love and sovereign grace, and not for any worthiness of theirs; and how great obligations they are under to glorify God: and to glorify Christ, who hath purchased this blessing with his own blood.[^004-note78] What manner of persons ought you to be! pray consider it! Do you hope that God has thus highly advanced and exalted you? And will you not be careful indeed to live to his glory, and to exalt and magnify his name? Will you dishonor Christ, who has thus honored you? Will you regard him but a little, who has shown such infinite regard to your welfare? Shall the world have your heart, and Christ and his glory be neglected after all? Will you not rather watch against your corrupt, worldly, proud dispositions? Will you not seek opportunities to do something

<!-- p. 173 -->

for God, who, as you think, has been thus kind to you? And for that Savior, who has purchased this, at the cost of such extreme sufferings? And that for you— worms!— vipers! Will you not every day, with the Psalmist, be ready to say, as in Psalms 116:12, "What shall I render unto the Lord for all his benefits towards me?" What could God have done more for you? What privileges can you think of now, that would have been better, and more worthy to engage your heart in gratitude and thankfulness, and in all holy living? And consider, how you live! How little you do for God! How little for his honor! How much to his dishonor! How little this lies with weight upon your heart, that you may do something for God and Christ! Consider how you ought to live, and the inexpressible obligations you are under to live so. And then consider how you do live, and how vast the distance is. How should such as you, who are so highly privileged, at all times carry towards God, in all filial love, thankfulness, strict obedience, quiet submission! And how should you live towards your neighbors, walking humbly, inoffensively, meekly, charitably, doing good to all, to their souls and bodies as you have opportunity, always fervent in spirit, serving the Lord, with the greatest and most earnest diligence.[^004-note79]

<!-- p. 174 -->

### SERMON THREE: NOTHING CAN MAKE UP FOR WANT OF SINCERITY IN THE HEART

> *And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing*.

I CORINTHIANS 13:3.IN the former verses the necessity and excellency of charity was set forth by its preference to the greatest privileges, and the vanity and insignificance of those privileges without it. The privileges particularly mentioned are those which consist in the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit of God, which are the highest kind of privileges which are ever bestowed on natural men. In this verse things of another nature are mentioned, viz. those which are of a moral nature; and it is declared that none of those are anything without charity. And particularly,

1. That no performances can avail without it. Here is one of the highest kinds of external performances mentioned, viz. a man's giving all his goods to feed the poor. Giving to the poor is a duty very much insisted on in the Word of God, and particularly under the Christian dispensation. And the case and circumstances of the church in the primitive times of Christianity were such that persons were sometimes called to part with all they had and to give it to others, both because of the extreme necessities of many Christians in their persecuted circumstances; and also because the difficulties which attended being a follower of Christ and doing the work of the gospel to which they were called, were such as called for a person's disentangling himself from the affairs and embarrassments of worldly possessions, and to go forth, as it were, without gold or silver, or brass in their purse, or scrip, or two coats apiece [Luke 10:4].[^004-note80] The apostle Paul tells us that he had suffered the loss of all

<!-- p. 175 -->

things for Christ, and so the primitive Christians in the church at Jerusalem sold all that they had and gave it into a common stock, and none said that aught that he had was his own, Acts 4:32. The duty of giving to the poor was a duty which the Christian Corinthians at this time had particular occasion to consider of, as also many other churches in that and the neighboring country, by reason of a great dearth or famine which sorely distressed the brethren in Judea; on which occasion the Apostle had already moved it to the Corinthians, as their duty, to send relief to them, and is particular in speaking of it in this epistle, and particularly in the sixteenth chapter; and also insists on it in his second[^004-note81] epistle to the same church throughout the eighth and ninth chapters. And though the Apostle says so much in both these epistles to stir them up to the duty of giving to the poor, yet he here takes care to inform them that, let them go ever so far in it, yea, though they should bestow all their goods to feed to the poor, and had not charity, it would profit them nothing.

2. He teaches them that not only no performance but also no suffering would avail anything without charity. Men are ready to make much of what they do, but more of what they suffer. They are ready to think it a great thing when they put themselves much out of their way, or are at great expense and suffering in religion. The Apostle here mentions a suffering of the most extreme kind, suffering even to death, and that one of the most terrible sorts of death, and says it is nothing without charity. When a man has given away all his goods, he has nothing remaining which he can give but himself. And the Apostle teaches us that if a man does not only give his possessions, but when he has done that proceeds further, and gives his own body, and that to be utterly consumed in the flames, it would avail nothing if the heart is withheld. The time at which the Apostle wrote to the Corinthians was a time when Christians were often called not only to give their goods but their bodies. The church then was generally under persecution, and Christians were often persecuted unto death, and then, or not long after, many were put to very cruel deaths. Many were called to many and great sufferings in life, but to suffer a cruel death was the greatest thing that they were called to go through. But this would not avail without charity. What is meant by this charity has been already fully explained in former discourses from this

<!-- p. 176 -->

and the preceding verses. In what has been said in those discourses, it has been shown that charity is the sum of sincere, distinguishing religion of the heart. And here[^004-note82] the doctrine, which I would observe from the words, is this.

*Doctrine*

*All which men can do, and all which they can suffer, will not make up for the want of sincerity in the heart*.

*Prop*. I. There may be great performances and great sufferings without sincerity.[^004-note83]

*First*. There may be great performances without sincerity. Nothing that men can do in religion will ever be accepted instead of truth and uprightness. The apostle Paul in the beginning of the third chapter of Philippians tells us what things he did before his conversion, and while he remained a Pharisee; and says, ver. Philippians 3:4, "If any other man thinketh that he hath whereof he might trust in the flesh, I more." Many of the Pharisees did great things. They abounded in religious performances. The Pharisee mentioned in Luke 18:11–12 boasted of great things which he did both towards God and towards men, and thanked God that he so exceeded other men. "The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God I thank thee, that I am not as other men are."

Many of the heathen have been eminent for moral performances. Some of them have been eminent for justice, and others for their great deeds which they have done for the public good. Many men without any sincerity in their hearts, and that have in some other respects been vicious men, have been exceedingly munificent in their gifts for pious and charitable uses, and have got themselves a great fame by it, and their names have made a great figure in history on this account, and have been handed down to posterity with great glory. Many have done great things from fears of hell, hoping thereby to appease the Deity, and make atonement for their sins; and many have done great things from pride and from vainglory. And though these things are not wont to influence men to a constant and universal respect to God's commands, and to carry along an even thread of Christian performances and practice of all duties towards God and men through the course of a man's life, yet it is hard to say how far natural principles may carry men in particular duties and performances.

<!-- p. 177 -->

*Second*. There may be great sufferings in religion, and yet no sincerity. Persons may undergo great suffering in life, as the Pharisees, some of them, used themselves to great severities; and many among the Pharisees put themselves to severe penance and many voluntary afflictions. Many have undertaken wearisome pilgrimages, and have shut themselves out from the comforts and pleasures of the society of mankind, and have spent their lives in deserts, called recluses. And some have suffered death who there is no reason to think had any sincerity. Multitudes among the Papists have voluntarily gone and ventured their lives in bloody wars in hopes of meriting honor by it. There was formerly a war maintained with the Turks and Saracens, which was called the holy war, which was carried on in this way. Thousands went volunteers into those wars in the Pope's encouragement that they should have the pardon of their sins, and rewards in another world for it. And many thousands, yea, some millions by this means lost their lives, even to the depopulating many European countries in a considerable measure. And the Turks are, many of them, exceedingly encouraged by this to venture their lives and, as it were, to run upon the points of the swords of the enemy, because Mahomet has promised that all who die in war in defense of the Mahometan religion shall go directly to Paradise. And history gives an account of some who have yielded themselves to voluntary death out of mere stoutness or sturdiness of spirit, who have braved it out and died rather than yield to the demands of others when they might have saved their lives. And there are accounts of some who have died martyrs to false religions, though not in any way in such numbers, nor in such a manner, as those who have died martyrs to the true religion. But if many may expose themselves to death for a false religion from natural principles, so without doubt they may from the same principles expose themselves to suffer for the true religion.

*Prop*. II. Whatever men do or suffer, they cannot by all make up for the want of sincerity in the heart. If they lay out themselves ever so much, if the things which they do in religion are ever so many; if there be many acts of justice, and many acts of liberality, and many acts of devotion; if prayers and sufferings are multiplied ever so much; if men should spend their time ever so much in acts of religion, continuing night and day in it, and should deny sleep to their eyes and slumber to their eyelids, and should be ever so laborious and spend their strength in religious exercises; if the things which they did in religion were ever so great, such as to get them a name through the world, and such as should make their name famous in after generations and should perpetuate their memory

<!-- p. 178 -->

in history to the end of future ages; whatever men should give to religious or charitable uses, if a man possessed the richest kingdom, and should give all, if a wealthy prince should make himself a poor beggar, and should not stop there but when he has done all this yield himself to undergo the severest sufferings, and when he is himself stripped of all possessions and his body stripped of its princely robes, and clothed with rags instead of them, should give up that body to be mangled and tortured as much as the wit of men could invent: all would not make up for the want of sincerity in the heart, and that for the following reasons.

*Reason* 1. It is not the external work done, or the suffering undergone, that is in itself anything worth in the sight of God. The motions and exercises of the body, or anything done by it, if considered separately from the heart, the inward part of the man, are no more worth in the sight of God than the motions of anything without life. And if anything be offered or given, it is not the external thing given, whether it be silver or gold or thousands of rams, or ten thousand of rivers of oil that is anything in itself, as an external thing, of any value in the sight of God. If God stood in any need of these things, they might be of value to him in themselves considered, and separately from any sincerity of heart that they flow from. We stand in need of external good things, and therefore such things offered or given to us may be of value to us in themselves. But God stands in need of nothing. He is not fed by the sacrifices of beasts, nor is he enriched by the gifts of silver or gold, or pearls. Psalms 50:9–12, "I will take no bullock out of thy house, nor he-goats out of thy folds. For every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills. I know all the fowls of the mountains: and the wild beasts of the field are mine. If I were hungry, I would not tell thee: for the world is mine, and the fullness thereof." 1 Chronicles 29:14–16, "But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly after this sort? For all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee. For we are strangers before thee, and sojourners, as were all our fathers: our days on the earth are as a shadow, and there is none abiding. O Lord our God, all this store that we have prepared to build thee an house for thine holy name cometh of thine hand, and is all thine own." Acts 17:25, "God is not[^004-note84] worshipped with men's hands, as though he needed anything, seeing he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things."

And as there is nothing profitable to God of men's performances, so

<!-- p. 179 -->

there can be nothing amiable in his sight in a mere external work without sincerity of heart; for God sees not as man seeth. He sees the heart; that is as naked and open to him as the external actions. And therefore he sees our actions not merely as external motions as of a mere machine, or piece of clock-work; but as human actions, or the actions of rational, intelligent creatures, and voluntary or free agents; and therefore there can be no amiableness in his eyes without sincerity of heart.

So also God takes no pleasure in any sufferings which any undergo, in themselves considered. He is not profited by their sufferings, nor does he delight to see them putting themselves to sufferings, unless it be from some good principle or good end. We may need that our fellow creatures, our neighbors, should suffer for us, should help bear our burdens and put themselves to inconveniences for our sakes. But God stands in no such need of us, and therefore our sufferings are not acceptable to him, considered merely as such sufferings undergone by us. And therefore if men have not sincerity in their hearts, neither doing nor suffering, let what may be done or suffered, will make up for that defect before God. For beings are not profitable or lovely to God in themselves. They cannot make any atonement for the want of sincerity, which is the great thing that God requires of us.[^004-note85] Psalms 51:6, "Behold thou desirest truth in the inward parts: and in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom." And ver. Psalms 51:16–17, "Thou desirest not sacrifice, else would I give it: thou delightest not in burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise."

*Reason* 2. Whatever is done or suffered, yet if the heart is withheld there is nothing really given to God. The act of the man in what he does or suffers is, in this case, looked upon not as the act of a lifeless engine or machine, but as the act of an intelligent, voluntary being. For surely a machine is not properly capable of giving anything. If any thing which is without life being moved by springs or weights casts anything before us, it cannot be said to give anything to us. Harps and tinkling cymbals and other instruments of music were used of old in God's praises. But those lifeless instruments could not be said to give God anything, because they had no understanding or will, or no heart, whence that pleasant sound proceeded. So if man, that has an heart, an understanding, yet when he gives without his heart, there is no more truly given to God than if he had none. He who has no sincerity in his heart has no real respect to God in what he seems to give in his performances or sufferings.

<!-- p. 180 -->

And therefore God is not his end in what he does or gives. What is given is given to that which the man makes his end in giving. If his end be only himself, then it is given only to himself, and not to God. If his aim be his own honor, then the gift is something offered to his honor; if it be his care or worldly profit, then the gift is to these. The gift is his to whom the man's heart directs and designs it. It is the aim of the heart which makes over the gift; and if the sincere aim of the heart is not to God, then there is nothing given to God, let what may be performed or suffered. So that it would be a great absurdity to suppose that anything which can be offered or given to God can make up for the sincerity of the heart; for without sincerity of the heart there is nothing really given. Nothing cannot make up for the want of something.

*Reason* 3. The truth of this doctrine appears from this, viz. that love or charity is the sum of what God requires of us. And it is most absurd to suppose that anything can make up for the want of that which is the sum of all that God requires. Charity or love is something which has its seat in the heart, and is that in which sincerity does consist; and all that is saving and distinguishing summarily consists in it. And how can we make up for the defect when we do in effect withhold the sum total of what God requires of us? It would be an absurd thing to suppose that we can make up for the want of one thing required by offering another thing required, to make up for one debt by paying another; but more absurd still to suppose that we can make up for the whole debt without paying any, and continuing still to withhold all that is required. As to external things without the heart, God speaks of them as being not the things which he had required. Isaiah 1:12, "When ye come to appear before me, who hath required this at your hand, to tread my courts?"

*Reason* 4. If we make a great show of respect to God in what we do without sincerity in the heart, it is but dissimulation, and a practical lying unto God. It is to make a great show of respect where there is no respect in the heart, as if we could deceive God. And therefore when the children of Israel offered praises to God at the Red Sea without sincerity of heart, they are said to lie to him with their tongues. Psalms 78:36, "Nevertheless they did flatter him with their mouth, and they lied unto him with their tongues." But certainly it is absurd to suppose that men can make up for the want of sincere respect by fallacy[^004-note86] and guise, or that they can make up for the want of truth by falsehood and lying.

<!-- p. 181 -->

*Reason* 5. Let what may be done and suffered, if there be no sincerity of heart, it is all but an offering to some idol, as was observed. But that is nothing really given to God, and therefore it will follow that we give that to some other which we should give to God, and so make an idol of it. It is true that by doing great things and suffering great things something is worshiped; but it is not God that is worshiped. If men do great things and suffer great things merely out of self-love, that is but to offer that to themselves which is due to God, and so making an idol of themselves. And how absurd is it to suppose that we can make up for withholding that from God which is his due by offering something to an idol. As absurd as it is to suppose that a woman can make up for want of love to her husband by giving that which is due to her husband to another man, or that she can make up for the want of faithfulness to him by committing adultery.

*Application*

I. Use may be of self-examination. If it be so, let this put us upon examining ourselves whether or no we have sincerity of heart. There are many here present who make a profession and a show of religion, and it may be some who seem to do considerable things in religion. And possibly they may think that their suffering is considerable, that they put themselves much out of their way for God. But let us inquire whether we have sincerity of heart. Doubtless if we examine ourselves aright, we may see abundance of hypocrisy; but is there any sincerity? God abominates great things without sincerity; but he accepts and delights in little things when there is sincerity. A cup of cold water given to a disciple in sincerity is more worth in God's sight than all one's goods to feed the poor; yea, than the wealth of a kingdom given away, and besides a body offered up in the flames, without sincerity.

And God accepts also of a little sincerity. Though there be a great deal of hypocrisy, yet if there be any sincerity, that little sincerity shall not be rejected because there is so much hypocrisy with it.[^004-note87] And here it may be

<!-- p. 182 -->

profitable for you to observe that there are these four things which belong to the nature of sincerity, viz.[^004-note88]

*First*. Truth, or that there be truly that in the heart of which there is an outward show. When there is indeed that respect to God, that love, that honor, that humility, that praise, something of it, of which there is a show made in the words or in outward actions, will appear. In a beforementioned place in the fifty-first Psalm it said that God desires truth in the inward parts [ver. Psalms 51:6]. And because truth belongs to the notion of sincerity, hypocrisy its opposite is called lying in Scripture. And so a sincere person is said to be such that is such indeed as he appears to be, without guile. John 1:47, "Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile!" Examine yourself with respect to this. There is an appearance, a show in you of respect to God, of [honor, of love or of praise to him].[^004-note89] Are these things indeed in your heart, or are they only external, without any real love or charity or humble honor?

*Second*. Another thing in the nature of sincerity is freedom. Upon this account especially obedience is called evangelical,[^004-note90] or the obedience of children, not legal, slavish and forced; but that which is performed from love and with delight. God is chosen for his own sake; holiness is chosen for its own sake, and for God's sake.[^004-note91] [[Christ is chosen and followed because he is loved, and religion because it is loved, and the soul rejoices in it, finding in its duties its highest happiness and delight. Examine yourself faithfully on this point, whether or no this spirit is yours. The

[[*Third* thing belonging to the nature of this sincerity is integrity. The word signifies wholeness, intimating that where this sincerity exists God

<!-- p. 183 -->

is sought, and religion is chosen and embraced with the whole heart, and adhered to with the whole soul. Holiness is chosen with the whole heart. The whole of duty is embraced and entered upon most cordially, whether it have respect to God or to man, whether it be easy or difficult, whether it have reference to little things or great. There is a proportion and fullness in the character. The whole man is renewed. The whole body and soul and spirit are sanctified. Every member is yielded to the obedience of Christ. All the parts of the new creature are brought into subjection to his will.[^004-note92] The seeds of all holy dispositions are implanted in the soul, and they will more and more bear fruit in the performance of duty and for the glory of God. The

[[*Fourth* thing that belongs to the nature of sincerity is purity. The word "sincere" often signifies pure. So in 1 Peter 2:2, "As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby"; i.e., pure, unmixed, unadulterated. This appears in the opposition of virtue to sin. The one is spoken of as defilement, and impurity, and uncleanness; the other, as that which is free from these things. The Apostle compares sin to a body of death, or a dead body, which of all things is most polluting and defiling, while holiness is spoken of as purity, and holy pleasures as pure pleasures, and the saints in heaven as without spot before the throne of God. Inquire then whether this purity is yours, and whether in its possession you find the evidence that you sincerely love God. This subject may also[^004-note93]

[[II. Convince those who are still in an unregenerate state of their lost condition. If it be indeed so that by all you can either do or suffer you cannot make up for the want of a holy, sincere principle of love in your heart, then it will follow that you are in an undone condition till you have obtained God's regenerating grace to renew a right spirit within you; and that do what you will, or undergo and suffer what you will, you cannot be delivered from your wickedness without the converting grace of God. If you make ever so many prayers, that will not make your case less miserable unless God, by his mighty power, is pleased to give you a new heart. If you take ever so much pains in religion, and cross and deny yourself, and do or suffer ever so much, all will not avail without this.

<!-- p. 184 -->

Therefore whatever you have done, though you can look back upon a great many prayers offered and much time spent in reading and meditation, you have no reason to think that these things have made any atonement for your sins, or rendered your case any the less deplorable, or left you any other than a wretched, lost, miserable, guilty and ruined creature.

[[Natural, unrenewed men would be glad to have something to make up for the want of sincere love and real grace in their hearts, and many do great things to make up for the want of it while others are willing to suffer great things. But alas, how little does it all signify! No matter what they may do or suffer, it does not change their character; and if they build their hopes upon it, they do but delude themselves and feed upon the east wind. If such be your case, consider how miserable you will be while you live without hope in the only true source of hope, and how miserable when you come to die when the sight of the King of terrors will show the nothingness and vanity of all your doings! How miserable when you see Christ coming to judgment in the clouds of heaven! Then you will be willing to do and suffer anything that you may be accepted by him. But doings or sufferings will not avail. They will not atone for your sins, or give you God's favor, or save you from the overwhelming storms of his wrath. Rest, then, on nothing that you have done or suffered, or that you can do or suffer; but rest on Christ. Let your heart be filled with sincere love to him; and then, at the last great day, he will own you as his follower and as his friend. The subject

[[III. Exhorts all earnestly to cherish sincere Christian love in their hearts. If it be so that this is of such great and absolute necessity, then let it be the one great thing that you seek. Seek it with diligence and prayer; and seek it of God, and not of yourself. He only can bestow it. It is something far above the unassisted power of nature; for though there may be great performances, and great sufferings too, yet without sincere love they are all in vain. Such doings and sufferings may, indeed, be required of us as the followers of Christ, and in the way of duty; but we are not to rest in them, or feel that they have any merit or worthiness in themselves. At best they are but the outward evidence and the outflowing of a right spirit in the heart. Be exhorted, then, as the great thing, to cherish sincere love or Christian charity in the heart. It is that which you must have; and there is nothing that will help your case without it. Without it, all will, in some respect, but tend to deepen your condemnation, and to sink you to but lower depths in the world of despair.]]

<!-- p. 185 -->

### SERMON FOUR: LONG-SUFFERING AND KINDNESS

> *Charity suffereth long and is kind*.

I CORINTHIANS 13:4.THE Apostle in the foregoing verses, which have been already insisted on, sets forth how great and essential a thing charity or a spirit of Christian love is in Christianity; how it is more necessary and excellent than any of those extraordinary gifts of the Spirit which the Corinthians had among them, and how it exceeded all external performances or sufferings; and that it was the greatest and most essential thing, and indeed the sum of all that is essential, distinguishing and saving in Christianity, and was, as it were, the very life and soul of all religion, without which all extraordinary gifts, such as prophecy and the gift of tongues, and knowledge, and miracles, and all morality and religion, even to such great things as giving all one's goods to feed the poor, and the body to be burned, were nothing. He now proceeds, as his subject naturally led him, to show the excellent nature of charity by describing the several amiable exercises and fruits of it in ver. 1 Corinthians 13:4–7. The words which I have now read to insist on at this time show us two of these fruits of charity mentioned. The first, viz. suffering long, has respect to ill received from others; and the other, viz. being kind, respects good to be done to others.

*Doctrine*

*A Christian spirit disposes persons meekly to bear ill that is received from others, and cheerfully and freely to do good to others*.

I say a Christian spirit because it has been observed already that that charity or Christian love, which is here spoken of, is the summary of the Christian spirit. I would consider each part of this doctrine distinctly.

<!-- p. 186 -->

[II. That a Christian spirit disposes persons meekly to bear ill received from others.][II. That a Christian spirit disposes persons freely to do good to others.][^004-note94] And

1. I would show how a Christian spirit disposes persons meekly to bear ill which is received from others, or the injuries which others do them. Meekness is a great part of the Christian spirit. Christ in that great call and invitation which we have in the close of the eleventh chapter of Matthew, where he calls all that labor and are heavy laden to come unto him, particularly mentions this as that in which he calls upon them who come to him to imitate him. "Learn of me, for I am meek and lowly in heart." And meekness, as it respects injuries received from men, is called long-suffering in Scripture, and is often mentioned as an exercise of the Christian spirit. Galatians 5:22, "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, long-suffering."[^004-note95] And Ephesians 4:1–2, "I therefore, the prisoner of the Lord, beseech you that ye walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called, with all lowliness and meekness, with long-suffering, forbearing one another in love." Colossians 3:12–13, "Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, long-suffering; forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye." In speaking to this point, I would, first, briefly take notice of some of the various kinds of injuries which persons receive from others; second, what is meant by meekly bearing such injuries; third, how this love that is the sum of the Christian spirit will dispose men to do thus.

<!-- p. 187 -->

*First*. I would briefly take notice of some of the various kinds of injuries that persons suffer from others. Some injure others in their estates by unfairness in their dealings, by being fraudulent and deceitful with them, or at least leading them in the blind, and taking advantage of their ignorance; or by oppressing them, taking advantage of their necessities; or by unfaithfulness towards them, not fulfilling their promises and engagements, and being slack and slighty in any business in which they are employed by their neighbors, aiming at nothing but first to get their wages, not being careful to improve their time which they are hired to work for their neighbor; or by asking unreasonable prices for what they do; or by withholding what is due from their neighbor unjustly, neglecting to pay their debts, or unreasonably putting their neighbor to trouble and difficulty to get what is due from them.

There are many other ways in which men injure others in their dealings one with another. There is abundance of wicked and perverse ways which men have in their dealings, in which they are far from doing to others as they would that others should to them, and by which they provoke and irritate one another. Some injure others in their good name, by reproaching them, or speaking evil of them behind their backs. Abundance is done in this way. No injury is so common as this. The iniquity which is committed by men in all our taverns[^004-note96] by what they say of one another behind their backs is beyond account. Some injure others by making or spreading false reports of others, and so slandering them. And others, although what they say is not a direct falsehood, yet a great misrepresentation of things, represent things in their neighbors in the worst colors, and strain their faults, and set them forth beyond what they are, and speak of them in a very unfair manner. A great deal of injury is done among neighbors by uncharitably judging one another, putting injurious constructions on one another's words and actions. Persons may greatly injure others in their thoughts by unjustly entertaining a mean opinion and low esteem of them. Some men are intolerably injurious to others in the contempt they have of them in their hearts, and also by a forwardness to think the worst of them. A great deal is done in injuring others in words. Men commonly make use of their tongues as their weapons. This therefore is represented as their "scourge," Job 5:21. And wicked men's tongues are in this respect compared to the tongues of some very poisonous kinds of serpents, whose weapon is their tongue, with which they mortally sting others. Psalms 140:3, "They have sharpened

<!-- p. 188 -->

their tongues like a serpent; [adders' poison is under their lips]."

Sometimes men injure others in their behavior and actions towards them, or in the injurious deeds they do them. Sometimes persons who are vested with authority carry themselves very injuriously towards those over whom they have authority, by behaving themselves very injuriously and tyrannically towards them. And sometimes they who are under them that are in authority carry themselves very injuriously towards them, by denying them that respect and honor which is due to them in their places. Some carry themselves very injuriously towards others by the exercise of a very selfish spirit. Some men seem to be all for themselves, and in their carriage among men to have no regard to the good or benefit of their neighbor, but all their contrivance is to aggrandize themselves. Some carry themselves as if they would set themselves above everybody, as though none was as good as they, and nobody was to be regarded but themselves. This appears in their talk and in their actions. When men carry themselves so, all who are about them, look upon themselves as injured by it, and very justly.
