Every true Christian has the spirit of a martyr. And as Christ says, Mark 4:13, "Know ye not this parable? How then will ye know all parables?"[^004-note264] So if you cannot bear such little sufferings as have hitherto been laid in your way, how will ye bear all sufferings? How will you answer what is said in the text, charity beareth all things? And so that may be explained to you, Jeremiah 12:5, "If thou hast run with the footmen, and they wearied thee, then how canst thou contend with horses? And if in the land of peace, wherein thou trustedst, they wearied thee, then how wilt thou do in the swelling of Jordan?"

II. Use may be of exhortation, to exhort professors of piety to a ready spirit for Christ's sake to undergo those sufferings which are laid in the way of their duty. Here consider

*First*. How happy such persons are represented in Scripture, as have a spirit to suffer, and do actually suffer for Christ. Matthew 5:10–12, "Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake. Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in

<!-- p. 323 -->

heaven." Luke 6:21–23, "Blessed are ye that hunger now: for ye shall be filled. Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh. Blessed are ye, when men shall hate you, and when they shall separate you from their company, and shall reproach you, and cast out your name as evil, for the Son of Man's sake. Rejoice ye in that day, and leap for joy: for behold your reward is great in heaven." Philippians 1:28–29, "In nothing terrified by your adversaries: which is to them an evident token of perdition, but to you of salvation, and that of God. For unto you it is given in the behalf of Christ, not only to believe on him, but also to suffer for his sake." Here suffering without being terrified is mentioned as a token of salvation, and suffering for Christ's sake is mentioned as a glorious gift of God beyond what they have who only believe. And again James 1:12 it is said, "Blessed is the man that endureth temptation." And 1 Peter 3:14, "But if ye suffer for righteousness' sake, happy are ye: and be not afraid of their terror, neither be troubled."[^004-note265] And Christ calls upon his disciples when they have suffered for his sake to be of good cheer. John 16:33, "In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world." When the apostles had been put in prison, and brought before the counsel and beaten there, we are told they departed from the presence of the counsel rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name, Acts 5:40–41. Paul and Silas, when they were suffering for Christ, looked on themselves happy. We read, Acts 16:24–25, that when they were thrust into the inner prison, and their feet made fast in the stocks, they sang praises unto God, and the prisoners heard them. And the Apostle teaches us in Romans 5:3 that Christians who suffer for Christ's sake have reason to glory in tribulations. And the Apostle tells us of himself, and the sufferings he underwent for Christ, 2 Corinthians 6:10, that though he was sorrowful, yet he was always rejoicing. And the Apostle commends the Christian Hebrews, chapter Hebrews 10:34, that they took joyfully the spoiling of their goods, knowing in themselves that they had in heaven a better and an enduring substance.

And the apostle James directs Christians to count it all joy when they fall into diverse temptations, knowing this, that the trial of our faith worketh patience, James 1:2–3. And the apostle Peter directs Christians to rejoice in their sufferings. 1 Peter 4:12–13, "Beloved, think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened unto you: But rejoice, inasmuch as ye are partakers of Christ's sufferings; that,

<!-- p. 324 -->

when his glory shall be revealed, ye may be glad also with exceeding joy." And ver. 1 Peter 4:16, "If any man suffer as a Christian, let him not be ashamed; but let him glorify God on this behalf."

*Second*. Consider what glorious rewards are promised to be hereafter bestowed on those who do willingly suffer for Christ. It is said that they shall receive a crown of life, James 1:12. And Christ promises that those who forsake houses or lands, or father or mother, or wife, or children for his name's sake, shall receive an hundredfold and shall inherit everlasting life, Matthew 19:29. And we are told that such shall be accounted worthy of the kingdom of God, 2 Thessalonians 1:5. And to the like purport the same Apostle tells us in 2 Timothy 2:11–12, "It is a faithful saying: For if we be dead with him, we shall also live with him. If we suffer, we shall also reign with him: if we deny him, he also will deny us." And so Romans 8:17, "If so be we suffer with him, that we also may be glorified together."[^004-note266] [[And we have, also, the most glorious promises made to those that overcome, and gain the victory over the world. "To him that overcometh," says Christ, "will I give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the midst of the paradise of God," and "he shall not be hurt of the second death"; and "to him will I give to eat of the hidden manna"; and "to him will I give power over the nations"; and "I will give him the morning star"; and "he shall be clothed in white raiment, and I will not blot out his name out of the book of life, but I will confess his name before my Father, and before his angels"; and "him will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out, and I will write upon him my new name"; and "to him that overcometh will I grant to sit with me in my throne, even as I also overcame, and am set down with my Father in his throne," Revelation 2:7, Revelation 2:11, Revelation 2:17, Revelation 2:26, Revelation 2:28; and Revelation 3:5, Revelation 3:12, Revelation 3:21. Surely promises so rich and abundant as these should make us willing to undergo all sufferings for the sake of Christ, who will so gloriously reward us for them all. Once more, consider,

[[*Third*. How the Scriptures abound with blessed examples of those that have suffered for Christ's sake. The Psalmist, speaking of the reproach and blasphemy he had suffered from the enemy and avenger, says, "All this is come upon us, yet have we not forgotten thee, neither have we dealt falsely in thy covenant," Psalms 44:17; and again, "The proud have had me greatly in derision, yet have I not declined from thy law;

<!-- p. 325 -->

many are my persecutors and mine enemies, yet do I not decline from thy testimonies; princes have persecuted me without a cause, but my heart standeth in awe of thy word," Psalms 119:51, Psalms 119:157, Psalms 119:161.[^004-note267] And the prophet Jeremiah spake boldly for God, though he was threatened with death for so doing, Jeremiah 26:11, Jeremiah 26:15. And Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refused to bow down and worship the golden image that the king of Babylon had set up, though they knew they would be cast into the fiery furnace, Daniel 3; and Daniel himself would still faithfully pray to his God, though he expected for it to be shut up in the den of lions, Daniel 6:10. But the time would fail me to tell of apostles, and prophets, and martyrs, and saints, and of Christ himself, who were faithful alike through good report and evil report, and in sufferings and trials, and who counted not their lives dear, so that they might be faithful to the end. "Wherefore seeing we, also, are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us, looking unto Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him, endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God," Hebrews 12:1–2. "Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer. Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life" [Revelation 2:10].]]

<!-- p. 326 -->

### SERMON TWELVE: CHRISTIAN GRACES CONCATENATED TOGETHER

> *Believeth all things, hopeth all things*.

I CORINTHIANS 13:7.AS these words are commonly understood the Apostle means that charity disposes men to believe the best and hope the best of our neighbor in all cases. But I would take leave to suppose that is not the Apostle's meaning in this place; but rather that charity is a grace which cherishes and promotes the exercise of other graces, as particularly those two graces of faith and hope. Here are two graces mentioned, viz. believing and hoping, or faith and hope; and the Apostle here shows how the exercise of these are promoted by charity. My reasons for understanding the Apostle in this sense are these.

1. The Apostle had just before mentioned the fruit of charity in thinking the best of our neighbor, and we have no reason to think he repeats the same thing over again in these words. He had mentioned that fruit of charity in the last words of the fifth verse, "Charity thinketh no evil."[^004-note268]

2. It seems plain that the Apostle had done speaking of those fruits of charity towards our neighbor, and summed them up in the last verse, as was observed before, when we were speaking on the first words of this verse, "beareth all things."[^004-note269] He had before been mentioning many good practices towards our neighbor to which charity tended, and then sums up all in this, "rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth."[^004-note270] That is as much as to say, it is needless to mention any more particulars of good behavior towards our neighbor to which charity tends; for it tends to all good behavior, and no ill. And then the Apostle in this verse proceeds to mention other fruits of charity, quite of another kind, and among others, that it believeth all things and hopeth all things; that is,

<!-- p. 327 -->

charity tends to promote all manner of exercise of those other two great graces of the gospel: faith and hope.[^004-note271]

3. We find that the Apostle does more than once mention the three graces, faith, hope and charity together; and it is but reasonable to suppose that each time he does so, he means the same three graces. In the last verse of the chapter we find these three mentioned and compared together. "And now abideth faith, hope, charity." Here by faith and hope the Apostle does not mean chiefly believing and hoping the best of our neighbor. But by faith, hope and charity the Apostle intends the three great and principal graces of the gospel which have God and Christ as their main and immediate object. And so we find here in this place the Apostle mentions the same three graces of charity and believing and hoping; or charity, faith and hope. And why should we not suppose that he means the same three things as in the last verse of the chapter, seeing that he calls them by the same name as he does there, and mentions them together as he does there; and it is in the same chapter, and in the same discourse, and where the Apostle is upon the same argument.

4. And lastly. This is agreeable to the drift of the Apostle through the chapter, which is to show the preference of charity to other graces, and particularly to faith and hope. This is what the Apostle does through the whole. And therefore when he comes to draw the conclusion of the matter in the last verse, after having discoursed much upon it, he says, "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, and the greatest of these is charity," where he has reference to what he had said before in the words upon which we now are, "charity believeth all things, hopeth all things." Which shows that charity is the greatest, as they show how charity is the sum of all grace; and is the most essential ingredient in faith and hope, and that by which they are cherished, and their exercises promoted in the soul. And therefore the doctrine which I would observe from the words is this.

*Doctrine*

*There is a concatenation of the graces of Christianity*.[^004-note272]

That is, the graces of Christianity are all linked together or united one to another and within one another, as the links of a chain; one does, as it

<!-- p. 328 -->

were, hang on another from one end of the chain to the other, so that if one link be broken, all falls; the whole ceases to be of any effect. In speaking to this I would

I. Briefly show how the graces of Christianity are concatenated together.[^004-note273]

II. Give the reasons, and then make application.

I. I would briefly explain the manner in which the graces of Christianity are concatenated.[^004-note274] It may be shown in three things.

*First*. All the graces of Christianity always go together, so that where there is one, there are all; and when one is wanting, all are wanting. Where there is faith, there is love and hope and humility. Where there is love, there is also trust; and where there is a holy trust in God, there is love to God. Where there is a gracious hope, there also is a holy fear of God. Psalms 147:11, "The Lord taketh pleasure in them that fear him, in those that hope in his mercy." Where there is love to God, there is a gracious love to men; and where there is a Christian love to men, there is love to God. Hence we find that the apostle John at one time gives love to the brethren as a sign of love to God. 1 John 4:20, "If a man say, I love

<!-- p. 329 -->

God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar." And again two or three verses after, he mentions love to God as a sign of love to the brethren, as ch. 1 John 5:2, "By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God, and keep his commandments."

*Second*. The graces of Christianity depend one on another. There is not only a conjunction whereby they are always joined together, but there is a mutual dependence of one grace and another, so that one cannot be without another. To deny one would be in effect to deny another, as to deny the cause would be to deny the effect, and to deny the effect would be to deny the cause. Faith promotes love, and love is the most essential ingredient in a saving faith. And love tends to promote and cherish faith, and therefore the Apostle says in the text, "believeth all things." Love is dependent on faith. For a being cannot be truly loved, and especially loved above all other beings, which is not looked upon as a real being. And again love cherishes[^004-note275] and promotes faith, because those whom we love we are more apt to believe and give credit to, and disposed to trust in. So faith begets hope; for faith sees and trusts in God's sufficiency to bestow eternal life, and in his faithfulness in the promises he has made, that he will do it. All gracious hope is hope arising from faith, and hope encourages and draws forth acts of faith. So love tends to hope. For a spirit of love is the spirit of a child. And the more one feels within himself this spirit of a child, the more natural it will be for him to look on God and go to God as his Father. This childlike spirit casts out the spirit of bondage or slavish fear. Romans 8:15, "Ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear, but ye have received the spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father." The apostle John tells us that perfect love casts out fear. 1 John 4:18, "There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear." And so again a true and gracious hope tends greatly to promote love. When a true Christian has most of a right hope of an interest in God's favor, and those eternal blessings which are the fruits of it, this tends to draw forth the exercises of love, and oftentimes does so. Romans 5:3–5, "Tribulation worketh patience; and patience experience, and experience hope; and hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost, which is given unto us."

Faith promotes humility. For the more entirely anyone depends on God's sufficiency, the more it will tend to a humble sense[^004-note276] of their own insufficiency. And so humility tends to promote faith. For the more a

<!-- p. 330 -->

person has of an humble sense of his own insufficiency, the more will his heart be prepared to trust alone in God, and depend entirely on Christ. So love promotes humility. For the more the heart is ravished with God's loveliness, the more will it abhor itself and abase and humble itself for its own unloveliness and vileness. And humility promotes love. For the more anyone has of a humble sense of his own unworthiness, the [more] he will admire God's goodness to him, and the more will his heart be drawn out in love to him for his glorious grace. Love tends to repentance. For he that truly repents of sin, repents of it because it is committed against a being whom he loves. And repentance tends to humility. To repent of sin tends to humble the heart for sin. So repentance, faith and love all tend to thankfulness. He who by faith trusts in Christ for salvation will be thankful to him for salvation, and he who loves God will be disposed thankfully to acknowledge his kindness. And he who truly repents of his sin will be disposed humbly to thank God for all mercies to one that is so sinful. A true love to God tends to love to men, who have the image of God. And a spirit of love and peace towards men cherishes a spirit of love to God, or love to the image cherishes love to the original. And so it might be shown how all the graces do depend one upon another, by mentioning many other particulars. Humility cherishes all grace, and all other graces promote humility. So faith promotes all grace, and all grace cherishes faith. And the like might be shown of every one.

*Third*. The different graces of Christianity are in some respects implied one in another. They are not only always together, and do arise one from another; but one is, in some respects, implied in the very nature of another. In many of them one is essential to another, and belongs to the essence of it. Thus, for instance, humility is implied in the nature of a true faith so as to be of the essence of it. It is essential to a true faith that it be an humble faith. It is essential to a true trust in God that it be an humble trust. And so it belongs to the nature and essence of every other true grace. It is essential to Christian love that it be an humble love. And it is essential to Christian submission that it be an humble submission. And so of repentance, thankfulness, and reverence.

So love is implied in a gracious faith. It is an ingredient in it, and belongs to its essence. Yea, it is, as it were, the soul of it, as its working, operative principle or nature. As that working, operative nature which is in man is his soul, so the working and operative nature of faith is love. For the apostle Paul tells us that faith worketh by love, Galatians 5:6. And the apostle James tells us that faith, without its working nature, is dead, as

<!-- p. 331 -->

the body without the spirit is dead, James 2:26. And so also faith is in some respects implied in love, for it is essential to a true Christian love that it be a believing love. So saving repentance and faith are implied in one another. They are both one conversion of the soul from sin to God through Christ. This act of the soul in turning from sin to God through Christ, as it respects the [object][^004-note277] from which the turning is, viz. sin, is called repentance. And as it respects the [object] to which, and the mediation by which [[it turns]],[^004-note278] is called faith. But it is the same motion of the soul, as when a man turns or flies from darkness to the light. It is the same motion though it may be called by different names, as it respects the darkness fled from, and the light fled to; with respect to one, it is called fleeing from, and the other, receiving, or embracing.

So there is love implied in thankfulness. True thankfulness is no other than the exercise of love to God on occasion of his goodness to us. So there is love in a true and childlike fear of God. A childlike fear differs from a slavish fear in this, that a slavish fear has no love in it. So there are these three graces implied in a gracious, childlike submission to the will of God, viz. love, and humility and reverence. So weanedness from the world and heavenly-mindedness do consist in these three, love, and faith, and hope. So a Christian love to men is a kind of mediate exercise of love to Christ. And that justice and truth towards men which are truly Christian graces have love in them, and it is essential to them. And love and humility are what constitute Christian meekness towards men. So it is love to God and faith and humility which are the ingredients in Christian patience, and contentment with our own condition. Thus all the graces of Christianity are concatenated, or linked together.[^004-note279] I would proceed now

<!-- p. 332 -->

II. To give some reasons of it.

*First*. They are all from the same Spirit of Christ. 1 Corinthians 12:4, 1 Corinthians 12:6, "There are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit. Diversities of operations, but it is the same God that worketh all in all." The graces of Christianity are all from the Spirit of Christ sent forth into the heart, and dwelling there as an holy principle and divine nature. And therefore all graces are only the different ways of acting of the same divine nature, as there may be different reflections of the light of the sun. But it is all the same kind of light originally, because it all comes from the same fountain, the same body of light. Grace in the soul is the Holy Ghost acting in the soul, and there communicating his own holy nature. As it is in the fountain, it is all one and the same holy nature; and only diversified by the variety of streams sent forth. These streams must be all [[of the same nature]],[^004-note280] seeing that they thus come from the same fountain. And the difference of many of them, whereby they have different denominations, is chiefly from the various respects to those and those objects and manners of exercise rather than a real difference in their abstracted nature.[^004-note281]

*Second*. They are all communicated in the same work of that Spirit, viz. the work of conversion. There is not one conversion to bring the heart to faith, and another[^004-note282] to infuse love to God, and another humility, and another repentance, and another love to men. But all are given in one work of the Spirit. All these things are infused by one conversion,[^004-note283] one change of the heart; which argues that all the graces are united and linked together, as being contained in that one and the same new nature which is given in regeneration; just as it is in the first generation, several faculties are communicated in one generation of the child, the sense of seeing, hearing, feeling, speaking and tasting, and the power of moving, breathing and digesting. It is all therefore one common nature, one common life manifoldly diversified.

<!-- p. 333 -->

*Third*. All graces have the same root and foundation, viz. the knowledge of God's excellency. The same sight or sense of God's excellency begets faith, and love, and repentance, and all other graces.[^004-note284] One sight of this will beget all those, because the sight of God's excellency shows the ground and reason of all holy disposition, and all holy behavior towards God. They who know God's name will love him, and trust in him, and have a spirit to submit to him, and a spirit to praise and to obey him. Psalms 9:10, "They that know thy name, will put their trust in thee." John 6:40, "He that seeth the Son, and believeth on him, may have everlasting life." 1 John 3:6, "Whosoever abideth in him, sinneth not; whosoever sinneth hath not seen him, neither known him." Jeremiah 22:16, "Was not this to know me?"

*Fourth*. All gracious dispositions have the same rule, viz. the law of God; and therefore must be linked together. For seeing they all have respect to this rule, they all tend to confirm the whole of that rule, and conform the heart and life to it. For he who has a true respect to one of God's commands, will have [[respect]][^004-note285] to all; for they are all established by the same authority, and are all jointly an expression of the same holy nature of God. James 2:10–11, "Whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all. For he that said, Do not commit adultery, said also, Do not kill. Now if thou commit no adultery, yet if thou kill, thou art become a transgressor of the law."

*Fifth*. *They* have all the same end. God is the end to which all the graces tend. As they are from the same cause, rising out of the same fountain, all standing on the same foundation, growing on the same root, and directed by the same rule, so they are all directed to the same end, viz. God, his glory, and our own happiness in him; which shows that they must be nearly related, and very much linked together.

*Sixth*. And lastly. They are related to one grace as the sum of them all; and that is charity, or divine love. This, we have before shown, is the sum of all true Christian grace,[^004-note286] however many names we may give the different ways and manners of the exercise of grace; yet if we strictly examine them, they are all related to one. Love is the fulfilling of them all. They are but so many diversifications, and different habitudes and relations and manners of exercise of the same thing. One grace does in

<!-- p. 334 -->

effect contain them all. Whence it is no wonder that they are nearly allied, and are always together, and dependent on one another, and implied one in another.

*Application*

The use may be of instruction.

*First*. This may help us to understand in what sense old things are said to be done away, and all things become new in conversion. This is what the Apostle teaches in 2 Corinthians 5:17, "If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature; old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." This doctrine, and what has been said under it, may in some measure show us how this is; for by this we learn that all the graces of Christianity are infused[^004-note287] in this, inasmuch as all are concatenated; when one is infused, all are infused; there is not one grace wanting. A [convert][^004-note288] at the same moment that he is become such is possessed of all holy principles, all gracious dispositions. There is a seed of every kind of holy behavior towards God, and towards men. There are as many graces in a [true Christian][^004-note289] as there are in Jesus Christ himself; which is what the evangelist John means in John 1:14–16, "And the word was made flesh, and dwelt among us. And of his fullness have all we received, and grace for grace." And it cannot be otherwise; for they are renewed after Christ's image, as Colossians 3:10, and have put on the new man, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him who created them. But that is no true image or picture of another which has some parts wanting. An exact image has part answerable to part; the copy answers the original throughout in all parts, though it may be an obscure image, and not represent any part perfectly, as grace answers to grace. Grace in the soul is a reflection of Christ's glory. It is a reflection of his glory, as the image of a man is reflected from a glass which exhibits part for part [2 Corinthians 3:18].

It is in the new birth, as it is with the first birth. The infant in the womb has all the parts of a man. Though they are in a very imperfect state, yet unless it be a monster,[^004-note290] there is not one part wanting. Such an infant has as many members as a man in full stature and strength. And

<!-- p. 335 -->

therefore what is wrought in regeneration is called the new man; not only new eyes, new ears, or a new head or new hands, but a new man in all the members.[^004-note291] [[But all the graces of the Christian are new. All of them are members of the individual after conversion, and none of them were members before conversion. And because there is, as it were, a new man, with all these members, begotten in conversion, therefore Christians are said to be sanctified wholly, in soul, body and spirit, as in 1 Thessalonians 5:23.]] So old things are done away, and all things become new; for as the new man is put on, the old man is put off; so that the man in a sense becomes new entirely.

If there be all graces infused[^004-note292] in this work, it will follow that all corruptions are mortified. For there is no corruption but what has a grace opposite to it to answer it. And the infusion of the grace mortifies its opposite corruption, as the infusion of faith mortifies unbelief, or as love mortifies enmity, humility high-mindedness, meekness revenge, or thankfulness[^004-note293] [[a thankless spirit, etc.]]. As one of these takes place, the other gives place, just as darkness in a room withdraws in proportion as light enters. Thus old things pass away; all old things pass away in a degree, though none perfectly; so all things become new, though also imperfectly. This shows that conversion when it is wrought is a glorious work, and a great change, though grace may be very imperfect. He must have a great change wrought in him who before had no corruption mortified, and now has all mortified; and before had not one grace, but now has all graces.[^004-note294]

<!-- p. 336 -->

*Second*. Hence persons who hope they find grace in their hearts may try one grace by another; for all graces are linked together, and one does, as you have heard, in some respects imply another. If persons think they have faith, and think they have come to Christ, they should inquire whether their faith was accompanied with repentance, whether they came to Christ in a brokenhearted manner, sensible of their own utter unworthiness and vileness by sin, or whether they did not come in a presumptuous manner taking encouragement from their own supposed goodness. They should try their faith by inquiry whether it was accompanied with humility, whether they trust in Christ in an humble, lowly[^004-note295] manner, delighting to renounce themselves, and to give all the glory of their salvation to Jesus Christ. So they should try their faith by their love. If their faith seems to have light in it, but no heat or warmth, it is not the true light. They should inquire whether their faith worketh by love.

So persons should examine their love by their faith. If they seem to have an affectionate love towards God and Christ, they should inquire whether this be accompanied with a real conviction of the soul of the reality of Christ, of the truth of the gospel which reveals him, with a conviction that he is the Son of God, that he is the only Savior, the glorious and all-sufficient Savior. Herein is one great difference between false affections and true affections: false affections and [a delusory][^004-note296] saving love to God and Christ are not accompanied with this conviction; they do not withal see the truth and reality of divine things. And therefore their affection is little to be depended on. It is much like the affection which one may have towards a person of whom he reads in a romance, whom he at the same time supposes to be a feigned person. Such affections as are not accompanied with conviction will never carry men very far, or influence them to any great matters.[^004-note297]

<!-- p. 337 -->

So persons should examine that in them which seems to be the grace of hope in them. They should inquire whether their hope be accompanied with faith, and arises from faith in Jesus Christ and a trust in his worthiness, and his alone; whether their hope is built on this rock,[^004-note298] or whether it does not arise from an high opinion of something in them. So they should examine in what way their hope works, and what influence it has upon them; whether it be accompanied with humility. A true hope humbles a man, tends to make him reflect on himself with shame and brokenness of heart, lying in the dust before God; and that comfort which arises from it is a lowly, humble joy and comfort. On the contrary, a false hope is wont to lift persons up with a high conceit of themselves, their own experience and doings. They should also inquire whether their hope be accompanied with a spirit of obedience, and a spirit of self-denial, and weanedness from the world. A true hope is accompanied with those other graces, as by a concatenation;[^004-note299] whereas a false hope is without them. It does not engage the heart in obedience, but flatters and hardens it in disobedience. It does not mortify carnal appetites, and wean from the world, but it indulges carnal appetites, cherishes them, and makes men the more easy in them.

So persons should examine their weanedness from the world by inquiring whether it be accompanied with and arises from a principle of love, whereby their hearts are drawn off from the things of the world to those spiritual and heavenly objects, to which their love carries them more than to the things of the world. John 21:15, "Lovest thou me more than these?" Herein a true weanedness from the world differs from false weanedness. A false weanedness is not from love, but commonly either from fear and distress of conscience, or from their outward afflictions whereby they have not their hearts sweetly drawn off from the world to something which they see is better, and which seems sweeter to them, but are driven and, as it were, beaten off from the world, while the heart would cleave to the world as fast as ever if it could enjoy it free from those terrors and troubles. Whereas he that has a true weanedness from the world contemns[^004-note300] those things at their best, because his heart is drawn after something better.[^004-note301]

So they should try their love to God by love to the people of God. And

<!-- p. 338 -->

also their love to the brethren by the love of God, by inquiring whether it arises from love to God, agreeably to the apostle John's directions in 1 John 5:2, "By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God, and keep his commandments." False grace is always like a monster,[^004-note302] wherein many essential parts are wanting. There is an appearance only of some graces. It may be there is an appearance of some good disposition to God; at the same time they are destitute of Christian dispositions towards their neighbors, unjust, uncharitable, spiteful. If they seem to have good dispositions towards their neighbor, to be good-natured, civil, just, generous; without love to God[^004-note303] [they are half roasted].[^004-note304]

On this account God complained of Ephraim of old. Hosea 7:8, "Ephraim is a cake not turned." That is, his goodness is partial and not universal, he is good on one side but wicked on the other, like a cake which is half baked, and half raw,[^004-note305] [[generally burnt on one side, and raw on the other, and good for nothing on either. Such a character we should studiously avoid, and endeavor that each grace that we have may testify to the genuineness of all our other graces, so that we may be proportioned Christians, growing into the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto perfect men, unto the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.]][^004-note306]

<!-- p. 339 -->

### SERMON THIRTEEN: GRACE NEVER OVERTHROWN

> *Endureth all things*.

I CORINTHIANS 13:7.THERE are three expressions in the description which the Apostle gives of the nature and tendency of charity in this place which, as they are vulgarly understood, all signify the same thing, viz. that in the beginning of the fourth verse, "charity suffereth long," that in the beginning of this seventh verse, "charity beareth all things," and this in the latter part of the same verse, "charity endureth all things." All these seem commonly to be taken as so many synonymous expressions, as though the Apostle in all of them only said the same thing over and over in different words. But this doubtless is from a misunderstanding of the Apostle.

If we closely consider those various expressions, and the manner in which the Apostle uses them, we shall find that every one of them signifies a distinct fruit of charity. Two of these expressions have been already considered, viz. that in the fourth verse, "charity suffereth long," and that in the beginning of this verse, "charity beareth all things"; and it has been shown that they signify different things. That in the fourth verse, "charity suffereth long," has respect to meekly bearing injuries from men, or receiving them without disturbance of the calm of the mind. But the expression in the beginning of this seventh verse, "charity beareth all things," respects that suffering spirit, which Christians are of, a disposition of mind to undergo all sufferings to which we shall be called in the cause of Christ and for a good conscience, and rather to undergo any, yea, all sufferings than to desert Christ and our duty. And this expression, "endureth all things," which we have in the end of the same verse, signifies something different still from either of the foregoing. It expresses the lasting and abiding nature of a principle of true grace or charity; how that, whatever opposition it meets with it does not fail, but

<!-- p. 340 -->

remains or endures. The two expressions in this verse, "beareth all things, endureth all things," in our English translation, are in common use much of the same import. But it is not so in the original. The expression which is translated, "endureth all things," is in the original *panta hypomenei*, which in the most liberal translation is, "remains under all things"; that is, it remains under all opposition.[^004-note307] Whatever attempts are made against it, whatever assaults are made upon it, yet it remains, it endures, it does not cease, but remains under all this opposition.

By the explanation which has been given of the expressions in this verse, "beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things," the sense of the Apostle in the words appears easy and natural, and consistent with the context. The Apostle, designing to set forth the universal benefit of charity or a spirit of Christian love, and to show how it is the sum of all that is good in the heart, first shows how it disposes to all good behavior towards men, and then sums up that matter in the foregoing verse, "charity rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth." And then proceeds and declares that charity does not only dispose to doing but to suffering in the cause of Christ. It gives a suffering spirit, and beareth all things. And this it does by promoting those two other graces of faith and hope, which are chiefly concerned in suffering in the cause of Christ. For such sufferings are the trials of our faith; and what upholds Christians under them is a hope of a more exceeding and eternal weight of glory which those slight sufferings, which are but for a moment, are not worthy to be compared with. But charity cherishes this faith and hope. It believes all things and hopes all things. And as the fruit of these it endures all things, or perseveres and holds out, and cannot be conquered by all opposition which is made; for their faith overcomes the world, and their hope in God makes them always to triumph in Jesus Christ.

<!-- p. 341 -->

*Doctrine*

*True Christian grace is that which nothing that opposes it can ever overthrow*.

*Prop*. I. There are many things which do greatly oppose the grace which is in the heart of a Christian. This holy principle has innumerable enemies, as it were, constantly watching and warring against it. The Christian is encompassed around with enemies on every side. Being a pilgrim and a stranger in the earth he is, as it were, in an enemy's country. There are thousands of devils[^004-note308] that are bitter enemies to the grace which is in the heart of a Christian, and do all in their power against it. And the world is an enemy to it. It abounds with persons and things that make opposition to it. And the Christian not only has many enemies without, but multitudes within his own breast which he carries about with him, and of which he cannot divest himself; many corruptions which have footing in his heart, which are the worst enemies of grace, and are under the greatest advantages of any in their warfare against it. Those enemies are not only many but exceedingly strong and powerful, and bitter in their enmity, implacable, irreconcilable, mortal enemies, seeking nothing but the utter ruin and overthrow of grace. And they are unwearied in their opposition. So that the Christian, while he remains in this world, is represented as being in a state of war; his business is the business of a soldier. Many are the powerful and violent assaults which the enemies of grace make upon it; they are not only constantly besieging it, but sometimes they assault it as a city which they would take by storm. They are always lurking and watching advantages against it, but sometimes they rise up in a dreadful rage against it. Sometimes one enemy, and sometimes another, and sometimes all together with one consent besetting it on every side, covering it like a flood, ready to overwhelm it and as though they would swallow it at once. Sometimes grace in the midst of the violent opposition of its enemies, besetting it with united strength, is like a spark of fire encompassed with swelling billows, or raging waves, which appear as if they would swallow it up and extinguish it in a moment. Or like a jewel of gold in the midst of a furnace of raging heat, enough to consume anything but pure gold, which is of that nature that it will not consume in the fire.

It is very much with grace in the heart of a Christian, as it is in the

<!-- p. 342 -->

church of God in the world. It is God's post[^004-note309] and it is but small, and great opposition is made against it by innumerable enemies. The powers of earth and hell are engaged against [it],[^004-note310] if possible to destroy it. And oftentimes arise with such violence and such great strength that, if we were to judge only by what appears, would swallow it up immediately. It is with it as it was with the children[^004-note311] of Israel in Egypt, against which Pharaoh and the Egyptians with all their host and force set themselves to endeavor to extirpate it. And as it was with David in the wilderness, who was hunted as a partridge in the mountains, and driven about by those who sought his life from one desert and cave to another, and several times chased out into strange lands. And as it has been with the Christian church under the heathen and antichristian persecution, when all the world did, as it were, unite their strength and will to extirpate the church of God for many ages with their utmost cruelty and most bloody persecutions, destroying many thousands and millions without respect to sex or age.

*Prop*. II. All the opposition which is made against true grace can never overthrow it. The enemies of grace in many respects may gain great advantages against it; they may exceedingly oppose it and reduce it, and bring it into such circumstances that it may seem to be brought to the very brink of utter ruin. But yet it will live. The ruin which seemed impending shall be averted. Though the roaring lion sometimes comes with open mouth, and no visible refuge appears, yet the lamb shall escape; yea, though it be in the very paw of the lion and bear, yet it shall be rescued and not devoured. Yea, though it seems to be actually swallowed down as Jonah was into the belly of the whale, yet it shall be vomited up again, and shall live. It is with grace in the heart in this respect as it was with the ark upon the water. However terrible a storm may come; yea, though it may be such as to bring a universal deluge, which shall overwhelm all other things, yet it shall not overwhelm that. Let the flood rise ever so high, yet it shall be kept above water. Though the mighty waves of it may rise above the tops of the highest mountains, yet they shall not be able to rise above this ark, but it shall still appear above water. Or as it was with the ship in which Christ was; though there arose a great storm, and the waves were high, insomuch that it seemed as if the ship would be instantly swallowed up, yea, though it was actually covered with the waves, yet it did not sink; and a good reason

<!-- p. 343 -->

why it did not, Christ was in the ship. So grace in the heart is like the church[^004-note312] of Israel in Egypt, and in the Red Sea and the wilderness. Though Pharaoh strove ever so much to destroy it, yet it remained and grew. And when at last he pursued with all his army and chariots and horsemen, when they were pent up by the Red Sea, and saw no way to escape, and were just on the brink of ruin, yet they did escape, and were not delivered a prey to their [[foes]]. Yea, they were preserved in passing through the very sea; when they were in the midst of the sea, the waters did not and could not overflow them. And they were preserved for a long time, even in a desolate wilderness in the midst of pits, and drought, and fiery flying serpents.

Thus as the gates of hell can never prevail against the church of Christ, so neither can they prevail against grace in the heart. The seed remaineth, and none can root it out. The fire is kept alive, even in the midst of floods of water. Though it appears oftentimes as if it were almost out, there is no flame but only a little smoke; yet the smoking flax shall not be quenched [Matthew 12:20]. And grace shall at last have victory, though it may pass through a long train of conflicts, and may suffer many disadvantages, and receive many wounds; yet it will live, and not only so but will finally prosper and prevail and triumph, and all its invaders shall be subdued under its feet. As David in the wilderness, though he was long kept in very low and distressed circumstances pursued by his potent enemies, and several times appeared on the very brink of ruin, there seemed to be but a step between him and death, when Saul encompassed him round ready to apprehend him. Yet at last he prevailed; and instead of being a fugitive in the mountains and caves of the earth, he came to sit on the throne of all Israel, and to wear the royal crown in great prosperity and glory. And like Joseph who, though he was designed for death by his brethren, and was cast into a pit by them, and then sold a slave into Egypt, and there cast into the dungeon, yet at last was exalted over the land of Egypt, and over all who had before opposed him. So it is with grace in the heart. It can never be overthrown by its enemies, and all the opposition which is made against it. And so it endures all things; it stands all shocks, and remains under all opposition. The reason of this may be seen in these two things.

*First*. There is much more in the nature of true grace which tends to

<!-- p. 344 -->

perseverance than in false grace. False grace is a superficial thing, consisting in external show, or in superficial [[affections]] and not in any change of nature. But true grace reaches the bottom of the heart, consisting in a new nature; and therefore it is no wonder that it is more abiding. When there is nothing but counterfeit grace, corruption is unmortified.[^004-note313] Whatever wounds may seem to be given, they are but slight wounds which do not at all reach the life of corruption, or diminish the strength of the principle; but sin remains in its full strength in the soul still; and so it is no wonder, that it ultimately prevents[^004-note314] and bears down all before it. But true grace really mortifies sin in the heart. It strikes at its vitals, and gives it a wound in its very heart; a wound which is mortal when it first enters the soul, and begins its conflict with sin. And therefore no wonder that it keeps possession, and finally prevails over its enemy. Counterfeit grace never dispossesses sin of the dominion of the soul, or the reigning power there; and therefore no wonder it does not last. But true grace is of that nature that it is inconsistent with the reigning power of sin, and dispossesses the heart of it as soon as it enters, and takes the throne from it, and therefore is more likely to keep its seat there and finally to prevail against its enemy. Counterfeit grace, though it may affect the heart, yet is not founded in any real conviction of the soul. But true grace is begun with real and thorough conviction. And having such a foundation has a much greater tendency to perseverance. True grace is of a powerful nature, it is something divine, something supernatural and heavenly. True grace naturally causes desires of perseverance and hungerings and thirstings after it, and makes men sensible of the dangers with which they are encompassed, and has a tendency to excite more to watchfulness, and care, and diligence in order to perseverance, and to look to God for help, and trust in him for preservation from the many enemies which oppose it.

*Second*. God will uphold true grace where he has implanted it against all the opposition which is made to it, and will never suffer it to be

<!-- p. 345 -->

overthrown. Though there be much more in true grace which tends to perseverance than in counterfeit grace, yet merely what is in the nature of grace considered abstractedly from God's powerful influence to uphold it would not be sufficient to render it unconquerable, or effectually to secure it from final overthrow. 1 Peter 1:5, "We are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation." An holy principle in the hearts of our first parents, where it had no corruption to conflict with, was overthrown. Much more might we expect that a little seed of grace in the heart of fallen man in the midst of so much corruption [[and exposed to]][^004-note315] such violent opposition against it, would be overthrown, did not God uphold it. But God will uphold it. He has undertaken to defend it from all its enemies, and to give it victory at last; and therefore it surely never shall be overthrown.

Here I would, first, briefly show how it is evident that God will uphold true grace, and will not suffer it to be overthrown; and then, second, give the reasons why he will not suffer it to be overthrown.

1. Show how it is evident. And in one word, it is evident by God's promise. God has promised that grace never shall be overthrown. It is promised in Psalms 37:23–24 that though a good man fall, yet shall he not be utterly cast down, because God will uphold him with his hand. And he has declared with respect to those into whose hearts he puts his fear, that they shall not depart from him, Jeremiah 32:40. And Christ has declared that it is the will of his Father that not one of those little ones should perish, Matthew 18:14; and signifies that it is impossible that the elect should be fatally deceived, Matthew 24:24. And has promised concerning grace that it shall be in the soul as a well of water springing up into everlasting life, John 4:14. And told us that it is his Father's will that of all which the Father hath given him he should lose nothing, John 6:39. He has promised that his sheep shall never perish, and that none shall pluck them out of his hand, John 10:28. And it is declared in Romans 8:30 that they who are called are justified, and they who are justified are also glorified; and that nothing can separate true Christians from the love of Christ; neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord, ver. Romans 8:38–39. And it is promised that where God has begun a good work, he will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ, Philippians 1:6. And that Jesus Christ shall confirm them to the end. 1 Corinthians 1:7–9, "Waiting for the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ; who shall also confirm

<!-- p. 346 -->

you unto the end, that ye may be blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is faithful, by whom ye were called unto the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord." And it is said of him who is born of God that his seed shall remain in him, so that he should not fall away, 1 John 3:9. And many other promises of the like nature might be mentioned.

2. I would briefly give some reasons why God will keep a principle of grace from being overthrown.

(1) Unless the redemption of Christ secured man's perseverance through all opposition, it would not be a complete redemption. Christ's redemption was to redeem us from the misery to which we were subject under the law, and bring us to glory. But if it brought us no further than the state in which we were at first, and left us as liable to fall as before, then all this redemption might be made void, and come to nothing. If man before he fell, being left to the freedom of his own will, fell from his steadfastness, and lost his grace when he was comparatively strong, and had not those enemies to encounter, what then would fallen man with weak imperfect grace do in the midst of his great and manifold enemies, if his perseverance was left to him only? Certainly a redemption which did not secure this would be very incomplete.

(2) The second covenant was introduced to supply what was needed in the first, of which a sure ground of perseverance was the main thing. The first covenant had no defect on God's part who constituted it. It was a holy, just and wise, and perfect constitution; but yet it proved that on our part it was wanting, that we needed something more in order to its being effectual for our happiness; and the thing wanting was some sure ground of perseverance. All the ground which we had under the first covenant was the freedom of our own will, and that was found not to be depended on. God, therefore, has made another covenant. The first was liable to fail, and therefore another was introduced which could not fail, and therefore it is called an everlasting covenant, Isaiah 55:3. The things which can be shaken are removed to make way for that which cannot be shaken. The first covenant had a head and surety which was liable to fail; therefore God has provided one which cannot fail, even his own Son.

(3) It is not fit that, in a covenant of mercy and saving grace, the reward of life should be suspended on man's perseverance, as depending on the strength and steadfastness of his own will. It is a covenant of works and not a covenant of grace, which suspends eternal life on that which is the fruit of a man's own strength to keep him from falling. If all be of free and sovereign grace, then free grace has undertaken the matter to finish

<!-- p. 347 -->

it, and has not left it to men themselves, to the freedom of their own wills, as under the first covenant.

(4) Our second surety has persevered already, and done what our first surety failed of, and therefore we shall surely persevere. Adam, our first surety, did not persevere, and so all fell with him. But if he had persevered, all would have stood with him, and never would have fallen. So our second surety has already persevered, and therefore all who have him for their surety will persevere with him. When Adam fell he was condemned, and all his posterity was condemned with him, and died with him. But if he had stood, he would have been justified, and so would have partook of the tree of life,[^004-note316] and been confirmed in a state of life, and all his posterity would have been confirmed. And by parity of reason, now Christ our second Adam has stood, has persevered, and is justified and confirmed in life;[^004-note317] [[all who are in Christ and represented by him are also accepted, and justified, and confirmed in him. The fact that he, as the covenant head of his people, has fulfilled the terms of that covenant makes it sure that they shall persevere]].

(5) The believer is already actually justified to life, and therefore God will not suffer him to come short of life. Justification is an actual acquittance of a sinner, a final[^004-note318] acquittance from guilt, and deliverance from hell, and acceptance to a free[^004-note319] title to life. But this is inconsistent with a deliverance from hell, and abiding life being yet suspended on an uncertain perseverance.

(6) The Scripture teaches that the believer has grace and spiritual life as partaking of the life of Christ's resurrection, which is immortal, everlasting life. The Scripture teaches this, Colossians 2:12, "Ye are risen with him." Ver. Colossians 2:13, "You hath he quickened together with him." Ephesians 2:5–6, "Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ; and hath raised us up together." Galatians 2:20, "I live, yet not I, but Christ liveth in me." Which shows that the believer's spiritual life cannot fail. For Revelation 1:18, "I am he, that liveth and was dead; and behold, I am alive forevermore." Romans 6:9, "Knowing that Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more; death hath no more dominion over him."

(7) Grace is that which God hath implanted in the heart against great

<!-- p. 348 -->

opposition of enemies, and therefore he will doubtless maintain it there against their continued efforts to root it out. The enemies of God and the soul used their utmost endeavors to hinder grace being implanted in the heart. But God manifested his glorious, all-conquering grace in introducing it there in spite of them. And therefore will not at last suffer himself to be conquered by their expelling that which he has so brought in by his mighty power.

*Application*

*First*. Hence we may learn one reason why the devil so exceedingly opposes persons' conversion, viz. because if they are once converted they are forever put out of his reach, so that he can never overthrow them. If there was such a thing as falling from grace, doubtless the devil would greatly oppose their having grace; but more especially when he knows that if once they have it he can never overthrow it, but that such persons are finally lost to him, forever out of the reach of his destroying power. This may show us something of the reason of that violent opposition with which persons meet who are under awakenings, and are seeking conversion, by so many and great temptations by which they are assaulted. The devil is wont to bestir himself greatly on such occasions, and heap mountains in persons' way if possible to hinder any saving issue of their conversion. He labors to his utmost to quench convictions, and if possible to bring persons who are under them to return to ways of sin and flesh. Sometimes he endeavors to flatter them, and at other times to discourage them. He labors to entangle and perplex their minds, and to his utmost stirs up exercises of corruption in envy, or quarrelling with God, and blasphemous thoughts. He endeavors by many subtle temptations to make them think that it is in vain to seek salvation by tempting them from the doctrine of God's decrees, or their own impotency and helplessness; or that all which they do is sin; or endeavors to persuade them that their day of grace is past, or terrify them that they have committed the unpardonable sin; or tells them that their pain and trouble is needless, that there is time enough hereafter; and if possible he will deceive them with a false hope, and flatter them that they are in a safe state already. And innumerable other ways there are in which Satan endeavors to hinder their conversion; for he knows the truth of the doctrine we have insisted on, that if once grace be infused[^004-note320] he can never overthrow it, that the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.

<!-- p. 349 -->

*Second*. Hence we may infer that those whose seeming grace fails, and is overthrown, may conclude they never had any true grace. That is not true grace which is like the morning cloud and early dew that passeth away. When persons seem to be for a time awakened and terrified, and to have considerable sense of their own sin and vileness, and after that to be much affected with the mercy of God, and to have seeming discoveries and much comfort; but when the newness of the thing is over, all goes away, and there is no abiding change answering what the Apostle says of him that is Christ Jesus' in 2 Corinthians 5:17, "If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature; old things are passed away, behold all things are become new." If the heart have again forsaken God and Christ and spiritual things, and those things are become tasteless and insipid to it, and the heart be again gone out chiefly after vanity and the world, and the man is again returned to ways of sin, neglecting in a stated way diligent attendance on the known duties of religion, and again going on in a way of gratifying the lusts of the heart, and living a careless, vain life: this proves that all those seeming appearances of grace are nothing, and that they have been woefully deluded.

*Third*. Here is matter of great joy and comfort to those who have good evidence that they have indeed true grace in their hearts. Those with whom it is thus, are possessed of an inestimable jewel, that which is more worth than all the jewels of gold and precious stones, and all the earthly crowns and treasures in the world. And this may be matter of great comfort to them that they never shall lose t, his jewel, but that he who gave it to them will keep it for them; and that as he has brought them into an happy state so he will uphold them in it, that the mighty power of God which is able to subdue all things to itself is on their side, and will strengthen them so that none of their enemies shall be able to destroy them. They may rejoice in it that they have a strong city, unto which God has appointed salvation, for walls and for bulwarks. And whatever bitterness their enemies manifest against them, and however subtle and violent they are in their attempts to destroy, they may stand on high, on the mountains of rocks on which God has set them, and may laugh at the power of the enemy, and may triumph over them, glorying that the Most High is their refuge, and underneath an everlasting arm, and that Jehovah rides on the heavens in their help, and in his excellency on the sky, who has promised finally to subdue all their enemies under their feet; and the things he has promised, he is able to perform.

*Fourth*. Here is matter of great encouragement to the saints earnestly to fight against the enemies of their souls. What a disadvantage is it to an

<!-- p. 350 -->

army, or soldiers who go forth to war, when they go to battle with little hope of conquering,[^004-note321] [[but with the prevailing expectation of being overcome! As hope in the one case might be half the victory, so despondency in the other would be likely to ensure defeat. The latter would debilitate and weaken, while the former would cooperate with and increase strength. You that have good evidence that you have grace in your hearts have, then, all that you can need to encourage you. The captain of your salvation will assuredly conduct you to victory in the end. He who is able to uphold you has promised that you shall overcome, and his promise shall never fail. Resting on that promise be faithful to your part, and ere long the song of victory shall be yours, and the crown of victory he will place, with his own hands, upon your head.]]

<!-- p. 351 -->

### SERMON FOURTEEN: DIVINE LOVE ALONE LASTS ETERNALLY

> *Charity never faileth; but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away*.

I CORINTHIANS 13:8THIS chapter is an encomium on charity, and the drift of the Apostle through the whole is to show the preference of charity to all other gifts of the Spirit. He sets forth the excellence of charity in this chapter by three things. (1) By showing that it is the most essential thing, and that all other gifts are nothing without it, in the three first verses. And (2) by showing how charity is that from which all good dispositions and behavior do arise, the stock on which all good fruit grows, and the fountain in which all that is good is contained and from whence it flows, in the four next verses to the end of the seventh.[^004-note322] And (3) he shows its preference above other gifts in its being more durable, and in its remaining when the church of God shall be in its most perfect state after other gifts of the Spirit are vanished away, beginning with this eighth verse, the verse of the text, to the end of the twelfth verse. And then the Apostle sums up his conclusion in the thirteenth verse, and so ends the chapter. In the text may be observed

1. A property of charity by which the excellency of it is set forth, viz.

<!-- p. 352 -->

that it is unfailing and everlasting. Charity never faileth. This naturally follows the last words of the foregoing verse, "charity endureth all things." There the Apostle declared the durableness of charity, as it appears in its standing the shock of all the opposition which is made against it in this world. He now proceeds further and declares how it not only endures to the end of time, but also throughout eternity. "Charity never faileth." When all tongues and things shall fail, this shall abide.

2. We may observe how that herein it is distinguished from other gifts of the Spirit, such as prophecy, and the gift of tongues, and the gift of knowledge. "Whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away." By that knowledge which the Apostle here says shall vanish away he does not mean spiritual and divine knowledge in general, for surely there shall be knowledge hereafter as well as now; there is knowledge in heaven as well as on earth, and vastly more than there is on earth, as the Apostle himself observes in the following verses. "For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away. For now we see through a glass darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known" [ver. 1 Corinthians 13:9–10, 1 Corinthians 13:12]. So the knowledge which Christians have of God and Christ and heavenly things shall not vanish away, but shall only be gloriously increased, and brought to perfection.

But by that knowledge which the Apostle here speaks of, which he says shall vanish away, he means only a particular, miraculous gift which there was in the church of God in those days; for the Apostle is here comparing charity with the miraculous gifts of the Spirit, as has been heretofore observed.[^004-note323] There were various extraordinary gifts of the Spirit given by inspiration which were then common in the church. There was the gift of prophecy, and another gift which they had was the gift of tongues, or languages, which they had never learned. Both these gifts are mentioned in the text, and the Apostle says they shall fail and cease. And another gift which they had in those days was called the gift of knowledge, or the "word of knowledge," of which we read in the foregoing chapter [1 Corinthians 12:8]. In the fourth verse the Apostle says there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit. And in the eighth, ninth and tenth verses he tells us what those diverse gifts are. "To one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge by the same Spirit; to another faith by the same Spirit; to another the gifts of

<!-- p. 353 -->

healing by the same Spirit; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discerning of spirits; to another divers kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of tongues."

You see that a gift of knowledge is mentioned among these, which was a different thing both from that speculative knowledge which is obtained by reason and study, or that spiritual and divine knowledge which persons have by the saving influence of the Spirit on the soul. It was a particular gift of the Spirit with which some persons were endued[^004-note324] whereby they were enabled by immediate inspiration to understand mysteries, or the mysterious prophecies and types of Scripture. The Apostle speaks of this in the second verse of this chapter: "Though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge." It is this miraculous gift which the Apostle says shall vanish away, together with other miraculous gifts of the Spirit, such as prophecy and the gift of tongues.

*Doctrine*

*That great fruit of the Spirit in which the Holy Ghost shall not only for a season but everlastingly be communicated to the church of Christ is divine love*.

That the meaning and truth of this doctrine may be better understood I would speak to it under the following propositions.

I. The Spirit of Christ is given to his church and people forever, everlastingly to influence them and dwell in them.

II. There are other fruits of the Spirit besides divine love wherein the Spirit is communicated to his church.

III. These other fruits of the Spirit are but for a season, and they either have already ceased or the time will come when they will cease. But,

IV. This divine love is that great and everlasting fruit of the Spirit in which his everlasting influence indwelling[^004-note325] in his church appears.

*Prop*. I. The Spirit of Christ is given to his church and people forever, everlastingly to influence them and dwell in them. The Holy Spirit is the great purchase of Christ. God the Father is the person of whom the purchase is made; God the Son is the person who makes the purchase, and the Holy Spirit is the gift purchased. The sum of all those good things in this life, and the life to come, which are purchased for the

<!-- p. 354 -->

church is the Holy Spirit. And as this is the great purchase, so it is the great promise of God and Christ. Acts 2:33, "Having received of the Father the promise of the Holy Ghost, he hath shed forth this, which ye now see and hear." And this great purchase of Christ is forever given to his church.[^004-note326] [[He has promised that his church shall continue, and expressly declared that the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.]] Therefore when Christ promises his Spirit, he promises the continuance of it forever. John 14:16–17, "And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you forever; even the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive; because it seeth him not, neither knoweth him; but ye know him, for he dwelleth with you, and shall be in you."

Man in his first estate had the Holy Spirit, but he lost it; [it was thrown][^004-note327] away. But a way is found out that it may be restored, and now it is given a second time, never again to depart. The Spirit of God is so given to the saints as to become theirs. The Spirit of God was communicated to our first parents in their state of innocence, and dwelt in them. But the Spirit was not given to them in the same sense that it is to believers in Christ. They had no proper right or sure title to the Spirit. It was not finally given and made over to our first parents as it is to believers in Christ. If it had been, they never would have lost it. But the Spirit of Christ is not only communicated to those who are converted, but it is made over by a sure covenant,[^004-note328] so that he is become theirs. Christ is become theirs, and therefore his fullness is theirs, his Spirit is theirs, the Spirit of Christ is their purchased and promised possession. I come now to

*Prop*. II. The second thing proposed, viz. that there are other fruits of the Spirit besides that which summarily consists in divine love wherein the Spirit of God is communicated to his church; as particularly,

*First*. The Spirit of God has been communicated to the church in many extraordinary gifts, which are the gifts of miraculous inspiration. The Spirit of God seems to have been communicated to the church in such gifts formerly to the prophets under the Old Testament, and to the Apostles, and prophets, and evangelists, and to the generality of ministers of the gospel, and great multitudes of common Christians under the New Testament who had such gifts as the gifts of prophecy and tongues,

<!-- p. 355 -->

and the gift called the gift of knowledge, and others mentioned in the context and in the foregoing chapters.

*Second*. Besides these there are the common and ordinary gifts of the Spirit of God which in all ages have been bestowed on many natural men; such as common convictions of sin, common illuminations, common religious affections, which, though they have nothing of the nature of divine love or true and saving grace, yet are the fruits of the Spirit or the effects of his influence on the hearts of men. And as to faith and hope, if there be nothing of divine love within them,[^004-note329] there can be no more in them which is from the Spirit of God than what is common to natural men, as the Apostle in this chapter says: "Though I have faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing." Saving faith and hope have love as an ingredient in them and as the essence of them. And take out this ingredient, and what remains is but the body without the spirit. It is nothing, seeing it is at most but a common fruit of the Spirit. I now pass to the third thing proposed.

*Prop*. III. Which was to show that those other fruits of the Spirit are but for a season, and either have failed or will fail. As to those miraculous gifts of prophecy, and the gift of tongues, and others, they are but a temporary use. They have not continued in heaven. Those miraculous gifts were given only as certain means of grace which God was once pleased to grant to his church in this world. But when those saints who once had the enjoyment and use of those means of grace came to heaven, those miraculous gifts as well as other means of grace ceased. There is no occasion for any means of grace in heaven; either ordinary, such as the stated ordinances of God's house,[^004-note330] [as] sacraments and prayer, or extraordinary, as prophecy, and gift of tongues, and gift of knowledge. I say there is no occasion for any of these means of grace to be continued in heaven; because there the end of all means of grace is already fully obtained in the perfect sanctification and happiness of God's people.

<!-- p. 356 -->

The Apostle, speaking of the means of grace, tells us in the fourth chapter to the Ephesians, those means were given for the perfecting of the saints, till we all come to a perfect man. Ver. Ephesians 4:11–13, "And he gave some apostles; and some prophets; and some evangelists; and some pastors and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ; till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ." But when this is come to pass, when the saints are perfected and are already come to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, then there will be no further occasion for any of those means, or the Apostles, prophets, pastors, or teachers, or any of their gifts.[^004-note331] Much as it is with the fruits of the field; they need tillage, and rain, and the shining of the sun, till they are ripe and gathered in, and then they need them no longer.

And as those miraculous gifts of the Spirit were but temporary with regard to those particular persons who had them, so they are but for a season with regard to the church of God as a collective body. Those gifts are not fruits of the Spirit which are always given and continued to the church throughout all ages. They were continued in the church, or at least granted from time to time, though not without some considerable intermissions from the beginning of the world till the canon of the Scripture was completed. These miraculous gifts of the Spirit were granted in the church before the beginning of the canon of Scripture; that is, before the writing of the book of Job[^004-note332] and the five books of Moses. They had the word of God then in no other way than by immediate revelation from time to time given to eminent persons who were, as it were, fathers in God's church, and so it was handed from them to others by oral tradition. It was a very common thing then for the Spirit of God to communicate himself in dreams and visions, as appears by several passages in the book of Job, ch. Job 33: Job 33:15–16; ch. Job 4: Job 4:15–16. They had extraordinary gifts of the Spirit before the flood. God immediately and miraculously revealed himself to Adam and Eve, and so to Abel; and Enoch had the gift of prophecy, Jude, ver. Jude 14. And so Noah had immediate revelation made to him, and he warned the old world from God; and Christ by his Spirit on him went and preached to the spirits that are now in prison, who were sometime disobedient, when once the long-suffering of God waited in

<!-- p. 357 -->

the days of Noah, while the ark was preparing, 1 Peter 3:19–20. So Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were favored with many immediate revelations. And Joseph had extraordinary gifts of the Spirit, and so had Job, and his three friends, and Elihu.

From this time there seems to have been an intermission of the communication of the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit until Moses' time; and from his time they were continued in a succession of prophets, which was kept up not without some intermission till Malachi's time. After that there seems to have been a great intermission of several hundred years, till the dawn of the days of the gospel, when the Spirit began to be given in his extraordinary gifts to Anna, Simeon, Zecharias, Elizabeth, Joseph and Mary, and John the Baptist. Those communications of the Spirit were given to make way for him who hath the Spirit without measure, the great prophet of God, by whom the Spirit is communicated to all other prophets. And in the days of his flesh his disciples had a measure of the miraculous gifts of the Spirit, being sent forth to teach and work miracles. But after his resurrection and ascension was the most full and remarkable effusion of the Spirit in his miraculous gifts, beginning with the day of Pentecost following Christ's resurrection. And in consequence of this not only here and there an extraordinary person was endued with those extraordinary gifts, but they were common in the church, and were so in a great measure for an age, during the life of the Apostles, or till the death of the last of them, even the apostle John, which was about an hundred years from the birth of Christ.

So that the first hundred years of the Christian era, or first century, was the age of miracles.
