Now consider, all ye who are out of Christ, who were never born again, and never had any blessed renovation of your hearts implanting a spirit of divine love there, leading you to choose that happiness which consists in holy love as your best and sweetest good, and to spend your life in struggling after happiness. Consider your misery.[^004-note370] For this is the world to which you are under condemnation, and so the world to which you belong by the sentence of the law, and the world in which you are in danger every day of having your abode fixed; and if you are not greatly changed by God's almighty power, in a short time will inherit instead of a portion in that world of love of which you have heard. Consider it is indeed thus with you. These are no cunningly devised fables. They are the great and awful truths of God's word, and things which in a short time you will certainly know to be true. How therefore can you rest in such a state as you are in, and go about from day to day so careless and so negligent of your precious soul? Seriously consider these things, and be wise for yourself before it is too late, before your feet stumble on the dark mountains, and you fall into that world of wrath and hatred where is eternal weeping, and wailing, and gnashing of teeth, with spiteful malice and rage against God and Christ, and one another, and gnashing of teeth with horror and anguish of spirit.

III. Use may be of exhortation in two branches.

*First*. Let the consideration of what has been said of heaven stir you up earnestly to seek after it. If heaven be such a blessed world, then let this be our chosen country, and the inheritance we seek. Let us turn our course this way. It is not impossible that this glorious world may be obtained by us. It is offered to us. Though it be so excellent and blessed a country, yet God stands ready to give us an inheritance there, if this be the country we choose, and upon which we set our hearts, and spend our time chiefly in seeking it. God gives men their choice. They may have their inheritance where they choose it, and may obtain heaven if they

<!-- p. 393 -->

will seek it by patient continuance in well-doing, Romans 2:7. We are all of us, as it were, set here in this world as in a large wilderness with divers countries about it, with several ways or paths leading to those different countries, and we are left to our choice what course we will take. If we heartily choose heaven, and set our hearts chiefly on that blessed Canaan, that land of love, and love the path which leads to it, we may walk in it; and if we continue so to do, it will certainly lead us to heaven at last. Let what we have heard of the land of love excite us all to turn our faces towards that land, and bend our course thitherward. Is not what we have heard of the happy state of that country and the many delights which are in it enough to make us thirst after it, and to cause us with the greatest earnestness and steadfastness of resolution to press[^004-note371] towards, and to spend our whole lives in traveling in the way which leads thither? What joyful news might it well be to us when we hear of such a world of perfect peace and holy love, to hear that there is an opportunity for us to come, that we may spend an eternity in such a world.

Is not what we have heard of that blessed world enough to make us weary of this world of pride and malice and contention and perpetual jarring and strife, a world of confusion, a wilderness of hissing serpents, a tempestuous ocean where there is no quiet rest, where all are for themselves, and self-interest governs, and all are striving to set themselves up, and little regarding what becomes of others; all together seeking worldly good which is the bone of contention among them, where men are continually envying and calumniating and reproaching one another and multitudes otherwise injuring and abusing one another, a world full of injustice, where there is abundance of opposition and cruelty without any remedy? Ecclesiastes 4:1, "So I returned and considered all the oppressions that are done under the sun; and behold the tears of such as were oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the side of their oppressors there was power; but they had no comforter." A world where there is so much falsehood and treachery, fickleness and inconstancy, hypocrisy and deceit; where there is so little trust to be had in men, and where even good men have so many failings which tend to render them unlovely and uncomfortable. Truly this is an evil world, and so it is like to be. It is in vain for us to expect that this world will be any other than a world of pride and enmity and strife, and so a restless world. The times may hereafter be mended, yet those things will always be found in the world as long as it stands. Who would content himself with a portion in such a world? What man acting wisely and considerately would concern

<!-- p. 394 -->

himself much about laying up a store in such a world as this, and would not rather neglect the world,[^004-note372] [[and let it go to them that would take it, and]] apply all his heart and all his strength to lay up treasure in heaven, and to press towards that world of love? What will it signify for us to hoard up great quantities here in this world? How may the thought of having our portion here in such a world as this be sinking to a man when there is an interest in such a glorious world offered? and especially when if we have our portion here, when we have done with this world, we have our eternal portion in hell, that world of hatred, a world of the wrath of God, and cruelty and malice of devils and damned spirits.

We all of us naturally desire rest and quietness; and if we would obtain, let us seek that world of peace and love of which we have heard. Here is doubtless a sweet rest to be had. Hebrews 4:9, "There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God." If we obtain an interest in that world, then when we have done with this we shall leave all our cares and troubles, our fatigues and perplexities and disappointments forever. We shall rest from those storms, we shall rest from our wearisome travel. Revelation 14:13, "Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth; yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labors." You who are poor, and think yourselves despised by your neighbors, and little esteemed among men, do not much regard this, do not give yourselves much concern about the friendship of the world; but seek heaven where is no such thing as contempt, where none are despised, all are highly esteemed and honored, and dearly loved by all. You who think you have met with many abuses, and much ill treatment from others, care not for it; do not hate them for it but set your heart in heaven, a world of love; press towards a better country.

Here for direction how to seek heaven,

1. Do not let out your heart after the things of this world and indulge yourself in a pursuit of earthly things. This is the reverse of seeking heaven. This is to go the contrary way, which leads directly from heaven and not towards it. If you would seek heaven, your affections must be taken off from the pleasures of the world. You must not indulge in sensuality; you must take off your heart from the profits of the world, and not spend your time and strength only in heaping up the dust of the

<!-- p. 395 -->

earth. You must mortify a desire of the honors and vainglory of this world, and become poor in spirit, and lowly of heart.

2. You must in your meditations and holy exercises be much in conversing with heavenly persons and enjoyments. You cannot earnestly and constantly seek heaven without having your thoughts much there. Therefore turn the current of your thoughts and meditations towards that world of love, and that God of love who dwells there, and towards Christ who is ascended and sits there at the right hand of God; and towards the blessed enjoyments of that world. And be much in conversing with [God and Christ,] without which heaven is no heaven. Philippians 3:20, "Our conversation is in heaven."

3. Be content to pass through all difficulties in the way to heaven. Though the path is before you, and you may walk in it if you really choose it, yet it is a way which is strait, and there are many difficulties in the way; the whole way is ascending. That glorious city of light and love is, as it were, on the top of an high hill, an elevation which is exalted above the hill, and there is no arriving there without traveling uphill. Though this be wearisome, yet it is worth your while to come and dwell in such a glorious city at last. Be willing therefore to comply with this labor. What is it in comparison of the sweet rest which is at the end of your journey? Be willing to cross the natural inclination of flesh and blood, which is downward. Continue crossing this tendency; it will grow easier and easier, and you will be paid by more and more of the pleasant prospect which you will have the higher you rise, and a nearer view of the glorious city on the top of the hill, besides the glorious reward which you will have when you arrive there.

4. In all your way let your eye be to Jesus who is gone to heaven as your Forerunner. Look to him; behold his glory there in heaven to stir you up the more earnestly to be there. Look to him, and observe his example. Consider how by patient continuance in well-doing, and in patient enduring of great sufferings, he went before to heaven. Look to him, and trust in his mediation, in his blood, with which he has entered into the holiest of all, as the price of heaven. Trust to his intercession in heaven before God. Trust to his strength by his Spirit sent from heaven to enable you to press on and surmount the difficulties which are in the way to heaven. Trust in his promises of heaven to those who love and follow him, whom he has confirmed by entering into heaven himself as the Head and Representative and Forerunner of such.

5. And lastly. If you would be in the way to the world of love, you must

<!-- p. 396 -->

live a life of love. But I would make this a distinct exhortation.[^004-note373] And therefore

*Second*. The second exhortation is to all, to seek that they may live a life of love, a life of love to God and love to men. We all hope to have a part in heaven, that world of love of which we have heard, and that in a little time. Surely then we should endeavor to use the same temper of mind. Here let several things be considered as motives.

1. This is the way to be like the inhabitants of heaven. You have heard how they love one another; and therefore they, and they only, are conformed to them who live in love in this world. In this way you will be like them in excellence and loveliness, for their holiness and loveliness consists in being of such an excellent spirit. And this will be the way to make you like them in happiness and comfort. For this happiness and joy and rest lies in loving the inhabitants of that world. And by living in love in this world the saints partake of a like sort of inward peace and sweetness. It is in this way that you are to have the foretastes of heavenly pleasures and delights.

2. This is the way to have a sense of glory of heavenly things, as of God and Christ, and holiness, and heavenly enjoyments. A contrary spirit, a spirit of hatred and ill will greatly hinders a sense of those things. It darkens the mind and clouds such objects, and puts them out of sight. A frame of holy love to God and Christ, and a spirit of love and peace to men greatly disposes and fits the heart for a sense of the excellence and sweetness of heavenly objects. It gives a relish of them. It, as it were, opens the windows by which the light of heaven shines in upon the soul.

3. This is the way to have clear evidences of a title to heaven. There are no evidences of a title to heaven but in feeling that which is heavenly in the heart. But by what has been said, it appears that heavenliness consists in love. Therefore the way to have clear evidences of a title is to live a life of love, and so seek the continual and lively exercises of such a spirit. You will find that this will cast out fear and give a strong hope of heaven, and be, as it were, an exercise of heaven in your hearts.

4. By living a life of love, you will be in the way to heaven. As heaven is a world of love, so the way to heaven is the way of love. This will best prepare you for heaven, and make you meet for an inheritance with the

<!-- p. 397 -->

saints in that land of light and love. And if ever you arrive at heaven, faith and love[^004-note374] must be the wings which must carry you there.[^004-note375]

[^004-note1]: Chronological proximity with *History of Redemption* does not demonstrate JE's plan to publish the charity sermons. But there is internal evidence, which I will note, that JE probably wrote down the Scripture verses cited in these sermons.

[^004-note2]: See App. I and my Intro., pp. 3–5.

[^004-note3]: The original edition of TE reads "acquirements."

[^004-note4]: Bellamy crossed out "commonly" in his "What Persons commonly mean," and wrote "very often" above the line. See App. I for this and subsequent references to Joseph Bellamy's part-copy.

[^004-note5]: My conjecture is that, after "chap. 1 Corinthians 8," JE's sermon booklet listed verses "1 Corinthians 8:1, 1 Corinthians 8:2, 1 Corinthians 8:3, " followed by comments he intended to make upon them. The Andover copyist faithfully entered the three numbers, then the entire Scripture passage, followed by comments referring seriatim to the verse in question. This made his version somewhat awkward. Bellamy edited as he copied. He quoted the first verse followed by comment, then the remainder of the passage followed by comment. Bellamy crossed out the numbers 2 and 3 when deciding to proceed one verse at a time. The result was a smoother construction of JE's thought. See the synopsis of the three texts at this point in App. I.

[^004-note6]: Here TE (p. 3) reads "how knowledge usually puffs up." His "usually" was a mistaken transcription of "vainly." The context is about things that are "in vain" without charity. Bellamy reads "how knowledge vainly puffs up." Andover has no word.

[^004-note7]: JE's proof of his point from these verses in I Cor. has special significance, since the apostle Paul more frequently uses the word *agape* for love of neighbor.

[^004-note8]: The Andover copyist entered the words JE meant to deliver from John 9:40 and Job 11:12; or else (as TE asserts in his introduction) these sermons were "written out in full" by JE himself. My judgment is that JE did usually copy "preceptorial" passages from Scripture in these sermon booklets. Here the precept is the vanity of the wise. Bellamy goes at once to the pivotal passage from Matthew 7:22. TE eliminates all Scripture quotations thus reducing what he believed was JE's redundancy— and at once introduces the Doctrine.

[^004-note9]: Pages of Bellamy's copy are missing after this point. "Has" is a catchword for the first word on the next, missing, page.

[^004-note10]: TE's parallel (p. 5) omits the last two sentences, beginning with "And particularly faith..."

[^004-note11]: Here TE agrees with the Andover copy in using the term "infuses." Also, just below, in the second sentence under point 2, where TE twice uses "infuse," Andover uses the term only once. These three instances are the only places in the entire sermon series where TE allows that this was JE's usage. In the fourteen instances where Andover uses the language of infusion, which will be noted below, TE avoids such language. There are eight instances of such replacement or avoidance in the twelfth sermon on the concatenation of Christian graces, three in the tenth sermon on holy practice, and one each in the seventh sermon on a selfish spirit, in the thirteenth sermon on grace never overthrown, and the fourteenth sermon on divine love alone lasts eternally. See Intro., p. 59, n. 5, and App. IV.

[^004-note12]: JE's 1741 sermon on the distinguishing marks of a work of the Spirit had as its text Romans 4:1 on "trying the spirits whether they be of God." In this famous discourse, he invoked many other verses in this chapter, including ver. Romans 4:12–13, quoted above. The fifth distinguishing mark or test— whether the Spirit "operates as a spirit of love to God and man"— strikingly parallels this first sermon. In discussing that mark, JE lays out his belief that humility is the "surest character of true divine supernatural love"; *Distinguishing Marks*, in *The Great Awakening*, ed. C. C. Goen, Vol. 4 in *The Works of Jonathan Edwards* (New Haven, Yale Univ. Press [1972], 257–59). The charity sermons present a more complex depiction of the divine condescension and humility in "the human nature" of Christ. See Sermon Six and p. 224, n. 3, below.

[^004-note13]: The words "nature or spiritual image of God" are expressions for one and the same likeness to God— not to be confused with JE's familiar *distinction* between the "natural" and the "spiritual" image of God. The word *nature* in the text above is from 2 Peter 1:4, "Whereby are given unto us exceeding and precious promises: that by these ye might be *partakers of the divine nature*, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust" (Ed. italics). This was the first verse quoted in point *First* above. The first reference I find in the "Miscellanies" to being partakers of the divine nature is in No. 683, whose running title is "Join this to Num. 673. COMMON GRACE. SPECIAL GRACE." The first paragraph of this entry states: "Natural men have nothing of that nature in them that true Christians have, and that appears because the nature that they have is divine nature... Not only they alone partake of such degrees of it, but they alone are partakers of it. To be partakers of the divine nature is mentioned as peculiar to the saints in 2 Peter 1:1." Notably, there is a reference to the verses that are texts of the present sermon in the entry joined with the above, a previous Miscell. no. 673, entitled "SAVING GRACE differs not only in degree, but in nature and kind, from COMMON GRACE, or anything that is ever found in natural men" (probably composed after the Northampton revival, and only a year or so before the charity sermons): "Those who go furthest in religion, that are in a natural condition, have no charity; as is plainly implied in the beginning of the 13th chapter of the first of Corinthians, by which we must understand, that they have none of the kind of grace or disposition that is so called" (par. 3). For my use of Thomas A. Schafer's transcriptions of the "Miscellanies," see Intro., p. 9, n. 1. For further commentary on 2 Peter 1:4 in explanation of the meaning of *spiritual*, see the *Treatise on Grace* (*c*. 1741), in Alexander B. Grosart, *Selections from the Unpublished Writings of Jonathan Edwards of America* (printed for private circulation, 1865), pp. 40–42, 51–56; *Religious Affections*, ed. John E. Smith, in *Works, 2*, Pt. III, First, Fourth, and Seventh Distinguishing Signs, with the summary (pp. 392–96) of these three signs among the reasons for the Twelfth; *Distinguishing Marks*, in *Works, 4*, 255–60; and Related Correspondence below for JE's defense against an objector who questioned his notion of God's communicating his own proper nature (*Affections*, pp. 232–39).

[^004-note14]: "Those precepts" refers both to 1 Peter 2:17 and to Philippians 2:3. There is no need to suppose that JE meant to deliver the three precepts the copy omits from 1 Peter 2:17, which continues: "Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the king." There is remarkably frequent use of "precept" in reference to Scripture passages throughout the sermon series. The word and the concept served to make JE's exposition of 1 Corinthians 13 an integrated treatise on the Christian moral life. The most notable series of precepts are in Sermons Four and Six. A not unreasonable supposition is that JE himself wrote out the precepts or portions of verses that served his purpose. On the other hand, if we suppose that the Andover copyist supplied many or most of the selections from the scriptures cited, he was greatly assisted by the conceptual— *preceptorial*— character of the series. The remarkable accuracy with which precepts are selected is, cumulatively, strong internal evidence that JE wrote out the passages he meant to deliver, and is perhaps (as TE also claims) evidence that he planned to publish the series.

[^004-note15]: The internal quotation is Psalms 82:6, "I had said, Ye are gods; and all children of the most High." JE understands the entirety of Scripture to be the law of God; hence the reference to Psalms.

[^004-note16]: JE's reasoning seems to be that since the second commandment sums up the precepts of the second table of the law rehearsed in Romans 13:9, this must— in the unity of Scripture— be the meaning of it in Matthew 22:38.

[^004-note17]: TE (p. 19) reads "speculative faith" to explain the Andover copyist's construction. My sense is that the copyist is faithful to JE's style. Note also, just below, the identification of "true spiritual *consent* of the heart" with "the *love* of the heart"; and cf. *True Virtue*, Chs. I and II.

[^004-note18]: I. e., compared with Galatians 5:6. See also n. 4 above.

[^004-note19]: See Sermon Twelve.

[^004-note20]: The sermon's two points under Doctrine— on the *nature* of divine love and on the *truth* of the doctrine— are both paralleled by the entirety of ch. II of the *Treatise on Grace*, entitled "Shewing Wherein All Saving Grace Does Summarily Consist" (Grosart, *Unpublished Writings*, pp. 30–38). The only significant thematic difference is that the sermon's ordering of what reason teaches and what Scripture teaches is reversed in the treatise.

[^004-note21]: The "several inferences" that follow immediately in the Andover copy seem to belong to use of instruction. Therefore I insert just below from TE (pp. 23–25) a use of self-examination, which was announced to come first. In placing this passage from TE in the text above, where there is no break in the copy, I reject the suggestion that JE might have simply *said* that his congregation should first examine themselves, while himself elaborating only the use of instruction. Of course, JE may have delivered the first use extemporaneously, which he announced but for which he had no text in his sermon booklet. Readers should note that when, after this interpolation, the text returns to the Andover copy, only the second and sixth of the inferences could possibly be read as being of examination. TE also has a third use, of exhortation. My insertion in single brackets announces my reliance on TE for the ending of the sermon. That there was an exhortation in JE's booklet is supported by Bellamy. See the final footnote to this sermon. However, there is another plausible approach to the Andover copyist's version of the application— one that gives more credit to his accuracy and less to TE. JE's original sermon, written and delivered, may have combined the two uses, the "several inferences" being both of examination and of instruction, as is the case in other sermons. The second and sixth of the six inferences, then, could be cited in support of the Andover copyist's accuracy and TE's greater liberty in editing the booklets. Andover's careful numbering of the two announced uses, and Bellamy's knowledge of a use of exhortation, on balance, supports my reliance on TE for the textual reconstruction I have made.

[^004-note22]: The first of several inferences. See n. 9 immediately above.

[^004-note23]: On Christ's elevation to the Father's throne as Ruler and Judge according to the covenant of grace, sec JE's *Observations Concerning the Scripture Oeconomy of the Trinity and Covenant of Redemption*, ed. Egbert C. Smyth (New York, Charles Scribner's Sons, 1880), p. 45 et passim. Note also, just below, the reference to Christ's prayer, John 17:21–23; and cf. the role this plays in *End of Creation*.

[^004-note24]: Six and one-half lines blank in the Andover copy, which breaks off with the words "in giving" without terminal punctuation. To retain and elide with the words of the copy, I have made slight changes in TE's words.

[^004-note25]: With this word, a second Bellamy fragment begins, continuing almost to the end of the sermon. The fragment concludes with a four-line use of exhortation, ending with the words "then surely," where "surely" is a catchword indicating the first word on a next missing page. In this instance, Bellamy agrees with TE that the sermon ended with an exhortation.

[^004-note26]: Both Bellamy and TE (p. 30) cite ver. Romans 5:10 also, and quote its final words, "when we were enemies." The Andover copy omits this reference to enemies, and there is no blank space in his copy at this point. For discussion of the textual problem, see App. I, pp. 669–71.

There Andover is correct and Bellamy errs. TE has "sight" in the first instance as well as "light" in the second. These words in JE's booklet could easily be taken one for the other; and, of course, JE's pen did sometimes slip.

[^004-note28]: JE effectively paused here— where the reader may need to read "that" in place of the comma.

[^004-note29]: Bellamy reads instead: "If they are so, love is the sum & substance of them." TE (p. 31) agrees.

[^004-note30]: Here Bellamy's parallel contains an additional sentence: "Divine knowledge & Divine love go together." So also TE (p. 31).

[^004-note31]: Point *Third* follows immediately in Bellamy and TE.

[^004-note32]: Bellamy adds "a life of love is a pleasant life," followed by several dashes. TE (pp. 32–33) goes further and quotes Proverbs 3:13, Proverbs 3:17.

[^004-note33]: Here the Andover copy ends. TE extends the sixth instruction and adds a seventh instruction, closely paralleling Bellamy, whose fragment also begins a use of exhortation before breaking off. TE's version continues this exhortation for a page and a half. I draw upon TE (pp. 34–37) to fill out the Andover copy's abrupt end of the sermon, persuaded by Bellamy that there was in JE's booklet both a seventh instruction and a use of exhortation.

[^004-note34]: Here Bellamy's fragment ends, with "surely" a catchword indicating the first word— we may reasonably conjecture of only one more page of his copy, now missing.

[^004-note35]: Ver. 1 Corinthians 12:10 is needed to complete the rehearsal.

[^004-note36]: Explication of the text is considerably compressed in TE, pp. 38–41. Beyond question, the exegesis in Andover's text explication is closer to that of JE's sermon booklet.

[^004-note37]: The Spirit influences the minds of men primarily in two ways: by operating on them and by dwelling in them. The former is "common" to natural men and to saints. "*Legal* humiliation" is an example of "the mind's being assisted to a greater sense of... the natural perfections of God, such as his greatness, terrible majesty, etc." An example of the Spirit's dwelling in the minds of the saints is the "sense... given in *evangelical* humiliation, by a discovery of the beauty of God's holiness and moral perfection" (*Affections*, p. 311. Ed. italics).

[^004-note38]: About two lines blank in the Andover copy. Insert from TE, p. 42.

[^004-note39]: The *Treatise on Grace* lists "common grace, common illuminations and common affections" as influences that are "of the nature of the Spirit" but that do not make us "spiritual persons" (Grosart, *Unpublished Writings*, p. 42). In Sermon Fourteen below JE's concentration is on the common *ordinary* influences of the Spirit that have yet to pass away. There he lists "common convictions of sin, common illuminations, common religious[!] affections." In the present sermon he is concerned chiefly with the common *extraordinary* gifts that have already passed away.

[^004-note40]: The copyist first wrote "peculiar"; then crossed it out, and wrote "special" above the line. Two possible explanations for this (and like instances below) are: (1) he realized he made a mistake in transcription, his eye having lighted upon the word "peculiar" later in the sentence; or (2) "peculiar" was in JE's booklet in both places, and the copyist decided upon a bit of editing to avoid the repetition. Most likely, his was an error in transcription, which he then corrected. See text below, at n. 7, for another use of "special" for "saving" or "uncommon."

[^004-note41]: The Application of JE's sermon *Distinguishing Marks* drew this same distinction between the "ordinary gracious" and the extraordinary influences of the Spirit that may be "common"; "a man may have those extraordinary gifts and yet be abominable to God." Balaam, Saul, and Judas are mentioned, then Matthew 7:22, as above (*Works, 4*, 278–79).

[^004-note42]: Here at the end of JE's eloquent tribute to the great privilege it was for men of old to be "endued" with the extraordinary gifts listed by St. Paul, attention should be called to the meaning the word "extraordinary" has when used in *Distinguishing Marks* (1741) and *Affections* (1746). In the context of JE's interpretation of revival phenomena, "extraordinary" means unexpected, strange, unusual, out-of-the-ordinary. That is all the word could mean, since it was JE's view that real supernatural "extraordinary gifts" had ceased seventeen centuries before. JE's discrimination, among strange or unusual revival phenomena, was between those occurrences that are "no certain signs" [*Affections*, Pt. II) in contrast to twelve "Distinguishing Signs" (Pt. III) of truly gracious affections. And in *Distinguishing Marks*, his language was "what are *not* signs that we are to judge of a work by"; indeed, he used a double negative, i.e., "what are *no* evidences that a work wrought amongst a people, is *not* the work of the Spirit of God" (*Distinguishing Marks*, p. 228. Ed. italics).

[^004-note43]: The Andover copy reads: "I come now in the III Place to show...," with "III" on the left margin. Subsequent similar transitions to new par. numbers will be regularly edited as here.

[^004-note44]: Here, and at "his ordinary influences" in the next sentence, the copyist changed references to the Holy Spirit to "himself" and "his." These words are written over "itself" and "its," faintly discernible. "It" and "itself" were used before this point. Eight uses of the more personal pronouns follow immediately in the paragraph.

[^004-note45]: The *First* and *Second* points above— that saving grace is inherent in the *nature* of him that has it, and that in the ordinary gift of graced affections the Holy Spirit communicates himself as a vital principle, and not his effects alone— can be supplemented by *Affections*, especially in the First, Fourth, and Seventh Distinguishing Signs. There also JE mentions some of the same unusual phenomena, as in the sermon, that are "no certain signs." See n. 8 above. From the side of the human subject "participation" is at the center of JE's theology, here and in *End of Creation*.

[^004-note46]: See Sermon One, p. 133, n. 1. JE distinguished between the "natural" and the "spiritual" images of God. The latter is "the amiable image and likeness of Christ" (just below). He also speaks of the "blessed image of God" in those who have the "ordinary gracious influences" of the Spirit. (*Distinguishing Marks*, pp. 278–79.) See also *Freedom of the Will*, ed. Paul Ramsey, in *Works, 1*, 166 and n., and *Affections*, Pt. III, Third Sign, esp. p. 256.

[^004-note47]: Here in Andover and at the following insertion there are blanks that could each be filled with a single word. I judge none to be needed in the first instance. TE (p. 54) reads: "influencing us to holy and heavenly lives."

[^004-note48]: Here in Andover is a break of about three-fourths of a line. TE simply omits the words "He foretold many things." Because these words concerning Balaam seem to be needed, I place a period after "things" and suggest that nothing more need be said. This conveys a crispness like the references to prophecy that follow. The absence of terminal punctuation, however, and the fact that three-fourths of a line is blank in the copy at this point, may indicate that JE drew a line to remind himself to recite some of the things Balaam foretold.

[^004-note49]: At about this place TE (p. 56) proceeds to point *Fifth*.

[^004-note50]: JE's sense is: Hence we may argue from the infinitely superior excellence *of the fruits or effects* of the ordinary gifts over those of the extraordinary— since grace is saving, extraordinary gifts are not.

[^004-note51]: The end or purpose for which extraordinary gifts were given is more fully elaborated in Sermon Fourteen. There, too, as in *Distinguishing Marks*, pp. 280–81, JE classed such gifts as "childish" things.

[^004-note52]: Miscell. no. 379 (*c*. 1728–29): "That extraordinary and miraculous way was made use of once, only for the introducing of the more perfect way. This is the *end*of the other way; it is excellent in itself; but inspiration and miracles are good for nothing without it... Seeing the *end* is come, it would be impertinent to continue the means" (Ed. italics). JE cites the final verse of 1 Corinthians 12 and the first verse of 1 Corinthians 13 in support of his view. But extraordinary outpourings were both necessary, pertinent, and suitable in the *transitus* from the Jews, the church of old, to "the gospel state of the church, which is not any particular enclosure but is dispersed throughout the whole world."

[^004-note53]: From here to the end of this point *Eighth*, TE deletes and replaces far more than was needed to deal with the final page of this section in the original sermon booklet, of which Andover was a faithful reproduction. Evidently TE, writing in the nineteenth century, had little interest in the thoughts that JE was wrestling with from the verses in Hebrews. In its entirety TE's replacement (pp. 60–61) reads:They were instructed in Christianity, and through the common influences of the Spirit they received the word with joy, like those in Matt, xiii. 20; and withal received the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit; "were made partakers of the Holy Ghost, tasted of the heavenly gift, and the powers of the world to come"; spake with tongues; prophesied in Christ's name; and in his name cast out devils; and yet after all, openly renounced Christianity; joined to call Christ an imposter, as his murderers did; and so "crucified to themselves the Son of God afresh, and put him to open shame." Of these it is that the Apostle says: "It is impossible to renew them again to repentance." Such apostates, in their renouncing Christianity, must ascribe the miraculous powers which themselves had possessed to the devil. So their case became hopeless; and their condemnation must be exceedingly aggravated. And from this it appears that saving grace is of infinitely more worth and excellence, than the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit. Then follows point *Ninth*, below.

[^004-note54]: At this point Andover leaves about four and one-half lines blank. This was doubtless its equivalent for the long dashes in the sermon booklet by which JE reminded himself to summarize what he had previously said. The words I venture to insert, here and below, are from JE's "Notes on the Bible" in Sereno E. Dwight, *The Works of President Edwards: With a Memoir of His Life*. 10 vols. (New York, 1829–30), 9, 538–41. To fathom the meaning of Hebrews 6:4–6, JE reads the passage in the light of Acts 19:2–6 (the doctrine of baptisms), Matthew 13:18–23, with Luke 8:18 (the parable of the sower— which he correctly understood as a parable of the soils) and Numbers 22 (the story of Balaam's disobedience). In the same context, JE interpreted Hebrews 10:25–29 to mean the sin against the Holy Ghost, whose type in the Hebrew Bible was the presumptuous, willful sabbath breaker in Numbers 15:32–36. The source of the standard Puritan sermon on Hebrews 6:4–6 and the sin against the Holy Ghost was Calvin, *Institutes*, III, iii, 21–24.

[^004-note55]: Ver. Acts 19:2 continues: "And they said unto him, We have not so much as heard whether there be any Holy Ghost." Then, after comparison with John's baptism, "When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. And when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Ghost came on them and they spake with tongues and prophesied" (ver. Acts 19:5–6). Numerous entries in the "Miscellanies" combine these verses with those mentioned in the previous note in interpreting the meaning of the sin against the Holy Ghost.

[^004-note56]: Nearly two blank lines in Andover.

[^004-note57]: One-fourth line omitted, to the right of the page; then the same space on the next line on the left of the page.

[^004-note58]: Space for one or two words, on left of page.

[^004-note59]: Space for one, perhaps two, words in the middle of the line. Assuming the copyist faithfully represented the page in the sermon booklet, the location of words on the page has no great significance. JE simply set down these incomplete sentences where best to catch his eye, with dashes to indicate he was to extemporize. At the end of this sermon there likely was another such page. But there I use the third Bellamy fragment in construing the best text. See App. I, editorial comments on fourth example.

[^004-note61]: Ten lines blank. TE's reconstruction of the paragraph (see above, p. 163, n. 1) not only ignores the reference to Balaam but adds statements not implied in the copy-text or in JE's notes on these biblical passages, e.g., that those who received common graces and then apostatize "must ascribe the miraculous powers which themselves had possessed to the devil" (TE, p. 61).

[^004-note62]: I judge that JE's extemporized interpretation of the Hebrews passage would have been something like my text above. The difficulty in the way of the present-day reader is largely theological. Indeed it is intellectually difficult to understand how, on JE's view, it was possible to commit the sin against the Holy Ghost in Northampton seventeen centuries after the extraordinary gifts had passed away. See App. V.

[^004-note63]: See below, Sermon Fourteen, whose text I inserted above.

[^004-note64]: Full line blank in the copy. TE (p. 62) has JE repeat the Doctrine (abbreviated). Surely the preacher did so here. But the space in Andover was likely in the original booklet.

[^004-note66]: These words occur on a stray slip of paper in the Andover collection. The handwriting is that of the copyist. They obviously belong here, where there is a full line blank with no terminal punctuation after "Solomon."

[^004-note67]: This is the language of *Affections*, Pt. II. Here, however, JE is arguing that *even if* they were real, extraordinary gifts would be no "sure signs of saving grace" because, when they were, such gifts were "common."

[^004-note68]: The foregoing concise list of supposed evidences was given lengthy analysis by JE ten years later in his May 1748 sermon on 1 Corinthians 13:8–13— especially under that sermon's second and third uses, of self-examination and of warning, comprising most of the third preaching unit. The warning is "not to give heed to any pretended revelation in yourself or others" (MS l.69va). Experiences looked upon as of a "spiritual nature" are to be tested "whether or no they ben't such as suppose immediate revelation" (MS l.47va). Moved to preach against the excesses to which the Great Awakening led, with "wild" claims "all over the country" (MS l. 48ra) to Scripture— free inspiration, JE wrote (consistent with the charity series): "If there be any such revelation as those in these days they are not spiritual. They were not spiritual in the days when there were such things. There was then a vast difference between those things and the saving operations" (MS l.5ora). Transcribed for me by Stephen D. Crocco. The sermon booklet is not paginated. See p. 83, n. 5 above. I refer to this important sermon below in my notes to the present sermon and to Sermons Nine, Fourteen, and Fifteen.

[^004-note69]: The Andover copyist mistakenly transcribed "desiring." TE (p. 66) reads: "And the only way, therefore, in which any can know their good estate, is by discerning the exercises of this divine charity in their hearts, for without charity, let men have what gifts you please, they are nothing." He then proceeds immediately to point *Third*.

[^004-note70]: Space for only one line in the copy. For my insert, cf. above, n. 8.

[^004-note71]: Here JE grants that God "often does direct persons' thoughts to such and such scripture... to stir up the exercises of grace." This means the grace they have. Cf. his view that "secondary beauty" has "a tendency to assist those whose hearts are under the influence of a truly virtuous temper, to... enliven in them a sense of spiritual beauty" (*True Virtue*, p. 565 below, and Intro., p. 36). In *Affections* he stresses also a reverse influence, that truly gracious affections often stir up unusual experiences that are "no certain signs." Two remarkable and connected Miscellanies, no. 123. SPIRITUAL SIGHT and no. 126. SPIRITUAL UNDERSTANDING OF THE SCRIPTURES (*c*. 1724), bear upon the issue here, giving as they do a sort of Lockean explanation of the phenomena in question. "When upon an occasion I was more than ordinarily affected with the passingness of one generation after another," JE writes in No. 126, "how that all those who made such a noise and bluster now, and were so much concerned about their life, would be clean gone off from the face of the earth in sixty or seventy years' time, and that the world would be left desolate with respect to them, and that another generation would come on, that would be very little concerned about them, and so one after another; it was particularly affecting to me, to think that the earth still remained the same through all those changes upon the surface, the same spots of ground, the same mountains and valleys where those things were done, remaining just as they were, though the actions were ceased and the actors quite gone— and then this text came into my mind," i.e., the text "One generation passeth away, and another cometh; but the earth abideth forever" (Ecclesiastes 1:4) that in "a common frame of mind, seemed insipid," and its final words a non sequitur. "Hence we learn," a corollary tells us, "how places of Scripture are often suddenly brought into mind, which are almost forgotten perhaps, before; the motions that are then in the mind being so exactly agreeable thereto, that if there be any footsteps of it in the memory, it will bring them before the mind. So that the Spirit of God don't immediately suggest the places to us, as though by inspiration, but by stirring up correspondent affections of mind, whereby the mind is naturally put in mind of the text that is so agreeable to it; as much as one speech or sentence puts us in mind of another like it, or as one instrument of music answers of itself to another in harmony and concord."

[^004-note72]: Romans 11:25–26, "Blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles be come in. And so all Israel shall be saved."

[^004-note73]: By "Antichrist" JE meant the Roman apostasy. And cf: "It appears to me much more probably that God should give immediate revelations to his saints in the dark days of popery, than now in the approach of the most glorious and perfect state of his church on earth" (*Distinguishing Marks*, p. 281).

[^004-note74]: No space in Andover copy.

[^004-note75]: In his 1748 sermon on 1 Corinthians 13:8–13 JE frames an objection on behalf of "some wild people of late," namely, "that in times past God has given no new revelation since the apostles' times; yet he may do it now, being about to introduce a new dispensation" (MS l.31va— b). But he replies, "God don't remove one dispensation to make way for another unless it be better" (MS l.32vb– 33ra), or without a change of ordinances. No such new dispensation is to be expected (MS l.36rb). This discussion is introduced between the fifth and sixth arguments for the first inference under the first use of information. That inference, comprising the whole of the sermon's second preaching occasion, reads: "Hence we may learn that it is not to be expected that any of those gifts that imply divine revelation should be suffered in these days because the canon of Scripture has been complete, the church of God completely furnished with a standing rule of faith and practice, and means of grace all settled and established; and therefore the great end of all these gifts is abolished" (MS l.15vb). Transcribed by Stephen D. Crocco. In JE's alphabetical Table to the "Miscellanies" there are five listings in which there is reference to this May 1748 sermon, one a duplicate. These are under: "Canon: of the Scripture, complete"; "Dispensation: no new one to be introduced, *see* sermon on 1 Corinthians 13:8–13 (first inference, fifth argument in answer to the objection there)"; "Gifts of the Spirit, extraordinary, have ceased"; "Revelations: immediate, not given in these days"; and "Scripture: the canon finished." By contrast, there is but one reference in the Table to the 1738 sermon scries, to Sermon Thirteen, under "Perseverance, *see* sermon on 1 Corinthians 13:7." There is a second *unlisted* reference, to Sermon Fourteen, tucked away in Miscell. no. 756. The 1748 sermon, and citations of it in the Table, show JE's growing insistence on the foregoing topics a decade after their comparatively abbreviated treatment in 1738 in Sermons Two and Fourteen. No doubt JE preached many times on texts from 1 Corinthians 13, marking for revision and reusing the 1738 booklets, now missing. The 1748 sermon is the only evidence we have of his composition of a fresh sermon on a verse or verses from this chapter. See also my notes to Sermons Nine, Fourteen, and Fifteen.

[^004-note76]: A fragment of Bellamy's part-copy begins at this point, and continues on into Sermon Three. See App. I.

[^004-note77]: Here— and to the end of Sermon Two— I adopt the text of the third fragment of Bellamy's copy into the text of this edition. For explanation of the editorial problem, see App. I, fourth example.

[^004-note78]: TE (p. 69) adds after "his own blood," where there is no break in the copy, "and to glorify the Holy Spirit who hath sealed it to their souls." Thus TE composed a trinitarian formulation. In these sermons JE speaks simply of our duties to God and Christ.

[^004-note79]: TE concludes the sermon with a "use of exhortation." This was not announced in the copy, unless by the Roman numeral "I" preceding "Use may be of instruction" above, to which there is no corresponding "II" in the copy. Clearly Bellamy came to an end; moreover, his tone had already become that of an exhortation. Consistent with electing his ending, I deleted the "I" at the beginning of the Improvement. TE's exhortation and the sentences immediately preceding his replacement for "lies with," read as follows:how little this divine love hath wrought in your heart to incline you to live for God and Christ, and for the extension of his kingdom? O! how should such as you show your sense of your high privileges, by the exercises of love; love that is manifest toward God in obedience, submission, reverence, cheerfulness, joy and hope, and toward your neighbor, in meekness, sympathy, humility, charitableness, and doing good to all as you have opportunity. Finally, 5. *The subject exhorts all unrenewed persons, those who are strangers to this grace, to seek this most excellent blessing/or themselves*. Consider how miserable you now are while wholly destitute of this love, far from righteousness, in love with the vanities of the world, and full of enmity against God. How will you endure when he shall deal with you according to what you are, coming forth in anger as your enemy, and executing his fierce wrath against you. Consider, too, that you are capable of this love; and Christ is able and willing to bestow it; and multitudes have obtained it, and been blessed in it. God is seeking your love, and you are under unspeakable obligation to render it. The Spirit of God has been poured out wonderfully here. Multitudes have been converted. Scarcely a family has been passed by. In almost every household some have been made nobles, kings, and priests unto God, sons and daughters of the Lord Almighty! What manner of persons, then, ought all of us to be, how holy, serious, just, humble, charitable, devoted in God's service, and faithful to our fellowmen. As individuals and as a people, God has most richly blessed us, and as both individuals and a people, it becomes us to be a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people, showing forth the praises of him that hath called us all out of darkness into his marvellous light! "Now consider this, ye that forget God, lest I tear you in pieces and there be none to deliver. Whoso offereth praise glorifieth me, and to him that ordereth his conversation aright, will I show the salvation of God!" [Psalms 50:22–23]

[^004-note80]: I have broken JE's rather long sentence by inserting a semicolon after "circumstances." Nevertheless, there remains grammatical disagreement between "a person's disentangling himself" and "their" purse. Bellamy remedied this by replacing "were such as called for," etc., with a new sentence: "For such was the state of things that some were called to give up all things, and entirely disentangle themselves from the cares and cumbers of worldly possessions," etc. On the short title I give to this sermon, see App. I.

[^004-note81]: The fragment of Bellamy's part-copy ends at this point, with the catchword "second" indicated as the first word of the next, missing page.

[^004-note82]: Andover copy reads "there."

[^004-note83]: See nn. 8 and 9 below for the meaning of the word "sincerity."

[^004-note84]: The verse in Acts begins: "Neither is worshiped..." JE frequently changed words within quotations— from Scripture or from other writings— to elide with his text. This is cited as an example; similar occurrences will not be noted.

[^004-note85]: TE (p. 84) proceeds immediately to *Reason* 2.

[^004-note86]: Archaic usage meaning deception, trickery, a false statement or a lie. The *Oxford English Dictionary* (hereafter O. E. D.) illustrates: "the Folly of younge Men and the Fallacies of Women" (1641), "the Fallacies of Sense" (1654), "the fallacy of human friendship" (1837).

[^004-note87]: In Christian ethics in general and in Puritan piety and self-scrutiny in particular there is a strong tendency towards a morality of *inward intention*. The use of the word "sincerity" in the Doctrine and throughout this sermon— together with JE's use of the word "kindness" for "cheerfully and freely doing good to others" in Sermon Four, and the argument in Sermon One that "reason teaches that whatever performances or seeming virtues there are without love are *insincere* and *hypocritical*" (p. 137 above, Ed. italics)— manifest this impulse toward a *gesinnungs Ethik*. As a corrective JE taught both a doctrine of natural and infused virtues as well as the moral rule of Scripture. Norman Fiering affirms that "hypocrisy" did not have our meaning of the deliberate deception of others; a hypocrite was rather someone mainly self-deceived. (*Moral Philosophy at Seventeenth Century Harvard* [Chapel Hill, Univ. of North Carolina Press, 1981], p. 172). Granting this, JE's discussion of the mixture of sincerity and hypocrisy remaining in the heart (the seat of both) shows that he did not expect "purity of heart" in this life. The "little sincerity" acceptable to God means that the Christian life was always *in via* toward holiness.

[^004-note88]: This sentence announce *four* things that belong to sincerity in the heart. The copy treats only two: *truth* and *freedom*. TE completes the list with *integrity* and *purity*, under his use for self-examination. He also has uses of conviction and of exhortation. For JE on the ambiguity of "sincere endeavors," on direct and indirect willing of a thing, on sincerity as the *reality* of will and endeavor (vs. pretense) and on "virtuous sincerity," see *Freedom of the Will*, pp. 312–19; and the section on sincerity in Miscell. no. 1153. MORAL INABILITY FREEWILL. SELF-DETERMINING POWER (a lengthy entry composed not long after his dismissal from the church in Northampton, and marked for use or when used at that place in *Freedom of the Will*). JE uses but one of the alternative meanings of *sincere* or *sincerity* that O. E. D. lists. See Intro., p. 61, n. 8.

[^004-note90]: Andover reads "evangelical." On balance, the theological context does not favor TE's "filial" (p. 90).

[^004-note92]: On this point, see Sermon Twelve on the "concatenation" of the virtues or graces of a "proportionate Christian."

[^004-note93]: Having spoken of the third and fourth things that belong to sincerity in the heart, TE proceeds (pp. 92–95) to add a use of conviction and a use of exhortation. TE's ending, as noted above, is needed to complete the copy on the elements in the nature of sincerity. Andover's use of self-examination is *numbered* "I"; this suggests at least another use to come. Hence I complete the sermon by including TE's entire ending.

[^004-note94]: This sermon was delivered in three "preaching units." The first covered the first point of doctrine; the second, improvement of that doctrine, with objections and answers; the third introduced the second point of doctrine, with its application. Evidently it was important to JE to hold in even balance the two dispositions mentioned in the text to which love inclines: suffering long and being kind. Even under the first point, JE shows (pp. 189–90 below) the nature of "long-suffering" to be gentleness and kindness; it is not merely endurance under ills suffered but endurance in well-doing with love in the heart. Therefore, he states one doctrine, divided into two heads. Because of its organization into I. Doctrine/Application and II. Doctrine/Application, the sermon may be described as duplex. In the short title given it, I endeavor to suggest the evenhandedness, indeed the singularity, of the doctrine JE meant to convey. TE divided the sermon into two, the second part being the third preaching unit. For this reason, this edition of Charity prints fifteen sermons, one fewer than TE's "Lectures." Not only does the form of the Puritan sermon indicate the correctness of my editorial decision. There is additional support for this decision in the fact that the entire duplex sermon was copied in one booklet (no. 4), the text forty-four pages in length, numbered in sequence. Only the final sermon, preached on two occasions, approaches this length (forty-three pages, also a single booklet, no. 15).

[^004-note96]: TE omits any reference to taverns, a well-known occasion for some of the friction between JE and the church in Northampton. His sentence (p. 99) reads: "Other ways of injury are abundant; but the amount of injury by evil-speaking of this kind is beyond account."

[^004-note97]: See above, n. 2. Here "gentleness" is a specific qualification of *meekness*, whose meaning is further characterized in this section. In *Affections* "meekness" is listed among those "lamblike, dovelike" qualities of Jesus Christ that "may by way of eminence be called the Christian spirit"; the "little children" of Matthew 19:14 are its model as well as those animal types. Such meekness and the virtue of meekness spoken of in the sermon may seem, on a careful reading, to have little in common. But then in *Affections*, JE himself frames an objection that lamblike, dovelike, and childlike meekness seems not fit for the Christian's warfare, and is incompatible with the virtue of "Christian fortitude." In showing that there is no inconsistency, JE discovers *steadfastness* and *boldness* to belong to the strength of the meek (Eighth Sign, pp. 344–45, 349–52), even as here in the sermon there is kindness and gentleness in the *strength* of the long-suffering of the meek. Early in the improvement (the second preaching unit below), the movement is from Christ's "lamblike quietness of spirit" to a composure that will fit us to live in a world such as this, with Christian imperturbability and "greatness of soul."

We have shown how a Christian spirit disposes persons meekly to bear ill that is received from others, or the injuries that others do them. / *First*. We took notice of the various kinds of injuries which persons suffer from others. / *Second*. What is meant by meekly bearing such injuries. / *Third*. How that love that is the sum of the Christian spirit will dispose men to do thus. I come now to make some brief/ IMPROVEMENT." These introductory words in the copy are omitted from the text above. [^004-note125]: End of the second preaching unit. Andover's transition to the third preaching unit represents JE as simply repeating the same duplex doctrine announced at the beginning and in the introduction to the second preaching unit. TE made what follows in the text into a separate (and fifth) lecture. TE does not have Andover's detailed enumeration of answers to the final objections above, which probably reflects the sermon booklet's brief reminders of topics to extemporize. Still, the words with which TE concludes his fourth lecture (pp. 138–39) are roughly parallel to Andover's ans. to obj. 2 and 3. TE quotes from Romans 12:19 only the words, "Vengeance is mine, I will repay, saith the Lord"; and then completes his fourth lecture, going beyond the copy-text to say:He interposed wonderfully for David, as he has for very many of his saints; and if you do but obey him, he will take part with you against all that rise up against you. And in observation and experience of men, it is generally found, that a meek and long-suffering spirit puts an end to injuries, while a revengeful spirit does but provoke them. Cherish, then, the spirit of long-suffering, meekness and forbearance, and you shall possess your soul in patience and happiness, and none shall be permitted to harm you more than God in wisdom and kindness may permit. The third and final preaching unit, below, completes the sermon by taking up the second point of doctrine, with its Application. The word "kind"— and "kindness"— in JE's exposition is, of course, drawn from the King James version of the text. "Kindness" or "lovingkindness" was also one translation of Hebrew *chesed* in the Old Testament; "mercy" was another. Kindness as a virtue, a fruit of agape or *chesed*, may be compared with the kindness of the "instinctual kind affections" discussed in *True Virtue*, Ch. VI. Evidently the quality of kindness expounded in the sermon is referred to later by JE as "true virtue" "mixing its influence with the natural principle," guiding and regulating its operation, or alternatively as a quality excited or infused by a holy love operating alone. See below, pp. 616–18.

[^004-note131]: "Love of benevolence" and "love of complacence" were familiar concepts in seventeenth-and eighteenth-century discussions of morality. Miscellanies composed more than a decade before this reference in the charity sermons make use of the well-known distinction between these loves. See, e.g., Miscell. no. 92. END OF CREATION (*c*. 1723–24) and no. 314. FREE GRACE (*c*. 1726); and see *Treatise on Grace* (*c*. 1741), p. 37n The influence of Francis Hutcheson upon JE, or the thesis that his view of "moral sense" was the chief target of *True Virtue*, should not be made to rest upon a mistaken assumption that the loves of "benevolence" and "complacence" were *late* additions to JE's moral concepts and language. A. O. Aldridge, for example, sometimes comes close to this error in interpretation.

I, like the seed which the Orientals plant by scattering it on the waters when the floods are up, and which sinking to the bottom, there takes root, and springing up, is found again in the abundant harvest after many days." I say "explains the *type*" because if people in the eighteenth or the nineteenth century believed TE's construal of the verse, they read Ecclesiastes 11:1 as a "natural type" (affirmed, to be sure, in the Scripture verse) of which there were higher antitypical fulfillments in gospel times. In any case, JE's weaving together of Old and New Testament passages, above, should be read as an antetypical hortatory peroration.

[^004-note140]: Below in the text at n. 6, TE has an extended reference to Haman's envy of Mordecai (concluding with a reference to Joseph and his brothers), which has no parallel in the Andover copy. Therefore I call attention that at this point TE (p. 163) has the following single sentence: "And Joseph's brethren, we are told, Gen. xxviii. II, envied him when they had heard his dream, which implied that his parents and brethren were yet to bow down before him, and that he was to have power over him." Here the disposition is *envy*; in TE's later use of the Joseph story, this envy turns into dislike and hatred of persons.

[^004-note141]: From this point on, for two full pages, TE (pp. 164–66) is only roughly parallel to the Andover copy, down to their common reference to Joseph's brethren, just before Doctrine II. A number of sentences are alike in both, but TE interweaves an extended account of Haman's envy of Mordecai (Esther 5:13). The text above, beginning at this point, may be compared with TE's version:He is very much of the spirit of Haman, who in view of all "the glory of his riches, and the multitude of his children, and all the things wherein the king had promoted him," still could say (Esther v. Esther 5:13), "Yet all this availeth me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting in the king's gate." From such a spirit, the envious person stands ready to rejoice at anything that happens to diminish the honor and comfort of others. He is glad to see them brought down and will even study how to lower their estate, as Haman did how to humble and bring down Mordecai. And often, like Haman, he will show his uneasiness not only by planning and scheming, but by actual endeavors of one kind or another to bring them down; and the very first opportunity of pulling them down that offers, he will gladly embrace. And it is from this disposition that the sight even of others' prosperity often sets the envious on talking against them and speaking evil of them, even when perhaps they do not know them. Envying them the prominence they have obtained, they hope by speaking evil of them in some measure to diminish their honors, and lower them in the esteem of men. This suggests, again, 2. That the opposition of the envious to the prosperity of others will be manifest *in a dislike of their persons for it*. Seeing how others prosper, and what honors they attain, the envious dislike, and even hate them, on account of their honor and prosperity. They entertain and cherish an evil spirit toward them, for no other reason but that they are prospered. They are embittered against them in spirit only because they are eminent in name or fortune. Thus Haman, it is said (Esther v. Esther 5:9), "was full of indignation against Mordecai" because he saw him "in the king's gate," and because "he stood not up, nor moved for him"; and Joseph's brethren (Genesis xxxvii. Genesis 37:4, Genesis 37:5), "hated him and could not speak peaceably unto him," because his father loved him; and when he had dreamed a dream implying their inferiority, "they hated him yet the more." And so the envious generally resent the prosperity of others and their coming to honor, as if in it they were guilty of some injury to themselves. Sometimes there is a settled hatred toward others upon this account, leading as in the case of Joseph's brethren (Genesis xxxvii. Genesis 37:19–28), to acts of the greatest cruelty and wickedness. After their common reference to Joseph's brethren, Andover and TE come to the second point of doctrine.

[^004-note143]: TE's reading (p. 167) "will crucify" seems too strong a word in the context; "to mortify" is the next point.

[^004-note144]: Romans 13:13 mentions rioting, drunkenness, chambering, and wantonness just before "strife and envying." JE or the copyist omits these words and instead goes directly to the "precepts" that are pertinent to the subject of this sermon.

[^004-note145]: With the word "envying" JE had come to the "precept" he wanted to take from the verse. 2 Corinthians 12:20 continues, "wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults."

[^004-note146]: The words quoted are ver. 1 Timothy 6:4. This suffices for the needed moral "precept." Ver. 1 Timothy 6:5 and 1 Timothy 6:6, if spoken, would weaken the conceptual and rhetorical force of the sermon.

[^004-note147]: Under "how... the doctrines and history of the gospel hold forth to enforce those precepts" against envy in Scripture, JE develops the *moral notions* of "grudging" (or "begrudging") and "grudging not." These notions are extensively deployed in the next sermon on humility, and in Sermon Fifteen. In face of Philippians 2:8, JE denied that "humility" was a virtue of "the divine nature" of Christ; "grudging not" is the proper notion, as the text above says. Not only did the devil envy or "begrudge" man's happy state in Eden. JE also believed those angels who fell did so not so much from towering pride, but from that vice in their hearts in the form of envy or grudging, when they learned that God had determined to raise human creatures below them in creation to a higher destiny than theirs in glory, i.e., to the highest honor and blessedness in *union* with himself. On these angels' envy of the hypostatic union, see Intro., p. 75, n. 9. In fact, JE's notion of pride was not the simple one of storming heaven's battlements to usurp God's throne. His was a subtler concept, essentially that of a "comparative spirit." That is, pride is born of a creature's vulnerability to perceived threats to his dignity, not of inordinate strength or uncomplicated assurance. "Pride don't consist most essentially in a too high conceit of oneself, but in a disposition inordinately to affect our own *comparative dignity*" (Miscell. no. 747. SELF-RIGHTEOUSNESS PRIDE [roughly contemporary with the charity sermons. Ed. italics]). "Pride may be thus defined. It is that habit or state of a person's heart whereby he is inordinately disposed to exaltation amongst other beings as to his comparative dignity or worthiness of esteem and value.. /.. The immediate object of pride is not... a man's own excellency considered absolutely. 'Tis not a disposition in a person to seek his own excellency absolutely, or a disposition to be excellent. A man can't excessively affect his own excellency... he can't excessively desire to be excellent, to have those qualifications that will render him a just object of esteem... 'Tis only a comparative dignity that pride affects, or the height that one is in or may be conceived to be amongst other beings. Nor is it the love and esteem of others absolutely considered... It don't content pride to be esteemed and loved by others, and to be so much valued by them, but to be highly valued and esteemed comparatively. 'Tis a person's comparative exaltation [among superiors, equals or inferiors]... whether those other beings with whom we compare our exaltation or dignity be God or creatures" (Miscell. no. 95O. PRIDE. HUMILIATION [*c*. 1744]).

See above, pp. 219–21, nn. 5, 6. Joseph's brethren and Haman are equally appropriate examples of the theme of this sermon (envy of good possessed by another turning into hatred of that person). Andover makes no reference to Haman, nor is there textual evidence that the copyist omitted anything he found in JE's booklet. The blank in Andover just above is filled by completing the question the copyist had begun. I cite TE's three references to Haman to give an example of his deftness in improving JE's sermon by an additional scriptural illustration. Another possibility cannot be excluded, however, namely, that when preaching this sermon on a subsequent occasion JE himself wrote in the Haman example, and that the copyist chose to transcribe only the original sermon, leaving to Dwight the decision whether or not to include the clearly marked later passages.

[^004-note177]: On its face, JE applies to the Day of Judgment a verse that might better be read as referring to God's ruling and judgment in history: "The king shall mourn, and the prince shall be clothed with desolation, and the hands of the people of the land shall be troubled: I will do unto them after their way, and according to their deserts will I judge them; and they shall know that I am the Lord." Nevertheless, this is another instance of JE's accurately choosing his precept from a verse, bearing in mind the tradition of figural interpretation of Scripture. Historical judgment was seen as a type of the final Judgment.

[^004-note178]: Cf. *Affections*, pp. 311–40. This Sixth Sign of gracious affections may be the most subtle discussion of humility as a Christian virtue that JE ever wrote, in its intermingling of analysis of pride throughout. The sermon on humility, however, is purer and, it may be, more powerful in the following respects: (1) The sign lacks the sermon's affirmation of humility as an *essential* qualification of love, *implied* in it; and (2) the sign sets up the correlation, "legal humiliation: God's greatness:: evangelical humiliation: God's beauty and holiness," while in the sermon the divine love that implies humility is a love to God *also* "as an infinite superior," i.e., humility is a creature excellence related both to God's greatness and to his holiness. This sermon, more than the Sixth Sign, prepares the reader to understand the words in *End of Creation*, Ch. I, Sec. I, p. 423 below: "so that the *degree of regard* should always be in a proportion *compounded* of the proportion of existence and proportion of excellence, or according to the degree of *greatness* and *goodness* considered *conjunctly*." Also to understand the account of the spiritual beauty in moral agents in *True Virtue*, Ch. I, p. 548 below, to the effect that "the *degree* of the *amiableness* or *valuableness* of true virtue, primarily consisting in consent and a benevolent propensity of heart to Being in general... is not in the *simple* proportion of the degree of benevolent affection seen, but in a proportion *compounded* of the greatness of the benevolent being, or the degree of *being* and the degree of *benevolence*." This consent to Being in itself or benevolent propensity of heart to Being in general is identified in the next chapter as love to God. So, it can be suggested, true virtue tends to humility as an effect and also implies humility as an essential qualification, as JE says of divine love in this sermon. Humility's sense of comparative meanness is founded in the heart's sense of the aweful greatness and the beauty or holiness of God. The same is true of other virtues as well, both later in the sermon series and in the dissertation, since the sum, principle, and source of them all is charity.

[^004-note184]: See n. 2 above. No space before use of exhortation. After the quotation of Hab 2:4, TE's parallel (p. 222) expands the use of examination:and the fact that "God resisteth the proud" (James IV. James 4:6) or, as in the original, "sets himself in battle array against him," shows how he abhors a proud spirit. And it is not every show and appearance of humility that will stand the test of the gospel. There are various imitations of it that fall short of the reality. Some put on an affected humility; others have a natural low-spiritedness, and are wanting in manliness of character; others are melancholy or despondent; others under the convictions of conscience by which, for the time, they are depressed, seem broken in spirit; others seem greatly abased while in adversity and affliction, or have a natural melting of the heart under the common illuminations of the truth; to others there is a counterfeit kind of humility, wrought by the delusions of Satan: and all of these may be mistaken for true humility. Examine yourself, then, and see what is the nature of your humility, whether it be of these superficial kinds, or whether it be indeed wrought by the Holy Spirit in your hearts; and do not rest satisfied, till you find that the spirit and behavior of those whom the gospel accounts humble, are yours.

[^004-note186]: JE held this view from his mid-twenties, when he wrote in his "Miscellanies":The best philosophy that I have met with of original sin and all sinful inclinations, habits and principles is undoubtedly that of Mr. Stoddard's of this town of Northampton: that is, that it is self-love in conjunction with the absence of the image and love of God; that natural and necessary inclination that man has to his own benefit, together with the absence of original righteousness; or in other words, the absence of that influence of God's Spirit, whereby love to God and to holiness is kept up to that degree, that this other inclination is always kept in its due subordination. But this being gone, his self-love governs alone; and having not this superior principle to regulate it, breaks out into all manner of exorbitancies, and becomes in innumerable cases a vile and odious disposition, and causes thousands of unlovely and hateful actions. There is nothing new put into the nature that we call sin, but only the same self-love that necessarily belongs to the nature working and influencing, without regulation from that superior principle that primitively belongs to our nature, and that is necessary in order to the harmonious existing of it. This natural and necessary inclination to ourselves without that governor and guide will certainly without anything else produce, or rather will become, all those sinful inclinations which are in the corrupted nature of man. Then JE observes that all the exercises and actings of the powers and inclinations in the souls of men, whatever they be, are but God's continual and immediate influence. Such, indeed, was his understanding of every physical being or motion in the world of nature: these are from an immediate operation of God without which there would be nothing. So it seemed entirely reasonable to suppose that a moral inclination (such as self-love)is nothing but God's influencing the soul according to a certain law of nature; therefore the influence that upholds one inclination being withdrawn, and God continuing the same influence to the upholding of the other inclination, according to the former rule and method, according to that law which we call the law of nature, it naturally and of itself breaks out into all those exorbitances. It might easily be shown how this will unavoidably, without any new infusion, produce all those inclinations that we call pride, covetousness, lasciviousness, malice, envy, etc. [Miscell. no. 301. SIN AND ORIGINAL SIN (*c*. 1727–28] This sermon speaks mainly of the natural self-love of the creature (which is as necessary to human nature as a faculty of will is) left alone, without original righteousness to regulate and channel it, and of the work of the Spirit in restoring that spiritual image of God. But if in 1738 JE believed anything like the principles of common morality and the "laws of nature" governing the ordinary dispositions and behavior of men (not to mention "common" grace) set forth in *True Virtue*, Chs. III, then he must also have believed that self-love is never *left alone* between the Fall and the redemption which God is working in every age. Many entries in his notebooks, e.g., on conscience, attest that JE treated "self-love" and "selfishness" in one or another of these contexts. See App. II.

This reading of other-love as "a moral love" highlights the superior excellency of divine love, though JE's point here is that love of others arises naturally from the principle of self-love.
