## APPENDIXES

<!-- p. 643 -->

### APPENDIX ONE: JOSEPH BELLAMY'S COPY OF THE CHARITY SERMONS

IN his preface, Tryon Edwards stated that after Edwards' death his sermons on 1 Corinthians 13 were "selected for publication by Dr. Hopkins and Dr. Bellamy; and by the latter were in part copied out and prepared for the press, when for some reason he was interrupted in their preparation, so that now for the first time they are given to the public."[^008-note1] The recent discovery and identification of fragments of Bellamy's part-copy confirms TE's assertion that Bellamy began transcribing the charity sermons for publication. TE did not say how he knew this, nor how extensive a partial copy Bellamy made.

How shall we explain Tryon Edwards' knowledge that Bellamy began a copy of the charity sermons? In attempting an answer to this question, we begin with Tryon's relation to Bellamy's papers. He had access to these papers in the preparation of a "Memoir" of Bellamy published in 1858,[^008-note2] six years after his own edition of *Charity*. This might explain how Tryon came upon Bellamy's part-copy, if it be reasonable to assume that he was engaged for several years in preparing the memoir, or that *Charity's* publication was delayed. But the span of years between TE's preface to *Charity* and his subsequent "Memoir" renders this supposition concerning his knowledge of Bellamy's eighteenth-century part-copy quite implausible.

Plausible explanations come to mind if we turn our attention to the history of Edwards' papers. Following Bellamy and Hopkins, Jonathan Edwards, Jr., was responsible for the collection for a long time, and edited from it. Tryon was the grandson of JE, Jr., and the son of Jonathan Walter Edwards, who held the collection for a brief period after the death of his father. JE, Jr. died several years before TE (1809–94) was born. Nevertheless, it is not unreasonable to suppose that an oral tradition

<!-- p. 644 -->

about the papers' history was handed down to TE along with the collection.

Bellamy and Hopkins might have left in the collection the letters that passed between them concerning their project of editing some of the MSS. This correspondence could have been retained among the papers and been handed on in succession to Tryon. This conjecture (Thomas A. Schafer's) is based on the fact that there were many letters addressed *to Jonathan Edwards* in the collection when it came into Tryon's possession, practically all of which have disappeared. As executor, Tryon himself might have removed letters he judged extraneous. (If so, how letters from Grosart addressed to TE, and several pages of the *Treatise on Grace*, came into the Andover coll. is a mystery.)

Furthermore, nothing excludes the possibility that *the part-copy itself* was in the collection when TE became executor. If the source of TE's knowledge of Bellamy's transcription was neither oral tradition nor correspondence in the collection, but the copy itself, we could further speculate that TE himself transferred the part-copy to the Bellamy papers when he was working on the "Memoir" and before he maneuvered Edwards' papers into the libraries at Yale and Andover.

But let us take up the story at its beginning, a century earlier. Recall the no-if-ands-or-buts letter Hopkins wrote to Bellamy concerning some sermons the latter had undertaken to transcribe.[^008-note3] We need now to raise questions about those sermons, even though this will lead only to a series of relatively plausible suppositions. Hopkins' words— "transcribe some of the sermons you mention without any *ifs or ands*"— are consistent with a high esteem on Hopkins' part for the sermons Bellamy had begun to transcribe, and with Tryon's assertion that Bellamy partly copied the charity sermons for possible publication. Such were my conjectures about the identity of these sermons: first Bellamy and then Hopkins noted the special worth of the 1738 sermon series; Bellamy began to copy them.

Inquiry into the respective apprenticeships of Bellamy and Hopkins in Northampton tended to confirm my surmise that, among Edwards' many sermons, papers, and notebooks, Bellamy's editorial attention had been drawn to the charity sermons. The following detailed reconstruction of the early years of these two editors has as its upshot *that the young Bellamy may have heard the first three, and only three, charity sermons delivered*.

Samuel Hopkins' first stay in Northampton lasted from December

<!-- p. 645 -->

1741 through March 1742. He returned to his home in Waterbury, Connecticut, and was licensed to preach in April 1742. Instead of taking a pastorate immediately, however, he decided to return to Edwards' home— known by then as one of the "schools of the prophets." Hopkins' second period in Northampton was from the spring of 1742 until May or June of 1743. During this period he served as interim pastor of the congregation in Simsbury, Connecticut, but his time was apparently mostly spent under Edwards' tutelage.[^008-note4] Thus Hopkins' time in Northampton overlapped with the Great Awakening (1740–42).

Bellamy was the older of the two, and he also came earlier as an apprentice to Edwards. It is commonly said that he studied with Edwards in 1738 (nearer in time to the revival in Northampton, 1734–35). If Bellamy's year in Northampton was 1738, he in all probability heard JE preach the charity sermons in their entirety. No wonder then that, following JE's death, Bellamy's eyes lighted upon that particular set of sermon booklets, and he remembered their quality. But S. E. Dwight is the source of that date, and he only *implies* that the year was 1738.[^008-note5]

Glenn Paul Anderson, however, says the year must have been mid-1736 to mid-1737.[^008-note6] Anderson's chronology of events in Bellamy's life is as follows: 1736–37, with Edwards in Northampton; licensed to preach, May 1737;[^008-note7] preached occasionally in his home church, Cheshire, Connecticut, 1737–38;[^008-note8] settled in Worcester, Massachusetts, where he preached regularly from June to October 1738; and was settled in Bethlehem, Connecticut, in November 1738, where he was ordained in 1740.[^008-note9]

On its face Anderson's chronology seems to remove Bellamy from

<!-- p. 646 -->

Northampton in the year the charity sermons were preached. But the fact that Bellamy was licensed to preach in 1737 does not mean that was the end of his apprenticeship with Edwards. Like Hopkins, Bellamy may have planned to remain under Edwards' tutelage after licensure. Nor does the fact that there is record of his preaching from time to time into the early months of 1738 at his home church remove him from Northampton during that period. Bellamy's permanent removal from Northampton began with his settlement in Worcester, where he preached every Sunday from June to October 1738.

This means that, by Anderson's account, Bellamy could *not* have heard the entire charity series. But his chronology allows us to suppose that Bellamy heard Edwards deliver the first three charity sermons. The Andover copy dates sermon one sometime in April and sermon two in May of 1738. Although sermon three is undated, we have reason to conjecture only that Bellamy did not hear the remainder of the series from sermon four (dated June 1738) onward. Significantly, the recently discovered fragments of Bellamy's part-copy are pieces of *these first three sermons*.

Before 1982, no extant Bellamy copy was known. For that matter, we had no definitive proof that TE was correct in saying that Bellamy had begun to copy the charity sermons. Then Mark Valeri located, and he and I identified, three fragments of sermons one through three in Bellamy's hand. Valeri, a doctoral student in the Department of Religion at Princeton, was doing the research for his dissertation on Joseph Bellamy.[^008-note10] In spring 1982, he was reading in the largest collection of Bellamy manuscripts, at Hartford Seminary, Hartford, Connecticut. There, in "Doc. Box. No. 189, Folder No. 2942 Joseph Bellamy papers (sermons)," Valeri found three fragments of sermons in Bellamy's hand, classified as his sermons, on texts from 1 Corinthians 13. The three items, with Hartford's numerical designation and description, were:

81466 a sermon n. d. 4 p. (on I Cor. XIII: 1 Corinthians 8:1, 1 Corinthians 8:2, 1 Corinthians 8:3) (incomplete)

81467 a sermon n. d. 4 p. (on "Love") (incomplete)

81468 Sermons; (1) last part of Sermon No. II (on God's grace; incomplete) (2) Sermon No. III (on I Cor. XIIL3; incomplete); 4p.

Upon Valeri's returning to Princeton with photocopies of these and other Bellamy papers, he and I recognized almost at once that these were fragments of Bellamy's long-lost copy of Edwards' charity sermons.

<!-- p. 647 -->

Dr. Richard B. Eberhart, then Administrator, Educational Resources Center, Hartford Seminary, tells me that the seminary received its Bellamy papers as a gift from Bellamy's great-granddaughter, Miss Elizabeth Bellamy Loomis of Greenfield, Mass., in 1893. He presumes that the papers had been in the family before that.[^008-note11]

I suggested above that Bellamy's copy or part-copy might have been placed among the Edwards papers, where Tryon came upon it when he became executor. If so, we might also picture him using Bellamy's part-copy as a "pony" or "trot" in the transcription of the earlier sermons in the series. This surmise in no way discredits, nor is it meant to discredit, TE's claim that he edited from the original sermon booklets. But the conjecture would serve to explain (if more is needed) a number of remarkable agreements between TE and Bellamy that are in disagreement with Andover (noted in the examples below). However, in general, both the discrepancies and the agreements among our three sources are adequately comprehended from the fact that each transcribed and edited as he copied. The Andover copyist doubtless was given rules for editing while transcribing. Of the three, TE was by far the most "liberal" redactor.[^008-note12]

Before commenting on the texts, I should raise the question why Bellamy did not finish his copy of the sermons. TE says he was interrupted. A more reasonable conjecture is that he stopped. This supposition can be unfolded as follows. As a young apprentice under Edwards' tutelage, Bellamy was properly impressed with the charity series (or the first three sermons) when he heard them delivered in 1738. Hence, after Edwards' death, he chose these sermons for possible publication, while also transcribing *True Virtue*. But— now more than twenty-five years older— Bellamy's interest in the project waned rather more rapidly than did that of the younger Hopkins. Why might this have been so? For a combination of two reasons, I suggest. (1) Having recently entered the

<!-- p. 648 -->

theological arena with his own systematic theology,[^008-note13] Bellamy was deeply engaged in his own life's work, and could not be diverted from this for any considerable length of time by his debt of filial piety to Edwards. But also (2) the more he comprehended the sermons as a mature scholar, the less they were to his liking.

In the theological battles of their own day, the New Divinity men (Bellamy, Hopkins, Emmons) identified themselves as heirs of the master theologian of the eighteenth century. Their claims served mainly to impair the continuing influence of Edwards in the intellectual history of America in the national period and in the nineteenth century. Three foci of Bellamy's system of divinity were surely not Edwardsean: his legalism, his concept of disinterested love, and his computation of virtue in terms of happiness in the whole consequences.[^008-note14] The law of God was not Edwards' *emphasis* in theology. And, while the expression "disinterested love" can be found in Edwards' writings,[^008-note15] there could not be a more *interestedlove* than his (whether by this is meant the will/love of one's own

<!-- p. 649 -->

happiness on the part of any intelligent willing being, or such a being's *specific* determination to love to God and to fellow creatures). It is quite reasonable to suppose that sooner or later the charity sermons— and especially these sermons among Edwards' writings— would disturb Bellamy; and threaten his fond belief, and that of other New Divinity men, that they were only thinking Edwards' most intimate thoughts after him.[^008-note16]

The first four-page Bellamy fragment proved to be the beginning of Edwards' sermon one; the second four-page fragment, the ending of sermon one; and the third four-page fragment, the ending of sermon two and the beginning of sermon three. Bellamy numbered his pages consecutively throughout. Thus, page 1 of the first fragment was his facing page; then pp. 2 (verso), 3 (recto), and 4 (verso) began the expected use of odd numbers for recto, even numbers for verso. Bellamy's pagination of the second fragment, the four-page ending of sermon one, however, introduces a mistake: 17, 17, 18, 19. The first 17 is correct, since it is a recto page. I conclude, therefore, that the missing pages are 5 through 16; and that there were 20 pages in Bellamy's copy to the end of sermon one.

We have some reason to assume that Bellamy continued to use the even-odd number sequences (18, 19, etc.) begun by his repetition of 17 on verso, for when he came to the pages we now have in the third fragment, the first of the four pages is 44, and this is on a recto. That

<!-- p. 650 -->

would be the outcome if, on the missing pages, Bellamy continued the unusual even-odd sequence introduced earlier. Then Bellamy made another mistake. He repeated 44 on the next verso, which corrected the first mistake and brought him back to odd-even for the two final pages (i.e., 45, 46), which are recto-verso. I figure the pages of Bellamy's copy to total 48 plus at least one more page, because the fragment ends with a catchword on the right at the bottom. The significance of these details is, I suppose, that Bellamy numbered consecutively throughout, and we know from this that his copy was a full one as far as he went— which was at least one more, now missing page!

In footnotes to the text of the charity sermons, I have indicated the beginning and ending of Bellamy's fragmentary text, and also something of the importance of the discovery of his copy in the preparation of the Yale edition. The latter requires further explanation. The problem is how best to construe the now lost original sermons. Just below, the text of Bellamy's part-copy is published in its entirety for the first time.[^008-note17] This provides a consecutive reading. But Bellamy, Andover, and Tryon all three copied and edited from the original booklets. Therefore I have selected four passages of particular significance to serve as examples of editorial problems in construing the originals behind our sources, or as examples of what can be learned from Bellamy's copy— so far as it extends. These are cross-sections of my text, Bellamy, Andover, and Tryon, printed in parallel columns to aid readers in making their own comparisons line by line and in forming their own judgments. Each example is preceded by an Editor's Comment in which I point out signal disagreements, analyze the problems faced in editing the passage, and indicate where I rely on Bellamy in constructing a text. Sometimes he helped in major respects; sometimes in deciphering a word that in Edwards' hand Andover and Tryon found difficult to read. Students of Edwards can go beyond these explanations into the style of our available sources. The synopses also afford, I believe, interesting exercises in editing.

<!-- p. 653 -->

<!-- p. 654 -->

<!-- p. 655 -->

#### Fragment One: BEGINNING OF SERMON ONE

#### SERMON I: Love the Sum of all Virtue

[1 Corinthians 13:1–3 quoted]

IN these words may be observed, (1.) Something spoken of, as of special importance, and as peculiarly essential, in Christians, which the Apostle calls *CHARITY*. *CHARITY* is abundantly insisted on in the New Testament by Christ and his Apostles, and indeed there is no virtue so much insisted on by them. But then the word Charity, as 'tis used in the New Testament, is of much larger signification than as it is vulgarly used now in Common Discourse. What Persons very often mean by Charity, in their Common Conversation, is a Disposition to hope and think the best of others, and to put a good construction on their words and behaviour, and sometimes it is used for a disposition to give to the Poor. But these things are only particular branches or fruits of that great virtue of Charity, which is so much insisted on in the New Testament. The word properly signifies Love, or that disposition or affection whereby one is dear to another. The word (agape) in the original, which is translated Charity, might as well have been rendered Love, for that is the proper English of it. So that by Charity in the New Testament is meant the very same as Christian Love. and altho' it is frequently used for Love to men, yet sometimes it is used to signify not only Love to men, but also love to God. So it is manifestly used by this Apostle in this Epistle, for so he explains himself. Chap. VIII. 1 Corinthians 8:1. Knowledge puffeth up, but Charity Edifieth. in these words knowledge & Charity are compared together; and Charity is preferred before Knowledge; because knowledge puffeth up, but Charity Edifieth. and then in the two next verses he explains first how knowledge vainly puffs up. if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know. and then Secondly, how Charity Edifieth. but if any man love God, the same is known of him. So that what he calls Charity in the first verse, he calls loving God in the third: for he is evidently speaking of the same thing, and doubtless he means the same by Charity in this XIII.th Chap, as he there does in the VIII.th for he is here comparing the same two things

<!-- p. 656 -->

together, viz. knowledge & charity, as he was there ver. 1 Corinthians 8:2. Tho' I have all knowledge. & have no charity, I am nothing. So again ver. 1 Corinthians 8:8. Charity never faileth; but— knowledge, it shall vanish away. So that by Charity here are doubtless to understand Christian Love in the full extent of it, and with regard to all the objects of it, and whether it be exercised toward God, or our fellow-creatures, and,

THIS Charity is in our text spoken of as that which is in a distinguishing manner the great and Essential thing: which will appear more fully, when we observe in the

(2.) Place, What Things are mentioned as being in vain without it. viz. the most excellent privileges, & the most excellent performances. first, the most excellent privileges, such as speaking with tongues, the gift of prophecy, understanding all Mysteries, faith to remove Mountains. & Secondly, the most excellent performances, such as giving all their goods to feed the poor, & their bodies to be burnt. greater things than these no natural man ever had, or ever did. & yet the apostle asserts, that a man, possessed of all these excellent privileges, if he has no charity is nothing: and those excellent performances will profit him Nothing. Natural men are exceeding apt to trust in such great priviledges. Matt. VII. Matthew 7:22, Matthew 7:23. Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy Name cast out Devils? and in thy Name done many wonderful works? and then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me ye that work iniquity. And natural men are very ready to trust in their performances, especially such extraordinary ones as these, giving all their goods to feed the poor, & their bodies to be burned: yet all are nothing, & will profit nothing without Charity.

*Doctrine*

ALL that virtue that is saving, and distinguishing true Christians from others, is Summed up in Christian or divine Love.

THIS appears from the words of the text, because so many other things are mentioned, that natural men may have; and the things that are mentioned are of the highest kind, that it is possible that natural men

<!-- p. 657 -->

should have, both of Privileges & performances; and it is said, they avail nothing without this, if any of them were saving, they would avail something without it.

And by the Apostles Mentioning so many, & so great things; and then saying of them all, that they profit nothing without Charity; we may justly conclude that there is nothing at all, that avails any thing without it. Let a man have what he will, and let him do what he will, it signifies nothing without Charity, which surely implies that Charity is the great thing, and that every thing, which

### Fragment Two: END OF SERMON ONE

THE gospel reveals such Love as never before was heard of. Joh. XV. John 15:13. Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends. Romans 5, Romans 7, Romans 8, Romans 8:10. Scarcely for a righteous man will one die.— But God commendeth his love towards us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.— When we were Enemies. God and Christ appear in the gospel revelation, as being clothed with Love; as sitting, as it were, on a throne of Mercy & Grace, a seat of Love, all encompassed about with pleasant beams of Love. Love is the Light & Glory that is round about the throne on which God sits. This seems to be intended in the vision the Apostle John, that loving & beloved Disciple, had of God in the isle of Patmos. Rev. IV. Revelation 4:3. and there was a rainbow round about the throne, in light like unto a Emerald. that is, round about the throne on which God sat. So that God appeared to him, as he sat on his throne, encompassed round with a Circle of Exceeding sweet & pleasant Light; pleasant like the beautiful colour of the rainbow, like an Emerald, which is a precious stone of a very Exceeding pleasant & Beautiful colour. This represents, that the Light & Glory, which God appears surrounded with in the Gospel is especially the Glory of his Love and Covenant grace, for the rainbow was given as a token of God's love & covenant grace to Noah. Therefore this spirit, even a spirit of Love, is the spirit that the gospel revelation does especially hold forth Motives & enducements to. and this is especially & Eminently the Christian spirit, the right spirit of the Gospel.

2. IF it is indeed so, that all that is saving and distinguishing in a true Christian is summarily comprehended in Love, then hence proffessors of Christianity may try their Experiences, whether they are real Christian experiences or no. if they are so, love is the sum & substance of them, if persons have true light let into their souls it is not light without heat. Divine knowledge & Divine love go together, a spiritual view of Divine things always excites love in the soul, and draws forth the heart in Love to every proper object: true discoveries dispose us to love to God as the Supreme Good, they unite the heart in love to Christ, they incline the heart to flow out in love to God's

People. they dispose the heart to love all Mankind. When persons have a true discovery of the Excellency and sufficiency of Christ, this is the Effect, when they experience a right Belief of the truth of the Gospel, such a Belief is accompanied with love, they love him, whom they believe to be the Christ, the Son of the living God. When the truth of the Glorious Doctrines & promises of the Gospel is seen, these Doctrines and these Promises are like so many cords, which take hold of the heart, to draw it out in love to God and Christ. When persons experience a true trust and reliance on Christ, they Rely upon him with love; and so do it with Delight, and sweet acquiescence of soul. The spouse sat under Christs shadow with Great Delight, rested sweetly under the shadow of his protection, because she loved him. Cant. 2.2. When persons experience true Comfort & spiritual Joy, their Joy is the Joy of faith and love. They don't rejoyce in themselves, but God is their exceeding Joy.

When Contention comes into a place, it seems to prevent all Good, and if religion has been flourishing before, it presently stricks a damp to it, and every thing that is bad begins to flourish, and in the light of this Doctrine we may plainly see the reason of it. for Contention is directly against that which is the very sum of all that is essential and distinguishing in true Christianity, even a spirit of Love and Peace, no wonder therefore Christianity cannot flourish in a time of strife and contention among its professors, no wonder that Religion and Contention cannot live together.

4. WHAT cause have those to Bless God & live to his glory, who have received such a Privilege, if we do but seriously consider of it, those who have this inestimable Privilege of the sanctifying saving influences of the spirit of God, have Cause to bless God & live to his glory that cannot be expressed, the more we consider it, the more wonderful & inexpressible will it appear. When we read over the History of Moses, & how God appeared to him, & what wonderful works were wrought by his hands, & how he went up into the holy Mount, &, &. and when we read the History of Elijah, Elisha, Daniel, the Virgin Mary, the Apostle Paul who was cought up to the third heaven, & consider what Privileges these had & what high honors were done them, we are ready to admire at the greatness of those Privileges by which they were distinguished from others: But all those extraordinary Privileges, considered in themselves, separately from the saving grace of God, are nothing compared to this, let those, therefore, who are thus highly favoured, consider more than ever yet they have done, how great that Blessing is which God has bestowed upon them, of his mere free Love, & sovereign grace, & not for any worthiness of theirs; and How Great obligations they are under to glorify God: and to glorify Christ, who hath purchased this Blessing with his own blood. What manner of Persons ought you to be! pray consider it! do you hope that God has thus highly advanced & exalted you? and will you not be careful indeed to live to his glory, & to exalt & magnify his name? Will you dishonor Christ, who has thus honored you? will you regard him but a little, who has shewn such infinite regard to your welfare? shall the world have your heart, & Christ & his glory be neglected after all? will you not rather watch against your corrupt worldly, proud dispositions? will you not seek opportunities to do something for God, who, as you think, has been thus kind to you? and for that Saviour, who has purchased this, at the cost of such extreme sufferings? and that for you— worms!— vipers! will you not every day, with the Psalmist, be ready to say, as in Psal. CXVI. Psalms 116:12. What shall I render unto the Lord for all his benefits towards me? what could God have done

<!-- p. 662 -->

more for you? what would you have had God to have done better? what Privilege can could you think of now, that would have been better, and more worthy to Engage your heart in gratitude and thankfulness, and in all holy living? and consider, how you live! how little you do for God! how little for his honor! how much to his dishonor! how little this lies with weight upon your heart, that you may do something for God and Christ! Consider how you ought to live, and the inexpressible obligations you are under to live so. and then consider how you do live, and how vast the distance is. & how should such as you, who are so highly privileged, at all times carry towards God, in all filial Love, thankfulness, strict obedience, quiet submission! and how should you live towards your Neighbours, walking humbly, inoffensively, meekly, charitably, doing good to all, to their souls, & bodies, as you have opportunity, always fervent in spirit, serving the Lord, with the greatest and most earnest diligence.

Sermon III.

#### SERMON III: Nothing can make up for the want of Sincerity

[1 Corinthians 13:3 quoted]

IN the former verses the Necessity and Excellency of Charity was set forth by its Preference to the greatest Privileges, and the vanity and insignificancy of those Privileges without it. The Privileges particularly Mentioned are those that consist in the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit of God; which are the highest kind of Privileges that ever are bestowed on Natural Men. In this verse things of another Nature are Mentioned, viz. those that are of a Moral Nature, and it is declared that none of these avail any thing without Charity, and particularly,

1. THAT no Performances can avail without it. here is one of the highest kinds of external Performances mentioned, viz. a man's giving all he has his goods to feed the Poor. Giving to the Poor is a Duty very much insisted on in the word of God: and particularly, under the Christian Dispensation. And the case and circumstances of the Church in the Primitive times of Christianity were such, that Persons were sometimes called to part with all they had, and give it away to others, both because of the extreme Necessities of many Christians in their persecuted circumstances; and because of the Difficulties that attended a being a follower of Christ, and doing that work which the gospel called them unto, for such was the state of things, that some were called to give up all things, and entirely disentangle themselves the Cares & Cumbers of worldly possessions, and to go forth, as it were, without gold, or silver, or brass in their Purses, or scrip, or two coats apiece. The Apostle Paul tells us, that he had suffered the loss of all things for Christ. and so the Primitive Christians in the Church at Jerusalem sold all that they had, and gave it into a Common stock, and none said that aught that he had was his own. The duty of giving to the Poor was a Duty that the Christian Corinthians at this time had particular occasion to consider of, as also many other churches in that and the Neighbouring Country, by reason of a Great Dearth or famine, that sorely distressed the Brethren in Judea. on which

<!-- p. 664 -->

occasion the Apostle had already moved it to the Corinthians, as their Duty, to send relief to them, and is particular in speaking of it in this Epistle, chap. XVI. and also insists on it in his

second

### EXAMPLE ONE

IN this example, from the text explication of Sermon One, I direct the reader's attention to the fact that only the Andover copyist has Edwards quote the first sentence of 1 Corinthians 8:1. He then proceeds to copy the three first verses of 1 Corinthians 8 in uninterrupted sequence, then states the topics those verses compare (knowledge and charity), and only thereafter explains the first and the "two next verses" separately, coming finally to the two points Edwards took from this last pair of verses. (Andover numbers only the first of these points with a "1".) This is a perfectly logical exegesis, but it might be difficult to understand in the hearing of it. Bellamy and Tryon agree on a different ordering. First, only the last part of ver. 1 Corinthians 8:1 is quoted, followed by comment. Then, ver. 1 Corinthians 8:2–3 are quoted, followed by comment. Who was faithful to Edwards' original MS? This seems to me answerable from the fact that Bellamy first copied "*Chap*. VIII. 1 Corinthians 8:1–3." Then he crossed out "2, 3." and tried to change the comma after "1" to a period, before entering his abbreviated quotation from the first verse. Bellamy's deletion of "2, 3." confirms Andover's accuracy. So I conclude that Bellamy edited as he copied, as later did Tryon. The Andover copyist *copied*.

### EXAMPLE TWO

TWO comparisons of our three sources for the end of Edwards' first sermon are of interest. This first, brief one is notable for the inclusion of the words "when we were enemies" from Romans 5 by both Bellamy and Tryon and their omission by Andover. All three had Edwards' sermon booklets beside them. Likely the booklets gave citations only, and each of the three supplied the words from the King James. Yet the Andover copyist did not place a "10" after his "Romans 5, Romans 7, Romans 8, " and he omits the reference to enemies in that verse. There is no space left in his copy for these omissions, if he did indeed omit anything. Bellamy and Tryon included both the verse number and the phrase. The question, Did Edwards' booklet refer to enemies at this point? must remain open— until the fuller ending of this sermon (to which we have access only through Bellamy and Tryon) is taken into account. The next and longer example from the end of Sermon One indicates reasons for believing that the extensive agreement between Bellamy and Tryon was based on Edwards' original text. This includes a sixth instruction on love of enemies.

### EXAMPLE THREE

A second example from the end of Sermon One begins with the final *sixth* paragraph of the second Application (use of instruction), the last paragraph our three versions have in common. After only two sentences under this number, the Andover copy stops abruptly, with "to take heed to themselves as to this matter." In my reconstruction of the text, I continue from that point with Bellamy's version, until his second four-page fragment breaks off. The parallels printed here show quite clearly that Bellamy was truer to Edwards' style than Tryon was, while at the same time the synopsis with the Bellamy copy confirms that Tryon also worked from the original booklets. Indeed, an editor can proceed in the confidence that behind the Bellamy-Tryon agreement to extend the sermon there was a portion of Edwards' booklet that Andover failed to copy. The copyist's omission of love of enemies is inexplicable.

After completing the sixth instruction, both Bellamy and Tryon record a seventh. This concerns love of enemies. The agreement of these two versions on the topic of a seventh instruction is consistent with their agreement (*contra* Andover) that Edwards included ver. Romans 5:10, "while we were yet enemies," in his exegesis of Romans 5.

Before the second fragment of Bellamy's part-copy breaks off, a third Application, a use of exhortation, was begun. Bellamy recorded only an incomplete sentence of the exhortation, ending with "the sum of Christian virtue, then surely." With that word ends my incorporation of the Bellamy MS directly into the text. "Surely" is a catchword. There was more to come. Tryon's version continues the exhortation for one and one-half pages. My edited sermon text, pp. 147–48 above, concludes with these final words from TE, pp. 31–32. I am confident that Tryon also had before him Edwards' original.

#### EXAMPLE FOUR

I select a single extended example from the third and final fragment of Bellamy's copy. We are now at the fourth point under sermon two's use of instruction. This part continues on into the explication of the text of sermon three. In anticipation of that notation on p. 45 of the MS, the words "Sermon II" are centered here at the top of the page. The hand is not that of Bellamy. A reasonable surmise is that this title was written in by the person who catalogued the Bellamy papers at Hartford Seminary.

From the third sentence of Bellamy's copy, "The more we consider it, the more wonderful and inexpressible will it appear" onward, his text has a distinctive style in comparison with our other two versions. Andover and Tryon read much more smoothly to our ears than Bellamy. There is a jerkiness, or sudden movement from one statement to another, in Bellamy's copy. Couple this with the three successive gaps in the Andover copy following the references to the Virgin Mary, etc., and readers can set themselves a test in construing what was the nature of this page in Edwards' sermon booklet.

In his booklets Edwards often did not fully write out the sermon as delivered. Instead, at certain places he wrote a phrase here and a phrase there, an incomplete sentence, or a short complete sentence, at irregular intervals on the page, some beginning to the left, some to the right hand of the page. This, we may suppose, assisted the preacher in extemporizing. Our three copyists and editors seem to be struggling with such a page.

At another point, Andover simply copied down similar irregular notes concerning the sin against the Holy Ghost. I reconstructed that page from JE's biblical notes (sermon two, pp. 164–66 above). Here the copyist— we may conjecture— was confronted with a similar page. He tried to make the text readable consecutively, but failed at the three gaps, and gave up altogether when he came to "how little this lies with." While (for the information of the reader) I indicate in brackets the

<!-- p. 680 -->

approximate length of the three lacunae, this is of no aid in attempting now to improve on Andover's reading of Edwards' (hypothetical) irregularly outlined page. Bellamy, while doubtless adding words of his own in the spaces, renders the original page more faithfully. To test this, try to fill in words in the gaps in Andover *without changing the words he did set down* (Tryon's changes are to be avoided).

This explains why (after only two sentences into the fourth use of instruction, beginning with the words, "The more we consider it..."), I switched to the Bellamy text instead of following Andover. If we had recovered a nearly complete copy of the charity sermons by Bellamy, his would have been the obvious copy-text for this edition. Having only fragments of a part-copy, however, it seemed best to make use of Bellamy and Tryon in reconstructing the text upon the basis of Andover, printing Bellamy's version (as far as it goes) in its entirety in this appendix. So the question arises, Why switch to Bellamy where there is an Andover parallel? Why not do this only after Andover's "how little this lies with"? Or only (as in my previous, third example) where Bellamy confirms Tryon in extending Sermon Two significantly beyond Andover?

The reason for this decision— which I hope will be persuasive— was my failure to find a way to make sense of Andover while at the same time respecting the integrity of his text at these particular blank spaces in his copy. To respect the integrity of the copy-text, I needed not to change *his* words to elide with mine (or with words taken from the Bellamy or Tryon parallels).

Consider the first space. Bellamy's is a splendid Edwardsean sentence: "considered in themselves, separately from the saving grace of God, are nothing compared with this." Bellamy's "this" (and, I surmise, Edwards') must have seemed dangling to both Andover and Tryon. Their versions extend the sentence to mention "saving grace in the heart." But Bellamy had stated that earlier: "considered in themselves, separately from the saving grace of God"— to which his "this" refers. Instead of switching to Bellamy for this sentence only and back again to Andover, my decision was to incorporate the entire relatively brief and lively Bellamy passage.

The second blank space presented a similar problem. Andover's "let those, who hope..." cannot be followed by any words from Bellamy or any that I myself can think of. Moreover, Andover has "hope" also later in his sentence. Just as in the foregoing example to rephrase Bellamy's "saving grace of God" to fill the space would render Andover repetitive, so here to incorporate Tryon's words would be repetitive with Andover's "hope" later in the sentence. In addition, Tryon's "let those, then, that

<!-- p. 681 -->

hope they have this last blessing" seemed to me to be a bland rewrite.

The third, one-line, blank space in the Andover copy follows the words "who of" (no terminal punctuation). To strike these words out of the copy-text, and make no insert, would bring the three versions into entire agreement. A simple enough solution. But that would be an abrupt dismissal of one of my sources— the one there was ample reason to choose as copy-text for this edition, since we have only pieces of Bellamy's copy and none of Edwards' booklets.

Without Bellamy, there would have been a similar difficulty in construing the text, below, where Andover breaks off with the words "how little this lies with." Tryon is no help; an editor's creative imagination falters; but Bellamy continues: "lies with weight upon your heart."

Taking these problems all together I concluded that the most intelligible passage would be obtained by here giving up my own attempts at elision and composition, adopting instead Bellamy's version to the end of sermon two. Andover's extension beyond its parallel with Bellamy is printed in n. 9, p. 173 above.

The title of sermon three is of greatest interest. Titles are taken from doctrines, and we do not know how Bellamy worded the Doctrine of this sermon, if he copied that far. Our only clue is the title he chose (to be compared with Tryon's): "Nothing can make up for the want of Sincerity"— the brevity of which might have been determined by want of space. The words at the top of the final page, 46, are "Nothing can make up for" (a running head that doubtless was on the missing pages that followed). Still, Bellamy's title is remarkable for its simplicity, and for offering no elaboration on "Sincerity," which could be all he meant to write. The Andover copyist entered no title (as Edwards did not). His statement of the Doctrine, however, was: "All, which men can do, and all, which they can suffer, will not make up for the want of sincerity in the heart." If that was Edwards' wording (and also Bellamy's), then Bellamy composed a more forceful short title by changing "All" to "Nothing." In editing this sermon I adopt Bellamy's title, with the addition of Andover's "in the heart," in the belief that this is not an elaboration upon "sincerity." At least it is not an elaboration to be compared with Tryon's Doctrine: "for want of sincere Christian love in the heart." Edwards would not have needed those additional qualifications of sincerity (see Intro., p. 61, n. 8). Otherwise Tryon's statement of the Doctrine is rather like Andover's, viz., "That all that men can do, and all that they can suffer, can never make up for..." Tryon's variation upon that for his *title*— stressing Edwards' (and St. Paul's) examples of performances and sufferings in extremis— is somewhat unfortunate.

At that time Mr. Cuntz had also in his possession a letter from Egbert Smyth to TE in Hagerstown, Maryland, dated December 4, 1867. In this letter Smyth asked Tryon what he knew about two *copies* in the Andover coll. To identify the first, Smyth emulated distinctive features of the handwriting, so that Tryon might identify it. Then in a single sentence he asked about a copy, "Charity and its Fruits." If Tryon replied to this inquiry (received some fifteen years after his *Charity* was published), that letter is now lost. [^008-note15]: Cf. *Charity*, p. 264 at n. 2: "there is no other-love so much above a selfish principle as Christian love is, there is no love that is so free and disinterested." This quotation from Sermon Seven on a selfish spirit points especially to *freedom*, to the doctrine to be "willing cheerfully and freely to do good to others"— one of the two dispositions of charity commended in Sermon Four— not to *disinterest*. No intelligent willing being can will or love disinterestedly. Such love was not among Edwards' themes, either in its New Divinity or its contemporary sense. The notion of "disinterested love" enabled Hopkins to write, as Edwards did not, a "Dialogue between a Calvinist and a Semi-Calvinist," showing that a true Christian should be willing, if God so wills it, to be damned for the glory of God. See *The Works of Samuel Hopkins, D. D*. (3 vols., Boston, 1854), *3*, 143–57. In his mature years Hopkins went in quite different directions, in both substance and terminology, from those of his mentor. He used the Edwardsean language of "benevolence or good will to being in general." But this "term of art" for love to God in *True Virtue* he promptly turned into a characteristic of the Deity, an axiom from which to reason as follows: "This is love of pure, disinterested benevolence, to creatures infinitely odious and guilty... Hence it follows with certainty, that disinterested benevolence is primary and essential in the divine moral character... And it follows from this also, that the love to God which is required, is the love of disinterested benevolence" (*The System of Doctrines, Contained in Divine Revelation, Explained and Defended*... in *Two Volumes* (Boston, 1811), 1, 291. Cf. pp. 52–61; and 465 ff., "On Disinterested Affection," distinguishing "self-love and a desire or *love of happiness*" [!] from "disinterested benevolence"). Hopkins presumed to know enough about the divine wisdom to write (as JE would not) a treatise entitled Sin, *Thro' Divine interposition, an Advantage to the Universe* (Boston, 1759), in *Three Sermons from Rom. iii*. Romans 3:5–8 (Boston, 1773). His older associate Bellamy computed (in 1758) the happiness of the generations, whether destined for heaven or hell, so as to *prove* the advantage! The need for such theological investigations logically follows from the premise that "disinterested benevolence" is a quasi-philosophical "characteristic of the Deity."

[^008-note16]: Edwards himself may not have wholeheartedly approved his protégé's work. This depends on how one reads Edwards' preface to Bellamy's *True Religion Delineated* (in *The Great Awakening*, ed. C. C. Goen, *The Works of Jonathan Edwards* [New Haven, Yale Univ. Press, 1972], *4*, 569–73). >From the tone of the preface one could conclude that Edwards was quite willing to recommend his protege's work against their common theological adversaries as a useful rendition of Calvinism, but did not think much of it as high theology. "Such a discourse as this is very seasonable at this day," he wrote. "And although the author (as he declares) has aimed especially at the benefit of persons of vulgar capacity; and so has not labored for such ornaments of style and language as might best suit the gust of men of polite literature; yet the matter or substance, that is to be found in this discourse is what, I trust, will be very entertaining and profitable to every serious and impartial reader, whether learned or unlearned" (p. 572). A letter from Edwards to Erskine (July 5, 1750) concerning Bellamy's work (among other matters) spoke first of the lack of attention paid of late to "the exact distinctions between a saving operation of the Spirit of God, and its false appearances." It endorsed Bellamy as "one of very great experience in religion, as to what has passed between God and his own soul" and of his "earnest care exactly to know the truth in these matters." His recommendation that *True Religion Delineated* be published in England, however, may be read as somewhat hesitant: "It might have been well if he [the author] had had more years over his head... [Y]et if his youth, and the obscurity of his original, and the place that he lives in, etc., do not prevent his being much taken notice of, I am persuaded his book might serve to give the church of God considerable light as to the nature of true religion, and many important doctrines of Christianity" (Dwight, *Life*, p. 406).
