Having denied a communication of "Nature to Nature" and affirmed that "the properties of both natures become common *to the Person*" (Ed. italics), Turretin continues: "Whence the phraseology, or the manner of speaking concerning Christ arises, by which the properties of either nature are predicated of the Person of Christ, in whatever manner it is denominated. This is done either *directly*, when what belongs to the divine nature is predicated of the person denominated from the divine nature, and what belongs to the human of the person denominated from the human nature, as when the Word is said to have been in the beginning with God, and God, John i. I, when the Son of man, it is said, must be delivered to death and crucified, Luke [Luke 18:31–33]. Or *indirectly*, as often as what belongs to the Deity is predicated of the man Christ, and to the humanity of Christ as God, as when suffering is ascribed to God, Acts xx. Acts 20:28, and ubiquity, which is proper to Deity is ascribed to the Son of man, John iii. John 3:13." (Giger, Topic XIII, Q. VIII, sec. III.) JE's metaphors and names for Christ in the sermon and in Miscell. no. 1358 denominate his excellencies by predicating directly *of the person* what belongs to one nature or to the other. See also the extraordinary example of the communication of the attributes, Miscell. no. *z*. LOVE OF GOD, written when JE was twenty (quoted in Intro., p. 20, n. 6), and my proposed interpretation of *End of Creation*, Ch. II, Sec. II, position 12.

[^010-note55]: *Perichoresis* was sometimes used as the "rule" for interpreting the interrelation of the two natures of Christ, but its true home was in trinitarian theology. Two Latin translations were used. In the Middle Ages, the notion was of a *spatial* togetherness of the three persons of the Trinity, a dwelling in one another; all three "inexist" one another (as Barth says, *Church Dogmatics*, I/1, pp. 424–25, 456), they exist or have their being only in common. So the reference in medieval times was always to the eternal "session" of the Trinity. *Circuminsessio* expressed this notion or rule of trinitarian reflection. *Circumincessio* was an earlier understanding of *perichoresis* (going back at least as far as John of Damascus (*c*. 675– *c*. 749], probably earlier). Its meaning was that the three persons permeate one another mutually by, as it were, moving around, one into another; or, as Barth says, "passing into one another" in "a kind of circular course" (ibid.). In another metaphor that has been used (appropriate in reading JE, I suggest), the joyous innertrinitarian life of God is a kind of dance. The Latin root is a legal term meaning to cede, yield, grant, give over; yielding and leading in turn are the movements of a dance. The suggestion of temporal sequence was replaced in the Latin church by the spatial metaphor of "session." If, instead of a Reformed understanding of the communication of properties, one wanted to frame JE on the excellencies of Christ in terms of *perichoresis*, the more dynamic of these two rules of interpretation suggests itself, just as *circumincessio* seems the better summary for him of the innertrinitarian society. In any case, the root of *perichoresis* means "orchestrated movement." JE avoids the temptation to affirm, of the person of Christ, that there was "more of God" than was manifest in his divine nature (and avoids the objection to "Nature to Nature" communication) by understanding "nature" chiefly as activity. Participation in the divine life or the divine activity is JE's answer to the objection raised against his use of 2 Peter 1:4 in *Affections*. See Related Correspondence, above.

[^010-note57]: **review me.** 27

[^010-note58]: On "The Excellencies of Christ," I am especially indebted to Robert W. Jenson's *America's Theologian: A Recommendation of Jonathan Edwards* (New York, Oxford Univ. Press, 1988). In a chapter entitled simply "The End," Jenson argues that JE's Christology was "specifically required," "the very thing needed— if only it had been noticed." So also of JE's eschatology: the need for two centuries has been for a vision of "the End" plausible enough to be believed along with a cosmology in which the heaven of heavens can no longer be conceived to be above. JE's ultimate vision is of beatification in heaven without a *place* (in which, however, he still believed). His distinctive originality in these matters was to affirm that Jesus Christ takes his people with him into the beatifical vision, "into the society of the blessed Trinity." See pp. 177–85. On the theological issues this appendix raises, students of JE will find fruitful comparisons in Jürgen Moltmann's *The Crucified God* (New York, Harper and Row, 1974), pp. 227–78, and his subsequent writings on the trinitarian history of God; and in Karl Barth. Nowhere in his writings does Barth develop systematically the idea of heaven as a progressive state. Yet we must remember that Vol. V of the *Church Dogmatics*, on the doctrine of redemption, where one would have expected the full statement of Barth's eschatology, was never written. We do not know how he might have developed the exchange of properties in the history of the incarnate Christ (the themes of IV/1 and IV/2, the Lord as Servant and the Servant as Lord) if placed in the context of God's end in redemption. Nevertheless, there is much in Barth's later theology that parallels Edwards' themes: (a) the inexhaustible richness of the living, triune God, whose being-in-love is freely extended to his creatures; (b) the inexpungeable significance of Christ for human salvation as the eternal mediator in and through whom we ever know and love God; (c) salvation as participation in the triune life of God, which is far more than a *restitutio ad integrum* of our humanity prior to the Fall; (d) the prevenience of God's grace now and forever in all his relations with humanity, opening and empowering human response in joy, gratitude, and obedience; (e) the communal as well as personal reality of the new creation here and hereafter; (f) the new life in communion with God and fellow creatures not as the extinguishing but as the establishment and fulfillment of our true humanity as finite creatures. Among others, I am grateful to Daniel L. Migliore and David Willis of Princeton Theological Seminary, and Alexander J. McKelway of Davidson College, for reading these pages and for unveiling some of my ignorance of Reformed theology, past and present. Migliore even mentioned "those light-hearted (but not flippant) remarks of Barth about his intention to inquire in heaven about Augustine, Thomas, Luther, Calvin, and Schleiermacher only *after* inquiring about Mozart; his plan to spend, say, a couple of centuries conversing with Schleiermacher about proper theological method, etc. Remarks like these do not, of course, carry the same weight as what might appear in large or fine print in the *Church Dogmatics*, but they do indicate a certain direction of Barth's thinking which is not incompatible with Edwards' vision of the growth in perfection of the redeemed in heaven" (letter, March 31, 1986).

## APPENDIX IV

#### INFUSED VIRTUES IN EDWARDSEAN AND CALVINISTIC CONTEXT

ANYONE who reads Edwards on 1 Corinthians 13 (even when stripped of the language of "infusion"),[^011-note1] who reads him on the "gracious" affections, and who reads him on true virtue must instantly see that he teaches a doctrine of *infused righteousness*, and not only a doctrine of Christ's righteousness *imputed* to us. This he variously expressed as divine love and its fruits in virtues implanted in heart and life by the indwelling Spirit, as a new "simple idea" impressed upon the soul,[^011-note2] as uniting consent or a propensity to unition with the Being of beings and our fellow human beings. Quite evidently, these qualities are virtues "endued" and inhering in the souls of men; they are neither "common" external influences of the Spirit, nor the garments of imputed righteousness alone, nor only a new status of being forgiven of sin.

From early entries in the "Miscellanies" through the period of the 1738 charity sermons to the end of his life (as *True Virtue* makes manifest), Edwards' account of the Christian moral life is one of progressive sanctification firmly grounded in a doctrine of *infused moral virtues*. Saving grace is "a quality *inherent* in... the subject of it," making "a man's heart and nature excellent." So "the Spirit becomes an indwelling vital principle in the soul, and the subject becomes a *spiritual being*."[^011-note3] This is what Edwards means by being remade in the "spiritual image of God" as distinct from having been made in the "natural image of God," i.e., belonging by natural birth to the "moral part" of the creation. The Spirit indwelling, "grace infused," is the fountain of "love infused" in the heart; and love infused is the fountain of a variety of infused moral dispositions.

<!-- p. 740 -->

Edwards stated succinctly the point to be proved in an early Miscellany: "[I]t is evident to a metaphysical demonstration, that one of these things is true of that man that is become good: either there was a time wherein if he had died he would neither have gone to heaven nor hell, that is, neither to great happiness nor great misery; or else, the future state is not according to man's goodness or badness here; or else, there are infused virtues."[^011-note4] The thesis of a related entry is: "Those that deny infusion by the Holy Spirit, must necessarily deny the Spirit to do anything at all." Whatever the "something" is that the Spirit does in the soul, this we call infusion: "[H]e causeth some motion, or affection, or apprehension to be in the soul, that at the same time would not be there without him."[^011-note5]

Moreover, Edwards argues in this entry that "God's Spirit... doth so much as he doth, or he causes in the soul so much as he causeth, let that be how little soever. So much as is purely the effect of his immediate motion, that *is* the effect of his immediate motion, let that be what it will; and so much is infused, how little soever that be. This is self-evident." Suppose, Edwards continues, that the Spirit of God only assists man's natural powers, according to the views of those who say the Holy Spirit only "assists the man in acquiring the habit." What does this mean? It means perhaps that the habit is "acquired rather sooner than it would be otherwise," or that it has a strength it otherwise would not have, or the natural power is assisted "to act more livelily and vigorously than otherwise." In such a circumstance, Edwards concludes, "that liveliness and vigorousness must be infused, which is a habit and therefore an infused habit; it is grace, and therefore infused grace." Therefore, among those who don't say the Holy Spirit does nothing at all, the dispute is only how much is infused. One party "says, a great deal; the other says, but little."

In another early entry Edwards refutes the position of those who say that a man acquires true virtue by frequent exercises of it. This, he argues, is a contradiction. "For tell me [how] a man that has no true grace within him shall begin to exercise it: before he begins to exercise it, he must have some of it. How shall [he] act virtuously the first time? How came he by that virtue which he then acted?" A man cannot get a virtuous habit by the acting or exercise of it before he has it. Edwards is willing to grant that *if* a man acts virtuously, after a while it will become habitual to him. The question concerns who was the prime mover in the act "when the man first began to act from a truly virtuous principle."

<!-- p. 741 -->

This cannot be "by means of his using of himself to it" in that time when he had never before acted from a virtuous principle.[^011-note6]

Edwards' insistent question is: "Supposing a person most profligate and vicious in his life," who afterwards changes course and reforms, "how this man became better than he was before, in his first beginning to reform; how came he by that virtue from which he acted when he first began to reform?" If you say that he did not at first act virtue, that he began to reform from some other spring or principle of action, the question remains: "[H]ow came he by his virtue by which he first *did* act from a virtuous principle?" To a common answer to that question Edwards replied: "If you say that even the worst have some spark of virtue remaining in them, and by acting and exercising of them he strengthens them; if we allow it to be so, the case is the same." How came the man to begin to reform today and not yesterday— or tomorrow? How came he to act so "livelily" and vigorously when he did? Did he strengthen the strength or liveliness of his virtue in order to begin to reform when he did, and to begin with the degree of impulsion he put into willing that self-reformation? So, among those who don't say the Holy Spirit does nothing, the dispute is over how much is infused. One party says, a great deal; the other says, but little.

Edwards has forced the reader to stand before disjunctive alternatives. The alternatives can be stated in two ways. (1) Either "the future state is not according to man's goodness or badness here; or else, there are infused virtues." (2) Either human beings are already naturally good enough by their own powers to receive acquittal from a perfectly righteous Judge (and from their own clarified consciences), *or else there are infused virtues*. So were Arminians and semi-Calvinists to be put to rout, and "humanitarians" left shielded in battle by extravagant claims only. If we are to come before God in holiness of life, this must be by nature (already our condition), or else by grace.

Of "infused virtue," Edwards did not hesitate to use the term "habits"— in the plural. In addition to Miscell. nos. *l, p*, and 73 (entries quoted above), Edwards lists nos. 137, 967, 1003, and 1029 under the heading "Infused habits" in his alphabetical Table. Miscell. no. 1029 gathers together scriptures "that show *that grace* is infused by God and is from his arbitrary efficacious operation" (Ed. italics). "Infused *grace*" is the title of nos. 147 (137), 967, and 1003, also listed alphabetically under "Infused habits." No. 481. SPIRIT'S OPERATION (*c*. 1730–31, shortly before

<!-- p. 742 -->

Edwards' first published sermon, *God Glorified*) is equally pertinent to a study of Edwards on virtue.

The interchangeability of the terms Edwards uses shows that for him the *moral* and the *theological* doctrines were the same. No. 655 even by its title, "HABIT OF GRACE. NEW NATURE," links the two as one "work of the Spirit in a sinner's conversion." In short, to take up the question of "infused virtues" in Edwards is to consider his account of the Reformed theological-moral doctrine of regeneration. Miscell. no. 241. REGERATION (*c*. 1726) compares the "new birth" with the infusion of the rational soul upon the vivification of the fetus. This entry also gives Edwards' understanding of habits, they "being only a law that God has fixed, that such actions upon such occasions should be exerted."[^011-note7]

Two distinguishing features of Edwards' philosophical theology prevented any notion of merit or threat to *sola gratia* from becoming associated with the virtues as Edwards understood them. (1) His view that all God's actions (including his "laws") with respect to creatures were by immediate arbitrary determination, his "arbitrary" will being subject to nothing but his *wisdom*; and (2) his view of *continual* creation. If no "steady-state" of the universe was "matter" on its own once it was created, then no steady-state of the soul (the virtues) or of the moral order (God's laws of nature) could ever be a world on its own without God's sustaining, immediate, continual action. Thus without God's constant activity, everything would drop into nothingness, both the old creation and the "new creature." The preservation of a virtue the next moment is the same as its creation the first moment. Therefore, infused habits or virtues cannot deposit and accumulate merit to the person in whom those qualities and characters inhere.[^011-note8]

Such was Edwards' understanding of infused moral virtues. Indeed, dropping the language of infusion would require explanation, not Edwards' use of it. A brief look at Edwards' immediate background in the Reformed tradition will show "infusion" to be a common Reformed doctrine.

In theology Edwards was demonstrably dependent upon the writings of Francis Turretin (1623–87) and Peter van Mastricht (1630–1706), two of the greatest seventeenth-century theologians in the Reformed tradition. He refers to "the great Turretine,"[^011-note9] and again to "the great

So, among those who don't say the Holy Spirit does nothing, the dispute is over how much is infused. One party says, a great deal; the other says, but little.

Edwards has forced the reader to stand before disjunctive alternatives. The alternatives can be stated in two ways. (1) Either "the future state is not according to man's goodness or badness here; or else, there are infused virtues." (2) Either human beings are already naturally good enough by their own powers to receive acquittal from a perfectly righteous Judge (and from their own clarified consciences), *or else there are infused virtues*. So were Arminians and semi-Calvinists to be put to rout, and "humanitarians" left shielded in battle by extravagant claims only. If we are to come before God in holiness of life, this must be by nature (already our condition), or else by grace.

Of "infused virtue," Edwards did not hesitate to use the term "habits"— in the plural. In addition to Miscell. nos. *l, p*, and 73 (entries quoted above), Edwards lists nos. 137, 967, 1003, and 1029 under the heading "Infused habits" in his alphabetical Table. Miscell. no. 1029 gathers together scriptures "that show *that grace* is infused by God and is from his arbitrary efficacious operation" (Ed. italics). "Infused *grace*" is the title of nos. 147 (137), 967, and 1003, also listed alphabetically under "Infused habits." No. 481. SPIRIT'S OPERATION (*c*. 1730–31, shortly before

<!-- p. 742 -->

Edwards' first published sermon, *God Glorified*) is equally pertinent to a study of Edwards on virtue.

The interchangeability of the terms Edwards uses shows that for him the *moral* and the *theological* doctrines were the same. No. 655 even by its title, "HABIT OF GRACE. NEW NATURE," links the two as one "work of the Spirit in a sinner's conversion." In short, to take up the question of "infused virtues" in Edwards is to consider his account of the Reformed theological-moral doctrine of regeneration. Miscell. no. 241. REGERATION (*c*. 1726) compares the "new birth" with the infusion of the rational soul upon the vivification of the fetus. This entry also gives Edwards' understanding of habits, they "being only a law that God has fixed, that such actions upon such occasions should be exerted."[^011-note25]

Two distinguishing features of Edwards' philosophical theology prevented any notion of merit or threat to *sola gratia* from becoming associated with the virtues as Edwards understood them. (1) His view that all God's actions (including his "laws") with respect to creatures were by immediate arbitrary determination, his "arbitrary" will being subject to nothing but his *wisdom*; and (2) his view of *continual* creation. If no "steady-state" of the universe was "matter" on its own once it was created, then no steady-state of the soul (the virtues) or of the moral order (God's laws of nature) could ever be a world on its own without God's sustaining, immediate, continual action. Thus without God's constant activity, everything would drop into nothingness, both the old creation and the "new creature." The preservation of a virtue the next moment is the same as its creation the first moment. Therefore, infused habits or virtues cannot deposit and accumulate merit to the person in whom those qualities and characters inhere.[^011-note26]

Such was Edwards' understanding of infused moral virtues. Indeed, dropping the language of infusion would require explanation, not Edwards' use of it. A brief look at Edwards' immediate background in the Reformed tradition will show "infusion" to be a common Reformed doctrine.

#### INFUSED VIRTUES IN EDWARDSEAN AND CALVINISTIC CONTEXT

ANYONE who reads Edwards on 1 Corinthians 13 (even when stripped of the language of "infusion"),[^011-note28] who reads him on the "gracious" affections, and who reads him on true virtue must instantly see that he teaches a doctrine of *infused righteousness, and not only a doctrine of Christ's righteousness *imputed to us. This he variously expressed as divine love and its fruits in virtues implanted in heart and life by the indwelling Spirit, as a new "simple idea" impressed upon the soul,[^011-note29], p. 205. Cf. *Freedom of the Will, p. 43, n. 5. as uniting consent or a propensity to unition with the Being of beings and our fellow human beings. Quite evidently, these qualities are virtues "endued" and inhering in the souls of men; they are neither "common" external influences of the Spirit, nor the garments of imputed righteousness alone, nor only a new status of being forgiven of sin.***

From early entries in the "Miscellanies" through the period of the 1738 charity sermons to the end of his life (as *True Virtue makes manifest), Edwards' account of the Christian moral life is one of progressive sanctification firmly grounded in a doctrine of *infused moral virtues. Saving grace is "a quality *inherent in... the subject of it," making "a man's heart and nature excellent." So "the Spirit becomes an indwelling vital principle in the soul, and the subject becomes a *spiritual being."[^011-note30], pp. 157–58. Ed. italics. Cf. JE's extended discussion of the meaning of *spiritual in *Affections, pp. 201–08. This is what Edwards means by being remade in the "spiritual image of God" as distinct from having been made in the "natural image of God," i.e., belonging by natural birth to the "moral part" of the creation. The Spirit indwelling, "grace infused," is the fountain of "love infused" in the heart; and love infused is the fountain of a variety of infused moral dispositions.******

<!-- p. 740 -->

Edwards stated succinctly the point to be proved in an early Miscellany: "[I]t is evident to a metaphysical demonstration, that one of these things is true of that man that is become good: either there was a time wherein if he had died he would neither have gone to heaven nor hell, that is, neither to great happiness nor great misery; or else, the future state is not according to man's goodness or badness here; or else, there are infused virtues."[^011-note31]. INFUSED HABITS (*c. 1722–23). The thesis of a related entry is: "Those that deny infusion by the Holy Spirit, must necessarily deny the Spirit to do anything at all." Whatever the "something" is that the Spirit does in the soul, this we call infusion: "[H]e causeth some motion, or affection, or apprehension to be in the soul, that at the same time would not be there without him."[^011-note32]. INFUSED HABITS (*c. 1722–23).**

Moreover, Edwards argues in this entry that "God's Spirit... doth so much as he doth, or he causes in the soul so much as he causeth, let that be how little soever. So much as is purely the effect of his immediate motion, that *is the effect of his immediate motion, let that be what it will; and so much is infused, how little soever that be. This is self-evident." Suppose, Edwards continues, that the Spirit of God only assists man's natural powers, according to the views of those who say the Holy Spirit only "assists the man in acquiring the habit." What does this mean? It means perhaps that the habit is "acquired rather sooner than it would be otherwise," or that it has a strength it otherwise would not have, or the natural power is assisted "to act more livelily and vigorously than otherwise." In such a circumstance, Edwards concludes, "that liveliness and vigorousness must be infused, which is a habit and therefore an infused habit; it is grace, and therefore infused grace." Therefore, among those who don't say the Holy Spirit does nothing at all, the dispute is only how much is infused. One party "says, a great deal; the other says, but little."*

In another early entry Edwards refutes the position of those who say that a man acquires true virtue by frequent exercises of it. This, he argues, is a contradiction. "For tell me [how] a man that has no true grace within him shall begin to exercise it: before he begins to exercise it, he must have some of it. How shall [he] act virtuously the first time? How came he by that virtue which he then acted?" A man cannot get a virtuous habit by the acting or exercise of it before he has it. Edwards is willing to grant that *if a man acts virtuously, after a while it will become habitual to him. The question concerns who was the prime mover in the act "when the man first began to act from a truly virtuous principle."*

<!-- p. 741 -->

This cannot be "by means of his using of himself to it" in that time when he had never before acted from a virtuous principle.[^011-note33]. 723–24). JE used this argument many times thereafter, in different contexts. See *Freedom of the Will, Intro., pp. 29–34.*

Edwards' insistent question is: "Supposing a person most profligate and vicious in his life," who afterwards changes course and reforms, "how this man became better than he was before, in his first beginning to reform; how came he by that virtue from which he acted when he first began to reform?" If you say that he did not at first act virtue, that he began to reform from some other spring or principle of action, the question remains: "[H]ow came he by his virtue by which he first *did act from a virtuous principle?" To a common answer to that question Edwards replied: "If you say that even the worst have some spark of virtue remaining in them, and by acting and exercising of them he strengthens them; if we allow it to be so, the case is the same." How came the man to begin to reform today and not yesterday— or tomorrow? How came he to act so "livelily" and vigorously when he did? Did he strengthen the strength or liveliness of his virtue in order to begin to reform when he did, and to begin with the degree of impulsion he put into willing that self-reformation? So, among those who don't say the Holy Spirit does nothing, the dispute is over how much is infused. One party says, a great deal; the other says, but little.*

So were Arminians and semi-Calvinists to be put to rout, and "humanitarians" left shielded in battle by extravagant claims only. If we are to come before God in holiness of life, this must be by nature (already our condition), or else by grace.*

Mastricht."[^011-note46], p. 337. He expressed his enthusiasm for the theology of both these men in a letter to Joseph Bellamy in 1746 telling him where he might be able to locate copies of their works. In passing, he noted,

> They are both excellent. Turretine is on Polemical divinity; on the 5 Points, & all other Controversial Points; & is much larger in these than Mastricht; & is better for one that desires only to be thoroughly versed in Controversies. But take Mastricht for divinity in General, doctrine Practice & Controversie; or as an universal system of divinity; & it is much better than Turretine or any other Book in the world, excepting the Bible, in my opinion.[^011-note47] (April 1928), 230.

A concise summary by Turretin on infusion follows:

> Just as Christ sustains a twofold relation to us, of *Surety & *Head, of surety, to take away the guilt of sin by a payment made for it, of Head, to take away its power & corruption by the efficacy of the Spirit, so in a twofold way Christ imparts his blessings to us, by *a forensic Imputation, & *a moral & *internal infusion. The former flows from Christ as surety, & is the foundation of our Justification. The latter depends upon him as Head, & is the principle of sanctification. For on this account God justifies us, because the righteousness of our Surety, Christ, is imputed to us. And on this account we are renewed, because we derive the spirit from our Head, Christ, who renews us after the image of Christ, & bestows upon us inherent righteousness.[^011-note48], trans. G. M. Giger (unpublished manuscript, Speer Library, Princeton Theological Seminary), Topic XVI, Q. III, sec. VI. By the fourth quarter of the nineteenth century the decline of Latin as an academic language had rendered it largely useless in theological discourse. This factor, along with the need to address issues of the day, led to the substitution of Charles Hodge's *Systematic Theology for Turretin's *Institutio as the textbook of theology at Princeton. Hodge's volumes were heavily influenced by Turretin's thought, and this apparently satisfied any pressing need to make the *Institutio available to English readers. As a result the bulk of it has never been published in English. The quotation above is taken from a handwritten translation by George Musgrave Giger, D. D., professor of Latin at the College of New Jersey from 1854 to 1865. In his introduction to *Affections John E. Smith was in error when he wrote that Turretin's *Institutio appeared "in English translation as late as 1847 at Edinburgh" (p. 73). For support he incorrectly interpreted John T McNeill's remark in *The History and Character of Calvinism that the *Institutio "was republished in Edinburgh in 1847" (p. 406). The 1847 edition was "a work of more than two thousand closely printed pages, in Latin" which resulted "from the joint endeavor of enterprising publishers in New York and Edinburgh." (J. W. Alexander, *The Biblical Repertory and Princeton Review, XX [1848], 452).*************

<!-- p. 744 -->

Mastricht's discussion of infusion may be introduced by an extract from the *Theoretico-Practica Theologia,[^011-note49]. In its 1300 pages the whole of Christian theology and morality, theory and practice, is laid out with a minuteness and precision that bring a hundred years of methodizing to a stupendous fulfillment. Beyond this limit no mortal could go. Every chapter expounds a text, analyzes it grammatically, etymologically, rhetorically, logically, comparatively, extracts all possible doctrines from it, argues all the supporting ‘reasons,’ raises and answers every conceivable objection, makes the practical applications, and points the moral of every principle" (*The New England Mind [Cambridge, Harvard Univ. Press, 1939], 1, 96). translated from the Latin as *A Treatise on Regeneration.***

> For regeneration, strictly so called, finds man spiritually *dead, into whom it infuseth the first act, or principle of the spiritual *life; by which he hath a *power or ability to perform spiritual exercises. Therefore, without this, he *can neither *see the kingdom of God, that is *mentally, as he is blind... Nor if he could *see could he *enter into the kingdom of God, as "*he is not subject to the law of God," neither indeed *can be; "who also ‘*of himself is not sufficient to think any thing spiritually good.’" *Who therefore stands in absolute need of illumination by regeneration, in order to his *seeing the kingdom of heaven, and of a *renovation of his will, in order to his willing to *enter into it.[^011-note50] (New Haven, Thomas and Samuel Green, n. d.), (1769 in pencil in Evans, *American Bibliography), p. 14.****************

Later in the treatise Mastricht discussed regeneration as a "*physical act powerfully infusing spiritual life in the soul: which is proved, not only, (1) By the constant phraseology of the *Scriptures... But, (2) It may also be proved by the very nature of the thing, in as much as regeneration is an operation upon men spiritually *dead, infusing life into them; but what moral operation, in teaching, offering, persuading, can be rationally exercised upon a man that is *dead?[^011-note51] Mastricht also writes, "This spiritual life, animating and quickening the *whole regenerate man, and all the several parts and faculties of him, hath different *names according to those******

<!-- p. 745 -->

different faculties... In the meantime, this saving illumination in regeneration, is to be cautiously distinguished from the illumination, which is given in the external call, in which spiritual light is rather held up to view, than conveyed into the soul."[^011-note52]

Edwards would certainly not have agreed with Mastricht that the infused "spiritual" life— the several dispositions and virtues quickening the regenerate man— obtain their *names according to "the several parts and *faculties of him." Instead, the infused virtues were *specifications of charity itself, and therefore also "characters" of the whole man. The appropriate *names are not designations of the excellence of various faculties of the soul, but designations of the moral character or quality in question, mankind learning to agree on fitting terms to use whether the virtues are fruits of charity or of natural principles or of both.****

Edwards' Miscell. no. 847. REGENERATION or CONVERSION (*c. 1740–42, the Great Awakening), in particular, invites close comparison with John Calvin on regeneration and justification in Bk. III of the *Institutes, entitled "The Way in Which We Receive the Grace of Christ: What Benefits Come to Us from It and What Effects Follow."[^011-note53], ed. John T. McNeill (2 vols., Philadelphia, Westminster, 1960), Bk. III. This is not the occasion for such a comparison, but still a few points can be selected from Calvin that may help in understanding Edwards' doctrine of infused moral virtues as a Reformed account of regeneration, of the "new life" of believers.**

I begin with a small but significant point. In what Calvin says about the "ancient doctors" to distinguish his method from theirs, he anticipated and granted the appropriateness of Edwards' careful delineation of a panoply of fruits of the Spirit— habitual dispositions or virtues in heart and life— in the charity sermons. Calvin wrote:

> In composing exhortations on but a single virtue, the ancient doctors, as we see, became very prolix. *Yet in this they waste no words. For when a man sets out to commend any virtue in his discourse, abundance of material drives him to a style of such fullness that he seems not to treat it properly unless he speaks at length. But I do not intend to develop, here, the instruction in living that I am now about to offer *to the point of describing individual virtues at length, and of digressing into exhortations. Such may be sought in others' writings, especially from the homilies of the fathers. To show the godly man how he may be directed to a rightly ordered life, and briefly to set down some

<!-- p. 746 -->

 universal rule with which to determine his duties— this will be quite enough for me.[^011-note54]**

Calvin himself set forth one rule only, that men may not be left to wander about in their zeal for righteousness, namely, "that we must be made holy because our God is holy... that, *infused with his holiness, we may follow whither he calls."[^011-note55] Edwards delivered eighteenth-century "homilies of the fathers," prolix yet wasting no words.*

Indeed, Edwards' innovation, within the Reformed tradition of infused righteousness, was not that he delineated an array of the virtues of charity. He drew his precepts from I. Cor. 1 Corinthians 13, and in the distinguishing signs of the gracious affections from St. Paul's list of the fruits of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23) and from elsewhere in Scripture, as did the fathers in their homilies. So Calvin remarks, "As philosophers have fixed limits of the right and the honorable, when they derive individual duties and *the whole company of virtues, so Scripture is not without its own order in this matter, but holds to a most beautiful dispensation, and one much more certain than all the philosophical ones."[^011-note56] Nor was Edwards' innovation solely in that he more carefully delineated the infused virtues, conceptualized and arranged them more "methodically"— heedless of Calvin's warning that the Spirit of God did not adhere so exactly or continuously to a methodical plan (because the Spirit taught more without affectation than the philosophers!).[^011-note57] His innovation within the Reformed tradition, I suggest, was rather his *full account of natural principles. His principles are the source of several, at least, of the dispositions and virtues that true virtue or love to God operating alone infuses in heart and life. Both dispositions and virtues deserve, by the common consent of mankind in its use of moral terms, the same names, i.e., justice, kindness, compassion.[^011-note58] and discussed more fully in the final chapter of that dissertation. In his account of the totality of the moral life Edwards articulated the humanism often ascribed to Calvin in contrast to Luther.**

We noted above that Calvin was content to set forth one "universal rule" only by which to determine our duties, namely, holiness as God is holy. At another place in Bk. III "repentance" replaces and becomes Calvin's term for "regeneration." To comprehend this, it helps to note Calvin's doctrine of *duplex gratia (double grace), and the rather astonishing*

<!-- p. 747 -->

organization of Bk. III as a whole. Calvin takes up regeneration *first, and comes to justification only at ch. xi, 188 pages later in the English text. At that point he explains the reason for this procedure. By "partaking" of Christ "we principally receive a double grace." This requires explanation, because Calvin has taken up the "second" of these graces first.*

> Of regeneration, indeed, the *second of these gifts, I have said what seems sufficient. The theme of justification was therefore more lightly touched upon because it was more to the point to understand first how little devoid of good works is the faith, through which we obtain free righteousness by the mercy of God... Therefore we must now discuss these matters thoroughly. And we must so discuss them as to bear in mind that this is *the main hinge on which religion turns, so that we devote the greater attention and care to it.[^011-note59], III, xi, 1 (p. 725. Ed. italics). See also the editor's footnote to Calvin's earlier discussion of repentance, III, iii, 1, n. 2 (p. 593).**

In other words, Calvin's exposition was designed most clearly to refute the charges of those who did not give full weight to the reality of "double grace" from one and the same source or spring, by either separating or confusing regeneration and justification.

In his discussion of regeneration, repentance has special importance. The "sum of the gospel," Calvin writes, consists in two things: repentance and forgiveness of sins. "That is, newness of life and free reconciliation," he explains. Note that repentance does not mean sorrow; it is paired with, and it does not precede, forgiveness. Both are "conferred" on us, and both repentance (newness of life) and free reconciliation (justification) begin *at the same point. But here again Calvin chooses to discuss repentance *first. The immediate transition is "from faith to repentance." Then we come to the following passage:**

> For when this topic is rightly understood it will better appear how man is justified by faith alone, and simple pardon; nevertheless actual holiness of life, so to speak, is not separated from free imputation of righteousness. Now it ought to be a fact beyond controversy that repentance not only constantly follows faith, but is also born of faith [since both pardon and newness of life are offered in the preaching of the gospel].[^011-note60]

Repentance means a "true *turning of our life to God."[^011-note61] It requires "a*

<!-- p. 748 -->

transformation, not only in outward works, but in the soul itself."[^011-note62] Repentance consists of two parts, "mortification of the flesh and *vivification of the spirit." No one can discharge such duties as Scripture enjoins without a turning of life to God, "unless *the mind itself and heart first put on the inclination to righteousness, judgment, mercy. That comes to pass when the Spirit of God so *imbues our souls, *steeped in his holiness, with both *new thoughts and feelings, that they can be rightly considered *new."[^011-note63] "Repentance" is defined exactly as Edwards did in the Seventh Distinguishing Sign of the gracious affections.[^011-note64], pp. 340–44. The resemblance between Calvin and Edwards on repentance and faith is even more remarkable in the concatenation sermon. "[S]aving repentance and faith are implied in one another," as Edwards wrote:******

> They are both one conversion of the soul from sin to God through Christ. This act of the soul in turning from sin to God through Christ, as it respects the [object] from which the turning is, viz. sin, is called repentance. And as it respects the [object] to which, and the mediation by which [[it turns]], is called faith. But it is the same motion of the soul, as when a man turns or flies from darkness to the light. It is the same motion though it may be called by different names, as it respects the darkness fled from, and the light fled to; with respect to one, it is called fleeing from, and the other, receiving, or embracing.[^011-note65], p. 331.

This passage may serve for Edwards on *duplex gratia. For him as well as for Calvin, "pardon" and "newness of life" are always together, and from the same source, our "sharing in Christ."*

Indeed, Calvin's exposition of repentance (newness of life) entails so thorough and so constant a turning to God that it embraces the whole of regeneration, so far as this is ever conferred in this life. "Therefore, in a word," he writes, "I interpret repentance as regeneration, whose sole end is to restore in us the image of God that had been disfigured and all but obliterated through Adam's transgression." This restoration "does not take place in one moment or one day or one year." Through "continual and sometimes even slow advances God wipes out... the corruptions of the flesh... consecrates... to himself as temples renewing all their minds to true purity that they may practice repentance throughout their lives and know that this warfare will end only at death."[^011-note66], III, iii, 8 (p. 601)

<!-- p. 749 -->

Calvin's entire discussion under the head of regeneration begins, as do Edwards' charity sermons, with the indwelling Holy Spirit, the "secret energy" by which he "breathes divine life" into us.[^011-note67] "As long as Christ remains outside us," all that he suffered (to purchase our pardon) remains useless to us.[^011-note68] "As if we ought to think of Christ, standing afar off and not rather dwelling in us! For we await salvation from him, not because he appears to us afar off, but because *he makes us, ingrafted into his body, *participants not only in all his benefits but *in himself... But since Christ has been *so imparted to you with all his benefits *that all his things are made yours."[^011-note69] No student of Edwards can read those words without thinking of many themes in the charity sermons: the Spirit working "divine love" in the heart; communicating himself not only by external influence or "adventitiously" but in his own "proper" or essential nature; our becoming "partakers of the divine nature"; recreated in the "amiable image of Christ"; he having become *ours.******

The terms "faith," "righteousness," "repentance," "regeneration," "sanctification," "holiness" are used with overlapping if not shifting meanings in the Reformed tradition. Nevertheless, one thing is clear: free reconciliation and newness of life begin together at the same point and continue together throughout life. On the one hand Calvin writes "concerning our righteousness [reckoned to us] and sanctification," that "although we may distinguish them, Christ contains both in himself." To attain favor or pardon in God's sight, "you must first possess Christ; but you cannot possess him without being made partaker of his sanctification, because he cannot be divided into pieces." These benefits are bestowed "at the same time, the one never without the other." Thus we are "justified not without works yet not through works, since in our sharing in Christ, which justifies us, sanctification is just as much included as [imputed] righteousness."[^011-note70]

On the other hand, a righteousness not their own must always continue to be just as much included as sanctification if the salvation of believers *and their works is sure. Why must this be so? Because the whole life of believers must, as we have seen, be a life of repentance, a turning to God, because the story of redemption through the regenerative work of the indwelling Spirit (infused righteousness) is never complete in this life. "After forgiveness of sins is set forth, the good works that now follow*

<!-- p. 750 -->

are appraised otherwise than on their own merit [as was the doer of them, in free reconciliation]. For everything in them is covered by Christ's perfection, every blemish or spot is cleansed away by his purity in order not to be brought in question at the divine judgment." So the good works done by believers still need to be "accounted" or "reckoned" righteous, if only the pure in heart are to see God.[^011-note71]

So it made sense to Calvin— and it was an embassy to be published daily to the hearts of men— that "man is so justified by faith that not only is he himself righteous but *his works are also accounted righteous above their worth";[^011-note72] that "a work begins to be acceptable only when it is undertaken with pardon"; that "by faith not only we ourselves but our works as well are justified."[^011-note73] Having laid stress, and continuing to stress, moral newness of life, Calvin demands (by his standard of being steeped in holiness) to be shown one virtue or work that can claim "any right to be raised up either to destroy or becloud justification of faith."[^011-note74] "Let one of Adam's children come forward with such uprightness. If there is no one, they must either perish out of God's sight or flee to the shelter of his mercy."[^011-note75] So justification by faith remains, for believers, the main hinge on which religion turns.*

Now, of course, we do not know that Edwards was steeped in the works of John Calvin.[^011-note76], p. 131). In fact, no Puritan ever believed that final truth had broken forth from the Scriptures in the writings of that man of God in Geneva. Still, no one can read Calvin, or the foregoing summary of his views, on the two forms of righteousness without noting the deep family resemblance between them and Edwards' views.

<!-- p. 751 -->

Mastricht."[^011-note77], p. 337. He expressed his enthusiasm for the theology of both these men in a letter to Joseph Bellamy in 1746 telling him where he might be able to locate copies of their works. In passing, he noted,

> They are both excellent. Turretine is on Polemical divinity; on the 5 Points, & all other Controversial Points; & is much larger in these than Mastricht; & is better for one that desires only to be thoroughly versed in Controversies. But take Mastricht for divinity in General, doctrine Practice & Controversie; or as an universal system of divinity; & it is much better than Turretine or any other Book in the world, excepting the Bible, in my opinion.[^011-note78] (April 1928), 230.

A concise summary by Turretin on infusion follows:

> Just as Christ sustains a twofold relation to us, of *Surety & *Head, of surety, to take away the guilt of sin by a payment made for it, of Head, to take away its power & corruption by the efficacy of the Spirit, so in a twofold way Christ imparts his blessings to us, by *a forensic Imputation, & *a moral & *internal infusion. The former flows from Christ as surety, & is the foundation of our Justification. The latter depends upon him as Head, & is the principle of sanctification. For on this account God justifies us, because the righteousness of our Surety, Christ, is imputed to us. And on this account we are renewed, because we derive the spirit from our Head, Christ, who renews us after the image of Christ, & bestows upon us inherent righteousness.[^011-note79], trans. G. M. Giger (unpublished manuscript, Speer Library, Princeton Theological Seminary), Topic XVI, Q. III, sec. VI. By the fourth quarter of the nineteenth century the decline of Latin as an academic language had rendered it largely useless in theological discourse. This factor, along with the need to address issues of the day, led to the substitution of Charles Hodge's *Systematic Theology for Turretin's *Institutio as the textbook of theology at Princeton. Hodge's volumes were heavily influenced by Turretin's thought, and this apparently satisfied any pressing need to make the *Institutio available to English readers. As a result the bulk of it has never been published in English. The quotation above is taken from a handwritten translation by George Musgrave Giger, D. D., professor of Latin at the College of New Jersey from 1854 to 1865. In his introduction to *Affections John E. Smith was in error when he wrote that Turretin's *Institutio appeared "in English translation as late as 1847 at Edinburgh" (p. 73). For support he incorrectly interpreted John T McNeill's remark in *The History and Character of Calvinism that the *Institutio "was republished in Edinburgh in 1847" (p. 406). The 1847 edition was "a work of more than two thousand closely printed pages, in Latin" which resulted "from the joint endeavor of enterprising publishers in New York and Edinburgh." (J. W. Alexander, *The Biblical Repertory and Princeton Review, XX [1848], 452).*************

Mastricht's discussion of infusion may be introduced by an extract from the *Theoretico-Practica Theologia,[^011-note80]. In its 1300 pages the whole of Christian theology and morality, theory and practice, is laid out with a minuteness and precision that bring a hundred years of methodizing to a stupendous fulfillment. Beyond this limit no mortal could go. Every chapter expounds a text, analyzes it grammatically, etymologically, rhetorically, logically, comparatively, extracts all possible doctrines from it, argues all the supporting ‘reasons,’ raises and answers every conceivable objection, makes the practical applications, and points the moral of every principle" (*The New England Mind [Cambridge, Harvard Univ. Press, 1939], 1, 96). translated from the Latin as *A Treatise on Regeneration.***

> For regeneration, strictly so called, finds man spiritually *dead, into whom it infuseth the first act, or principle of the spiritual *life; by which he hath a *power or ability to perform spiritual exercises. Therefore, without this, he *can neither *see the kingdom of God, that is *mentally, as he is blind... Nor if he could *see could he *enter into the kingdom of God, as "*he is not subject to the law of God," neither indeed *can be; "who also ‘*of himself is not sufficient to think any thing spiritually good.’" *Who therefore stands in absolute need of illumination by regeneration, in order to his *seeing the kingdom of heaven, and of a *renovation of his will, in order to his willing to *enter into it.[^011-note81] (New Haven, Thomas and Samuel Green, n. d.), (1769 in pencil in Evans, *American Bibliography), p. 14.****************

Later in the treatise Mastricht discussed regeneration as a "*physical act powerfully infusing spiritual life in the soul: which is proved, not only, (1) By the constant phraseology of the *Scriptures... But, (2) It may also be proved by the very nature of the thing, in as much as regeneration is an operation upon men spiritually *dead, infusing life into them; but what moral operation, in teaching, offering, persuading, can be rationally exercised upon a man that is *dead?[^011-note82] Mastricht also writes, "This spiritual life, animating and quickening the *whole regenerate man, and all the several parts and faculties of him, hath different *names according to those******

<!-- p. 745 -->

different faculties... In the meantime, this saving illumination in regeneration, is to be cautiously distinguished from the illumination, which is given in the external call, in which spiritual light is rather held up to view, than conveyed into the soul."[^011-note83]

Edwards would certainly not have agreed with Mastricht that the infused "spiritual" life— the several dispositions and virtues quickening the regenerate man— obtain their *names according to "the several parts and *faculties of him." Instead, the infused virtues were *specifications of charity itself, and therefore also "characters" of the whole man. The appropriate *names are not designations of the excellence of various faculties of the soul, but designations of the moral character or quality in question, mankind learning to agree on fitting terms to use whether the virtues are fruits of charity or of natural principles or of both.****

Edwards' Miscell. no. 847. REGENERATION or CONVERSION (*c. 1740–42, the Great Awakening), in particular, invites close comparison with John Calvin on regeneration and justification in Bk. III of the *Institutes, entitled "The Way in Which We Receive the Grace of Christ: What Benefits Come to Us from It and What Effects Follow."[^011-note84], ed. John T. Mastricht's discussion of infusion may be introduced by an extract from the *Theoretico-Practica Theologia*,[^011-note111] translated from the Latin as *A Treatise on Regeneration*.

> For regeneration, strictly so called, finds man spiritually *dead*, into whom it infuseth the first act, or principle of the spiritual *life*; by which he hath a *power* or ability to perform spiritual exercises. Therefore, without this, he *can* neither *see* the kingdom of God, that is *mentally*, as he is blind... Nor if he could *see* could he *enter* into the kingdom of God, as "*he is not subject to the law of God*," neither indeed *can be*; "who also ‘*of himself is not sufficient to think any thing spiritually good*.’" *Who therefore stands in absolute need of illumination* by regeneration, in order to his *seeing* the kingdom of heaven, and of a *renovation* of his will, in order to his willing to *enter* into it.[^011-note112]

Later in the treatise Mastricht discussed regeneration as a "*physical* act powerfully infusing spiritual life in the soul: which is proved, not only, (1) By the constant phraseology of the *Scriptures*... But, (2) It may also be proved by the very nature of the thing, in as much as regeneration is an operation upon men spiritually *dead*, infusing life into them; but what moral operation, in teaching, offering, persuading, can be rationally exercised upon a man that is *dead*?[^011-note113] Mastricht also writes, "This spiritual life, animating and quickening the *whole* regenerate man, and all the several parts and faculties of him, hath different *names* according to those

<!-- p. 745 -->

different faculties... In the meantime, this saving illumination in regeneration, is to be cautiously distinguished from the illumination, which is given in the external call, in which spiritual light is rather held up to view, than conveyed into the soul."[^011-note114]

Edwards would certainly not have agreed with Mastricht that the infused "spiritual" life— the several dispositions and virtues quickening the regenerate man— obtain their *names* according to "the several parts and *faculties* of him." Instead, the infused virtues were *specifications* of charity itself, and therefore also "characters" of the whole man. The appropriate *names* are not designations of the excellence of various faculties of the soul, but designations of the moral character or quality in question, mankind learning to agree on fitting terms to use whether the virtues are fruits of charity or of natural principles or of both.

Edwards' Miscell. no. 847. REGENERATION or CONVERSION (*c*. 1740–42, the Great Awakening), in particular, invites close comparison with John Calvin on regeneration and justification in Bk. III of the *Institutes*, entitled "The Way in Which We Receive the Grace of Christ: What Benefits Come to Us from It and What Effects Follow."[^011-note115] This is not the occasion for such a comparison, but still a few points can be selected from Calvin that may help in understanding Edwards' doctrine of infused moral virtues as a Reformed account of regeneration, of the "new life" of believers.

I begin with a small but significant point. In what Calvin says about the "ancient doctors" to distinguish his method from theirs, he anticipated and granted the appropriateness of Edwards' careful delineation of a panoply of fruits of the Spirit— habitual dispositions or virtues in heart and life— in the charity sermons. Calvin wrote:

> In composing exhortations on but a single virtue, the ancient doctors, as we see, became very prolix. *Yet in this they waste no words*. For when a man sets out to commend any virtue in his discourse, abundance of material drives him to a style of such fullness that he seems not to treat it properly unless he speaks at length. But I do not intend to develop, here, the instruction in living that I am now about to offer *to the point of describing individual virtues* at length, and of digressing into exhortations. Such may be sought in others' writings, especially from the homilies of the fathers. To show the godly man how he may be directed to a rightly ordered life, and briefly to set down some

<!-- p. 746 -->

 universal rule with which to determine his duties— this will be quite enough for me.[^011-note116]

Calvin himself set forth one rule only, that men may not be left to wander about in their zeal for righteousness, namely, "that we must be made holy because our God is holy... that, *infused with his holiness*, we may follow whither he calls."[^011-note117] Edwards delivered eighteenth-century "homilies of the fathers," prolix yet wasting no words.

Indeed, Edwards' innovation, within the Reformed tradition of infused righteousness, was not that he delineated an array of the virtues of charity. He drew his precepts from I. Cor. 1 Corinthians 13, and in the distinguishing signs of the gracious affections from St. Paul's list of the fruits of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23) and from elsewhere in Scripture, as did the fathers in their homilies. So Calvin remarks, "As philosophers have fixed limits of the right and the honorable, when they derive individual duties and *the whole company of virtues*, so Scripture is not without its own order in this matter, but holds to a most beautiful dispensation, and one much more certain than all the philosophical ones."[^011-note118] Nor was Edwards' innovation solely in that he more carefully delineated the infused virtues, conceptualized and arranged them more "methodically"— heedless of Calvin's warning that the Spirit of God did not adhere so exactly or continuously to a methodical plan (because the Spirit taught more without affectation than the philosophers!).[^011-note119] His innovation within the Reformed tradition, I suggest, was rather his *full account of natural principles*. His principles are the source of several, at least, of the dispositions and virtues that true virtue or love to God operating alone infuses in heart and life. Both dispositions and virtues deserve, by the common consent of mankind in its use of moral terms, the same names, i.e., justice, kindness, compassion.[^011-note120] In his account of the totality of the moral life Edwards articulated the humanism often ascribed to Calvin in contrast to Luther.

We noted above that Calvin was content to set forth one "universal rule" only by which to determine our duties, namely, holiness as God is holy. At another place in Bk. III "repentance" replaces and becomes Calvin's term for "regeneration." To comprehend this, it helps to note Calvin's doctrine of *duplex gratia* (double grace), and the rather astonishing

<!-- p. 747 -->

organization of Bk. III as a whole. Calvin takes up regeneration *first*, and comes to justification only at ch. xi, 188 pages later in the English text. At that point he explains the reason for this procedure. By "partaking" of Christ "we principally receive a double grace." This requires explanation, because Calvin has taken up the "second" of these graces first.

> Of regeneration, indeed, the *second* of these gifts, I have said what seems sufficient. The theme of justification was therefore more lightly touched upon because it was more to the point to understand first how little devoid of good works is the faith, through which we obtain free righteousness by the mercy of God... Therefore we must now discuss these matters thoroughly. And we must so discuss them as to bear in mind that this is *the main hinge* on which religion turns, so that we devote the greater attention and care to it.[^011-note121]

In other words, Calvin's exposition was designed most clearly to refute the charges of those who did not give full weight to the reality of "double grace" from one and the same source or spring, by either separating or confusing regeneration and justification.

In his discussion of regeneration, repentance has special importance. The "sum of the gospel," Calvin writes, consists in two things: repentance and forgiveness of sins. "That is, newness of life and free reconciliation," he explains. Note that repentance does not mean sorrow; it is paired with, and it does not precede, forgiveness. Both are "conferred" on us, and both repentance (newness of life) and free reconciliation (justification) begin *at the same point*. But here again Calvin chooses to discuss repentance *first*. The immediate transition is "from faith to repentance." Then we come to the following passage:

> For when this topic is rightly understood it will better appear how man is justified by faith alone, and simple pardon; nevertheless actual holiness of life, so to speak, is not separated from free imputation of righteousness. Now it ought to be a fact beyond controversy that repentance not only constantly follows faith, but is also born of faith [since both pardon and newness of life are offered in the preaching of the gospel].[^011-note122]

Repentance means a "true *turning* of our life to God."[^011-note123] It requires "a

<!-- p. 748 -->

transformation, not only in outward works, but in the soul itself."[^011-note124] Repentance consists of two parts, "mortification of the flesh and *vivification* of the spirit." No one can discharge such duties as Scripture enjoins without a turning of life to God, "unless *the mind itself and heart first put on the inclination to righteousness*, judgment, mercy. That comes to pass when the Spirit of God so *imbues* our souls, *steeped* in his holiness, with both *new thoughts and feelings*, that they can be rightly considered *new*."[^011-note125] "Repentance" is defined exactly as Edwards did in the Seventh Distinguishing Sign of the gracious affections.[^011-note126] The resemblance between Calvin and Edwards on repentance and faith is even more remarkable in the concatenation sermon. "[S]aving repentance and faith are implied in one another," as Edwards wrote:

> They are both one conversion of the soul from sin to God through Christ. This act of the soul in turning from sin to God through Christ, as it respects the [object] from which the turning is, viz. sin, is called repentance. And as it respects the [object] to which, and the mediation by which [[it turns]], is called faith. But it is the same motion of the soul, as when a man turns or flies from darkness to the light. It is the same motion though it may be called by different names, as it respects the darkness fled from, and the light fled to; with respect to one, it is called fleeing from, and the other, receiving, or embracing.[^011-note127]

This passage may serve for Edwards on *duplex gratia*. For him as well as for Calvin, "pardon" and "newness of life" are always together, and from the same source, our "sharing in Christ."

Indeed, Calvin's exposition of repentance (newness of life) entails so thorough and so constant a turning to God that it embraces the whole of regeneration, so far as this is ever conferred in this life. "Therefore, in a word," he writes, "I interpret repentance as regeneration, whose sole end is to restore in us the image of God that had been disfigured and all but obliterated through Adam's transgression." This restoration "does not take place in one moment or one day or one year." Through "continual and sometimes even slow advances God wipes out... the corruptions of the flesh... consecrates... to himself as temples renewing all their minds to true purity that they may practice repentance throughout their lives and know that this warfare will end only at death."[^011-note128]

<!-- p. 749 -->

Calvin's entire discussion under the head of regeneration begins, as do Edwards' charity sermons, with the indwelling Holy Spirit, the "secret energy" by which he "breathes divine life" into us.[^011-note129] "As long as Christ remains outside us," all that he suffered (to purchase our pardon) remains useless to us.[^011-note130] "As if we ought to think of Christ, standing afar off and not rather dwelling in us! For we await salvation from him, not because he appears to us afar off, but because *he makes us*, ingrafted into his body, *participants* not only in all his benefits but *in himself*... But since Christ has been *so imparted* to you with all his benefits *that all his things are made yours*."[^011-note131] No student of Edwards can read those words without thinking of many themes in the charity sermons: the Spirit working "divine love" in the heart; communicating himself not only by external influence or "adventitiously" but in his own "proper" or essential nature; our becoming "partakers of the divine nature"; recreated in the "amiable image of Christ"; he having become *ours*.

The terms "faith," "righteousness," "repentance," "regeneration," "sanctification," "holiness" are used with overlapping if not shifting meanings in the Reformed tradition. Nevertheless, one thing is clear: free reconciliation and newness of life begin together at the same point and continue together throughout life. On the one hand Calvin writes "concerning our righteousness [reckoned to us] and sanctification," that "although we may distinguish them, Christ contains both in himself." To attain favor or pardon in God's sight, "you must first possess Christ; but you cannot possess him without being made partaker of his sanctification, because he cannot be divided into pieces." These benefits are bestowed "at the same time, the one never without the other." Thus we are "justified not without works yet not through works, since in our sharing in Christ, which justifies us, sanctification is just as much included as [imputed] righteousness."[^011-note132]

On the other hand, a righteousness not their own must always continue to be just as much included as sanctification if the salvation of believers *and their works* is sure. Why must this be so? Because the whole life of believers must, as we have seen, be a life of repentance, a turning to God, because the story of redemption through the regenerative work of the indwelling Spirit (infused righteousness) is never complete in this life. "After forgiveness of sins is set forth, the good works that now follow

<!-- p. 750 -->

are appraised otherwise than on their own merit [as was the doer of them, in free reconciliation]. For everything in them is covered by Christ's perfection, every blemish or spot is cleansed away by his purity in order not to be brought in question at the divine judgment." So the good works done by believers still need to be "accounted" or "reckoned" righteous, if only the pure in heart are to see God.[^011-note133]

So it made sense to Calvin— and it was an embassy to be published daily to the hearts of men— that "man is so justified by faith that not only is he himself righteous but *his works are also accounted righteous above their worth*";[^011-note134] that "a work begins to be acceptable only when it is undertaken with pardon"; that "by faith not only we ourselves but our works as well are justified."[^011-note135] Having laid stress, and continuing to stress, moral newness of life, Calvin demands (by his standard of being steeped in holiness) to be shown one virtue or work that can claim "any right to be raised up either to destroy or becloud justification of faith."[^011-note136] "Let one of Adam's children come forward with such uprightness. If there is no one, they must either perish out of God's sight or flee to the shelter of his mercy."[^011-note137] So justification by faith remains, for believers, the main hinge on which religion turns.

Now, of course, we do not know that Edwards was steeped in the works of John Calvin.[^011-note138] In fact, no Puritan ever believed that final truth had broken forth from the Scriptures in the writings of that man of God in Geneva. Still, no one can read Calvin, or the foregoing summary of his views, on the two forms of righteousness without noting the deep family resemblance between them and Edwards' views.

<!-- p. 751 -->

Mastricht."[^011-note139] He expressed his enthusiasm for the theology of both these men in a letter to Joseph Bellamy in 1746 telling him where he might be able to locate copies of their works. In passing, he noted,

> They are both excellent. Turretine is on Polemical divinity; on the 5 Points, & all other Controversial Points; & is much larger in these than Mastricht; & is better for one that desires only to be thoroughly versed in Controversies. But take Mastricht for divinity in General, doctrine Practice & Controversie; or as an universal system of divinity; & it is much better than Turretine or any other Book in the world, excepting the Bible, in my opinion.[^011-note140]

A concise summary by Turretin on infusion follows:

> Just as Christ sustains a twofold relation to us, of *Surety* & *Head*, of surety, to take away the guilt of sin by a payment made for it, of Head, to take away its power & corruption by the efficacy of the Spirit, so in a twofold way Christ imparts his blessings to us, by *a forensic Imputation*, & *a moral* & *internal infusion*. The former flows from Christ as surety, & is the foundation of our Justification. The latter depends upon him as Head, & is the principle of sanctification. For on this account God justifies us, because the righteousness of our Surety, Christ, is imputed to us. And on this account we are renewed, because we derive the spirit from our Head, Christ, who renews us after the image of Christ, & bestows upon us inherent righteousness.[^011-note141]
